HOLLAND
One of the quick selling Philips EP records now
is one by Soeur Sourire, a
nun from Belgium who
sings her own chansons with
guitar accompaniment.
Original Broadway cast recording album of Rodgers & Hammerstein’s “Flower
Drum Song,” featuring Pat Suzuki, has been released here by L. C. Phonogram
on Philips. The Trio Siboney from Spain has a unique, very personal
sound,
as can be heard on the Philips album “On Tour With El Trio Siboney,” recorded
in Holland. Recordings that were made during the European tour
of
gospel
singer Mahalia Jackson last spring, have been released on the
Philips album
“Tell The World.” Famous Dutch composer Jan
Pieterszoon
Sweelinck was
born in Deventer, 400 years ago. To remember this, an LP by the world known
Netherlands Chamber Choir conducted by Felix de Nobel has been released on
Philips, with Sweelinck’s Psalms and Cantiones Sacrae.
The Concertgebouw Orchestra
is having tremendous success on their Japa-
nese tour.
Les Freres Jacques, famous French singing quartet on
Philips,
will
revisit
Holland next October.
To mark the 75 years jubilee of the Dutch Salvation Army, an album has
been made by L.C. Phonogram, which is an overwhelming success.
Vico Torriani, accompanied by an orchestra directed by Bert Paige, cut Dutch
versions
of
the American
hit
“Caterina”
and
the
Italian
song
“Permetete
Signorina”
(Signorina Capucina)
in the Phonogram studio at Hilversum.
The
French
Pathe-label,
represented
in
Holland by Bovema-Gramophone-
house, this week released a
45 rpm recording by
filmstar Anthony
Perkins,
including one
of the songs from the motion picture “Aimez-Vous Brahms?”,
entitled “Quand Tu Dors Pres De Moi.”
The Dovells’ new delight “Do The Continental” has been released by Bovema’s
Columbia-label in Holland.
Bob Weiss, Warner Bros’ European top-exec, visited Bovema’s Gramophone-
house recently in order to discuss the new releases of the label.
Singer-comedian Eartha
Kitt
will

“NEW EXCITING LATIN SOUNDS !”—Manuel
—MGM E 4029
With
the
exception
of
a
spirited
flute/piccolo
player Manuel’s orchestral sound is based entirely
on strings and this top-drawer sound album, part
of MGM’s 21 channel sound
series,
is noted for
its remarkable definition, depth and acute separa-
tion. The ork and chorus gets things
off
to de-
lightful
start with “Cachita” and offers superior
renditions of “Jealousy” and “Adios.” Fine fare
for
hi-fi bugs or the non-twistin’ set.
“TWIST WITH CUGAT”—Xavier Cugat—Mer-
cury SR 60705
Cugat, a
prolific producer of LP’s, has come up
with one of his best to date with this sock set of
tunes from the past few decades. The orkster ap-
plies
his
Latin rhythms and a twist beat
to an
almost incongruous package of standards and the
results are highly effective. Top-notch tracks are
“Johnson Rag,” “Woodchopper’s
Ball,” “Chatta-
nooga Choo
Choo,” and
“Fascinating Rhythm.”
This is a first-rate disk and should step out sales-
wise.
“KISS ME, KATE”—Earl Wrightson, Lois Hunt,
Mary Mayo—Columbia CL 1768
Cole Porter’s whimsical “Kiss Me, Kate” is given
spritely treatment by the concert
hall voices of
Earl Wrightson, Lois Hunt, and Mary Mayo. The
lyrics,
a
subtle
blending
of
Elizabethan
with
earthy modern, are delivered convincingly by the
performers.
Some
noteworthy
tracks
are
Earl
Wrightson’s “Where Is The Life That Late I Led”
and “Were Thine That Special Face;” Lois Hunt’s
“I Hate Men” and Mary Mayo’s “Always True To
You.” This
excellent revival
of the Porter show
should appeal to many theatre tune fans.
“TWISTIN’ AT
THE
ROUNDTABLE WITH
THE ORCHIDS”—Roulette R 25169
The Orchids, who came into the limelight via New

form with an exuberance that is evident in every
note they play. Their twist beat is solid and force-
ful
and
should
have
wide
appeal
for
teen-age
twisters.
Some
top-notch
dancing
tracks
are
“Slow
Walk,” “La Paloma
Twist,” and
“Night
Train.”

LIBERTY MOVES TO
EXPANO DOMESTIC SALES
HOLLYWOOD—Liberty
Records
has
made
several key
exec appointments
as part of its plans to expand domes-
tic
sales.
As
announced
last week
by
Don
Bohanan,
sales
head,
Dick Bowman,
formerly
in
distributor
sales,
will
serve as
divisional
sales manager for
the
Southern
states,
headquartering
in Cincinnati.
Joe
Zaleski, from the
label’s
inter-
national
sales
department,
has
been
upped to
divisional
sales manager
in
the
mid-west. He
will
be
based
in
Chicago,
and
be
responsible
for
the
sales
picture
in
15
states,
reporting
directly
to Ken Revercomb,
assistant
national
sales manager.
Bohanan
said
that both would
act
as
liaison between
distributors, rack-
jobbers and retail
outlets.
“They
will
also attempt,” Bohanan
noted, “to further embellish the vari-
ous
activities
of Bob
Skaff’s promo-
tion men
in these
territories, Ed
Sil-
vers in the mid-west, Joe Sadd
in the
South.”
The
exec
said
that
the
label
ex-
pects to accelerate
its expansion proj-
ect
shortly with
similar
additions
in
the
east and west coasts.

Jazz Stays At Newport;
Wein To Sponsor Fest
NEW YORK—They’ll
have
a
jazz
festival
again
at Newport,
R.I.
this
July,
this
time
to
be
tagged “New-
port
’62.”
Announcement of the event, to take
place July
6,
7 &
8, came
last week
from George Wein,
producer-director
of the offering who was also involved
in
the
famed “Newport
Jazz
Festi-
val,” which ended
its seven-year run
in 1960
after
riots by youngsters.
Last year,
Sid Bernstein and
local
Newporters
sponsored
a
“Music
at
Newport”
show,
but
a
recent
an-
^nouncement
said
that
the show was
nqt.j.returning
this
year.
The roster of artists for “Newport
’62’’
is in the glittering Newport tra-
dition.
It
includes
Duke
Ellington,
Gerry
Mulligan,
Count
Basie,
Dave
Brubeck,
Dinah
Washington,
Paul
Desmond, Coleman Hawkins, Carmen
McRae
and
others.
Charlie
Mingus
and Max
Roach, who
left
the “New
port Jazz
Festival”
in
1960
to form
their own
“festival”
in the
city,
will
also make
the
fete.
Carol
Sloane,
a
surprise hit of
last- year’s show (now
recording
for Columbia)
is
slated
to
appear.
Gospel
music
will
be
represented
by the Clara Ward
Singers.
There
will be
four major
concerts
Friday
(6),
Sat.
(7)
and
Sun.
(8)
evenings and Sun. afternoon.
Festival
headquarters
will
be
the
Viking Hotel and Motor Inn
in New-
port.

Wed., afternoon.

in

hour and a half.
Record retailers are offered the fol-
lowing
subjects: “How
to Buy
Rec-
ords and
Set Up a Simple Inventory
Program,”
“How
Can
the
Record
Store
Profitably
Diversify?,” “How
the Department Store Sound Depart-
ment
Can

Successfully,”
“Organizing
a
Profitable
Trade-In
Program,”
and
“Ways
to
Economi-
cally Organize and

retailers

cover “Ways
to Move
Dead
Stock”
and “How
to
Display^
Demonstrate
and
Sell
Phonographs,
Radio & TV
Sets.”
Radio program
directors
will
pick
from
“Programming
the
Automated
Station—Its
Problems &
Prospects,”
“Successful
Selection, Development &
Use
of
Personalities”
and “How
to
sions
for
various
labels,
including
Liberty.
Otis’
association
with
Liberty,
about a year, was highlighted by
his
role in the success of songstress Timi
Yuro, now
a
major
singles
and LP
performer on the
label.
Before
coming
to
Liberty,
Otis
spent many
years
as
an A&R
pro-
ducer for Mercury Records. His
stint
at Mercury
included

sessions by

Benton
(“It’s

“Kid-
dio,” “Boll Weevil”), Dinah Washing-
ton
(“What A

(“Bro-
ken-Hearted

Op-
erator”),

mita

re-

more time
to

estab-
lished

“ERROLL GARNER MOODS”—Mercury
Wing
SRW 16134
Erroll Garner, who has probably won more laurels
for keyboard artistry than almost any other 88’er
in jazz
history, displays
his
original,
distinctive
approach
on
this
first-rate
set
from
Mercury
Wing. The pianist
dishes up some
potent,
free-
flowing renditions of “Deep Purple,” “Minor With
The Trio” and “The Quaker.” A host of Garner’s
many fans should come out in force for the disk.
“CHILDHOOD MEMORIES”—Disneyland WDL
3045
This delightful collection of new songs, geared for
the kiddies, were written and performed by Rica
Owen Moore to supplement Disneyland’s long
list
of children’s LP’s. Disk
is
attractively packaged
in a jacket which includes the lyrics of four of the
songs. Included in the fifteen tunes are “The Baby
In The Mirror,” “The Shadow Horse,” and “Little
Touslehead.” Album should have appeal for par-
ents.
IlLLYGULUr
PO THE HITS
irw||r»i|iis
“PARIS IN THE SPRING”—Michele Arnaud—
Capitol ST 10317
This new
offering by
Capitol features the vocal
talents
of
Michele Arnaud,
a newcomer
to
the
American scene. Her premiere album in this coun-
try shows
off her
strong
interpretive
skills and
a
rich velvety voice. The
lark
delivers,
in
a
so-
phisticated manner, a collection
of French songs
with emphasis on romance. Some first-rate bands
are
“Le
Bleu
De
L’Ete,”
“Pour
Un
Grand
Amour,” and “L’Amour,
II N’y En Avait Guere.”
This appealing LP should bring new admirers to
the chanteuse.
“HULLY GULLY TO THE HITS”—Mel “Pigue”
Robbins—Smash SRS 67012
Mel “Pigue” Robbins
unleashes some
fine musi-
cianship as he
serves up
a generous
helping
of
current
hits with a marked
hully gully
beat.
In
contrast
to
the
hard
rock
tempo
purveyed
by
many instrumental
groups,
Robbins
and ensem-
ble have captured the
spirit
of the pop rhythms
and added a sophisticated jazz flavor. Some note-
worthy tracks are “White Silver Sands,” “Mother-
In-Law,” “Hey Baby,” and “Young Blood.” Strong
wax with good potential.
“EDDIE’S GOLDEN SONG BOOK”—Eddie
Cal-
vert—ABC Paramount 422
Eddie Calvert, a trumpeter who follows a straight
melodic line, plays a dozen evergreens in the lush
manner of Spivak and James, but with a very dis-
tinctive style of his own. An international favorite
since
his memorable “Oh
Mein
Papa,”
Calvert
could have a strong seller in this LP. The trum-
peter’s
mellow
and
vibrant
interpretations
of
“Moonlight And
Roses,”
“Catari,
Catari,”
and
“And
This
Is My
Beloved”
make
this
disk
a
worthy addition to any collector’s shelf.
“ROLLICKING SEA SHANTIES”—Oscar Brand
—Audio Fidelity AFSD 5966
Oscar
Brand,
accompanied
by
Dave
Sear
and
Eric Weissberg, sings and plays the sea shanties
that were
inherently
necessary
to
the hard
life
of
a
sailor. Most of the tunes
are familiar, and
the folk singer gives fresh, subtle readings of the
lyrics. Starting with “Hullabaloo Belay,” the LP
also includes “Blow Ye Winds In The Morning,”
“Whiskey
Johnny,”
and
ten
other
rollicking
tunes. The
disk
is
well
done
and
should
evoke
enthusiasm among folk music admirers.
“ORLANDO MARIN AND
HIS ORCHESTRA
VOLUME 1”—Alegre LPA 814
Orlando Marin
is one
of the most popular
ork-
sters around today rendering
Latin themes. On
this
high-spirited
Alegre LP
Marin
comes
up
with a pleasant group
of fast-moving
terpsicho-
rean delights. On hand
to
offer the vocals
is the
well-known Latin chanter Chivirico Davila. Non-
twisters should
find “La
Casa,” “Ritmo Bembe”
and “Aprovechate”
first-rate
for
dancing.
JAZZ
“2° EAST,
3° WEST”—Various
Artists—Pacific
Jazz PJ-44
A
strong jazz package featuring
the piano and
arranging artistry of John Lewis with some ex-
cellent tenor solos by
Bill Perkins, as well as in-
teresting improvisations by guitarist Jim Hall
is
this PJ etching. You feel warmth and simplicity
throughout the record, however there
is
still evi-
dence of modern overtones in such tracks as “Al-
most Like Being In Love,” “I Can’t Get Started,”
and the
jazz
favorite “Love Me Or Leave Me.”
Top drawer jazz album.
“THE STRAIGHT HORN OF STEVE LACY”—
Candid 8007
This new Candid release has Steve Lacy unleash-
ing his talents on the soprano saxaphone in a set
of six jazz pieces composed by some of the
top
jazz names around today. Lacy starts the session
with an imaginative piece by
Cecil Taylor called
“Louise,” and then rides into “Introspection” by
Thelonious
Monk, and “Donna
Lee” by
Charlie
Parker. The
flip
side
is devoted almost
entirely
to
the
complex
melodic
themes
of
Thelonious
Monk
with
a
pair
of
tunes
entitled
“Played
Twice”
and
“Criss
Cross.” The
last
is
a
tune
called “Air,” again by Cecil Taylor. Potent jazz.
“BILL DOGGETT SWINGS”—Warner
Brothers
WS1452
Pointing
to
the
fact
that
the
organ
is
rapidly
gaining
in
popularity
in
jazz
circles.
Bill
Dog-
gett, who swings equally well on the 88, offers an
entire
session
of
sure-fingered
organ
items
on
this compelling Warner Brothers entry. On
this
outing of sturdies and
originals, the
spotlight
is
focused almost entirely on Doggett. The organist
renders
“The
Sparrow,”
“Coffee’s
Theme”
and
“High Low”
in
his
distinctive
fluid, free-flowing
approach. Top-notch jazz set.
“SOMETHING ELSE”—Meg
Welles
Quintet—
Columbia CL
1777
The Meg Welles Quintet
is a new group featur-
ing
the
vocal
talents
of
the
leader on
a
dozen
folk-flavored
items.
The
quintet’s
arranger-con-
ductor
Fred
Karlin
has
come
up
with
some
melodic
jazz

for
the
Welles-read
tunes.
Unfortunately,
the
marriage
of
jazz
coupled with traditional folk selections falls short
of
perfection.
Although
each
member
of
the
group
is an accomplished musician the
only av-
erage material clouds their respective
talents. A
few
interesting
items
here
are
“Ev’ry

and “No More Booze.”
CLASSICAL PICK OF THE WEEK
“WILD,
WONDERFUL
WYNONA”—Wynona
Carr—Reprise R 6023
With
a highly
listenable warmth and
the
unre-
strained
intensity
of
a
real
pro, Wynona
Carr
demonstrates
the
contagious,
uninhibited
self-
release of her early gospel background. She was
a member of the Wings Over Jordan Choir and
the
Sister Rosetta Tharpe group. Although
this
Neal
Hefti-arranged
package
has
definite
jazz
overtones,
the
lark
fares
better
on
fervent
rhythms.
The
one
time
Mahalia
Jackson
88’er
turns
in
first-rate
renditions
of “Down By The
Riverside,” “Love, Love, Love” and “Strange.”
MAHLER: Symphony No. 9—Bruno Walter con-
ducting the Columbia Symphony Orchestra—Co-
lumbia M 2L 276
Columbia has come up with a superlative set spot-
lighting the highly-acclaimed
talents
of the
late
Bruno Walter. The three-disk set boasts the con-
ductor rendering the intricate strains of Mahler’s
Symphony No.
9. Walter demonstrates a magni-
ficent
control
and
a
firm
understanding
of
the
music as he firmly leads the ork through the sym-
phony. The
set boasts a talking
portrait of the
conductor
with
Walter
discussing
his
life
and
work
with
Arnold
Michaelis.
Additionally,
the
diskery
has included
a working
portrait
of
the
actual recording of the symphony. Package looms
as a hot item with
all
classical
collectors.

Goodman
Reigns As
'^King^'
In
Russia
NEW YORK—From
Premier Khrus-
chev
on
down, Benny Goodman
and
his orchestra have made the grade
in
Russia.
Opening
a
six-week
tour
of
the
Soviet
Union
in
Moscow
last
week
(30), the Goodman ensemble,
includ-
ing
vocalist
Joya
Sherrill,
was
re-
ceived with warmth and appreciation,
an
appreciation that stems from
the
fact
that
at
last Russian
jazz
fans
were
able
to
get in-person
jazz
per-
formances by American
artists.
Premier
Khruschev,
who
attended
the
initial
concert
in
the
Central
Army
Sports
Arena,
certainly
gave
jazz
a
strong
(and
official)
boost
in
Russia when
he remarked
after
the
performances;
“I
enjoyed
it
.
.
1
don’t dance myself, so
I don’t under-
stand these things too well.”
The
Soviet
leader
also
had
kind
words
about
the
singing
of
Joya
Sherrill,
approving
of
her
“warm,
wonderful manner as
if
it had
been
a delight for her to perform.”
Print-
wise,
Tass,
the
official
Soviet
news
agency, termed
the
concert “a
great
hit.”
Khruschev’s
and
Tass’
public
A-OK’s
for
the
Goodman
tour
is
bound to make Russian jazz fans ex-
press their feelings on jazz, often de-
cried as “decadent” by Soviet
officials
and
press, more
openly.
Goodman’s
first night audience was
more or less an official one, thus lend-
ing a reserve
to the reception
to the
performances. A
younger, more
en-
thusiastic
attendance
the
next
night
displayed
much
greater
excitement,
bringing
the band
back
for
25
min-
utes
of
encores.
Some remarks were made after the
first Goodman concert that his brand
of Swing Era
music was somewhat,
if
enjoyably,
behind
the
times,
even
for Russia, where the West has been
inclined
to
believe that current Rus-
sian
jazz was somewhere where
the
U.S. was
in the 30’s.
It would be a
surprise
to many
if
the hip
coterie
in Russia were ready
for
the
likes
of
such
far-out
U.S.
jazzists
as
Ornette
Coleman
and
Charlie Mingus.

A new record has been established by the single, “Amor,” cut by Copacabana

As reported last week, the situation between our record companies and the
musicians is ended. In view of the deadlock created by both parties, the compa-
nies insisting in not paying Cr. $1,000 per hour and the musicians refusing to
work for less than that fee, the labels decided to contract exclusive musicians
to make
all recordings. Copacabana Records, as an example, formed in Rio de
Janeiro its own orchestra and from now on, all the records will be waxed there,
even those with artists from Sao Paulo. Other companies are doing the sarne.

“BY SPECIAL REQUEST”—Guv Lombardo —
Decca DL4280, DL 74280
Guy Lombardo and the band adapt their sophisti-
cated
and
danceable
arrangements
to
a
dozen
tunes currently among the nation’s favorites. The
orkster
launches
the
session
with
the
popular
“Midnight In Moscow” and includes some smooth
renditions
of “A
Little
Bitty
Tear,”
“Afrikaan
Beat,” “Moon
River,” “Norman,”
and “When
I
Fall
In
Love.”
Vocals
are
delivered
by Kenny
Gardner,
Bill Flanagan, and the Lombardo
Trio.
Lombardo’s fans should
find
this
a winning
set.
“PONCIE PONCE SINGS”—Warner Brothers—
WB 1453, WS 1453
Poncie Ponce, the singing, uke-strumming cabbie
of TV’s “Hawaiian Eye,” waxes his premiere LP
for
Warner
Brothers
singing
a
collection
of
Hawaiian “pupule” (crazy) songs. The songster’s
delivery
is
spiced with
a nonchalant mixture
of
pidgin, English, and Hawaiian which lends an air
of
authenticity
to
the
island
ditties. Some
fine
tracks
are
“There’s
No
Place
Like
Hawaii,”
“Little
Brown
Gal,”
and
“The
Pidgin
English
Hula.”
“THE EXOTIC MOODS OF MARTITA”—Mar-
tita Ramirez—Columbia EX 5074
Here’s
a
pleasant
folk-flavored
Latin
package
spotlighting the feelingful vocal charms of Mar-
tita Ramirez. The lark displays a vibrant,
origi-
nal. sensuous voice as she goes through her paces
with superb range and nitch. The versatile song-
stress penned seven of the tunes here and accom-
nanies herself on the guitar on all the selections.
Some fine examnles of her artistrv are evidenced
on “Caboclo,” “Voigue” and “El Bannanero.”
“GERMANY’S GREAT WOLFGANG SAUER”—
Canitol ST 10307
Wolfgang Sauer, a favorite in Germany since the
end
of WW
II, makes
his
American
debut
on
Canitol
vdth
a
collection
of
international
ever-
greens. The German
baritone
has
a
big warm
voice that
is readily at home with both pop and
jazz tunes. Singing in German, the crooner gives
easy
relaxed
renditions
of “Heartaches By The
Number,”
“The
Three
Bells,”
and
“I’ll
Come
Back Again Some Day.” The LP
is
a
fine
first
entrv which should make many American friends
for Sauer.
“RICHARD
DEYER-BENNETT”—Decca

9102, DL 79102
This

features the singing and guitar playing of Rich-

JAZZ
PICKS
OF THE WEEK
“SAN FRANCISCO SCENE”—George
Shearing
—Capitol ST 1715
The George Shearing Quintet have been turning
out
first-rate albums for quite a while and
this
new entry ranks as a superlative addition to the
Shearing catalog. The session was cut live at the
Masonic
Auditorium
in
San
Francisco
and
the
pianist gives each number an
effective introduc-
tion. The pace is extremely varied here including
such
smooth
standards
as “When
April Comes
Again” and a high-spirited Afro-Cuban percussion
rendition of “My New Mambo.” Once again 88’er
displays
his
expected,
distinctive
feelingful
ap-
proach on
this
set which
is sure
to appeal to a
wide coterie of his admirers.
OUL BATTLE
Oliver nelson
king: curtis
jimmy forrest
“SOUL
BATTLE”—Various
Artists—Prestige
7223
Here’s a triple-threat jazz package featuring the
tenor artistry of Oliver Nelson, King Curtis and
Jimmy Forrest on an ultra-melodious
session
of
improvisation. Everyone gets chance to show his
own distinctive horn
style on some potent
solos.
The wax marriage of these three makes for su-
perior listening as
their respective and
different
approaches compliment each other on “Blues At
The Five Spot,” “Perdido” and “In Passing.” Set
should bring out jazz buffs in droves.
“LES McCANN LTD. IN NEW YORK”—Pacific
Jazz PJ 45
Les McCann has earned many laurels in the past
for
his keyboard
artistry
and
this new
Pacific
Jazz date with Stanley Turrentine as guest artist
should win the talented jazz 88’er a flock of new
admirers. The
session was
cut
live
at Gotham’s
Village Gate and the crew read five McCann origi-
nals with verve and straight-forward blues
lines
with enough good soul stuff in
it to appeal to a
wide variety of jazz fans. The set also boasts some
colorful trumpet solos by Blue Mitchell. Best lis-
tening bets here are “Chip Monck” and “Maxie’s
Changes.”
“THE SOUL OF HOLLYWOOD”—Junior Mance
—Jazzland JLP 63, JLP 963
Movie themes, which have provided a gold mine
of material for LP producers, are given some ex-
ceptionally fresh and inventive treatments in this
superb package by Junior Mance. Melba
Liston
has come up
with
effective and imaginative
ar-
rangements which allow the 88’er to take a new
approach to such goodies as “Never On Sunday,”
“Maria,”
“The
Apartment,”
and
“Spellbound.”
The disk
is strong wax with wide appeal for jazz
fans.
“HEADIN’ SOUTH”—Horace Parian—Blue Note
4062
Horace Parian is teamed up with an accomplished
group
of jazzman
including George
Tucker
on
bass, A1 Harewood on drums and Ray Barretto on
conga for this free-flowing Blue Note session of
ballads and uptempo
items. The
88’er does
not
rely on gimmicks but renders the eight selections
here with an honest,
straight-forward, emotion-
packed
style. Some
of
the
best bands here
are
“The Song Is Ended,” “Summertime” and “Prel-
ude To A Kiss.”
“CLASS IN SESSION”—Jack Quigley—Sand CS
30
Multi-talented Jack
Quigley
superbly showcases
his dynamic talents on this provocative,
distinc-
tive session from Sand. Quigley penned eight out
of the ten tunes here and served as the arranger
for the entire session. Although he is no new-wave
experimenter, Quigley dishes up some highly pro-
fessional free-flowing jazz items with “Celestial,”
“Homeward Bound” and
“I’ll Follow You” taking
top
honors.
Top-notch
listening
enjoyment
throughout.

JOHANN STRAUSS: The Gypsy Baron, Vienna
Philharmonic Orchestra, Heinrich Hollreiser, Con-
ductor, Various Artists—Angel BL 3612
This delightfully entertaining operetta by Johann
Strauss is performed by a European cast with the
Vienna Philharmonic Orchestra ably and artfully
conducted by

Hollreiser. The
excellent
soprano
voices
of

Rothenberger
as
Arsena and Hilde Gueden
as
Saffi do
justice
to
the lyrical melodies of the composer. The album is
attractively packaged and includes the complete
libretto in translation. Angel’s top-drawer produc-
tion of “The Gypsy Baron” should be a desirable
addition to any collector’s
shelf.

bevy of young collectors.

A long time ago there was created by M. Canetti for the
Philips label the
series
called
“Trefle
a quatre feuilles.” Not much
is
left
of that
series now
with the exception of a Brunet composition called “Le Tango Polaire,” which
has just been re-recorded by Fernand Reynaud. On the other hand. Vogue an-
nounced a new collection to be known as Contact and which
is being launched
to bring new, young talent to the record-buying public and
to
enable young
recording artists to get a hearing. Among the five newcomers already waxed
in the series are Jose Salcy, whose tune “Barbara” shows must promise; Micky
Ameline; an Italian vocal and instrumental quintette called
I 'Trovatori; Jean
Ridez and Jean-Louis Bleze (whom we’ve already heard favorably at the Olym-
pia). Let’s not forget that Vogue president Leon Cabat started Marino Marini
on his career and one shouldn’t be surprised
if something didn’t come out of
this new
series
of promising youngsters.
Frank Sinatra’s coming visit to Paris to sing for charity continues to make
the headlines. The town
is covered with Sinatra posters. Too bad that his ap-
pearance
will be limited to a very small section of the Sinatra fans and that
the real Parisian public won’t hear him.
Note “The Memphis Slim Story,” which
is on the market as part of the col-
lection
marking
Vogue’s
10th
anniversary.
With
summer
just
around
the
corner, already in hand
is the report that the rock combo, Les Fantonies, have
a hot-weather date
at the Vieux Colombier
in Juan-les-Pins, the
club which
has already featured stars such as Sydney Becht, Claude Luter and, more re-
cently, Johnny Hallyday. Les Copains, the rock
’n’ roll duo, are
still on the job
and have recently recorded
a
series of “Madisons,” the dance which
is very
much a
la mode in Paris these days, though
it can hardly be said that
it has
taken the town by storm in the same way as the twist did. Those who can afford
to frequent the swank night clubs in Paris are dancing
(or trying
to dance)
The Madison, but the rest of the Paris public
is continuing
to alternate the
twist with the tango.
Jocelyne Jocya has just waxed the female version of Becaud’s hit tune, “Sur
La Plus Haute Colline.” Latest female vocal quartet
is called Les Gams. Their
first studio session for Vogue comes up
shortly.
Every single record dealer in France received this week a 45 single bearing
only
a blank
label. On listening to the
disk,
it seemed
like
a
practical joke
being played by some rank amateur trying his hand at singing. A rather ex-
pensive joke, folks thought. But the truth came out at last, for “the truth will
out” and especially
in the record
business. The
disk was by a fellow whose
A&R
director
calls merely “Le
roi
de
la
Nouvelle
Orleans.”
He’s
one
Aldo
Franck, composer-lyricist-arranger-interpreter and according to
Philips’ pub-
licity people, the release of this record
is an event which we
will hear more
about later. Just the opposite is true of another Philips recording star—Robert
Nyel, whose first disk is really worth listening to.
Serge Gainsbourg, about whom
little has been heard during the last several
months,
is back in the public eye (and ear) with a 10-inch album. One of his
tunes on the platter
is called “Requiem Pour Un Twisteur.”
Yves Montand, back from a tour in Japan, just made a television appearance
in
Paris. The singer had an enormous
success
in the Far East and brought
back a new tune of which he hummed just enough to make us wish we could
hear
it
all. On the other hand, he sang all of “Napoli Joli,” which is one of the
songs on
his
latest issue. Received a
disk from him
in
Italian. Back
to the
source, we might say.
A lyricist who’s getting much attention these days is Bernard Dimey, whose
efforts are nicely finished
off and so much so that even Michel Simon has re-
corded a Dimey composition, “Memere.” Johnny Hallyday’s latest EP includes
“Jardin d’amour” and “Laissez-nous Twister,” which just might make a
lot of
people forget all about The Madison. Nana Mouskouri’s latest session in French
comprised waxings of “Ce Soir A Luna Park” and “Savoir Aimer,” the latter
a French adaptation of “Stranger On The
Shoi’e.”
News from Barclay: Eddie Barclay
is back in Paris from the Riviera after
a detour by way of Rome. “Le Twist Du Canotier,” already mentioned
in this
column (Maurice Chevalier and Les Chausettes Noires),
is more than a suc-
cess. Les Chausettes Noires have two new sides on the market—“Roly Poly”
and “Hey,
Let’s
Twist.” Barclay’s
Gary,
I’ange
noir
et
ses demon have
re-
corded “The Fly.”
Festival’s Les Loups Garous are
definitely on The Madison train and have
waxed “Apprenez A Danser Le Madison.”
“Voyage De Noce” by Jean Valtay
(edited by Madame Breton)
will repre-
sent France at the Italian Television’s song festival, “Canzone Per I’Europa.”
Last but not least, a few words on Jacques Brel. Not about his lawsuits but
about the veritable triumph which was
his on the
last Musicarama program,
Europe No.
I’s famous broadcast. The public simply
didn’t want
to
let him
leave the mike. More and more, Brel looms as the really big singer of tomor-
row! With him on the program were Isabelle Aubret, Jennifer, Pierre Perret,
et
al. But for the public, Brel was the man!
Happy
Birthday
TOKYO—Celebrating her sixth birth-
day above
is Kumiko
Goto, probably
one
of
the youngest pop
singers
in
the
world
today.
Her
recent
wax
debut, “Pretty Little Baby” and “Too
Many
Rules,” A&R’d
by
Columbia’s
Takayasu
Yoshioka, made
a
big
hit
throughout
the
country
and
sky-
rocketed
the
youngster
to
fame. A
follow-up
deck, “Cute
Li’l Baby But
I’m A
Marshall” and
“Indian
Girl,”
will be released July
7.

TORONTO—A rather strange appari-

downtown area here. The phoney
ele-

Stan
Doi-ling.

promo

dreamed
it

to
help
promote
Lawrence Welk’s Dot noisemaker
of
“Baby Elephant Walk.” In the above
photo the elephant gets the once over
from CHUM’s
head
librarian,
Millie
Moriak,
and
the
station’s
morning
man, Al
Boliska.

Big triumph for Frank Sinatra on the occasion of his two personal appear-
ances in Paris. The Lido welcomed the singer with
all
flags
flying, admission
was extremely dear and very much sought after, and the newspapers played
up Frank’s charity stint there as one of the year’s biggest and very “Parisian”
events. Then came
his one-nighter
at the Olympia where
the general
public
greeted him with equal enthusiasm. After
Paris,
Sinatra’s tour took him on
to Monte Carlo and an appearance at the Sporting Club there under the patron-
age of Prince Rainer and Princess Grace.
Jack Mills may soon visit Paris, where he will discuss with Gerard Tournier
the handling of his
edition
here. Pathe’s rock
’n
roll recording
star, Richard
Anthony,
is
off for a tour of Argentina towards the end of June.
Sir Joseph
Lockwood is currently touring the European capitals for the purpose of study-
ing the
different problems attendant on
the
distribution
of the EMI
line
in
relation to the Common Market. He visited Paris two weeks ago.
Roger Maruani, who holds a post for EMI, reports that trumpetist Georges
Jouvin’s
latest recording, “African Beat” comprises
a
classical
study
of
the
trumpet with drum accompaniment and the result
is an
excellent twist. Jean
Yatove has signed the musical score for the film, “Le Roi de la Montagne” and
it’s Ducretet-Thomson’s vocal ensemble Les Hommes who interpret the main
theme, “Le coeur des
brigands.” Rock
’n
rollers,
Les Chats Sauvages, with
their new
side “L’amour
que
j’ai pour
toi,” have
just
attained
the
million
mark
in
record
sales. A new recording by
Christian Marin has
four comic
songs, among which
are
“Arthur,
la
friture”
and
“J’ai
des
ailes
sous
les
pieds.”
Success
noted
on
the
movie,
“Le
Gueare
des
Boutons.”
The
music
belongs to Editions Tutti and the EMI recording of the track has been made
by the “fanfare” of the famous Beaux Arts school here
in Paris.
This
year’s song
Festival
in
Enghien,
near
Paris, went
off
as
scheduled,
marking the attribution of the
first 1962 GRAND PRIX DE LA CHANSON
FRANCAISE. The winning tune was “Ma melodie” sung
in
the
contest by
Ghislaine
(Claude
Carrere
is
the composer)
and
Gilda
Gil. The
latter
will
record the tune for Philips and the former for RCA. The
tune, an
excellent
one, has
also been waxed by Richard Anthony
(Pathe). Madame
Breton
is
the
song’s
very happy
publisher whose
files
include
a
whole
series
of
hit
tunes
quite apart from “La grosse
caisse” and “Sur
la plus haute
colline,”
Becaud’s latest successes.
Quite
a few people
are
surprised by
the growing
success
of
“L’Horrible
tango,” published by Chappell, a song which, when
it was launched,
did not
seem to hold much promise. The composer
is Charles Trenet. This tango can
be compared rhythmically speaking
to
the
best
of the tango
standards and
should become one of those tunes which have their permanent place in
all the
popular dance
halls. One more
hit to be added
to the growing
score
of pro-
motor Soula.
Good news from
Versailles
Records by way
of
Jean-Pierre
Perrier, who
reports that on the occasion of the re-issue of the
film, “Nous irons a Paris,”
Christian Deffes has waxed a new version of the musical
track.
In
addition,
the original track
(the film was circa 1949)
will be re-issued. Ricordi’s
Public
Relations expei’t is Marie Wencel, and
it is through her that Cash Box learned
that
Francis
Linel’s
latest waxings
include “La
serenade
de
Toselli”
(in
a
twist version)
and
a
tune, which
believe
it
or
not,
is
called “La musique”
(from the pen of Drejac). Robert Ripa, who makes his appearance from time
to time in the song world has recently waxed “Magali,” a Robert Nyel tune.
Rosalie
Dubois’s
latest
platter
includes
“Dieu
soit
loue.” Another
of
her
latest
recordings, from
Chappell’s
catalog,
is
“Toi, mon
habitude.”
Ricordi
has released “Johnny Angel” on the Colpix label.
News gets scarcer as summer approaches and thoughts turn towards slow-
up and vacation. Fortunately, foreign artists do manage to keep things moving
in Paris during such
periods. The
latest was
Errol Gamer, who
did
a
one-
nighter
here.
Philips
director,
Mr.
Meyerstein,
threw
a
highly
successful
cocktail at his home for Errol, where
all the biggies of the Philips organiza-
tion were on hand, as well as the “who’s who”
of radio, records,
press,
etc.
Caravelli (and his Magic Strings)
is rapidly becoming a top star in France.
The demand is so great for his pressings that Versailles can hardly keep up
with incoming orders. Much elation at Arteco
in view of the big response
to
the launching
of
Billy
Bridge
in
France. The
16-year-old
singer,
signed on
the Odeon label, made his debut with “Twist Up” a few weeks ago. His second
EP features a series of “Madisons” and the orders are rolling
in. Thirty-four
years after
its original release. “Pedro”
is being re-issued by Odeon.
It was
one of the biggest comic hits of its creator, Marie Dubas.
Two requests for corrections with respect to recent columns. The
first, from
Rudi Revil, asks
to mention that “Le
lion
est mort ce
soir”
is sub-published
by Editions
Tropicales. What
is
really important
is that the
success
of the
tune in question
is due to Henri Salvador’s disk and to
it alone. The second
is
that Timmel and not Dumay
is the one who
will
replace Roger Maruani
in
handling the Capitol catalog.

Philips Records
just had
a
cocktail
party
for the
press and
disk jockeys
celebrating the appearance
of the
first
Polydor, Deutsche Grammophon and
Archiv records. The meeting, including the presentation of the
first
releases,
and speeches by Maximo Wyngaard, head of Philips, and Heddo Heide, DGG’s
representative
in South America. Heide announced that there
is
a
plan
for
local recordings
in Argentina, which will be distributed through
all the DGG
chain to the rest of the world.
Los Cinco Latinos have
started
their new European
trip, which
will
last
a couple of months. They will have to return to Argentina
in October because
of several contracts they
still have to
fulfill.
RCA reports the release of “Good Luck Charm” by Elvis Presley, “Natural
Boy” by Esquivel, “Mood Indigo” and “Samt Antonio Rose” by Floyd Cramer,”
and a new LP by Francisco “Charro” Avitia, Mexican singer of good success
in Argentina.
Luque
of Disc Jockey
records
reports
about the
promotion
of
Begin The
Beguine,”
the
old

Eddie Clark, member of the Serenata Records roster, has cut “La Charanga”
and
Suba A1 Tren
(Twisting Train),” and “Peppermint Twist.” Clark
is the
son of the well known orchestra director, Barry Moral, and is a good showman.
Juan Carlos Menna, Odeon’s promotion man, married Susana Esther Garcia
June
22.
The visit of Emilio Vitale, head of Vitale Publishers of Brazil, has been de-
layed some weeks. Vitale plans
to coordinate
his
visit to Buenos Aires with
the opening of the Sbat-Sbacem-Sadembra (Brazilian Composers Associations)
office opening
in Porto Alegre,
in the South of Brazil, and the return
of Ri-
cardo Korn, head of Julio Korn Publishers, who

The

of

plans
to

in

all the Latin

will be present. The

last year
in Rio de Janeiro,

NEW YORK — A more professional
approach
to
completely-assembled
hifi
stereo sound systems
is
respon-
sible
for
the
current
success
of
home
instrument
manufacturers
in
the music and sound market, accord-
ing to Raymond W. Saxon, vice-pres-
ident
of
marketing
for RCA
Sales
Corp.
“The introduction
of improved and
larger
speakers,
professionaly
styled
record changers, and the development
of FM
stereo radio have enabled the
so-called
ready-to-play
producers
to
achieve a greater success in the con-
sumer sound market.”
Saxon issued
his statement as
the
RCA
Victor
“Studiomatic”
record
changer was being demonstrated
for
the first time at the National Associa-
tion of Music Merchants Show in the
New York Trade Show Building
last
week.
The
RCA-developed
“Studiomatic”
record changer, which Saxon termed
“a major advancement in music repro-
duction,”
will be
used
in
the
deluxe
models of the
1963 RCA Victor
line
of
radio
phonograph
combination
units, stereo portables and color tele-
vision—stereo—FM-AM
models.
This
record
changer
incorporates
a
12-inch
turntable
that
minimizes
vertical rumble, because of its greater
mass, with more
constant
turntable
speed
to
minimize wow
and
flutter.
The new tone arm has been designed
at a professional angle to insure
ac-
curate tracking and compliance. The
four
speed
changer
plays
all
sizes
of same-speed
records
intermixed
in
any sequence.
Calling
the phonograph market
a
“highly competitive
field for
all
pro-
ducers
of
sound
equipment,”
Saxon
said current indications are that more
than
four
million
complete
phono-
graph
units,
with
an
approximate
retail value
of
$475
million,
will
be
sold in
1962. “This figure could very
easily go
higher,
depending
on
the
public’s interest in FM stereo radio.”
Saxon
said the combination of the
“professional
approach”
in
building
components and
the
industry’s
radi-
cally new
cabinetry
styling
“should
mean
an
even
larger
share
of
the
total sound market for manufacturers
of complete sound instruments.”
“The 1963 RCA Victor phonograph
line
has more
technical
and
styling
improvements
than we
would
have
thought
possible
a few
years
ago,”
Saxon said. “Every type of consumer
interest is covered in the portable line,
for example, from a smart low priced
poi’table
to the
‘float down’ changer
in the new stereo portable line.”
Saxon
said the growing
public
in-
terest in FM stereo radio
is reflected
in
the
fact
that
all
thirteen
stereo
combination units will be offered with
factory built-in tuners
to receive the
new type broadcasting now available
in most
areas.
Last
year’s
line had
only six models so equipped.

Don’t Live For Future,
Brief Warns Retaiiers At
NAMM Meet Seminar
NEW YORK—The
retailer
shouldn’t
be carried away with advancements in
the phono
and
record
business
that
are years in the future.
Instead,
he
should
be
more
con-
cerned with what he
can
do
to
sell
today what
is available today to the
customers
of today.
This was
one
of
the
observations
made
last week by Henry
Brief,
ex-
ecutive-secretary
of
the
Record
In-
dustry
Association
of
America
(RIAA),
who
spoke
as
keynote
speaker on the topic of “What’s Ahead
for Phonographs & Records”
at the
Electronic
Industries
Association’s
Symposium
on
“What’s
Ahead
for
Consumer
Products”
during
the
NAMM
music
show
in New
York.
Glenn Wallichs, Capitol Records head
and
RIAA
prexy,
was
originally
scheduled
to
speak, but
couldn’t due
to
a world-wide
tour.
“You don’t stop selling automobiles
today because somewhere
olf
lin the
vague
future we
will have new
en-
gines, new fuels, new types of propul-
sion,”
Brief
stated.
“In
any
discussion
of
“What’s
Ahead for Phonographs”
it
is there-
fore seems appropriate to talk about
what we
can
sell today
in
order
to
reap tomorrow.”
Some
of
the
guidelines
listed
by
Brief for sales based on the
present
include: how
enterprising, how crea-
tive, how
forceful, how
imaginative
shall we be ?
; how can we make peo-
ple want to buy phonos and records ?
how
can we
make
people
want
to
listen to our equipment, to
see
it, to
touch it?
Brief said today’s consumer is more
interested
in
quality than
gadgetry,
in performance rather than conversa-
tion pieces, in simplicity of design and
operation rather than a confusion of
technical jargon.
When
selling phonos,
Brief
added,
the
retailer
should
not
eliminate
“half
the
sales
talk” by
failing
to
dramatize
“the wealth

Decca Cuts Fortune
In
Fiddles
NEW YORK—A
fortune
in
fiddles
were used
in a disk session made by
Decca
Records
last week.
Fifteen violins, worth $750,000 were
used by American
violinist Ruggiero
Ricci
in
the
course of cutting music
covering
four
centuries
of
violin
repertoire in the ballroom of the New
York
Technical
Institute,
this
city.
Guarded
at
the
studio
by
armed
detectives, the violins were assembled
from
private
collections
throughout
the
U.S.
at
the
request
of
Ricci by
Rembert
Wurlitzer,
the
stringed
in-
struments
authority.
LP,
tentatively
titled
“Ruggiero
Ricci & The Sounds Of Cremona,”
is
intended
to
provide
connoisseurs
of
violin
tone
with
an
opportunity
to
compare
the
sounds
of
the
instru-
ments
in
relation
to
different
types
of music under uniform performance
conditions and to convey, via today’s
hi-fi standards, the subtle differentia-
tions of tone which were the mark of
early Italian violin makers.

Exhibitors, Buyers
NEW YORK—The
1962
Music
In-
dustry Trade Show, sponsored by the
National
Association
of
Music Mer-
chants
(NAMM),
set new
highs
in
exhibitors
(294)
and buyers
(4,219)
at its recent gathering in New York.
Sizing up
the turnout at the
61st
annual trade show, William R. Card,
executive
secretary
of
the
National
Association
of Music
Merchants,
the
show’s
sponsors,
noted:
“Optimism
seemed
to be
the
prevailing keynote
at the show, both at the retailing and
manufacturing levels. Exhibitors gen-
erally were happy with the big turnout
of buyers from the very
first day of
the show.”
Attendance
figures
reached
11,515
for
the
five-day
show
at
the
Hotel
New
Yorker
and New
York
Trade
Show Building, which opened for the
first time
at an
early hour on
Sun.
and closed at midday Thurs. This fig-
ure was a new record for a New York
show, but below the
all-time high of
11,878
at the Chicago show
in
1961.
Buyers totaled 4219 at the 1962 show,
which
was
higher
than
the
4,028
buyers at last year’s show in Chicago
and
an
all-time high
for
the
music
trade show.
Previous
high
in
exhibiting
firms
was 274
in
1953, topped by
294
ex-
hibitors
this
year.
Biggest
increases
from past shows were in band instru-
ments with 56 exhibitors compared to
45
in
1961,
accordions with 34 com-
pared with 20 the previous year and
stringed instruments with 46 in con-
trast to 33 in 1961. Radio and phono-
graph
exhibits
increased
to
64 from
52
in 1961, tape recorders and sound
equipment up to 57 from 47 and tele-
vision up to 20 from 14 in 1961.
A
record number
of foreign
firms
were exhibitors at the show, ranging
from more than a dozen Japanese elec-
tronics
firms
to
several
European
piano manufacturers.
Ted P. Korten of Korten’s in Long-
view, Wash., was re-elected president.
Other officers reelected were Eldred S.
Byerly, Byerly Bros. Music Co. in Pe-
oria,
111.,
as
vice-president
and
R.
Gregory Durham of Lyon & Healy in
Chicago
as
treasurer,
in
addition
to
assuming the post of secretary.
Columbia
Plants Keep
Full Summer Sked
Columbia
Records’
four
factories
will maintain a full production sched-
ule
throughout
the summer
months.
This will enable Columbia Record Pro-
ductions to provide continuous service
for
its custom record
customers,
ac-
cording
to
Floyd
Glinert,
national
sales
manager
of
Columbia
Record
Productions.
For the past ten years the plants
at Pitman, New Jersey;
Bridgeport,
Connecticut;
Terre
Haute,
Indiana
and
Hollywood,
California—have
re-
mained
open
for
business
through
July and August.
The
practice
is
based
on
Colum-
bia Records’ belief that interruptions
of
manufacturing
would
severely
hamper
the
daily
service
require-
ments of the record industry.

en-

selected specifically for this affair.

Injection-Molded Vinyl
Disks From Golden Crest
NEW YORK.—Golden
Crest Records
is now making vinyl phono
disks by
the injection molding process, thanks
to
GC’s
subsidiary.
Shelly
Products,
which
has
developed
this new
tech-
nique by using a screw type of plas-
ticizer that molds vinyl at controlled
heat levels.
Vinyl, the highest quality material
on today’s disks, has heretofore been
used only
in compression molding,
a
process
in which the master
disk
or
stamper
is subject to deterioration so
that successive pressings do not pro-
duce disks of uniform quality.
According to GC, injection molding
of
disks
does
not
deteriorate
the
stamper, making every disk produced
from
the
same
master
identical
in
quality.

“IRA HAYES AND OTHER BALLADS”—Peter
La Farge—Columbia CL 1795
Take

part

rate guitarist, one part rodeo rider and the result

own but the influence of his mentor. Josh White
can be detected on “Ira Hayes,” “I Gave My Love
A Cherry” and “Alabama Bound.” If this album
is any indication, the songster seems destined for
stardom.
“TED WEEMS’ GOLDEN HITS”—Mercury SR
60708
Mercury comes up
with
a
platter
of
nostalgia
served up in fine style by the band of Ted Weems
which
scored many a ballroom triumph
during
the big band era of the 20’s and 30’s. Some of the
arrangements might sound a bit schmaltzy today,
but the Weems band follows
a
straight melodic
line and
can’t be beaten for sheer musicianship.
The orkster launches the set with his biggest hit,
“Heartaches,” and
includes “Mickey,” “Oh
Mo’-
nah,” “That Old Gang Of Mine,” and “One Man
Band.” An excellent reissue of a
fine band.
VIVA
PALMIERI”—Charlie
Palmieri—Alegre
LPA 816
The Charanga La Duboney of Charlie Palmieri is
an
orchestral
sound
unfamiliar
to
the
ears
of
most Americans until a few years ago. Unusual
arrangements in which the melody
is carried by
flutes and strings highlight each orchestration in
a very effective manner. Some interesting tracks
are
“El
Vendedor
De
Mangos,”
“Lagrimas Y
Tristeza,” “Mi Amor No
Esta De
Moda,”
and
“Estuve Pensando,”
all with a variety of tempos
and rhythms. Good dance wax with a Latin flavor.
“CHRIST
IN
CONCRETE”—Eli
Wallach—
DaVinci D205
Eli Wallach gives a moving and powerful reading
of Pietro Di Donato’s “Christ In Concrete,” with
original music composed by Harold Seletsky. The
thespian proves himself a great dramatic talent
and a skillful master of character integration in
this portrayal of the author’s avant-garde work.
Side 2
is devoted to a reading of Chekhov’s one-
act “Swan Song,” and again Wallach emerges as
an actor with great depth
of feeling. A superb
dramatic
disk
that merits
the
attention
of
the
actor’s and author’s admirers.
JAZZ
PICK
OF THE WEEK
“LONELY WOMAN”—Modern
Jazz
Quartet
Atlantic 1381
John
Lewis
and
the MJQ
have
earned many
laurels
in the past and this new Atlantic LP of
impressive
jazz
items
read
by
the group
with
their expected style and verve should go down the
hitsville
path
in
winning
fashion.
The
session
highlights the group’s ability to inject symphonic
statements along modern jazz
lines. The quartet
shines as they offer top-rung readings of “Lonely
Woman,” “New York 19” and “Lamb, Leopard.”
An
eye-catching
cover
of
a
pretty
lass
should
help spark
sales.
LOU DONALDSON
“GRAVY TRAIN”—Lou Donaldson—Blue Note
4079
The most difficult thing in jazz is sounding differ-
ent. Although he is strongly influenced by Charlie
Parker, Lou Donaldson has developed a free-flow-
ing style in the modern mainstream that is all his
own. Donaldson is teamed up with Herman Foster
on
piano, Ben Tucker on
bass, Dave
Bailey on
drums and Alec Dorsey on conga on this new Blue
Note
entry. The alto saxophonist gets a chance
for some smart solos on the seven originals and
standards included here. The group really swings
on “Gravy
Train,” “Avalon” and “Twist Time.
“2
SIDES
OF
CALVIN JACKSON”—Reprise
R-6022
This
jazz
offering
from
Reprise
features
the
keyboard
stylings
of
Calvin
Jackson,
a
triple-
threat composer, conductor, and pianist. Jackson’s
playing
is jazz flavored but without the abrupt
departure from the melodic line that characterizes
much of the modern jazz. An adept arranger, the
88’er uses lush strings to complement his playing.
First-rate bands
are “Moon
River,” “Moonlight
Sonata,” “I’ll Remember April,” and “Like Some-
one In Love.” Jazz buffs should go for this one.

entry Joy

fine premiere show-
ing.

“FRENCH PIANO MUSIC”—Andre Previn-Co-
lumbia ML 5746
The music of the French composers Roussel and
Poulenc
is interpreted by the skilled and artistic
Andre Previn
in
his highly
individualistic
style.
The
pianist
begins
with
the
shorter
pieces
of
Poulenc whose
melodies are
fused with French
folklore and rich with
clarity. On the other
side
Previn plays the longer works of Roussel which
include “Trois Pieces” and the “Sonatine.” This
subtle but delightful blending of two sharply de-
fined
schools
of composition
is masterfully exe-
cuted by the young performer. An excellent clas-
sical
disk.
iWisT PolKA
“TWIST POLKA”—Ray Henry—Dana DL
1297
Dana offers its latest in the polka field, this time
the music of Ray Henry and his polka band play-
ing a
collection of polkas, waltzes, obereks, and
a twist polka tossed in for added measure. With
emphasis on
reeds and
strings and toned-down
brass, the lilting melodies are given a refreshing
treatment. Polka fans will enjoy “Twist Polka,”
“Hop-Top-Jump
Polka,”
“Tony, The
Bachelor,”
and “Goodnight My Love.”
“MOISEIWITSCH PLAYS SCHUMANN”—Dec-
ca DL 710048
Benno
Moiseiwitsch plays
a
collection
of
short
romantic works of Robert Schumann, pieces which
reflect the composer’s feelings and emotions. The
pianist has a light, delicate touch as he plays the
“Kreileriana,” eight
short
pieces
depicting
Ger-
man romanticism. Also included are the “Kinder-
scenen,” which contains the very beautiful “Trau-
merei”
(Dreaming), “Arabesque,” and the “Ro-
mance
In F
Sharp
Major.”
First-rate
listening
enjoyment throughout.

Neil Sedaka was the “visitor of the week”
in Buenos Aires. The American
singer performed on television and at dance parties organized by Escala Musi-
cal.
His
main
engagement
took
place
at
the Luna
Park
Stadium,
July
8.
Previously, Sedaka spent several days in Santiago, Chile.
Daniel Gutierrez, artist manager, reported to Cash Box that Ives Montand,
the French
actor, singer and pianist will be
in Buenos Aires Nov.
12. Manolo
Munoz, Mexican twister who has been already in Argentina this year, will re-
turn in October to perform with Chubby Checker at the Luna Park. This event
(combined with “Twist Festivals”)
is also organized by Escala Musical.
Columbia
is continuing its “artist of the month campaign.” The
first artists
of the month were Los Cincos Latinos, before they started their new European
trip. Now, Waldo de los Rios (arranger and orchestra director) will receive spe-
cial promotion during July and August. As part of the plan, he will visit record
stores and sign records for
his admirers. All
his records
(he has
several
al-
bums, like “Gold Music” and “South American
Suite”)
will be highlighted in
stores and on radio stations.
More about Columbia: the label reports record sales of “West Side
Story,”
the LP with the music from the flick, in its first week of sales. This album has
been also released in its stereo version, considering that there is a good market
for this type of record. Besides, Columbia will put to sale a “Sing Along With
Mitch” album in August. Previously, it had cut two LP’s by Los Alegres Can-
tores, with popular “sing along” music in Spanish,” with very good success.
Jose A. Rota, International A&R of Odeon (EMI representative
in Argen-
tina), has started a new tour of several provinces. The main reason for this
visit is to promote Odeon records through the TV stations in the cities of Mar
del Plata, Cordoba and Mendoza. Odeon has been promoting its newest “Favu-
lozo”
Selection LP through the Buenos Aires channels, with four
daily one-
minute spots, besides
its normal radio exposure.
Alberto Martinez, coordinator of Southern Music operations in South Amer-
ica, has returned from a several weeks tour of Mexico, Brazil, Colombia, Peru
and
Chile, started after Mrs. Ralph
S. Peer’s
visit to South America about a
month ago. Martinez has been visiting the Peer representatives in these coun-
tires, to see the form
of improving cooperation between them.
Julio Korn Publishers working on the foreign promotion of “Mami,” a Chico
Novarro
local
hit that seems
to have good
international value. The pubbery
has recorded a acetate with all the available versions of the tune and sent it to
Editions Intro of Germany, with some other Novarro songs. Another JK item
is “Don’t Let Her Go,” already recorded by Dean Reed
(Capitol)
and Tony
Vilar (Columbia-in Spanish).
More about JK: The high rating of a Channel
9 Saturday night fight pro-
gram has been used as theme for two new tunes, which are being
sold very
well by Odeon Pops in the Pat Clipper version: “Las Barbas De Karadagian”
and “Dedos
Magneticos
(Magnetic
Fingers).” Both tunes
are
controlled by
Julio Korn. The diskery gave a dinner to the press celebrating the first 15,000
records, with Martin Karadagian and El Indio Comanche,
stars
of the
fight
program, as special guests.
Columbia plans to release the “Los Panchos Sing Tangos” LP nearly at the
same time in Argentina, Uruguay, Mexico, Chile, the United States and Japan.
The album contains tango evergreens, sung as boleros.
Lucio Milena has been inked to

back Juan Carlos Mareco
in

13, while Tony

(who’s doing very well with his version of “Nacida Para Mi” and now has re-

during July. Both artists record exclusively for Columbia.
Violeta Rivas

“DOO WACKA D00”—The Doowackadoodlers
RCA Victor LSP-2509
Marty
Gold
doubles

on

outing for
Victor which features

of the Kora

Some
first-rate

are
“Tiger
Rag,” “Yes
Sir,
That’s My Baby,”
“Toot,
Toot,
Tootsie!
Goodbye”
and
“Doo Wacka
Doo.” An
amusing and entertaining disk with a refreshing
novelty flavor.
“WALTZING WITH GUY LOMBARDO”—Capi-
tol ST 1738
Guy Lombardo adds another stanza to his exten-
sive repertoire with this session of waltzes played
in
a very danceable tempo by
the
Royal
Cana-
dians. The orkster surveys a group of evergreens
that have
always
been
favorites with
waltzers.
A
few
good
listening
and
dancing
bands
are
“Girl Of My Dreams,” “When
I Grow Too
Old
To Dream,” “Tennessee Waltz” and “A Beautiful
Lady In Blue.” Enjoyable dance wax.

“DE MEXICO A LA HABANA”—La Sonora San-
tanera—Columbia EX 5075
Latin music
lovers
should come out
in

for

The band renders a dozen fast-moving and dance-

HIGH FIDELITY
“MISTER COUNTRY MUSIC”—Cowboy Copas—
Starday SLP 175
Cowboy
Copas, who
has
established
himself
as
one of the biggest luminaries in the country field
with a long
string
of
hits, unleashes
his potent
vocal
and
instrumental
talents
on
the
Starday
LP
outing. The
songster
starts
things
off with
“Sal,”
his
recent country
chart-rider, and
turns
in professional renditions
of “A Thousand Miles
Of Ocean,” “Soft Rain” and “You Are One.” All
of Copas’ many fans should come out in strength
for the package.
“STERLING MOSSMAN AT THE BAREFOOT
BAR”—Decca DL 74178
Sterling Mossman and his “gang” give out with
a
lively assortment
of Hawaiian melodies
inter-
spersed with comedy monologs delivered by Moss-
man. Recorded live at the Barefoot Bar in Hono-
lulu,
the boys
do “Hawaiian
Calypso,”
“There’s
No
Place
Like Hawaii,”
“Little Hula
Coquette”
and “Yellow
Bird.” The
musical portions
of the
disk are entertaining but Mossman’s humor falls
short and he
is at best mildly funny. Album could
evoke mild
response among
those who
like Ha-
waiian music.
“AL DEXTER”—Capitol ST 1701
A1 Dexter, whose
first taste
of fame came with
his
self-penned
“Pistol
Packin’ Mama,”
renders
the while back smash in addition to eleven other
country items on this new disk from Capitol. The
chanter’s
feelingful,
authority-filled
vocal
style
carries him in good stead on “Down At The Road-
side
Inn,”
“Texas
Waltz”
and
“Too
Late
To
Worry.” A natural for airplay with the country
deejays.
JAZZ
PICKS
OF THE WEEK
“FREE SPIRITS”—Chris Connor—Atlantic 8061
Chris
Connor’s
versatility
as
jazz
singer
has
earned
a
reputation
of
being
able
to
deliver
a
tender
ballad
with
the
same
finesse
that
she
gives
to uptempo items. On the
Atlantic outing
the
lark
dishes up
eleven
tunes which
fall
into
both the lament and swingin’ categories. All the
selections were penned by famous
jazz
writers
and the thrush pays her dues to these tunesmiths
in
her
usual
superlative
manner.
Jazzophiles
should
dig
the
Connor
readings
of “Jump
For
Joy,” “Night Bird” and “Things Are
Swingin’.”
“BURNIN’ BEAT”—Gene Krupa, Buddy Rich-
Verve V6 8471
The wax marriage
of two
of jazzdom’s greatest
drummers, Gene Krupa
and Buddy
Rich,
offers
an excellent opportunity to compare their respec-
tive
talents
on
this
top-notch
Verve
set. Each
artist
is given an ample chance
to express him-
self with extended solos showcasing their distinc-
tive
styles.
Additionally,
the boys play together
complementing each other on eight potent sturd-
ies. Best listening bets here are “Jumpin’ At The
Woodside,” “Night Train” and “Perdido.”
“BLUE MOODS”—Miles Davis—Fantasy 6001
Here’s
an
interesting
session
cut
quite
a
while
ago displaying an introspective Miles Davis play-
ing
old, standard blues with an impressive,
lyric
simplicity. The
disk
is
noteworthy
for
it show-
cases the artist in an interim stage of his career
before he
attacked more
adventuresome
things.
With
an
able
assist
from
Britt Woodman
on
trombone, Teddy Charles on vibes, Elvin Jones on
drums and Charles Mingus on bass, Davis offers
top-flight
renditions
of
“Nature
Boy,”
“Easy
Living” and “Alone Together.”
“THINK WELL OF ME” — Jack Teagarden —
Verve V 68465
Jack
Teagarden, who
through
the
span
of
his
40-year career has won countless laurels for
his
distinctive
horn-vocal
expressiveness,
comes
up
with one of the best disks that he has cut in quite
a while
on
this new Verve
outing. The
session
spotlights the trumpet artistry of Don Goldie and
the combined
arranging
and
conducting
talents
of Russ Case and Bob Brookmeyer. Teagarden’s
trombone
injects a wistful, sentimental touch
to
his vocal statements on “Where Are You,” “Cot-
tage
For
Sale”
and
“Old
Folks.”
Jazzophiles
should come out in droves for the
set.

ALBUM REVIEWS
"ODETTA AND THE BLUES"—Riverside RLP
9417
Odetta, long thought of as a folk
artist, demon-
strates a moving communicative feel for the blues
on
this
top-notch
offering from
Riverside.
The
thrush
covers
a
wide
range
and
dramatic
and
emotional
effects as she dishes up some passion-
filled
renditions
of
“Believe
I’ll
Go,”
“Yonder
Come The Blues” and “Go Down, Sunshine.” An
impressive
disk.
•
'
'
“RUSSIAN
SONGS AND
CHORUSES”—Don
Cossack Choir, Serge Jaroff, Conductor—Deutsche
Grammop'hon SLPEM 136 235
The Don Cossack
Choir, under the very capable
direction of Serge Jaroff, has been a favorite of
the American concert stage for many years, and
the choir’s legion of admirers will want this new
offering
for
their
shelves. The
Cossacks
sing
a
group
of Russian folk songs which are not well
known,
but
they
are
delivered
with
the
same
verve and power
that has become
a trademark
with the choir. Included are “Song Of The Brave
Major,” “Marching
Song,” “On The
Hill,” “The
Broken
Heart,” and “Along The
Road.”

“I’LL WALK WITH GOD ”—Mario Lanza—RCA
Victor LM-2607
Despite
his untimely death
in
1959, the voice
of
Mario Lanza
is
still much
in demand, and Victor
has responded with this LP of songs of love and
devotion.
Some
of
the
tunes
have
been
taken
from
other albums,
but
Victor
has added some
new ones taken from
Lanza’s
radio
series. The
dynamic
voice
is
at
its very
best
in
“I’ll Walk
With God,” “Guardian Angels,” “Somebody Big-
ger Than You And
I,” and “Addio Alla Madre.”
The
tenor’s legion
of admirers
will
surely want
this one.
“THAT’S
ALL”—Herman
Chittison—L’elegant
LES
1000
Herman
Chittison
unleashes
his
talents
on
the
piano and comes up with some sparkling arrange-
ments in this potent bag of oldies. As a box man,
he is not only nimble-fingered, but fleet-footed too
as he pedals and pounds his way through uptempo
versions
of
“Little
Girl
Blue,” “Smoke
Gets
In
Your Eyes,” “My Funny Valentine,” and “Danc-
ing On
The
Ceiling.”
Playing
sans
accompani-
ment, the 88’er proves himself a keyboard
artist
of the first order.

“MY FAVORITES OF HANK WILLIAMS”—
George Jones—United Artists UAS 6220
George Jones, who is currently riding high on the
country
charts with “She
Thinks
I
Still
Care,”
offers
a dozen musical tributes to the
late Hank
Williams on this new United Artists session. The
selections
include
songs which were
written by
Williams and others which have become standards
as
a
result
of
his performances. The
songster’s
feelingful vocal
style
is aptly suited
to such
old
favorites as “Wedding
Bells,” “You Win Again”
and “Your Cheating Heart.” Plenty of
sales po-
tential here.
“GEORGE JONES SINGS FROM THE HEART”
—Mercury SR 60694
Here’s
a
top-drawer
package
of
country
love
songs from George Jones cut during his days with
Mercury. The
chanter
has
the
ability
to
inject
the necessary conviction and authority on
all the
tunes he dishes up here. Jones’ professional, wide-
range
voice
is
firmly
evidenced
on
“Aching,
Breaking
Heart,”
“Candy
Hearts”
and
“Cold,
Cold Heart.” The
set should prove popular with
the country spinners. A fine showing.
“MOODY AND MAGNIFICENT”—Harry Robin-
son—Riverside 97528
The
music
of Harry
Robinson
is
characterized
by rich instrumentation, a soaring string section,
inventive
arrangements,
and
adherence
to
the
melodic
line. This entry from Riverside features
the orchestra from England playing a set of bal-
lads intended to set a mood, and does
it effective-
ly in “Me And My Shadow,” “I’m In Love Again,”
and “All In The Game.” Potent wax for spinners.
“SONGS BY JIMMY NEWMAN”—MGM E4045
Jimmy Newman gives some soulful readings to a
bevy of country-flavored ballads on this new out-
ing from MGM. The chanter has a sincere, feeling-
ful delivery that comes off well on such numbers
as
“I’d Just Be Fool Enough,” “What’cha Gonna
Do,” “You’re Makin’ A Fool Out Of Me,” “Crying
Over You,” and
“Please Accept My Love.” The
country
singer’s
loyal
coterie
of fans
will want
this enjoyable
session.
JAZZ
PICKS
OF THE WEEK
“SONNY’S
TIME”—Sonny
Rollins—Jazzland
JLP 972
Sonny Rollins, whose return from a self-imposed
retirement
last year was greeted with apprehen-
sion by the jazz world, offers proof positive that
he
still has an imaginative, harmonic tenor style.
On this Jazzland set the artist is teamed up with
an accomplished group of sidemen including Oscar
Pettiford
on
bass. Max
Roach
on
drums
and
Sonny Clark on piano. The sounds here are free-
flowing, impressive and professional. Some
first-
rate tracks include “The Last Time I Saw Paris,”
“Cutie” and “My Old Flame.” Jazzophiles should
come in droves for the package.
“CHAZZ !”—Charles
Mingus
Quintet—Fantasy
6002
Here’s a top-drawer experimentative set cut seven
years ago at Gotham’s Club Bohemia spotlighting
the controversial talents of Charlie Mingus. The
bassist’s amazing control and technical skills are
aptly showcased on such adventuresome works as
“Septemberly,” “Jump Monk” and “Serenade
In
Blue.” All the artist’s many admirers should come
out in strength for the set.
“COLTRANE PLAYS THE BLUES”—John Col-
trane—Atlantic 1382
John Coltrane, who has established a solid reputa-
tion as one of the leaders in the avant-garde jazz
tradition, reverts to
his
early musical
roots
for
this
first-rate
set
of
six
blues
selections.
The
soprano
saxist
does
not
rely
on gimmicks
but
utilizes a fresh, straight-forward approach on the
self-penned
items
on
the
set.
Each
track
is
a
dramatic, personal statement in the best Coltrane
style.
Best
listening
bets
are “Blues To
Elvin,”
“Blues To You” and “Mr. Day.” Powerful
jazz
package.
CLASSICAL
“DANCIN’
THE
GOLDEN
20’s
GERMAN
STYLE”—Philips PHS
600-030
The syncopated rhythms of the roaring twenties
are rejuvenated in this new offering from Philips
which features a host of tunes of that era—melo-
dies that were popular on both
sides
of the At-
lantic. The band has
a bouncy, catchy beat and
employs the banjo, tinkling piano, and an organ
to recreate the musical spirit of the 20’s. Playing
24
melodies
in medley form,
the
band
includes
“Whispering,”
“Mack
The
Knife,”
“San
Fran-
cisco,”
and
“Valencia.”
Disk
is
a
pleasant
late
hours companion.
PUCCINI: Madame Butterfly; Andre Kostelanetz
—Columbia CL 1787
The
orchestra
of
Andre
Kostelanetz
plays
the
music of Puccini’s most melodic opera, “Madame
Butterfly,”
in
a
pleasing,
straight-forward man-
ner that should satisfy the most discerning opera
fan.
For
those whose
likes
are
limited
to
pop
music, the Kostelanetz treatment
of the Puccini
score
should
be
a
sheer
delight. The
orchestra
plays the entire first act, and the first part of the
second act, and the second part of the third
act.
A very enjoyable session.
32

Frank Russell Expands
Russ-Fi Music Operations
HOLLYWOOD—Flick producer Frank
Russell, who launched his record com-
pany
subsidary Russ-Fi with
the
re-
lease
last month
of
two
Vince
Ed-
wards
sides
recorded
before
the
artist’s TV
success
as “Ben
Casey,’’
announced
last week
that
he
is
ex-
panding his music operations with the
addition
of
three
more
labels,
the
acquistion
of
several
pubberies
and
the building of a talent roster under
A&R
chief Jack Moon.
Russ-Fi last week released a second
platter,
“Daybreaker”
and
“Beat,”
recorded
by
Skip
Batten
and
Kim
Fowley. Scheduled for August release
is a third deck and another Vince Ed-
wards wax, “Hole
In The Head.”
Other labels under the Russell ban-
ner
include
Gift,
to
specialize
in
al-
bums,
first of which will be a Christ-
mas
package
of
ballads
by Champs
Butler, who has been inked to a long-
term contract by the diskery.
Philip-
pine
88’er Pomping
Villa and
organ-
ist Frank Perry have also been signed
to
record
for
Gift.
Russell
will
also
release country
sides under the RRE
banner, with the Victoria
label
to be
added
for r&b
sides.
Russell’s Mamaleen publishing firm,
which
holds
the
rights
to
the
tunes
recorded
by
Edwards
is
augmented
by
two
more
firms
brought
in
by
Moon, Moontunes (ASCAP) and Hol-
lyvale
(BMI)

Dis-

to

will handle promo and Larry Hosmer,

HOLLAND
The Blue Diamonds,
are having
a
top-hit
in
their
recent
repertoire with
“Marching Along With The Blue Diamonds,” are most popular
in Germany.
For that reason, Mr. John Ros of Dutch Decca told us, a new single was
re-
leased in German hardly a month after their popular
soldiers’ medleys.
It
is
the German
hit “Lady Sunshine And Mr. Moon,” backed with the charming
“Angelina, Lass Das Weinen,” a song based on old German folk tunes.
The TV performance
of Zizi Jeanmaire in Holland, on July 13th, caused a
little trouble. Her manager agreed
in
Paris that she would
do
her
tour-de-
chant show for one hour on Dutch TV. When Zizi arrived
in Holland, to ap-
pear as the top attraction in a “Miss Eye-Glasses” contest,
it turned out that
Zizi had not been informed about a personal TV appearance in Holland, and
that a movie company in France, moreover, did not allow her to appear on TV
at
all. However, when
Zizi learned that the misunderstandings were not the
fault of Dutch TV officials, she agreed upon a twenty minutes show. She went
on for almost forty minutes, in fact, giving a fine performance, including her
famous “True de plumes”—the feathered fan dance, together with the Roland
Petit Dancers. The songs she sang were those on the recently recoi'ded Philips
LP in the “Music Hall” series, a live recording of Zizi in Paris.
Gene Pitney’s (“The Man Who Shot) Liberty Valance” on the United Arists
label, with the
plaintive
fiddle
introduction, could become an
excellent
sales
item in the C & W
field, Mr. Otto Vriezenberg of L. C. Phonogram observed.
Flip-side “Take
It Like A Man”
is also being plugged in Dutch C & W pro-
grams.
Sales
of
jazz
recordings
are
getting much
better
in
Holland,
Mr.
Leo
Boudewijns, general label manager of L. C. Phonogram, told us. The excellent
quality of modern jazz on Riverside, London, Fontana, Philips and many other
leading labels are certainly a vital influence upon the increasing jazz market,
but
it turns out that
old jazz-recordings
in new presentations
are
also
well
received. There
is a tendency in demands for
historic recordings—one
of the
reasons why London’s “Jazz
Festival
Series”
in Holland
released
a
Charlie
Parker recording lately, featuring Miles Davis and Jay Jay Johnson, from the
early
fifties.
CNR reports that Ben
Steneker’s “Lonely River Rhine”/“I Used To Love
You” is a hot seller—in Holland as well as in Denmark, Germany and Belgium.
Colpix releases of the month: “Conscience” by Jimmy Darren and “Johnny
Loves Me” by Shelley Fabares.
Still a big seller on Colpix is Jimmy Darren’s
“Her Royal Majesty.”
Joe Brown’s “Picture Of You” on the Pye label
is a big surprise. Probably
this disk
will enter Holland’s Top Twenty. Mr. Hans van Zeeland
told Cash
Box that Jimmy
Justice, whose “Little Smiling Girl”
is very popular in Hol-
land, will pay a visit to our country.
Holland’s
top
trumpeter Gerard
Engelsma,
a.o.
first trumpetman
in The
Skymasters’ brass-section, scored a sensational success with his one and only
trumpet version of the current hit parader “Heisser Sand.” Engelsma, who has
often been' nicknamed
as the “Dutch Harry James” recorded the number on
Bovema’s Columbia label, which had the disk on the market within two days
after the
session!
The same rush release took place for the Number 1 Hitparader in the U.S.,
Bobby Vinton’s “Roses Are Red,” which also appeared on Bovema’s Columbia
label—commercially supported by posters and broadcast plugging.
Bovema, already running exclusive agencies for U.S. labels

of the Stateside label
(artists
a.o. Freddy Cannon, Dee Dee Ford and Sharon

in Holland.

NEW YORK—The winner of London
Records
nationwide
Mantovani
Con-
test is a supermarket clerk from Mil-
ford, N.
J. The
prize, a trip to Eng-
land
for
two, was won
by
Angeleo
Ruggiero.
His
entry
choosing
the
songs and
title
for
Mantovani’s
next LP
was
selected
from
thousands
of
entries.
The
title of Ruggiero’s LP
is “Latin
Rendezvous” and
includes
“Siboney,”
“Granada,” “Amapola” and nine other
popular Latin American numbers.
Contest
entries
were
screened
by
London’s A&R
staff
with
the
final
choice made by Mantovani.
The
Mantovani
contest
was
fea-
tured in a broad national advertising
campaign,
trade
advertising
and
at
point of sale. The only way a person
could enter the contest to recommend
Mantovani’s next LP was to buy his
then
current
release
“American
Waltzes,”
and
use
the
official
entry
blank enclosed in the LP. The contest
ended June
30.
Every contestant who submitted
a
qualified entry to the Mantovani Con-
test
received
a
special
six
selection
Mantovani LP including some of the
performer’s most requested items.
Ruggiero and
his wife
vdll depart
for England
via BOAC on
Sept.
15.
They
will be
greeted upon
their
ar-
rival
in London
by
Maestro Manto-
vani.
Subsequently
they
will
attend
the actual recording
session
of Rug-
giero’s LP.
The
couple
will be
hosted by
Mr.
Joe
Bott and
his
wife.
Mr.
Bott
is
London Records’ national
sales man-
ager. Their itinerary includes
shows,
night
clubs and
tours.
Mr. Ruggiero
is an avid Mantovani
fan owning 32
LP’s
by
the famous
British
conductor.
Until
now
his
favorite LP has been Italia Mia.
The
contest
vdnner
has
attended
every
local
Mantovani
concert
and
has his autographed photograph.

NEW YORK—A
star
talent
lineup
has been set for a benefit concert here
this Sat. (11) at the Apollo Theatre to
raise funds for the Southern Student
Freedom Fund.
Appearing
will
be
Tony
Bennett,
Sonny
Rollins,
The
Caravans,
The-
lonious Monk, Art Blakey,
Bill Hen-
derson, Lloyd Price, “Moms” Mabley,
Billy 'Taylor and Lambert, Hendricks
& Bavan.
Set up by the U.
S. National
Stu-
dent
Association, SSFF
seeks
to
aid
those students in the south who have
been expelled from school because of
their
leadership
and/or
participation
in
civil
rights
activities.
Funds
are
also being used for bail and jail fines
for sit-in students and freedom riders
and will also be applied to voter reg-
istration projects in the south.
Producing the
benefit
is
C. B. At-
kins,
head
of
Progressive
Talents
management
office, this city.
New ASCAP
Rubbery
In Tannen
Set-Up
NEW YORK—Natson Music, an AS-
CAP pubbery, has been formed here
by Paul Tannen.
New firm
is the only ASCAP firm
in the Tannen
set-up, which
also
in-
cludes Tannen Music, Ridge Music and
Tanridge
Music,
all BMI
firms.
Ac-
cording
to
Tannen,
Natson’s
catalog
will be varied, covering pop, country
and showtunes.
Additionally, Tannen
said
that
he
was on
the
lookout for
writers who
clear through either BMI or ASCAP.
Paul Tannen took
over
the
opera-
tion of Tannen Music—^which has one
of the top country catalogs—after his
dad, vet music man Nat Tannen, died
in March, 1962.
Tanridge Music, formed last Jan., is
currently hot with Johnny Tillotson’s
smash
on
Cadence,
“It Keeps
Right
On
A-Hurtin’.”

Spain—Last 12 Months
(Continued from page 26)
The capacity for absorption of new
records depends upon the number
of
phonographs
in
existence
(around
700,000)
and the
economic
status
of
the
buyers. The demand
for
phono-
graphs
is
increasing
and
so
is
the
number of types and models produced
by different manufacturers. However,
the teenagers, who are without doubt
the sector most interested in records,
do not have
sufficient means to make
large purchases, especially bearing in
mind the fact that most of the Span-
ish production consists
of
E.P.’s, the
price
of which
almost consumes
the
weekly pocket money of a young per-
son
of
the
middle
class. Some
com-
panies
already
have
a
good
produc-
tion
of
singles
which
are
enjoying
more and more
success.
Exploitation
of the
single, however,
is
difficult
as
there are very few suitable radio pro-
grammes
and
most
stations
are
lo-
cated
in
Madrid
and
Barcelona. Up
to the present
publicity
in the
press
has
been
practically
nil
and
few
companies
run
an
organised
depart-
ment
for
promotion
although
there
are
some,
such
as
RCA,
who
are
pioneering in
this respect.
The
great mass
of
the
public
is
beginning
to demand
melodies
sung
in Spanish and
for this reason some
American and European
artists have
made recordings in this language with
the
Spanish
and
Spanish-American
market
in mind.
At
present
there
is
an
extensive
inclination
towards American
music.
In
all
the
big
cities
a
multitude
of
orchestras have been formed, mostly
by
students,
which
are
being
con-
tracted by
the main
companies. One
of
the
infinite
number
of
junior
grouns,
the
ones
which
stand
out
are
“Los
Sonor” who
have
already
recorded three albums for RCA: “Los
Estudiantes”
(Philips)
is
another
group
of
youngsters
which
is
also
successful.
The main
radio
stations,
with several talent-scout programmes,
is
contributing
to
the
spreading
of
what has become known as “The New
Spanish Wave.”
The preference of the Spanish pub-
lic
leans
towards
Elvis
Presley—in-
disputable King in the record market
—Paul
Anka,
Cliff
Richard,
Johnny
Hallyday, Sacha
Distel, Connie Fran-
cis; Italian artists Mina, Milva, Celen-
tano, Fidenco, Modugno and Dallara;
Mexican Miguel Aceves
Mejia,
Chil-
ean
Antonio
Prieto whose
recording
of “La Novia” was
the
hit
of
1961
in
Spain and
a
considerable
part
of
Europe
and
Spanish
artists
Alfredo
Kraus, Duo Dinamico, Lolita Garrido,
-Toselitn,
Jose
Guardiola,
Elia
Fleta,
Sara Montiel, Marisol. Paquito Jerez,
Manolo Escobar and Dolores Vargas.
In recent years the Spanish record
industry
has
experienced
a
number
of innovations including the introduc-
tion of the Compact 33%rd by RCA
which failed to make sufficient impact
on the market
to
justify
its continu-
ance.
Equally
unsuccessful
was
the
introduction by Hispavox of “Disco-
flex”—a
two-selection
record pressed
on
paper
bound
plastic.
Despite
its
low price and curiosity value the pub-
lic soon lost interest. Another develop-
ment has been
the launching
of
the
Readers
Digest
Record
Library
by
RCA
who
report
that
distributors,
after a period of opposition, now real-
ise that it constitutes a very powerful
promotion
drive for the record
busi-
ness
in general.
The
future
seems
hopeful.
The
three largest companies, RCA, Philips
and
Gramofono-Odeon,
have
thrown
themselves energetically into the task
of
promoting
their
records
and
in-
creasing the
overall
national
figures.
Also, the increase
in tourism and the
popularity
in
Europe
of
everything
that
is
Spanish
have
aroused
inter-
national
interest
in
the
folkloric
music
and
there
is
a
good
level
of
sales and
distribution for records
of
this type abroad.

JERRY WILLIAMS
is the feotured singer with THE VIOLENTS.
He began

in
1957, working
together
with
Little Ger-
hard. He formed
his own
band
three

later and
joined

now
touring
with
this
group. He
has
appeared
on TV
in
Sweden and
Finland. This spring
he smashed
with "DARLING
NELLY GREY" and his latest recording
is "HELLO GOODBYE."

break came when a Swedish DJ played

first record, "AL-
PENS ROS," an
old

ore
"TRINK,
BRUDERLEIN

BORIS started out as a rock and
