######## cb 1962-08-11 p273  [pacific\s+jazz]

AAA
^^^<^ERMANY^>
With the summer season still in full swing, the strongest collection of singles
that has ever been issued in this usually weak season has been released by the
record firms here. Although no novelty such as “Ahab The Arab” in America
has come on the market
to
bring buyers
into
the
shops,
the
industry
has
answered by shooting their strongest guns and issuing strong records by art-
ists usually reserved for better selling periods. Electrola opened the competi-
tion by
releasing
a new
platter from Conny who was
still
riding
on
the
wave of her hit “2 Kleine Italiener” which passed the % million mark months
ago. Her new waxing, “Lady Sunshine & Mr. Moon” passed the 100,000 mark
in a very short time after release. Polydor answered the competition with new
waxings by top
selling
stars such
as Gus Backus and Connie
Francis, and
Teldec rushed out a new platter by Gerd Boettcher, their strongest teenager
and a strong waxing by Caterina Valente of two top American
hits sung in
German, “Roses Are Red” and “Johnny Get Angry.” The firm also has the new
Billy Vaughn recording of “Swinging
Safari” which
is
selling here like hot-
cakes. The song was written by Germany’s world star Bert Kaempfert. Philips
is riding high with Gerhard Wendland and Nana Mouskouri who failed to cool
off after each had a million seller on their last release. Although many of the
names
listed above are unknown internationally, they
all mean
top
sales
in
Germany.
Ariola has also not been sleeping, and their recording of “El Rancho Grande”
by Peter Hinnen can also be listed as a top summer
seller.
It’s a fine summer
sales wise and should open the door for a great fall and winter sales season.
Philips started pushing their new Interdisc jazz program by issuing 70 LP’s
of top material from Riverside, GTJ, Contemporary, Pacific Jazz, and Jazzland.
Electrola records has had many changes in their distribution set-up. As re-
ported a few weeks ago in Cash Box, Wilfried Jung from Frankfurt has taken
over the distribution chief’s job
in Cologne. A board of distributors has
also
been formed to advise the new chief and help
fulfill
this important position.
The committee of 4 will be headed by the oldest regional distrib chief of the
firm Hans Breunig from Munich. The former distribution assistant Heinz Vill-
mann has also been promoted to
first position under Mr. Jung. New regional
distribution
chiefs include the former Berlin
chief Werner Wewiasinski who
will now take over the Frankfurt bureau, Rolf Nietsche who
is now in charge
of Berlin, and Wolfgang Zimmerhansl who
is now in charge of the Mannheim
area.
Electrola which belongs to the world wide EMI group will also play a more
important part
in
the
classical
international catalog
of the
label. The new
“International Classical Repertoire Committee” for the firm has announced that
Germany will deliver 3 complete operas, 2 large choir works and many other
recordings. The new head of the German department for Electrola
is Sigfrid
Hoffman. In addition the production is being enlarged, and for this purpose, a
new classical A&R team has been started in Munich with new equipment and
studios there as an addition to the Berlin set-up for the firm. Hans Ritter who
for years has produced for D.G.G. is joining the Electrola team as head of the
artist production
in the classical
sector and
Fritz Ganss
is leaving the
firm.
The production head of the classical department remains under the leadership
of Director Max Ittenbach in Cologne.
The summer
classical season
in Germany and Austria began
late
in July
with the Bayreuth Festival of Wagner operas and followed with the Salzburg,
Austria festival of operas and concerts with the works of Salzburg born Wolf-
gang Mozart featured. Both
festivals were, as
usual,
sold
out.
Polydor reports top action on new summer releases of “Speedy Gonzales”
done in German by Lou Van Burg, “I Can’t Stop Loving You” in German by
Ivo Robic and U.S. discings of Brenda Lee’s “Heart In Hand” and Sue Lyon’s
“Lolita Ya Ya” with the
film mnning now in Germany
to help
sales along.
Heino “Calcutta” Gaze writes that Warner Bros. Records have recorded
a
new “Calcutta” LP with Raoul Meynard and that he’s got two new songs en-
tering the hit parade sweepstakes in the U.S. within the next few weeks.
Metronome Records
is cashing in on the Italian vacation goers by releasing
the top
selling “St. Tropez Twist” by Peppino Di Capri
in Italy. The record
was tested in Munich radio and won 1st place 3 times in row.
That’s
it for this week in Germany.

JAZZ
PICKS
OF THE WEEK
“COLTRANE”—John
Coltrane
Quartette—Im-
pulse A 21
The accomplishments, thus far, of John Coltrane
rank him
as
one
of the most
significant
forces
in the new-wave jazz movement. On this new Im-
pulse
set Coltrane along with his quartet, which
consists
of Elvin Jones on drums, Jimmy Garri-
son
on bass and McCoy on
piano,
offer
five
su-
perbly-read selections in the distinctive style that
has
become
associated with
their
hard-driving,
potent brand of jazz. Some top-notch tracks here
are
“Out
Of
The
World,”
“Soul
Eyes”
and
“Miles’s Mode.” Package should bring out a host
of
jazzophiles.
“MY HOUR OF NEED”—Dodo
Greene—Blue
Note 9001
Blue Note
long-associated
with
the
top
instru-
mental
names
in
jazz,
makes
a
dramatic
de-
parture on this disk by showcasing the emotion-
packed
vocal
abilities
of Dodo
Greene,
recently
pacted
by
the
label
to
an
exclusive
contract.
With
a
first-rate
backing from
the
Ike Quebec
Quintet
the
lark
displays
an
imaginative,
per-
sonal,
spontaneous
approach
on
a
fine
bag
of
evergreens
including
“You
Are My
Sunshine,”
“Lonesome
Road”
and
“Little
Things Mean A
Lot.”
If
this
premiere
session
is any indication
the thrush has
a most promising
future.

“3 BLIND MICE”—Art Blakey—United
Artists
Jazz 14002
United
Artists
spearheads
their new
jazz
drive
with
this
top-drawer
entry
showcasing
the
tal-
ents of Art Blakey’s Jazz Messengers. This
ses-
sion which
spotlights
Blakey on
drums, Jimmy
Merritt on bass, Cedar Walton on piano, Curtis
Fuller
on
trombone,
Wayne
Shorter
on
tenor
and Freddie Hubbard on trumpet, has the crew
rendering
six
sturdies
and
originals
with
their
expected verve and
polish. The group
wails
su-
perbly on “Three Blind Mice,” “Blue Moon” and
“Up Jump
Spring.” One

the Messengers have
cut
in
quite
a
while.
“WINTERS
AGAIN”—Jerri
Winters—Charlie
Parker PLP
808
There are many jazz larks around today but few
possess the top-drawer phrasing and understand-
ing
of
lyrics
that
Jerri
Winters
eloquently
ex-
presses on this superior LP from Charlie Parker.
With
exactly
the
right
backing
from
Mundell
Lowe’s
crew, the thrush
displays an impressive,
wide range vocal
style on such superb
oldies
as
“Elmer’s
Tune,”
“Through
Again”
and
“Did
I
Remember.” Disk should attract attention in both
the jazz and pop markets.
CLASSICAL PICKS OF THE WEEK
“CARNIVAL
IN VIENNA”—The
Philadelphia
Orchestra, Eugene Ormandy—Columbia ML 5752
Here
is a superb classical entry from Columbia’s
new
fall
release
collection
which
features
the
best-selling
Philadelphia
Orchestra
under
the
baton of Eugene Ormandy. The maestro expertly
leads
the men through
lilting waltzes and
fiery
polkas from the pens of Johann and Josef Strauss.
First-rate
bands
here
are
“Fire-Bell
Polka,”
“Thunder And Lightning Polka,” and “Thousand
And One Nights.” The disk should cause plenty
of sales excitement and could be a strong conten-
der for the charts.
SHOSTAKOVITCH
:
Symphony
No.
5,
Vienna
Philharmonic
Orchestra,
Constantin
Silvestri
—Angel S 35760
The 5th Symphony by Shostakovich marks
his
“arrival” as a composer inasmuch as he adheres
more
closely
to pure symphonic
structure, with
more
lyrical
and
dramatic
results
than
in
his
earlier works.
This performance by
the Vienna
Philharmonic is brilliant under the baton of Con-
stantin Silvestri who gives to the work a dynamic
quality.
This
excellent
classical
offering
merits
the attention of
all collectors of the classics.

Decca's New Nashville Offices Make Official Bow
NASHVILLE—Last Wed. (8) marked
the
official
opening
and
dedication
festivities of Decca Records’ new per-
manent
headquarters
in
Nashville,
long the focal point
of extensive
re-
cording
activity by the
label.
Located
at
803
Sixteenth
Avenue
South,
in
the
heart
of
Nashville’s
center
of recording and
music
pub-
lishing
activity, often referred
to
as
Music City, U.S.A., the new building
is a two-story structure of modernis-
tic
design,
featuring wood
panelled
walls
and
soft
lighting,
created
by
W.
B. Cambron and Company,
Inc.,
architect and builder.
The
building
will
house
executive
offices, reception, audition and rehear-
sal
facilities.
A&R
Director Owen
Bradley
will
be in charge of Decca’s new Nashville
offices. He will be
assisted by Harry
Silverstein, who
also
oversees
Decca
promotion for the
area.
Also housed
in the building will be branch
offices
of
Northern
and
Champion
Music
Decca’s
affiliate
publishing
firms.
These are co-managed by Gerald Nel-
son and Jerry
Crutchfield.
Top
label
executives
including
Leonard W. Schneider, executive vice
president, and
vice president Martin
P.
Salkin flew to
Nashville
to be on
hand
for
the
opening-day
activities
and to greet the many Decca
artists
who
live and work
in
the
Nashville
area.
Decca’s
association with
Nashville
can be traced to the very early days
of the company’s
history
in
the mid
30’s
when
A&R
producers
made
periodic flights to Nashville to record
the
ever-increasing number
of
local
artists
bidding
for
national
recogni-
tion. Many
top-name
talents
in
the
country
field
rose
to
world
wide
prominence
via
a
recording
associa-
tion with
Decca. A number
of these
remain active, best-selling attractions
today,
including
Ernest Tubb,
Kitty
Wells, Red
Foley, Webb
Pierce,
Bill
Monroe,
and Jimmy
Davis.
Others,
have been discovered and gone on
to
become potent
factors
in
the
record
industry. Among these: The Wilburn
Brothers, Bobby
Helms,
Goldie
Hill,
Roy
Drusky, Jimmie
Martin,
Grady
Martin, Bob Beckham, Loretta Lynn
and Connie Hall.
Several
of
Decca’s
top
pop
talent
record
exclusively
in
Nashville.
Brenda
Lee,
Burl
Ives
and
Patsy
Cline each has recorded
their
recent
string of hits in Nashville.
Commenting on the new edifice, ex-
ecutive
vice
president
Leonard
W.
Schneider
said, “This
stands
in
en-
during brick and concrete as evidence
of our continued faith in the city and
the people of Nashville.
It
is an
ex-
pression of our confidence in the con-
tinuation
of
a
venture
that
is
both
economically
sound
and
rich
in
its
musical
heritage. We’re proud
to be
a part of this heritage that enriches
so many throughout the world.”
CBS Earnings Up
For 2nd Quarter Of '62
NEW YORK—The Columbia Broad-
casting System
Inc., the parent com-
pany of Columbia Records, racked up
record
sales and earnings
in
the
six
months ended on June
30, according
to
announcement
last week
by
Wil-
liam
S.
Paley, chairman, and Frank
Stanton,
prexy.
The
second-quarter
net
earnings
were
$6,388,000, equal
to
72
cents
a
share.
This
was
almost
double
the
3.383.000 and 38 cents realized
in the
quarter
ended
June
30,
1961.
The
organization’s net sales rose to $118,-
105.000 from $114,760,000 a year ago.
CBS showed net earnings
of
$14,-
153,308
for
the
first
six
months
of
this
year.
This
is
equal
to
$1.59
a
share
against
$9,409,332 and
$1.06
a
year
earlier.
Earnings
before
taxes
rose to $31,069,308 as opposed to $20,-
476,332 a year ago.
The
Paley-Stanton
report
also
noted that net sales for the 26 weeks
to June 30 rose
to $246,656,296 from
$240,767,745 for the 1961
period.

Mauricio Brenner, head of Producciones Fermata, reported to Cash Box that
his diskery has arranged the representation of Festival Records
of France in
Argentina. First releases will take place in a few weeks, and special emphasis
will be put on Marie Jose, Maria Candido, Jacques Helian and Fred Gerard.
^
Besides,
several
of
Festival’s
“disques
litteraires”
will
be
also
put_ in
the
market, mainly those by Jean
Cocteau, Albert Camus, Gerard
Philipe and
Paul Geraldy. “We don’t suppose to find a big market for these literary rec-
ords,” Brenner said, “but we consider them very important and worth being
released. Marie Jose, Maria Candido, Helian and Gerard have good
possibili-
ties in Argentina.”
Big news on the charts this week. Several changes, a new topper and many
new tunes are forcing several chart riders to disappear. The new number one
is “King Of Clowns,” which has been helped a
lot by Neil Sedaka’s
visit to
^
Argentina several weeks ago. But there are a couple of rivals for this King:
RCA
and
Fermata—the
publisher—are
already
promoting
Sedaka’s
latest
recordings, in English and Spanish: “Breaking Up
Is Hard To Do” and the
other songs in his albums. Since it very seldom happens that an artist has two
titles on the charts (although Sedaka made it once, with “Calendar Girl” and
“Little Devil”)
there may be some friction between “King Of Clowns” and
“Breaking Up.” The other
rival for
this
chart topper
is
“Africkaan Beat ”
the Bert Kaempfert waxing, which is running extremely well after a slightly
slow start. A bit lower is “Munequita” (Roly Poly) and “Cuando Calienta El
Sol.” Both are published by Edami, and seem to have big force, too. “Mune-
quita” has been
cut
in Mexico by Enrique Guzman, who
is becoming
well
known in Argentina, and there
is also a local version by Johnny Tedesco. The
lists show also the name of Elvis Pesley, who
sells very well but seldom gets
into the top
fifteen. In this case
it’s “Little
Sister.”
New Philips
releases:
a new LP by folk
singer Horacio Guarany, a new
album
of the “South America By Night”
series, with
tropical
music,
and
several Polydor
releases.
In the
single
line, new
titles
are “Dale
Dale” by
Rudy Machado, “Midnight In Moscow” by Gasparin, “Camino de Traicion” by
Los Abriles and “Exaltacion” by Los Hue Quillen, new folk group.
Anibal Alverdi of Music Hall informs that Siro San Roman, who’s becoming
a big
star, will soon travel
to Ecuador and Colombia
to perform
there. He
would stay in that country about two months, and maybe visit Mexico. Carlos
Vega
Pereda,
folk
singer,
will
also
travel
to
Mexico, and
afterwards
visit
Venezuela. He will be back in Dec. Raul Shaw Moreno will go to Chile, to per-
form on Radio Mineria of Santiago. His trip will last about four weeks. Elizte
Cardoso, the Brazilian songstress, will stay about one month in Buenos Aires,
recording a new LP there. Arrangements will be made by Lito Escarso, who
^
will also direct the orchestra.
More about Music Hall: the diskery reports that “Barbara,” MH’s new pro-
motional record, has already got to the 10,000 mark, in only fifteen days. The
album is already in the charts. It contains tunes by MH’s most popular artist's,
including Los Santos, Lito Escarso, Siro San Roman and others, and has been
priced at 285 pesos (regular LP’s cost: 455).
Disc Jockey Records are
all smiles with the sales of its “promotional” LP,
“Golosinas

It
also
got
onto

in
a few

seems that

well.

ALBUM REVIEWS
“BAD BUT BEAUTIFUL”—Eartha
Kitt—MGM
E 4009
The sultry songstress puts her own special trade-
mark on a set of standards and newies perfectly
suited
to
her
somewhat
sensual
delivery.
The
lark’s
supper
club
sophistication
and
intimate
stylings come
off well
in such goodies
as
“All
I
Want
Is
All There
Is And Then
Some,” “Love
For Sale,” “Diamonds Are A Girl’s Best Friend,”
and “Lola-Lola.” Eartha’s loyal fans will want to
have this one.
“SING A LITTLE SOMETHING”—Sholom
Se-
cunda—Liberty LST 7254
Sholem Secunda, who has earned a long string of
laurels
in
the
field
of
Jewish
liturgical
music,
comes up with a first-rate, Yiddish sing-along on
this LP outing from Liberty. Secunda’s
classical
approach
is
eloquently
evidenced
in
impressive
renditions
of “Hava
Nagilah,”
“Flaker
Feieril”
and
a
delightful arrangement
of “Tzena Tzena
Tzena Tzena.” A clever, eye-catching cover show-
ing a table of goodies should help spark sales.
“OFF
HIS
ROCKER”—Pat
Buttram—Warner
Brothers WS
1455
Pat Buttram, who earned his reputation as Gene
Autry’s
flick
sidekick, gets the
solo
spotlight on
this
yoek-filled
comedy
LP
from
Warner
Brothers. Buttram’s
delivery
is slow and
laconic
and his material
is in an extremely funny home-
spun
vein.
The
laughman
effectively
aims
his
satric
guns
at
such
diverse
things
as
“Teen-
agers,” “Etiquette” and “The High Cost Of Dy-
ing.” Many laughs to be had here.
“THE TEMPERANCE SEVEN”—Kapp KL 1287
Kapp, who has had a significant success with trad
efforts
(via the Kenny Ball singles and albums),
showcases another swingin’ British group on this
new danceable session. Tagged “The Temperance
Seven,” the crew offers a dozen instrumental and
vocal tracks
in the lighthearted Dixieland
style.
There’s plenty of listening and terpsichorean en-
joyment as the band dishes up attractive arrange-
ments
of
“Hard-Hearted
Hannah,”
“Black
Bot-
tom” and “Home In Pasadena.” Loads of airplay
potential here.
“GOLDEN REUNION IN RAGTIME”—Various
Artists—Stereoddities C 1900
Ragtime
authority Bob
Darch, who
acts
as
the
emcee on
the
disk, comes up
with
a
delightful,
nostalgic
package
spotlighting
the
talents
of
Eubie Blake, Joe Jordan and Charles Thompson,
three
of the
greatest composers and
pianists
of
the ragtime era playing their own compositions.
The three artists, who had not seen each other in
50 years were brought together expressly for this
disk. Jazzophiles as well as pop collectors will dig
this fine session.
“WALT DISNEY PRESENTS
SONGS FROM
THE MICKEY MOUSE CLUB SERIALS” —
Various Artists—Disneyland DQ 1229
Here’s a delightful kiddie package of some of the
most popular tunes from the now-defunct “Mickey
Mouse
Club”
TV’er
rendered
with
professional
artistry and
polish by
the crew from
the show.
Highlight of the set is a few tracks featuring the
new
famous
teen
lark
Annette.
The
LP
has
enough
built-in success ingredients
to
appeal
to
a
legion
of youngsters.
JAZZ
PICKS
OF THE WEEK
“WHAT’S NEW?”—Sonnv Rollins—RCA
Victor
LSP 2572
Sonny
Rollins, who has never been
afraid to
at-
tempt
something
new,
explores
the
complex
strains of the bossa-nova on this excellent Victor
set.
Rollins has not compromised
his
distinctive
style of playing but instead he launches full-blast
into the Latin rhythms with a drive which comes
from
the music
itself. Some
outstanding
tracks
here include “If Ever
I Would Leave You,” “Jun-
goso” and “The Night Has A Thousand
Eyes.”
One of the best LP’s that Rollins has cut in quite
a while.
“THELONIOUS MONK, GREATEST HITS” —
Riverside 9421
Thelonious Monk, whose
artistry
as
a musician
and talents as a composer have made him one of
the
most
important
names
in
the
jazz
world,
brings together on one disk six of his most widely
played compositions. The 88’er’s circle of admirers
is growing steadily as
his music gains
in
public
acceptance. In addition to playing such
fine num-
bers as “Little Rootie Tootie,” “Ruby, My Dear,”
and
“Brilliant
Corners,”
the
pianist
includes
“ ’Round
Midnight”
with
assists
by
Coltrane,
Coleman Hawkins and Art
Blakey. A must
for
jazzophiles.
e
“WONDERLAND”—Charles
Mingus —
United
Artists Jazz UAJ 14005
Charles Mingus, who has long been regarded as
one
of
the
most
versatile
new-wave
jazzmen,
opens up his accomplished musical guns full-blast
on
this
varied
set which
showcases
his
superb
control and understanding of his instrument. Min-
gus
is aptly backed by John Handy on
alto sax,
Booker Ervin on tenor sax and Danny Richmond
on drums for the four top-drawer jazz tracks
in
the
album. The
bassist
eloquently
rises
to
solo
challenges in his self-penned “Nostalgia In Times
Square” and “I Can’t Get Started.” Powerful jazz
merchandise.
“I DON’T WORRY ABOUT A THING”—Mose
Allison—Atlantic 1389
The
multi-talented Mose
Allison, who
functions
with admirable effort as a
pianist, composer and
singer, kicks off his premiere LP on Atlantic with
the album’s namesake,
“I Don’t Worry About A
Thing,”
a
self-penned
blues
item
which
he
de-
livers with a
distinctive, wry, lyrical blues
style.
Although
Allison
receives
a
fine
backing from
Addison Farmer
on
bass
and
Osie
Johnson
on
drums top kudos here are his alone. Smart tracks
on the set include “Let Me See” and “Stand By.”
CLASSICAL PICK OF THE WEEK
MOZART:
Violin
Concertos,
Yehudi
Menuhin,
Bath
Festival Chamber
Orchestra—Angel
35745
Yehudi Menuhin directs his
artistic and interpre-
tive
skills
to
a
pair
of Mozart
violin
concertos,
written when the composer was still a young man.
The
celebrated
virtuoso
plays
the
No.
3
in G
Major and the No.
5
in A Major, both of which
are
soft, subtle, melodic, and devoid of the thun-
derous
bravado
finales
inherent
in
other
violin
concertos. Menuhin executes them with sensitivity
and complete control. Disk is a first-rate classical
offering.

-4
“YAMEKRAW”—James
P.
Johnson—Folkways
FJ 2842
The
late James
P. Johnson, who earned
quite
a
reputation as a composer of popular hits, also had
a serious side as evidenced in this superb record-
ing
of “Yamekraw,”
the
first Negro
rhapsody.
The work utilizes blues to eloquently express the
religious fervor and happy moods of the American
Negro. The composition, which has a subtle touch
of Gershwin,
is rendered by the composer at the
piano
on
this
top-notch Folkways
offering. The
second
side
of the
disk boats four
tracks from
Perry Bradford.

Symphony No. 5 in C Minor
FERENC FRICSAY

lin

Orchestra,

Fricsay
Deutsche Grammaphon SLPM 138813

played Beethoven 5th to

pretive skills, and this superb version of the work

sional baton of the maestro. A superior classical

Latest Board of Trade figures show that manufacturers’ sales of records
in
June were valued at £900,000 and
five per cent less than in June
1961. Home
sales were 2 per cent less and export sales were 17 per cent
less. Taking the
first half of this year as a whole, home and export sales were
9 per cent and
6 per cent higher respectively, than
in
the corresponding period
last year.
Production
of gramophone records
in June was 20 per cent less than a year
earlier; output of 78 rpm records was 17 per cent less and 45 rpm 15 per cent
less. Production of 33
1/3 rpm’s has expanded strongly during the past year
and despite a sharp
fall
in June to a rate of 30 per cent below the level of a
year earlier, output in the
first half of this year was 26 per cent higher than
in
the comparable
period
in
1961.
Production
of both
78 rpm
and
45 rpm
disks during the first half of this year was 7 per cent less than
in the corres-
ponding months
of
1961.

Another
Austrian-Dutch
musical
cooperation
of
importance
has
been
pre-
sented by Philips: the recording of four 18th century Oboe Concertos by Dutch
oboe player Evert van Tricht with the Vienna Symphonic Orchestra conducted
by Bernhard Paumgartner. Apart from superb performance, the Dutch soloist
contributed
the cadenzas for the Concerto
in C Major by Karl
Ditters von
Dittersdorf. The three other concertos are one by Telemann and two by Handel.
Leo Boudewijns, general label manager of L. C. Phonogram, drew attention to
the outstanding sound-qualities of the recording.
From Bartok’s
six String Quartets, the Numbers 3 and 4 (from the years
1927 and 1928) demand the utmost degree of technical
ability when correctly
performed. Added
to the extremely complicated music
itself,
the works
are
hardly popular favorites. Hence, the release
of the
Philips recording
of The
Juilliard Quartet, brought out in Holland this month, commands the more ad-
miration. However, the release is quite well considered, as Bartok’s music has
many friends
in Holland:
there
is a Bartok
Society and
a
great number of
Bartok performances every year.
Since 1952, the demand in Europe for country music has been kept steadily
high, not
in the
least through
radio programs and
the promotion
of
active
Hillbilly Clubs. Several times tremendous top hits have come from the C & W
repertoire, but during the last few years, a new group of C & W buyers de-
veloped a taste for the genuine folk repertoire performed by American spe-
cialists in this field. Therefore, a new album on the Philips label by The Bar-
rier Brothers could be exactly the type of Blue grass music the connoisseurs
are after. The album, Otto Vriezenberg of L.C. Phonogram pointed out is simp-
ly entitled “Hillbilly Music,” but represents a collection of the purest Bluegrass
repertoire, including the 5-string banjo and the country-fiddle. Although many
years on the American
Stages, The
Barrier
Brothers
are not widely known
yet in Europe, but this recording will make them find many “pardners” here.
Folk music from Surinam was released on an EP in the Philips series, “Song
And Sound, The World Round”: four vocal numbers by singer “Big Jones” and
his Band. It represents music from the Kawina-river district. A photograph by
Herman van der Horst, Dutch prize winning photographer, was used
as the
cover, and he wrote the liner as well.

versal. The Government also attacked

was dissolved several weeks after the

.
MCA must make the following de-

to
sell,

no
rights

—with any major TV,

duction
or
distribution
Arms.

of
Charles
Mingus
to
a new two-year
contract;
the sponsorship of a Town Hall con-
cert
in New York on

12 which
will feature Mingus

of an

In addition to the current domestic
recording schedule, Douglas will leave
for Europe immediately following the
Town Hall concert where he will meet
with United Artists Records
affiliates
on the Continent and
cut a
series of
albums for release during 1963.
The second UA Jazz
Series release
is scheduled for
Oct., Douglas
stated,
and
will
include
a
never-before
re-
leased album by Billie Holiday as well
as a new Herbie Mann package. The
special packaging which marked the
initial release will be carried through
the new
product
which
will
be
out
next month, Douglas stated.
Signing of Mingus is a further step
in the program to build a strong artist
roster
for
the
Jazz
Series,
Douglas
stated. Other signings are now being
negotiated with top
artists.
The Town Hall concert will feature,
in addition to Mingus, such Jazz stars
as Don Butterfield, Jimmy Cleveland,
Eric Dolphy, Zoot Sims, Jerome Rich-
ardson, Jim Hall and other
all-stars.
The Ellington, Mingus, Roach wax-
ing
is
a
major
coup,
with
Douglas
working for months to bring the three
jazz
giants together for the
session.
Featuring both new and a few of the
old
Ellington
songs,
the
album was
recorded at a midnight session in New
York with all three stars flying in for
the
session,
then
dispersing
to
con-
tinue their personal appearances.

SYMPHO.NIY IN D .MINOR

urmm SYMPDONV DRCHFaTIU
PAUL PARAY
“FRANCK: Symphony In D Minor”; Paul Paray
conducting
the
Detroit
Symphony
Orchestra
Mercury Wing SRW8002
The amazing popularity of the Franck symphony
has perplexed classical purists for over 70 years.
At the time of its premier performance in Paris,
the work was called musical heresy by most ob-
servers.
Today,
even
the
most
narrow-minded
classical critics have come to accept the symphony
for
its
sincerity and throbbingly beautiful pass-
ages.
Paul
Paray
comes
up
with
a
sparkling,
electrifying
interpretation
of
the work on
this
Mercury Wing
offering.
Paray’s
understanding
and love of the music
is firmly evidenced as he
leads the orchestra through its paces with control
and verve. A
fine item for the younger classical
collector.

President Signs Bill;
Copyrights Extended 3 Yrs.
WASHINGTON—All
copyrights
in
effect on Sept. 19 have been extended
until
Dec.
31,
1965 by a
bill
signed
last week by
President Kennedy.
The
President signed
the
bill
into
law that keeps the work affected out
of the public domain while Congress
takes its time in mulling over a com-
plete revision of the copyright statu-
tes.
Under the
bill, authorized by Rep.
Emmanuel Celler (D-N.Y.) any copy-
rights
in
effect
on
the
date
of
the
signing are extended for the
3 year
time
period. Those copyrights
expir-
ing
after
Dec.
31,
1965
are
not
af-
fected.

HELEN SHAPIRO
NEW YORK—Epic Records has
an-

concluded with Electric Music Indus-
tries, Ltd. for exclusive American dis-
tribution
rights
to
single and album
releases by Helen Shapiro. Under the
terms
of
the
agreement.
Epic
will
release
material
recorded
by
Miss
Shapiro
in England
as
well
as any
material
she
records
in
the
United
States.
One
of
Europe’s
most
popular
singers. Miss Shapiro, who
is
fifteen
years old, currently holds three Silver
Discs
for
sales
exceeding
250,000
copies
of
a
single
record. Her
first
Silver
Disc
commemorated
sales
of
“You Don’t Know” which maintained
the number
one
position
on
British
best
seller
charts
for many
weeks.
Her other Silver Discs were awarded
for “Walkin’ Back To Happiness” and
“Tell Me What He Said.” In addition,
she was chosen earlier this month as
Top Female Singer
in
Britain’s 1962
Melody Maker Popularity Poll.
Miss
Shapiro
will
celebrate
her
sixteenth
birthday
on September 28
while on a personal appearance tour
of Australia and New Zealand. From
there she will travel to Honolulu, Los
Angeles
and
Las
Vegas.
She
will
arrive
in New York on
October
24.
While in New York, she
will appear
on Ed
Sullivan’s CBS-TV Show
on
October 28 and
will meet with Epic
Records
executives
to
discuss future
recording plans.

Beltone Sues King
For $3,000,000
NEW YORK—Beltone
Records
last
week
filed suit against King Records
and
its
president
Sid Nathan
in
the
Supreme Court of the
State of New
York for the sum of $3,000,000.
Beltone, which hit big last year with
Bobby Lewis’ “Tossin’ And Turnin’ ”
and the Jive Five’s “My True Story”
was at the time of these big hits dis-
tributed nationally by King Records.
The complaint charges that during
the run of these records Beltone was
“charged large and excessive sums of
monies” for “records manufactured by
King which was far in excess
of the
cost of such records.” The complaint
also charges that “King manufactured
for Beltone records far
in excess
of
the
demand
for
them
and
charged
Beltone
for them even though there
was no need for doing
so.”
The
complaint
goes
on
to
charge
that
King
distributed
and
sold
for
Beltone large quantities of records for
which it paid Beltone a sum far lower
than is customary in the trade and for
amounts
less
than
which
Beltone
would have sold its merchandise; that
King
and
its
president
gave
away
large quantities of record for nothing
or sold for sums much lower than the
actual
cost
for
which
Beltone
was
charged; that King paid Beltone 40^
per record
distributed when the nor-
mal
charge
for
the
distribution
of
records generally accepted in the trade
is
48^
per
record
distributed.
The
complaint
also charges that King
al-
legedly sold remaining inventory be-
longing
to
Beltone
as
scrap
for
5^
each for which King has refused
to
account to Beltone or to issue to Bel-
tone the proper credit therefor.
Attorney Martin
J. Machat
is rep-
resenting
Beltone.

NEW YORK—Michael Edwards, clef-
fer
of
the
standard,
“Once
In A
While,” and other popular tunes, died
here last week at the age of 69.
“Once In A While,” Edwards’
first
published
tune,
topped
radio’s
now-
defunct “Hit Parade” show for seven
consecutive weeks in
1937.
After World War
I, Edwards was
a

Cincinnati Sym-
phony
Orchestra. In recent years he
was
a music
editor
of
Mills
Music,
Inc., and an

other pubberies.
He
is
survived by
his
wife,
Mrs.
Marie Weber Edwards and three
sis-
ters.

FEDERAL ANTI-BOOTLEG BILL BECOMES LAW
Kennedy Signs Senate’s Amended Version
of
Biii
WASHINGTON—A
Federal
anti-
bootleg
bill against the manufacture
of bogus disks
is law.
President Kennedy last week signed
into law the Senate’s amended version
of
the
bill,
passed
by
the
House,
which makes disk bootlegging a Fed-
eral crime and provides for penalties
of up to one year in
jail or a $1,000
fine, or both. Tag for the
bill
is Pub-
lic Law 87-773.
The
House
had
previously
passed
the original version of the
bill, which
could
have
sent
those
convicted
of
disk bootlegging to
jail for
10 years
and
further
penalized them
with
a
$10,000
fine.
When the Senate passed its amend-
ed version of the
bill, industry lead-
ers
felt that a less
stiff Federal curb
on
bootlegging was
better
than no
curb
at
all
(see Cash Box
story
in
Oct. 6 issue).

Decca Sets New LP
Chronicle Of Music
Series
NEW
YORK—Decca
Records
has
announced the forthcoming release of
its new Chronical Of Music LP series,
a history of music on records designed
to represent a concise and interesting
library of the romance of music from
the
Middle
Ages
through
the
Twentieth Century.
Under
the
editorship
of
Ben
Deutschman, teacher and
lecturer on
music education, a staff of consultants
was

to
prepare
the
format.
The group divided the history of music
into
eight
periods:
Middle
Ages,
Renaissance,
Baroque,
Transition
from Baroque to
Classic,
Classicism,
Romanticism, Jazz, and the 20th Cen-
tury.
Each record in the eight-LP set is
registered with
the
Library
of Con-
gress and has
a complete
set of
in-
formational liner notes on the musical
era represented. Included in the pack-
age
are “The Play Of
Daniel” with

Musica, “French
Renaissance Vocal Music” with Nadia
Boulanger,
“Bach”
selections
by

“Francois
Couperin”
with the New York Chamber Soloists,
“Mozart”
Avith
the
Zimbler
Sinfo-
nietta, “Brahms” with the Stokowski
Symphony of the Air, Gershwin’s “An
American In Paris” and “Rhapsody In
Blue”
with
Arthur
Sandford,
and
Aaron Copland’s “The Red Pony” and
Virgil
Thompson’s
“Acadian
Songs
and Dances.”
Series was revealed at a press meet-
ing
held here
last week
(10), hosted
the label’s Marty Salkin, Leonard W.
Schneider,
Sidney
Goldberg,
Claude
Brennan,
Is
Horowitz,
and
Sonny
Burke. Ben Deutschman was on hand
to discuss the
series.

On the occasion of the Festivities around the Dutch Concertgebouw and the
Concertgebouw Orchestra this winter, commemorating the 76th Anniversary of
the building’s inauguration
in the spring of
1888,
Philips released a
special
LP edition of Mahler’s First Symphony. The symphony will be performed at
the Festival tour of the Concertgebouw Orchestra through Holland this winter-
season, conducted by Bernard Haitink. Mahler’s Symphony
is connected to the
Concertgebouw Orchestra in a very special way:
it was composed in 1888, the
very year of the Orchestra’s foundation, and w^as premiered and conducted by
Gustav Mahler personally in the Concertgebouw. Since, countless performances
have taken
place by the Concertgebouw Orchestra, many
of them under the
late Willem Mengeloerg. On Oct. 1, of this year, w'hen the Symphony was per-
formed
at the Festival Concert in Amsterdam, conductor Haitink presented
the first copy of the LP to Her Majesty Queen Juliana of The Netherlands.
The very
successful
Sept.-Oct.
tour
of Les
Freres Jacques
in
Holland
is
honored
with
high
praises
in
newspapers. The
LP, which was
released
in
connection with this tour, met with the same enthusiasm by press and public,
creating,
at the same time, a demand
for a recent
EP-recording. The EP,

to an LP-recording
of Anne Sylvestre
on the Philips-label.

Columbia has entered in music instrumental line after Victor and Toshiba.

on sale in the market. The product, called “Elepian,” has 75 keys and issues
sound thru
electric
devices, not thru piano
strings. The newly developed
in-

is on sale at $230.60 each. Columbia
is going
to

Victor's Nero Display Promo
Best In Label's History
NEW YORK—A
dealer window
dis-
play
contest
for
its
fourth
LP
by
pianist
Peter
Nero,
“For
the
Nero-
Minded,” and other Nero product last
summer
(June
15-July
15)
was
the
most
fruitful
display
promo
in
the
history of RCA Victor Records.
Build around the overall theme, “It’s
Time
For
Peter
Nero,”
the
contest
offered
500
specially
designed RCA
Victor
Gold
Record
clocks
as
prizes
for the best window displays. Special
Nero
four-color
display
units
were
made
available
to
dealers
via RCA
Victor
distributors. The
distributors,
in conjunction with Victor officials, se-
lected the winners from photos of the
displays which were submitted during
the contest period.
According to William
I. Alexander,
manager
of
advertising,
promotion,
and publicity, “Over 3,500 window dis-
plays
throughout
the
country
high-
lighted
our
Peter
Nero
promotion.
This was unquestionably the most suc-
cessful
point-of-sale window
display
contest in the history of RCA Victor.”
With the contest over, and the 500
clocks
already presented
to the win-
ners,
orders
for the purchase
of 741
clocks
have been
received from
dis-
tributors for dealers who entered but
did
not
win.
“This
tremendous
re-
sponse, with
dealers wanting
to buy
the Nero
clocks,
is
indicative
of the
overall industry praise for the promo-
tion,” stated Alexander.
Alexander also reports that he has
received many requests from depart-
ment stores who wish to merchandise
the clocks as a regular retail item.

Nashville
Style Welcome
NASHVILLE—When
the
over
2,500
country
music
deejays
gather
in
the
Music City on Nov.
9th and
10th for WSM’s
11th annual
National Country
Music Festival, they will be greeted with
street signs reading: “Welcome To
Nashville, Home Of The Grand Ole Opry, Music City U. S. A.” This is the first
time in Nashille’s 156 year history that welcoming signs of any kind have been
placed on the outskirts of the city. One of the signs was presented to Ott Devine
(left), manager of the Opry, by Mayor Ben West who in turn made the mayor
an honorary member of the Grand Ole Opry.
CMA Banquef Looks
Like Biggest Yet
NASHVILLE,
TENN. — Apparent
trade-wide
acceptance
of
the
annual
Country
Music
Association
anniver-
sary banquet has spurred an “unprece-
dented rush” on ticket orders at CMA
headquarters here, according to execu-
tive secretary Jo Walker.
The
$10-a-plate
dinner-dance
is
scheduled for the evening of Fri., Nov.
9,
at
the Hillwood Country
Club.
It
will be the focal point of the second
annual National Country Music Week,
Nov.
4-10, and
will occur during the
WSM
11th
Annual
Country
Music
Festival.
The CMA banquet, an optional dress
affair, annually attracts the cream of
the country industry. It offers a show-
case for the presentation
of
selected
honorees to the Country Music Hall of
Fame and a roster of talent to include
Jimmy Dean, Flatt and Scruggs, Leon
McAuliff
and
band.
Grandpa
Jones,
and Boots Randolph. McAuliff and his
Cimarron
Boys
will
play
for
after
dinner dancing, as well as the show.
Plans call for recording Grandpa Jones
and Boots
Randolph’s
act by Monu-
ment Records.
Details
of
the
banquet,
limited
in
attendance
to 500 persons, are being
woven together by CMA banquet co-
chairmen
Frances
Preston
and
Bill
Denny.
Attendance
is by
reservation
only
and tickets may be ordered from the
CMA
Office,
610 Exchange
Building,
Nashville. Any excess funds from the
$10 ducats go into the CMA treasury
and will be used to defray CMA op-
erating costs.

ALBUM REVIEWS
“TONI CARROLL SINGS HITS OF THE ROAR-
ING 20’S”—MGM E 4063
All of the perpetual gaiety of the 20s is captured
on
this
lively
set of
flapper-flavored
evergreens
by
Toni
Carroll.
The
songstress
is
completely
taken up in the high-spirited tone of the project
as she offers such fine
oldies as “I’m Just Wild
About
Harry,”
“Makin’
Whoopee”
and
“Five
Foot Two
Eyes
Of
Blue.”
Top-flight
listening
enjoyment throughout.
'Yojimbo
“YOJIMBO” — Original
Sound
Track — MGM
E-4''96
“Yojimbo”
is the new Akira Kurosawa film that
paradoxically has as
its roots the
classic Amer-
ican Western
tale
(a
hired gun cleaning up an
evil
town).
Masaru
Sato,
who
composed
the
score, has
effectively contributed to the ominous
feeling
of doom
and
tragedy
which
permeates
the
story.
Although
the
oriental
flavor
of
the
music falls a bit harshly on the Western ear, the
excitement engendered throughout does much to
dispell the
alien sounds. Art-film buffs
will
find
this
is a must for their collections.
“ERNIE FREEMAN’S SOULFUL SOUND OF
COUNTRY CLASSICS”—-Liberty LRP 3264
Ernie Freeman
cashes
in
on
the
current wide
acceptance
of country music
for
this,
his
first
LP outing for Liberty. All of the tunes here are
rendered with their original country flavor. How-
ever,
the
orkster has
given
each
item
his
dis-
tinctive modem
teen-oriented
beat
and
added,
on some
of the
tracks,
a
fine
chorus. Best bets
here
include
“I Walk The
Line,”
“I Don’t Hurt
Anymore” and
“It Makes No
Difference Now.”

“MY BIG BAND’S SHOWING”—Francis Bay-

The growing strength and importance

A top-drawer example is the big band of Francis

(Belgian), who

up
-with

and

of

dressed

fering from

“MIGIANI GRAND ORGHESTRE”—RCA Victor
International FPM 108
Ace
European

Armand
Migiani
has

ar-
rangements of popular tunes. Migiani has utilized

On

“GOLDEN FAVORITES”—Wayne King—Decca
DL74309
Wayne King, who has provided the country with
some very danceable music for
several
decades,
recalls twelve of his most requested tunes on this
easy
listening package from
Decca. With
first-
rate arrangements by Wayne Robinson and
the

oldies
as “The
Waltz You Saved For Me,” “Dancing With Tears
In My Eyes,” and “Meet Me Tonight In Dream-
land,”
terpsichorean
delights
are
in
abundance.
The orkster’s many admirers will find much nos-
talgic listening here.

818

ALBUM REVIEWS
Gash Box
“CHA CHA DE AMOR”—Dean Martin—Capitol
ST1702
Here
is
a top-drawer package
of evergreens by
Dean Martin cut during his
affiliation with Capi-
tol. The deep-voiced
chanter
delivers
a
host
of
lilting
ballads enhanced by some
pulsating
ar-
rangements by Nelson Riddle who also conducted
the
session. The tunes
all have
an Afro-Cuban
rhythm that makes for easy
listening and danc-
ing. Martin fans will find lots of listening pleasure
in
such
goodies
as
“Cha
Cha
D’Amour,”
“A
Hundred Years From Today,”
and “Two Loves
Have I.”
“THE WALTZES OF IRVING BERLIN”—Mela-
chrino
Strings &
Orchestra—RCA
Victor LSP
2561
The
genius
of
Irving
Berlin
has
captured
the
fancy of the American public for over fifty years.
On
this
pleasant
Victor
offering, George
Mela-
chrino effectively utilizes his mellow strings and
ork to capture all the romantic strains of a dozen
all-time great Berlin
waltzes. From
the
kick-off
tune of “All Alone” to the last track, “Reaching
For The Moon,” the package is filled with enough
top-drawer
sounds
to
please
a
wide
variety
of
record buyers.
“DON SHIRLEY PRESENTS MARTHA FLOW-
ERS”—Cadence CLP 3055
Pianist Don Shirley effectively plays talent scout
on
this
Cadence
set
which
showcases
the
im-
pressive
vocal
talents
of Martha
Flowers. The
lark’s
wide-range
soprano
voice
is
capable
of
great
diversity.
She
can
sing Rodgers & Hart
sturdies with
the same
super musicianship and
poignancy as she gives to spirituals. With a fine
instrumental backing from the
Shirley crew she
offers “Dancing On The Ceiling,” “I Had Myself
A True Love” and “Love Walked In.” A talent to
watch.
“LA
DOLCE
HENKE”—Mel
Henke—Warner
Brothers WS 1472
Here’s
a
delightful,
off-beat
creative
set which
spotlights
the
swingin’
arrangements
of
Mel
Henke and the voices of a few Hollywood thespi-
ans. The music is based on solid jazz lines but oc-
casionally departs and utilizes a novel pop twist.
Each track here
tells two
stories, one musically,
one
in
the
lyrics.
Best
bets
here
are
“The
Twisters,” “Put Out The
Lights” and “Farmer
John.”
“AN
EVENING WITH
ROMBERG”—Carmen
Dragon—Capitol SW1804
Sigmund Romberg, who was one
of the world’s
prolific composers, turned out a phenomenal num-
ber
of
beautiful
melodies,
and Carmen Dragon
plays some of his best on this newest outing on
Capitol.
Conducting
the
Hollywood
Bowl
Pops
Orchestra, the maestro begins the program with
the “Drinking Song” from “The Student Prince,”
and gives first-rate readings of “Close As Pages
In A Book” and
“Softly, As In A Morning Sun-
rise.” Lush arrangements coupled with the Rom-
berg melodies makes this LP a welcome addition
to any collector’s shelf.

r
'
“ONCE UPON A THEME”—Meg Welles Quintet
—Columbia CL 1889
Meg
Welles’
distinctive
jazz-based
approach
to
troubador items carries her in good stead on this,
her second Columbia LP outing. Although much
of the material is extremely intricate the quintet
effectively provides
a firm backing for the lark
on
all twelve tracks
here. Highlights
of the
set
include “Once Upon A Theme,” “Wheel The Keel
Row” and “Good Day My Heart.”
“THE MINSTREL MEN”—Various Artists—Col-
pix SCP 434
Colpix has assembled a delightful, nostalgic pack-
age
in
this
thoroughly
entertaining
full-length
minstrel show. The disk stars such famous name
vaudeville
stars
as
Jack
Benny,
Milton
Berle,
George Burns, Phil Silvers and Benny Fields. The
performers render a
fine
collection
of
oldies
in-
cluding “Hello My Baby,” “Darktown
Strutter’s
Ball” and
“In The Good Old Summer Time.” A
fine offering for the entire family.

PICKS
OF THE WEEK
umm m rm&
“BLUES
IN TIME”—Gerry
Mulligan &
Paul
Desmond—Verve V 8478
The wax teaming up of Gerry Mulligan and Paul
Desmond makes for one
of the most aggressive,
lyrical
sessions
that
either
saxist
has
cut
in
quite
a
while.
Mulligan’s
potent
baritone
sound
perfectly
compliments
Desmond’s
unobtrusive
work on the alto. With a fine backing from Dave
Bailey on drums and Joe Benjamin on
bass, the
two
wail
professionally
on
“Blues
In
Time,”
“Body And Soul” and “Stand
Still.”
“BIG BAND BOSSA NOVA”—Quincy
Jone^-
Mercury MG 20751
Cashing
in
on
the rapidly-increasing
popularity
of the bossa nova, ace orkster Quincy Jones has
come up with a top-flight set of the samba-flav-
ored
sounds.
Jones
makes
an
effective
bid
for
terpsichorean attention by using his big jazz band
for
all the tracks
here. With
exactly
the
right
amount of rhythmic emphasis the crew turns
in
excellent
performances
on
“Soul
Bossa
Nova,”
“Desafinado” and “Serenta.” Plenty
of
sales po-
tential here.
“SWING STREET”—Various
Artists—Epic SN
6042
For two decades (the 1930’s and 1940’s Gotham’s
52nd Street was a setting for every type of jazz.
Its
distinction was
such,
that musicians
simply
called
it The
Street. On
this
excellent four-disk
Epic set all the sounds and color of that exciting
era are vividly represented. Through a collection
of
masters,
the
label
has
assembled
a
stellar
group
of
performers
including
such
names
as
Fats Waller, Red Norvo, Teddy Wilson, Art Ta-
tum, Billie Holiday and Dizzy Gillespie. Although
sometimes the fidelity is not up to modern stand-
ards,
the package ranks
as
a superb tribute to
American jazz.

“DESAFINADO”—Coleman
Hawkins—Impulse
A-28
Vet

Coleman

tags

ing Latin tempos. With some

“Stumpy

“VIVA BOSSA NOVA!”—Laurindo & The Bossa
Nova All Stars—Capitol T 1759
Laurindo Almeida and a crew of first-rate
jazz
musicians including
Shelly Manne, Max Bennett
and Bob Cooper, have created a fresh approach
for the rhythmic bossa nova
strains. Instead of
drawing on the usual Brazilian choros for mate-
rial, the guitarist delivers a dozen popular stand-
ards
in the contagious new rhythm. Outstanding
bands here include “Naked City Theme,” “Ram-
blin’ Rose” and “Moon River.” Eye the package
for rapid acceptance.
CLASSICAL
BACH: Orchestral Suites, Ernest Ansermet Con-
ducting L’Orchestre De La Suisse Romande—Lon-
don CS6243
Two suites (No. 2 in B Minor and No. 3 in D) and
excerpts from
a
pair
of Cantatas by Bach
are
rendered by the Suisse Romande Orchestra under
the
guiding
hand
of
Ernest
Ansermet.
These
secular
works
transcend
the
somber
mood
of
Bach’s sacred compositions, and the maestro’s in-
terpretive
skills
permit them
to shimmer
with
orchestral brilliance. Devotees of Bach will surely
appreciate
this
excellent performance by one of
Europe’s finest orchestras.

AUSTRALIA
The “Mama Sang A Song” battle
is now on with the big three American
versions
in
the front
line.
Festival
Records
has
the
Bill Anderson
release
while EMI has the Stan Kenton and Walter Brennan versions.
It will be
in-
teresting to see just how well the number does in Australia because this type
of material
is not alway readily accepted by the Australian consumer.
In a very fast release move, RCA of Australia landed Paul Anka’s hot new
single “Eso Beso” on the market at about the same time as
it was issued
in
the United States. Jim Cuff, promotion boss for RCA Records in Australia, be-
lieves
it will be Anka’s biggest success for RCA to date, and judging by the
airplay
it
is receiving, Jim could be
right.
If anything
is going
to
establish
the new Bossa Nova trend in Australia, this could be the disk to do
it.
The
latest release from EMI includes
a big flock
of
singles; among them
being “If A Man Answers” (Bobby Darin)
; “Night River” (The Morgan Con-
dello Combo);
“Slightly Out Of Tune”
(Julie
London); “Keep Away From
Other
Girls”
(Helen
Shapiro); “Happy
Guitar”
(Reg
Owen);
“The
Music
From The House Next Door” (Toni Fisher) and a local production featuring
Teddy Bennett with “That Ring” and “The Life I Love.”
RCA
of
Australia has
released
three
singles
of
the
top
songs from
the
English show “Oliver!,” which will soon run on Broadway. Della Rose has “As
Long As He Needs Me” (which was a fairly good song here some time back
when
the show was running
in
Australia)
The
Limeliters have “Who
Will
Buy?” and The Norman Luboff Choir presents “Consider Yourself.” With the
tremendous interest being stirred up by “Oliver!”
in the United States there
is no real reason why these singles shouldn’t catch a good market—even though
the show has already been presented in this country.
There are two versions of “The Longest Day” available here now—one
is by
Mitch Miller on the Coronet label for the Australian Record Company and the
other is a locally produced version by The Firebirds, an instrumental group on
the W&G logo. “The Longest Day”
is,
of course, the theme tune that Paul
Anka wrote for inclusion in the Daryl F. Zanuck film production
of the same
title. Publishing rights
in Australia are shared by
J. Albert & Son Pty. Ltd.
and Spanka Music Pty. Ltd. Initial air play indicates that “The Longest Day”
could become an important melody over the next few months. The film
is ex-
pected to be shown in Sydney and Melbourne before the end of the year.
Popular local singer Warren Williams has an interesting new release out on
the Leedon banner through the Festival group. Topside is an Australian com-
position “Stand There And Cry”
and
the
coupling
is
“Absence Makes The
Heart Grow Fonder.” A good production and a record worthy of success.
English artists Adam Faith and John Leyton arrived in Australia recently
in preparation for their tour of this country and of New Zealand.
Had a wonderful letter recently from one of Australia’s leading stars, Elaine
McKenna, who has been working in the United States for many months now.
Elaine will be back in Australia to spend Christmas with her parents in Mel-
bourne during a break in her television and nightclub engagements in America.
It is understood that Elaine will feature in some Australian television produc-
tions during her visit home.
Norrie Paramor renewed acquaintance with some of his old associates dur-
ing his stay in Australia with the Helen Shapiro Show. Norrie spent some time
with the EMI executives
in Sydney and with John Sturman
of EMI
visited
several of the leading music publishers of Australia—including his contact of
several years ago Norman Whiteley who
is now general manager of the Be-
linda Music group of companies in this country.
Roy
Orbison’s
current American
hit “Working For The Man”
is making
good sales headway but the majority of the dealer lists coming in to Cash Box
indicate that “Leah” is the side that is actually selling the record. Sue Thomp-
son looks set to enjoy another good run of sales with her latest, “James, Hold
The Ladder Steady,” which is issued through Australian Record Company. Sue
has been one of the most consistent disk attractions we’ve seen over the past
twelve months.

Last summer’s coast-to-coast smash, “Loco-Motion,” was unveiled here this
month when
(Japan’s) King released three “Loco-Motion” disks at one time.
The
first one
is
Little Eva’s
original
hit version on Dimension
(but tagged
here as King International label)
as a single. The others are waxes by Yukari
Itoh
in
singles
and
album

respectively.
The new
dancing
teen
fad,
“Loco-Motion,”
then, was

and

Itoh
at
the
weekly TV
seg
of which

and

Watanabe
Production. By the way,

first

on King
in-
cludes “Loco-Motion.” “Vacation,” “Johnny Angel,” “Mugmates” and her big-
gest recent smash “King Of The Clown,” etc.

is due out by Victor next month. The firm’s star

• THIS THING CALLED LOVE”—Sy Rady Sing-
ers—Columbia CL1911
Two dozen evergreens (mostly ballads) from the
pens
of
the
country’s
greatest
composers
are
given a choral airing by the Sy Rady Singers on
this new
entry from
Columbia. With
so many
titles
included,
the
shortened
versions
of
these
fine tunes make
for
a very refreshing
listening
experience. The
singers
give
top-flight readings
of Jack Halloran-arranged “All The Things You
Are,” "The Way You Look Tonight,” and “You’d
Be So Nice To Come Tome To.”
“COME ON AND JOIN LITTLE WILLIE JOHN
AT A RECORDING SESSION”—King 802
Little Willie John has earned many laurels in the
past
for
his
distinctive
vocal
handling
of r&b
tunes. The wailer recently
struck pay dirt with
his single “Big Blue Diamonds” which
is included
here with
eleven
other
danceable,
listenable
se-
lections. All the songster’s many fans should dig
his first-rate readings of “Until Again My Love,”
“The
Masquerade
Is
Over”
and
“Without A
Friend.”
“NICK KENNY READS NICK KENNY”—Dot
DLP 3427
Nick Kenny has achieved an
international repu-
tation
for
his
distinctive,
sentimental
style
of
poetry and this excellent Dot offering boasts the
poet-journalist
reading
twenty-four
of
his own
compositions.
All
of
the poems
here
are
culled
from Kenny’s new volume
of verse, “Poems To
Inspire,” and are of a moving, inspirational na-
ture. Package should spark healthy sales.
“HAWAII AND I”—Jack La Forge—Purpletone
P 716
Jack La Forge displays a commanding keyboard
style on
this
first-rate
set
of Hawaiian-flavored
items
from
Purpletone.
The
talented
musician
effectively utilizes both the piano and the Ham-
mond Organ as he goes through his musical paces
with
a
fine
jazz-based
backing from Don
Ser-
besky’s
crew.
Best
bets
here
include
“Malia,”
“Orchid Twist” and
“It’s Time To Say Aloha.”
Fine
fare
for
terpsichorean
or
listening
enjoy-
ment.
“GOD’S
TROMBONES”—Fred
Waring—Decca
DL74345
“God’s
Trombones,”
a
poetical work by James
Weldon Johnson, is delivered in a musical setting
by Fred Waring and his Pennsylvanians. Featur-
ing a variety
of soloists and narrators, Waring
has come up with an
effective program with
a
genuine religious tone enhanced by the orchestral
and
choral
backing.
The
orkster
also
includes
renditions of standard spirituals such as “Count-
in’ My Blessings,” “Were You There” and “Some-
times
I Feel Like A Motherless
Child.”
“TAHITI:
ISLAND
OF
PARADISE”—MGM
E4082
Here is a package of tunes from Tahiti recorded
on location in Papeete during the filming of “Mu-
tiny On The Bounty.” Performed by the
native
singers of Tahiti,
all of the authentic flavor and
subtle rhythms of the islanders
is evidenced here
in “Umi Umi,” “Te Ume Horotini,” “Tiare” and
“Tapona Ura.” Growing interest in Hawaiian mu-
sic could spark some sales for this LP which has
a similar sound.

TCHAIKOVSKY: The Nut Cracker
Ballet, Lon-
don Symphony,
Antal
Dorati,
Conductor—Mer-
cury SR 2-9013
Tchaikovsky’s
enchanting and flamboyantly me-
lodic
ballet
“The
Nutcracker,”
normally
per-
formed as an orchestral suite,
is presented in its
entirety in this new two-disk
set from Mercury.
The
London
Symphony
is
expertly
guided
through the two-act ballet by Antal Dorati whose
definitive
interpretation
adds new warmth
and
lustre
to
this
great work. The many
beautiful
waltzes, the fiery trepak, the galop and the polo-
naise are as fresh and exciting as they were when
the “Nutcracker” was written. A superb classical
disk that should see plenty of sales action during
this holiday season.
“SWEET SAX”—Freddy
Gardner, Alvy West
Decca DL74317
Freddy Gardner and Alvy West each take a side
of this disk from Decca and showcase their indi-
vidual
talents
on
the
alto
saxaphone.
Gardner
was and West is an accomplished saxman but the
organ backing for Gardner and the instrumental
backing for West lack the
life and brilliance that
would
effectively
showcase
their
artistry.
In-
cluded
here
are
“Trees,”
“Love’s
Old
Sweet
Song”
and
“Will You
Remember.”
Despite
an
over abundance of schmaltz, the LP has merit in
the solos of the saxmen.
JOHANN STRAUSS:
Die
Fledermaus,
Various
Artists—Richmond RS62006
One of the entries in Richmond’s new opera cata-
log
is this fine performance of “Die Fledermaus”
by Johann Strauss with Hilde Gueden supported
by an excellent cast and the Vienna Philharmonic
Orchestra
and

conducted
by
Clemens
Krauss. The opera, lush with
lilting waltzes and
lyrical arias, was originally recorded on the Lon-
don label and the economy price of $2.98
is sure
to be a strong sales point with all opera buffs.

NARM Board
Sets N.Y. Meet
NEW YORK—^The board of directors
of the National Association of Record
Merchandisers, Inc., will hold its next
meeting on Jan. 5 and 6, at the Ameri-
cana Hotel in New York,
it was an-
nounced by Jules Malamud, the asso-
ciation’s
executive
director.
On the agenda for consideration by
the seven man Board will be member-
ship applications which have been re-
ceived by the
office
of the
executive
director since the last Board meeting,
and
the
finalizing
of
details
for
the
1963 NARM Convention at the Fair-
mont
Hotel
in
San
Francisco
on
March 3-7.
Presiding
at
the
meeting
will
be
NARM
President,
Glen
C.
Becker
(Music
City Record
Racks, Los An-
geles). In attendance at the meeting
will be NARM vice persident Alvin M.
Driscoll
(Pioneer
Distributing Com-
pany of Kansas and Texas), Secretary
Kenneth Sach
(Merchants Wholesale
Seiwice
Company,
Detroit,
treasurer
George
A.
Berry
(Modern
Record
Service, New Orleans), past president
and director Edward M. Snider (Edge,
Ltd.,
Washington,
D.C.),
director
Larry
M.
Rosmarin
(Record
Dis-
tributing
Company,
Houston),
and
director
Cecil
Steen
(Recordwagon,
Inc., Boston). Jules Malamud, execu-
tive
director, and Earl M. Foreman,
NARM legal counsel, will also partici-
pate
in the meetings.

FCC Orders Miami
TV Outlet Off The
Air By Jan. 4
WASHINGTON, D.C. — The Federal
Communications
Commission
(FCC)
has
set
a
definite
date—Jan.
4—for
the Biscayne Television Corp. to cease
its
operation
of TV
station WCKT,
Miami.
The agency made no deadline when
it ordered the
outlet
off the
air
last
year after
it had reached the conclu-
sion that Biscayne had used improper
attempts
to
influence
its
original
award
of
the
station
to
Biscayne
in
1956.
Succeeding
Biscayne
on
a
tempo-
rary basis will be the Sunbeam Tele-
vision
Corp. The FCC
declared
Sun-
beam must apply for a new
license
April

U.S. Library Exhibit On Musical Theatre
WASHINGTON,
D. C.—Noting
the
American
musical

one
of

“most

(19)
an

“The

On

Friml,

Tienery,

DeSylva,

Many hologranhs of hit shows plus

of performers,

respondence,

and
jf
other items
will

In

jh
of Congress

ican musical theater
is surely one of

^

,

SICAL VERSION OF RUMPELSTILTSKIN”—

The

for

*EL DEBKE”—Naif Agby—Audio Fidelity AFSD

Denis
Preston and
Lionel
Stevens,
both from
London,
visited
Milan and
Cash Box met them. First question they asked us was: “How is the Bossa Nova
going in Italy?”. We take this opportunity to give all readers a picture of Italy
Bossa Nova-wise. Twice this year, last Spring and then again at the end of
Summer, Enrique Lebendiger, the well known music publisher of South Amer-
ica, came to Milan and contacted a lot of people of our music industry to speak
to them of Bossa Nova with his personal, warm enthusisam. Meanwhile, news
on the Bossa Nova success
in the States came through foreign trade papers.
The two sources of information made the Italian music industry aware of the
possible commercial meaning of Bossa Nova and record houses started arrang-
ing a
lot of Bossa Nova numbers,
either domestic
or foreign. At that time,
the public
did not yet know anything about
it and ignored the word
itself.
Later this Autumn, a troupe called “Jazz USA” came to Italy and
guitarist
Charlie Byrd performed on Milan and Rome stages the Bossa Nova* So, first
to release the new South American “sound” in Italy were Enrique Lebendiger
and the exciting guitar of Charlie Byrd, whose
concerts became a good op-
portunity for our national papers to speak of Bossa Nova, and the public at
large became acquainted with the new word,
if not yet with the new music.
Incidentally, we can note that Bossa Nova
is such a word, such a “sound of
word” that it possesses a catchy quality for the Italian language. At this mo-
ment, that’s the situation: record houses have ready for release or have already
released a lot of Bossa Nova numbers (we feel too many); the public, on their
part, read in the papers about Bossa Nova, but do not yet know the music, do
not yet buy the records, and—in one word—isn’t yet crazy for Bossa Nova at
all. Meanwhile, recoi’d houses go on increasing their already too rich catalogs
of Bossa Novas. So many records are expected to create a disturbing sense of
confusion in the mind of future record buyers, whose attention will be drawn
away from the very few best Bossa Nova waxings, such as that by Joao Gil-
berto.
When Tony Renis sang this year on the stage of San Remo his marvelous
“Quando Quando Quando,” the Italian audience voted it fourth. But as soon as
the festival ended, the situation was upset: the song voted number one, “Addio
Addio” by Domenico Modugno,
died
one week
later
and “Quando Quando
Quando” came up fast and over 1962 has sold some 400,000 copies and
it has
not yet died. This Autumn, as in the past, our TV music contest Canzonissima
started its shows and at once “Quando Quando Quando” was voted number one
by the same audience. As an immediate result of its success on Canzonissima,
the record sales of “Quando Quando Quando” are coming up once again. 'Two
weeks ago, the number appeared 3 in Sweden, and 2 in Denmark, while in Fin-
land it was 8 in the version by Pat Boone.

two

year’s Down Beat
Readers’

claimed

ists—Buddy

Miscellaneous

ment award—Mercury steps ahead in

Beat
poll
further
re-
flects
this
in
its
listing of seventeen
other
jazz
meteors
on
Mercury. A
glance at these names
is proof that
the label’s jazz division today enjoys
an unparalleled rally of greats on its
roster.
Gerry
Mulligan,
represented
in the Mercury catalog, won the Bar-
itone Sax award as he has every year
since 1963, and three diversified cate-
gory mentions.
Bob
Brookmeyer,
Cannonball
Ad-
derley
and
Charlie
Mingus
nudged
the

in

with

spots. Quincy Jones got
multiple

under

Composer, Big Band:
Jazz and Big

Dance, while Maynard Fergu-
tK>n was a Hall of Fame nominee and
included
in Miscellaneous Instrument
and Trumpet mentions. In addition to
^ond
placer
in

ited
listings
under

poser and Combo. Terry Gibbs pulled
to qualify twice—Vibraharp and Big
Band:
Jazz,
and

Kirk,
also earned Flute
rec-
ognition.

MERCURY REVIEWS 1962
SETS PLANS FOR 1963
IRVING GREEN
IRWIN STEINBERG
KENNETH MYERS
President
[xeeutive VP
Vice-president,
Sales
CHICAGO—Mercury
Records
looks
back on
1962
as
a
year
of
achieve-
ment
in
many
areas.
From
the
achievements of the A&R staff, to the
“new look” of the classical division, to
the
parade
of
hot
singles.
Mercury
considers 1962 a year of which to be
proud.
According
to
Irving
Green,
Mer-
cury
prexy.
Mercury
is
ending
the
year with a 23 per cent increase
in
volume
over
the
previous
year,
a
growth
attributed
to
Mercury’s
con-
cern
with
constant
readjustment
to
the
changing market
conditions.
In
its
planning
for
1963, Mercury has
been carrying out a broad evaluation
program
of
all
its
merchandising
techniques. Under the direction of Ir-
win
Steinberg,
executive
veep,
this
has included surveys of the field staff,
disk
jockey
promotions,
advertising
and
public
relations
in
an
effort
to
determine to just what extent expen-
ditures
in
these areas
create a
con-
sumer sale. Another part of the pro-
gram was
a
review
of
artists and
number of releases. The Mercury label
is also in the process of expanding or
strengthening
its
sales
organization,
under the supervision of Kenneth
,S.
Myers,
director of
sales.
Purpose of
the expansion
is
to
sell more
effec-
tively
the
Mercury
catalog
to
the
various types of merchandisers, deal-
ers, rack jobbers and discount houses.
Much of Mercury’s
research
will be
used by the A&R staff to assist them
in
their
planning.
Shelby
Singleton,
David
Carroll,
Quincy
Jones,
Jack
Tracy,
Hal
Mooney,
Jerry Kennedy
and Jerry Reed are already busy pre-
paring for 1963
in terms of the art-
ists with whom
they
plan
to work,
and
the
areas
of music which
best
relate
to
these
artists and
best
re-
flect
the consumer demand
research.
The A&R
staff
will
be
the
prime
conduit
for
engaging
independent
producers when they feel this system
can best create for a given artist; and
when an independent producer may
provide outstanding new artist or re-
cording concept.

Mercury entered the phonograph
fleld in 1962 with the introduction of its
first two models. Pictured above is the AG 4026 fully transistorized portable.
Its sister model is the AG 9115 fully automatic stereo portable. 'The phono-
graph
line
will be expanded
in
1963,
according
to
Irving

SPOTLIGHT
ON HUMOR
Comedy
albums
came
into
their
own
in
1962, with a delighted public
snatching up the fun-fill^ albums as
fast as they appeared.
Mercury contributed three
top-sell-
ing
humor
albums,
all
of
which
landed.
Starting off Mercury’s humor year
was “Mike
Nichols and
Elaine May
Examine
Doctors,” an album which
not
only
racked up
sales but drew
comment from all segments of the na-
tion’s press and broadcast media.
Ray
Stevens,
the young man who
also answers to “Ahab The Arab,” is
featured on the album “1,837 Seconds
of
Humor.”
The
package
leads
off
with an extended version of “Ahab,”
followed
by
10
other
selections
of
satire and characterization.
Humor combined with serious sing-
ing
put
“The
Two
Sides
of
The
Smothers
Brothers”
on
the
charts.
The album
presents Tom and
Dick
Smothers
in one side of comedy, re-
corded
live
at the Crystal Palace in
St.
Louis, and one side of folk sing-
ing that shows
off the brothers’
se-
rious talents.
Sales
of “The Two
Sides
of The
Smothers Brothers” have also brought
new action for their first Mercury re-
lease,
“The
Smothers
Brothers
At
The Purple Onion.”

See Tape Sales Up 25% In ’63
NEW YORK—A
healthy
25%
in-
crease
in sales in
all segments of the
magnetic recording industry has been
forecast for 1963.
William
P.
Gallagher, president
of

sociation,
and
marketing
veep
for
Columbia
Records,
reported
that
a
survey conducted among members by
the industry association revealed that
this year’s sales generally were about
20% ahead of last year, with slightly
more optimism shown
in predicting a
25% figure for the new year.
“Right now ever>d;hing
is going for

said. “Four-
track stereo tape is established as one
of

finest
mediums
for
recorded

“Good Year For Talent”
Is ’62 Report By
Bill Grauer
NEW
YORK—Bill
Grauer
Prod.,
parent company to Riverside Records
and five other labels, had—as the firm
put
it—a
“good
year
for
talent”
in
1962.
Noting that jazz talent came at a
premium during the year and
artists
shuttled from one label to another for
greener pastures, the firm reports an
“extremely successful program to se-
cure new
talent
as
well
as
re-sign
artists
presently under
contract.”
According to Orrin Keepnews, veep
& A&R head, several of the firm’s top
performers
have
recently
inked new
long-term pacts for the Riverside and
Jazzland diskeries. They are guitarist
Wes
Montgomery,
pianist-composer
Bobby Timmons, vibist Johnny Lytle,
tenor
saxist Jimmy Heath
and
alto
saxist Frank Strozier.
For
Battle
Records,
Grauer’s new
gospel
and
spiritual
line, Keepnews
has inked the Rev. Cleophus Robinson,
as
well
as The
Duncanaires, a new
group of sacred singers from Chicago.
During
’62,
several
major
artists
who
had
established
themselves
as
solid
sellers
on
other
labels moved
over to Riverside. They include vibist
Milt
Jackson,
formerly
on
Atlantic;
drummer
Art
Blakey, who
cut
for
Blue Note for a number of years; The
Staple
Singers,
the
famed
sacred
group previously on the VeeJay label;
and Latin drummer Mongo Santama-
ria, who came to the label after a stint
with Fantasy.

######## cb 1963-01-26 p1  [three\s+sounds|art\s+blakey]

JAKUARY 26. 1963
It s rare in our industry to hear of an independent label celebrating
its S ilver Anniversary. But the consistently successful Blue Note
firiii formed
in January of 1939 should soon be turning the trick as
it begins
its 25th year as a leading company in the Jazz field. Formed by Alfred Lion (sec-
ond from left) and run today by Lion and Francis Wolff (left)
the diskery has been responsible for introducing many of today’s
jazz greats on
records, including Horace Silver (right) who has been with the label for the past ten years. The gentlemen are seen above with Silver’s new “Tokyo
Blues
LP inspired by the
artist’s recent tour of Japan. The company began with traditionalist Sidney Bechet and has since furthered the careers
of such names as Art Hodes, Sidney De Paris, Thelonious Monk, Milt Jackson, Lou Donaldson, Art Blakey, Jimmy Smith, the Three Sounds and an
endless
list that reads like a varitable Who’s Who of the
jazz world. There are now over 200 LP’s in the Blue Note catalog.

[ Blue Note Starts 25th Year
As Leader In Jazz Field
NEW
YORK—When
Alfred
Lion
started the Blue Note operation Jan.,
1939, the Depression had put the rec-
ord
business
in
bad
shape,
and
not
many tradesters gave him much hope
for
success
in
selling
nothing
but
jazz on
12"

Lion persevered and with

ner, Francis Wolff, the pair now have
the

in
the
U.S.
and
the
oldest
indie
as
the
firm
1
i
1
1
Ll'
fi
enters
its
25th
year.
Undoubtedly,
one
reason
for
their
success
is
their
long
dedication
to
jazz. Both are ardent jazz buffs who
record what they
like.
It turned
out
that
the
buying
public
likes
what
they
like,
with
the
result
that
their
Blue Note catalog is one of the fastest
moving in the business.
Starting

was “Summertime" which one
of the

refused

Bechet

cur-
rent
catalog.
Their

still

Not

has
Blue Note been

most exclusive jazz
label, but
it also
has been most helpful
in
giving

ented
young
musicians
their

The

is a

DeParis,
Edmond Hall, Ike Quebec, Thelonious
Monk,
Bud
Powell,
Tadd
Dameron,
Fats
Navarro,
Clifford
Brown,
Milt
Jackson
and Hank Mobley
are some
of the men who were featured during
the
first decade of Blue Note.
Blue Note’s record in this respect is
particularly
striking
in terms
of the
modern
jazz
men
it
has
helped
to
recognition. Horace
Silver, Lou Don-
aldson, Art Blakey, Jimmy Smith and
The
Three
Sounds
have
achieved
prominence during
their long
associ-
ation with Blue Note.
More
recently,
they
have
concen-
trated
on
other

active
musi-
cians
such

Donald
Byrd,
Dexter
Gordon,
Grant

Morgan,
Sonny Clark, Freddie Hubbai’d, Jackie
McLean, Horace Parian, Stanley Tur-
rentine,
Herbie
Hancock, and
vocal-
ists Dodo Greene and
Sheila Jordan.

deserved

Nat King Cole makes his second
visit to Japan
in February, the promoter,
Kyodo-kikaku Production, announced. On his way of travel to Far East coun-
tries including Hawaii and
Philippines, he stays
in Japan for about a month
at his own wish. The performances are
to be
held
in Tokyo and
other cities
from February 18 to early March, with much lower admission fees than those
of his last visit, according to his plan, which shows that he earnestly wants to
sing for those who could not come to
listen to him during his
last stay here.
In the course of his tour in our country, he is also scheduled to make TV films.
Top female singer of Nippon Columbia, Chiyoko Shiniakura,
left Japan on
January 3 to Hawaii and Los Angeles for her
first musical tour abroad. She
was invited by overseas Japanese and
nisei group’s to sing for them her
hit
numbers at theatres in Honolulu, Maui, Hilo and Los Angeles. After ten day’s
performance, she’ll spend a vacation.
The Platters arrived Tokyo on December 27, with their manager Buck Ram.
At their press conference held at Hanabasha, they sung some of their hits and
received a hearty welcome from
all of the audience. Tickets were sold out for
their stage performances leaving
so many fans disappointed that they have
additional performances for five days in the middle of January here
in Tokyo.

HOLLAND
Bovema’s
His

has
released new

in

“Great
Recoiding-s Of The

In

Van Een Zeeman”
(Repentance Of A

and “Hongkong” by

Imperial

by Duo

“The

.

The

“II

The

Angelica”
and
“Gianni
Schicchi” were

with

of

has
only
seldom
happened

let alone that recording companies would
risk
the ventui-e to release

The

Merrill.
Among

is one

of pos-
sibilities.

EXPOSITION OF JUKE BOXES IN AMSTERDAM
Recently, during four days
the yearly
exposition
of equipments
for
Hotel
&
Restaurants,
called HORECAVA, was
held
in
the immense RAI-Building
of Amsterdam. This was the seventh year this
exposition was
held and
the
exposition was
bigger
than
ever
before.
More
than
300
manufacturers
or
dealers
and
importers
showed
their
articles
in
a
space
of
25,000
square
meter, and everyone who
has something
to
do
with
the
catering
or
enter-
tainment business
visited
this
wonderful
exhibition.
This was the right opportunity for the public to meet with the 1963-models
of juke boxes and
all American makes were represented.
Rock-Ola represented by Brabo
Holland, drew
the
interest
of many
visi-
tors with
its new models, which were not shown before in Holland. Especially
the
Capri-type was met
with
approval.
Eight men
of
the
Brabo-Holland-
staff were on the stand
to give the public
information and
details.
Wurlitzer was shown on the
stand
of Elspor and here the system of Ten
Top Tunes was introduced for the
first time. We think however
this system
not
favorable
for the Dutch market because
of
the
Dutch
coins.
Ten
Top
Tunes can be played for one guilder (28 cents) and this
is not a big business
for
the
operators.
The
Seeburg
all-transistor
model was
shown
in
the
stand
of
J.
Schaap
and new AMI Consoles were demonstrated by
L. C. Denies.
New on the market was the introduction
of background music, brought by
Brabo-Holland. We
saw
a
full-automatic
tape-recorder
(manufactured
by
Viking USA)
to be played with cartridges containing each a two hours pro-
gram.
All
recordings
were
made
by
the
Dutch
firm
themselves
in
own
studios and the Dutch
public can hear
their famous
soloists and conductors
on Brabo Background Music.
Especially
for
the
better type
of
restaurants,
this kind
of music
is
highly
attractive and
it
is
very
interesting
that
the
equipment
is
exploited
on
a
rental
base,
assuring
the
restaurant-owner
a
monthly consignment of new programs. Even the hotel that has an orchestra
during
dinner-time, can use
this background music for
the time during
the
day,
that no music
is
heard. Because
there
are no
vocals
in
the
library
of
Brabo, the idea of music
in the background
is
fully
realised.

Italian
musicians,
as
of
this
writing, are
on
strike for more money. The
strike comes at a time when labels are busy cutting San Remo songs.
The Italian Record Producers Association (AFI)
has created a commission
to negotiate with the musicians’ reps and try to find a
solution. In fact, the
dispute seemed settled at one point, and the musicians returned to work, but
the
situation became
difficult again.
Therefore, just a few San Remo songs
were recorded.
It is felt that by applying collective bargaining, instead of each label settling
on
its own, a fair settlement can be expected soon.
By the way, regarding the AFI and referring to our column in the January
26 Cash Box
issue, there was a misunderstanding about their activity.
As a matter of fact, it is no longer forbidden for AFI to handle questions of
general
economic
interest for
record
producers,
but
this
activity must
be
mainly
connected
with
syndicated
matters,
taxes, common
advertising and
so on.
The new AFI
articles
of
association
don’t provide common
price
policy.
We vish
to stress that each record manufacturer follows his own judgement
about
prices:
as for the
last increase some leading record houses decided
it
separately to face new woi-k costs, and some other houses followed this
first
example: no common decision about prices was taken, as stated.

MEXICO
Bernard C. Solomon, president of Everest Enterprise, Inc. and Walter Hofer,
attorney at law, came to Mexico the last week to visit Mario Freidberg, Tizoc
Records manager, to sign a contract to represent in
this country the Everest
and Challenge labels at the same time that Bernard C. Solomon will represent
Tizoc
in the United States. The last record made by The Champs will appear
in Mexico immediately and
will be the
first
of
this commercial interchange.
Freidberg
also informed
Cash Box
that he
sigmed
a
contract
to
represent
Colpix Records and that the first album which will be released in this country
will be the “Barrabas” sound
track. He
also got the permission
to
press
in
Mexico records from the World
Pacific catalog. From another label he repre-
sents, Argentinia’s Disk Jokey, he released an album with Juan Ramon songs,
which
is selling well.
Cesar Costa, one
of the most popular young Mexican
singers, new record
contains the songs “Te Esperare”
(I’ll Wait For You) and “Baila Bossa Nova”
(Dance Bossa Nova) with strong arrangement made by Gustavo Pimentel and
Los Vocalistas chorus. We are sure that
this record
will be a top
hit. Cesar
will start a new TV series and one or two more pictures. There’s also a chance
he will record
in English, perhaps at Capitol Records.
Like
Costa,
Enrique Guzman
is
also
very
popular.
Enrique
recorded
one
of
the
songs
included
in
the past “Mexican Song
Festival” named
“Vida”
(Darling), which can be heard on almost
all the Mexican radio
stations. The
arrangements on
this record were made by Chuck Anderson. Enrique
is now
performing
in
Caracas,
Venezuela,
and
from
that
place
he
will
move
to
Argentina, where he probably
will work with another Mexican singer
of the
“new wave” named Manolo Munoz, who has in Mexico two of his records on
the charts “Speedy Gonzalez” and “Speedy in Tijuana.”
Back from Spain
is well known
singer Lucho Gatica and
his wife Mapyta
Cortez and their two children. Lucho is planning to stay in Mexico for a long
while, performing at different places.
Peerless Records released a new record made by Julio Jaramillo in Ecuador
with the songs “Falla Corazon” (Fail Darling) and “Tu Palida Voz” (Your Pale
Voice). Julio is trying to earn popularity again in this country and he is getting
a strong promotion.
Andre 'Toffel, BelArt general manager, is at the moment in New York trying
to get new contacts for his company, which promises
to be some of the most
important in Mexico
in the months to come.
Mona Bell
is getting strong popularity again with her version of the movie
“Tombola,” recorded
in Spain
at the Hispa Vox
studios. Monna
is preparing
her return to Mexico, and will perfoimi at theaters, on TV and cut records.
One of the youngest singers of the “new wave,” Oscar Madrigal,
is ready to
release his
first LP on which he includes
his biggest
hit, “Cosas”
(Things),
“El Ultimo Verano” (Sealed With a Kiss), “Que Clase De Amor Es” (What Kind
of Love It Is) and some of his unknown songs like “Rumores” (Rumors). Oscar
told Cash Box that he will appear in two weekly TV shows.
Perry Como, who was in the capital a few days ago, will return January 26
to film some scenes for one of his TV shows. It promises to be sensational and
Perry
will
take
some
location
shots
from
Xochimilco,
with
the
Amalia
Hernandez
ballet and will take some lessons with “matador” Carlos Arruza,
since he will appear as a “matador” on one of his next shows. Perry made a
videotape with Andy Russell to appear in Mexico on Andy’s show, having the
same sponsor that Perry has in the U.S.
Under the name of “Pasos Musicales” (Musical Steps)
there’ll be a new TV
series with Bobby Capo, Pablo Beltran Ruiz orchestra, Jose
Silva and young
Angelica Maria.
