ALBUM REVIEWS
“THE EXPLOSIVE SIDE OF SARAH VAUG-
HAN”—Roulette R 52092
In
recent
years
most
Sarah
Vaughan
sessions
have
featured
a
soft
collection
of
ballads. The
lark has met with great success with her brilliant
readings
of
low-key
romantic
items
but she
is
(as evidenced on this set) also capable of
belting-
out
swingin’
numbers.
The
artist’s
wide-range
vocal charms coupled with flawless diction carries
her
in winning fonn
on Benny
Carter-arranged
versions
of
“I
Believe In
You,”
“Trolley
Song”
and “I’m Gonna
Live
Until
I
Die.” One
of

Nippon Victor and Toshiba have just made awards for top songs of ’62.
At a party at Victor’s studio on Jan. 26, there were 23 songs named, includ-
ing a foreign composition that received a Triumph Trophy. Tune
is “Pretty
Little Baby,” recorded in Japan by Mie Nakao and published by Shinko Music.
The Japanese
lyricist of the song, Kenji Sazanami, was also given an award.
Toshiba’s annual Hit Show was held at the Daiichi Hotel
in Tokyo on Jan.
25. Nine compositions were named as top songs and awarded gold and
silver
prizes.
.
Foreign material getting gold prizes were: “Don’t Treat Me Like A Child,”
cut by Mieko Hirota and published by Shinko Music; “One Eyed Jack,” cut by
Shigeru Karsumi, and published by Folster Music; “He’s Not Just A Soldier,”
cut by Q. Sakamoto, and published by Shinko

“CARAVAN”-Art Blakey—Riverside RS
9438
Here’s a significant jazz set marking Art Blakey
and the Jazz Messengers
first disk for Riverside.
As with previous Blakey groups,
this crew per-
forms in stimulating fashion and has a powerful,
distinctive
method
of
communication. Although
the ace drummer
is somewhat subdued on most
of the tracks
his imaginative brushwork behind
Cedar
Walton’s

is

masterful.
The group swings superbly on “Caravan,” “This
Is For Albert” and “Thermo.” Potent wax.
“SCREAMIN’ ”—Brother Jack McDuflf—Prestige
PR 7259
Brother Jack McDuff unleashes his potent organ
talents
full-blast on
this impressive teaming up
with Leo Wright on
alto, Kenny Burrell on gui-
tar and Joe Dukes on drums. Unlike some
soft-
style
organists
currently
in vogue, McDuff
has
a rousing, earth-shattering approach highlighted
by his use of quick stop changes. Top-flight tracks
here
include
“He’s A
Real Gone Guy,”
“After
Hours” and “I Cover The Waterfront.” Eye the
disk for rapid acceptance.

on

“Theme

Jazzophiles
should come out in force for the package.

James
Darren
James
Darren,
who
is
currently
riding the Top 100 with “Pin A Medal
On Joey,”
is one of the hottest double-
barreled stars in the business. In ad-
dition to his vocal hits, he previously
triumphed with “Angel Face,” “Good-
bye Cruel World,” “Her Royal Majes-
ty,” “Conscience” and “Mary’s
Little
Lamb” on
Colpix, he has
starred
in
such
film
successes
as
“The
Gene
Krupa
Story”
and
“The
Guns
Of
Navarone” for Columbia Pictures, the
parent company of his
label.
The
chanter-thespian was
born
in
Philadelphia
on
June
8,
1936
and
studied at the Ephiphany School and
Southern High
School
there. As
far
back
as he
could remember,
Darren
always wanted to be a singer and an
actor, but
his schooling
(as an
actor
with
the
Stella
Adler
Group),
was
limited
to
a
bare
two
weeks when
fate gave him a remarkable
aid:
he
was in a Gotham office building, wait-
ing for an elevator, when a Columbia
Pictures
talent
scout
spotted
him;
only
three
days
later
he
signed
a
movie contract. The rest
is history.
New
Christy
Minstrels
The New
Christy
Minstrels,
who
are
currently
riding
the LP
charts
with “New Christy Minstrels In Per-
son,” were organized by
their leader
Randy Sparks, who at 27
is the oldest
member
of
the
fourteen
member
group.
Sparks was born July
29,
1933
in
Leavenworth,
Kansas
and
conceived
the idea and name
for
his
singer-in-
strumentalists from Edwin
P.
Chris-
ty, who,
in
1842, formed
the famous
Christy
Minstrels,
hailed
as
the
na-
tion’s foremost interpreters of Steph-
en Foster songs.
Sparks got
his start
in show busi-
ness while in college. He was seeking
a part-time job and made his first ap-
pearance at the Purple Onion
in San
Francisco.
Since
then
he
has
been
booked
at
the
Blue
Angel
in New
York, the
entire Playboy
circuit and
numerous TV appearances. The group
are
currently
regulars
on
the Andy
Williams weekly NBC-TV stanza.
The new Christies all sing and play
folk
instruments
(guitars,
banjos,
bass
violin and a variety of assorted
secondary
instruments:
harmonica,
fife,
etc.).

A

new

called

“Mars
Telephone
Simul-
tape,”
has
been
developed
by Mars
Broadcasting
Corp.
of
Stamford,
Conn.,
for
use
on
“The
Dick
Clark
Radio Show” of which
it
is the pro-
ducer and
distributor. The
technique
permits Clark to interview anyone in
the
world
with
the immediacy
of
a
face-to-face
studio
confrontation.
Using
the
“Simultape”
technique,
Clark, who
is usually in Philadelphia
or Stamford, can arrange to call any-
one
and
interview him
on
the
tele-
phone. At
the
same
time
they
are
talking on the phone, both Clark and
the
interviewee
also
speak
directly
into tape
recorders. When the
inter-
view
is
concluded,
the
tapes
are
spliced together at the Mars
studios,
resulting
in a taped “live” interview.

######## cb 1963-03-02 p43  [art\s+blakey]

English singer Shirley Bassey has been awarded £3,000
(Australian) dam-
ages by the Supreme Court in Sydney in a defamation case against Sungravure
Ltd., publishers of Fix, a weekly magazine;
this amount
is
in
the vicinity of
$6,000. The case was heard before Justice Macfarlane and a jury of four.
EMI has suddenly speeded up their release program of overseas
hits. There
used to be quite a time lag betwen a US or English release and the appearance
of the same record on the local scene through EMI but the situation
is vastly
improved now with a new rush-release program in operation. Records such as
“What Does A
Girl Do?”—Marcie
Blane; “Dance On!”—The Shadows;
“In
Dreams”—Roy Orbison; “Butterfly Baby”—Bobby Rydell and “The Puzzle” by
Gene McDaniels have already been
in Australia for the past couple of weeks.
Set for a concert season
in this country beginning late in March are Louis
!
Armstrong and His Jazz All Stars, together with the Eddie Cano Quartet. The
Australian tour
is being handled by Arthur J. Tait
in association with James
Dilena by arrangement with Harry Miller.
Chris Vaughan-Smith of Southern Music has secured the Australian and New
Zealand rights to the current worldwide smash “Walk Right In” which
is do-
ing great disk business
in this part of the world for Astor Records with the
single release by the Rooftop Singers. The Southem group also controls “What
Will Mary Say” and the English hit tune “Must Be Madison.”
Local boys The Deltones are making giant strides in progress with their fine
single on the Leedon label of “Come A Little Closer.” This is an excellent piece
of production and
is worthy of immediate worldwide
action.
George Taylor,
of Melbourne Records
(a subsidiary
of Rodeo
Records)
in
Canada, advises he
is planning to release the album “Frankie Davidson’s Big
I
16” which he has negotiated through W&G Records in Australia; a single from
I
the album will also be issued. Frankie moves out at the end of February for a
lengthy tour of New Zealand.
Dr. John Chapman, writer of such hits as “Southeim ’Rora” and “Xmas Gui-
tar”—both of which were successfully recorded by The Joy Boys, was a recent
visitor to Cash Box. John recently collected third prize in a playwriting contest
conducted throughout Australia by General Motors.
One of the recent big American hits “Up On The Roof” by The Drifters looks
like
it’s missing out on any really big success in Australia—a couple of cover
versions are making headway in England but
it seems unlikely that the song
will emulate its American and English success in this country.
Eydie Gorme will probably have the biggest Australian hit of her career with
her present CBS label single “Blame It On The Bossa Nova.” It is catching top-
notch airplay and should soon hit the high spots on sales charts. Eydie’s hus-
band, Steve Lawrence, is on the best-seller list with his CBS release “Go Away
Little Girl.”
As an illustration of a point we made in an editorial of a few weeks back on
the problem of local records gaining national recognition, we
cite the present
instance of “Surfside” by The Denver Men—which
is close to the number one
record in Sydney where
it was produced—and “The
Girl Behind The Bar” by
Johnny Ashcroft which has also done good business
in Sydney
.
.
. neither of
these records has done good
business
in Melbourne which
is regarded
as a
prime
disc market. Reversing the
situation, we
find
that two
of the
hottest
singles in Melbourne are “Summertime Blues” by Johnny Chester and “Leavin’
i
Town” and “Cry Of The Wild Goose” by The Strangers—both
disks
are by
Melbourne
artists and neither record has done anything
in Sydney
.
.
.
yet
each disk
is good enough
to
get top
action
in
their
local markets
so there
can’t be much wrong with these records
if they can enjoy fine sales
in their
home States. Since our first editorial on this problem. Cash Box
in Australia
has received many comments from disk-jockeys, record companies and publish-
ers
all condemning this sad
state of
affairs—but there has been
little or no
improvement. Again we say:
if the Australian record industry is to develop to
the stage of successful competition for a share of the international market,
it
must first solve its most urgent problem—that of national acceptance of Aus-
tralian recording talent.

Though we have
still a severe winter in Japan, people have been feeling the
approach of spring since celebrating the traditional Spring Starting Day, with
the colorful event of pitching beans against the imaginary demons
to chase
them away. We shall have a number of visitors for the early spring season, of
whom announced until this date are:
German popular singer, Caterina Valente,
in Feb. for the
first performance
here; Chubby Checker, well known to our fans as the King of Twist, in Feb.;
George Shearing, the jazz
pianist,
in Mar.; French singer Gilbert Becaud,
in
Mar.; Lionel Hampton, King of the Vibes, and originator of Two Finger Sys-
tem on piano, in Apr., with all his stars; Count Basie and his 16 members, hold-
ing big popularity among our fans as the leading orchestra of America, in May;
England’s Mantovani Orchestra, dominating our mood music world,
in May;
Marcel Amont, French popular singer, in May.
Ray Charles was honored by Nippon King Records for the big sales
of his
disks released from the company during the
last half-year, “All About Ray
Charles” (LP album), “Ray Charles Country Song 0 Utah” (LP album), and
many singles. He is the first artist to receive the Hit Prize of this company as
an American or as a male singer, and the third foreigner after the war, follow-
ing Caterina Valente and Kathy Linden. The Prize
is to be presented through
Samuel Clark, president of ABC-Paramount.
Victor Shuppan KK is releasing modern jazz albums, the original masters of
Prestige, including dates by Art Blakey, Horace
Silver, Miles
Davis, Sonny
Rollins and Stan Getz.
Nippon Grammophon Records established two
deals on new
labels: One
is
Ansonia, on which
it
is pushing Middle-South American Music. The
first re-
lease
will be
in March, an album of a native chorus group
Julito Rodorigez
Trio. The other one
is the original master of “Sounds Of Hawaii,”
to be re-
released on the Polydor Label. The
first such issue
is due March 20.
Nippon Columbia
is putting to sale two issues of coupled 30cm LP records.
“All About Connie Francis” is a collection of her
hits, while “Marty Robbins
For You” is the 4th issue of Columbia’s popular series, which features popular
singers in 30cm mono coupled records.

ALBUM REVIEWS
Cash Box
“RAMBLIN’ ROSE AND OTHER HITS”—Living
Voices—RCA Camden CAS748
Ten
of
the most
melodic
best-sellers
of
recent
months are
delightfully and harmoniously
deliv-
ered by the Living Voices on this excellent RCA
Camden
package.
All
of
the
tunes
here
saw
plenty
of
chart
action and
this new
version
of
them
is
sure
to
create
some
sales
excitement.
Best
bets
here
are
“I
Left My
Heart
In
San
Francisco,”
“What
Kind
Of
Fool Am
I”
and
“Roses Are
Red.”
“THE JOKER IS WILD” — Archie Campbell —
Starday SLP223
Archie Campbell comes up with some
sparkling
country-flavored humor on
this “Joker
Is Wild”
LP from Starday aptly subtitled “The Adult De-
linquent Teaches Indoor
Sports.” The laughman
pokes good-humored fun
at a variety of
institu-
tions (marriage, etc.,) people (women) and places
(the South)
in a tongue-in-cheek manner guaran-
teed
to invoke plenty of chuckles. Comedy
LP’s
are hot items and this one could spark some sales
for the gagster.
“ORGAN HOLIDAY” — Johnny Duffy — Liberty
LRP3281
The organ has always been one of the most ver-
satile
of musical instruments and Johnny Duffy
on a fine theatre pipe organ paints enough inter-
esting and
exciting
tonal
pictures
to
please the
most discerning record buyers. Duffy showcases a
distinctive, swingin’ style on “Cuban Love Song,”
“Come Back To Sorrento” and
“It Happened
In
Montery.” Fine fare for either listening or danc-
ing pleasure.
“CABBAGE GREENS”—Champion Jack Dupree
—Okeh OKM12103
Jazz and blues buffs should get excited about this
excellent LP featuring
sides
cut
in the
1940-41
period by Jack Dupree. The chanter’s jazz-based
singing
style
combines many
diverse
elements
and his piano playing is the exciting barrelhouse
style.
The
artist,
backed
by
a
small
effective
combo,
turns
in
top-drawer
readings
of “Gam-
bling Man
Blues,”
“Black Woman
Swing”
and
“Heavy Heart Blues.” A
collector’s item.
“NEW SOUNDS IN FOLK MUSIC”—Rod Mc-
Kuen—Horizon WP1612
The multi-talented Rod McKuen takes a crack at
folksinging on this new Horizon outing and comes
off amazingly well. The chanter has a fresh, un-
stereotyped wide-range voice aptly
suited to the
folk idiom. While backed by a small combo and a
chorus
called
the
Keytones, McKuen
dishes
up
top-drawer readings
of
“If
I Had A Hammer,”
“Empty Pocket Blues” and “Got To Roam.” De-
lightful
listening throughout.

Len Levy Upped To
Sen Mgr of Epic
LEN LEVY
NEW YORK—Len
Levy
has
been
promoted to general manager of Epic
Records,
it was announced
last week
by Norman
Adler,
exec veep
of
Co-
lumbia Records, the parent firm.
Levy, formally Epic’s national sales
manager,
will
report
directly
to
Bill
Gallagher, marketing veep
at Colum-
bia.
Gallagher noted that under
Levy’s
direction
the
label
“experienced
the
greatest
sales
volume
in
its
history
during
1962.”
In
his new
post,
Levy,
with
Epic
since
Oct.,
1961,
will
continue
to be
responsible for
all phases of the sales
operations of Epic and Okeh, a label
affiliate, including the development of
merchandising programs and the
di-
rection of such programs through the
efforts
of
Epic-Okeh
district
sales
managers and
distribs.
Levy
joined
Epic
with
14
years
experience in disk sales. He was veep
of Modern Sound,
Inc., an
indie pro-
ducing company and director of sales
and administration for Top Rank. He
has
also
been
involved
with
whole-
saling,
retailing
and
manufacturing
operations
in the disk industry.
With
Levy
at
the
helm.
Epic
achieved the greatest sales in
its nine
year history. Heading the sales show-
ing were Bobby Vinton, whose “Roses
are Red” was the label’s first million-
seller,
George
Maharis
and
Buddy
Greco. Label acquired the services of
Adam Wade and the Ames Bros, dur-
ing
’62.
Classical-wise
the
diskei’y
added The
Juilliard
String
Quartet.
Epic’s
top
long-hair
attraction
is
George
Szell &
The
Cleveland
Or-
chestra.

FTC Winds Up Its Case
Against Columbia; Label
Rebuttal Begins Apr. 15
NEW
YORK—The
Federal
Trade
Commission completed its case against
the Columbia
Record Club
last week
with
final
hearings
in New York on
Mar.
11-12.
The
Columbia
Record
Club
will
argue
its
case with
testi-
mony of witnesses beginning Apr.
15.
The
final
witnesses
for
the FTC
in
Gotham were David Rothfeld of Kor-
vette’s,
A.
Hirsch
of
Malverne
Dis-
tributing, Edwin
Ricotta
of Wunder-
man,
Ricotta
and
Kline
Advertising
Agency,
Randy
Wood,
president
of
Dot
Records,
and
Paul
Ackerman,
executive secretary
of ARMADA.
The most extensive testimony given
during the
final
sessions was that of
Randy Wood,
president
of Dot
Rec-
ords, and
Paul
Ackerman,
executive
secretary
of ARMADA.
Wood
was
questioned by
counsels on
both
sides
on
the
history
of
Dot
Records,
its
growth, ownership and current finan-
cial
status.
The
diskery
prexy
re-
vealed that in the past seven or eight
years
he has
negotiated with
repre-
sentatives of
all the record clubs for
distribution
of Dot product and
that
to
date
no
contracts had
ever
been
finalized. Wood also stated that in his
opinion the record clubs has probably
hurt
the
record
dealers
by
reducing
traffic
in
the
stores,
but
that
Dot
needs club distribution to increase the
exposure
of
its
artists, regardless of
his own personal feelings on the mat-
ter. Wood concluded by saying that he
thought discount houses and rack job-
bers were not good for the
industry.
David Rothfeld, who testified at the
beginning
of
the
hearings,
was
re-
called by the FTC
to give additional
information
on
Korvette’s record
de-
partments. Rothfeld stated that since
joining Korvette’s in 1958, the chain’s
gross from record sales has increased
from
$3
million
in
’58
to
13
or $14
million
in
1962.
The
sharp
upward
trend was
a
result
of
extensive ad-
vertising
and
the
opening
of
addi-
tional
stores,
Rothfeld
said.
In com-
paring Korvette’s advertising methods
with
those
of
the
Columbia
Record
Club, Rothfeld remarked, “Columbia’s
advertising has had a deflationary ef-
fect on records generally.” The Kor-
vette exec also remarked that of the
18
stores
operated
by
the
Korvette
chain,
10 showed an increase
in
vol-
ume
in
1962
over
1961,
while
8
showed
a
decrease.
The
Government’s
final
witness,
Paul Ackennan, was called as an ex-
pert on the music industry in general,
in that he was on
the
editorial
staff
of
Billboard
for
28
years
and
had
extensive knowledge on
all phases of
the business.
Ackerman
highlighted
his remarks
by
commenting
that
he
editorially
endorsed
the
Columbia
Record
Club
on two separate occasions because
in
its
initial
stages
the
club was
sup-
posed
to
enhance
business,
service
outlying areas which has been untap-
ped, and
that catalog product would
get greater exposure. In the ensuing
years,
said
Ackerman,
the
club
has
become
a
competitor
of
the
dealers.
He
also
remarked
that
discount
houses were no good for the industry,
but
that
rack
jobbers
did
serve
a
function.
Stuart Robinowitz, counsel for Co-
lumbia, asked Ackerman why he
did
not
reiterate
his
sentiments
toward
the Columbia Club
in
the
article he
wrote for Cash Box
(Dec.
29,
1962)
in which he discussed the
ills of the
record
industry.
Ackerman
replied
that by this time the “Club thing was
old hat” and that he was writing on
current problems.

Capitol Club Takes-On
1st
Outside LP: WB's “Gypsy"
NEW
YORK—The
Capitol
Record
Club
is handling
its
first non-Capitol
or Angel album. It’s the Warner Bros,
label’s soundtrack LP of “Gypsy.”
To
set
the record
straight,
it was
pointed
out by Dan
Bonright,
vice-
chairman
of
the
board
of
Capitol,
that
the WB album does not
consti-
tute “a change
in the Club’s general
pattern
of
releasing only Angel and
Capitol label records.”
He
added
that
no
agreement
has
been made as to any label or catalog,
but that the Club, however,
will con-
tinue to “review particularly desirable
recordings as they come up”
to
give
Club members recordings
of
“special
interest.”
“Insofar as labels and catalogs are
concerned,”
Bonright concluded, “We
believe
the
Capitol
and
Angel
cata-
logs represent the quality recordings
in the Club market.”
An interesting sidelight to the move
is that the Columbia Record Club has
been handling WB product. However,
Columbia
Records
has
the
original
Broadway cast LP of “Gypsy,” and
it
figures
that
the
label would
not
be
eager
to have
it competing with
the
WB version in
its own Club setup.
based
in
Philadelphia;
Philips: Jerry
Kennedy,
stationed
in
Nashville, Hal
Mooney and Herb Rosen, both in New
York.
Doug Moody, eastern regional man-
ager
for
Smash,
will
leave
his
post
in
the
field
to
serve

Victor's Ben
Selvin
Feted At Retirement Dinner
BEN
SELVIN
NEW YORK—Benjamin B. Selvin, for
the past 10 years A&R manager for
RCA Victor’s Custom Record Depart-
ment, who, for over 58 years has
left
his mark on
the musical world
as
a
UA Plans Ahead
(Continued from page 6)
Caiola, The
Exciters,
Mike
Clifford,
The
Highwaymen,
LeRoy
Holmes,
Tito Rodriguez, Jay and The Ameri-
cans, Ralph Marterie and other
con-
tract performances
will be forthcom-
ing
on
a
regularly
scheduled
basis
through
the balance
of
1963.
In
this
regard, Talmadge
said, a new three-
year pact has
just been signed with
Marv Johnson, one of the early artists
on
the
label,
and
the
first
release
under the new contract will be forth-
coming
shortly.
Leiber and
Stoller
will continue
to
produce
all new
artists for UA, Tal-
madge stated, and will also handle ses-
sions for many of the current pactees,
including The Exciters, Mike Clifford,
Baby
Jane
and
The Rockabyes
and
others. Album product will be turned
out by this team, while LeRoy Holmes,
who
serves
a dual function as
artist
and A&R
for
the
label,
will
con-
centrate
on packaged goods
produc-
tion.
UA, under a long-term distribution
contract,
will continue
to handle
the
Musicor label, with
all releases under
the Musicor banner
included. During
the UA
arrangement
-with
Musicor,
the

has
developed
one
of

top young

today.
Gene Pitney, whose first five releases
“I
Wanna
Love
My
Life
Away,”
“Town Without
Pity,”
“Liberty Val-
ance,”
“Only
Love
Can
Break
A
Heart,” and “Half Heaven-Half Heart-
ache” have all been major chart items.
A
new
Pitney
record,
“Mecca”
is
on the Top 100. The Musicor releases
are produced by Aaron Schroeder with
Wally Gold.
“From
all
indications,”
Talmadge
said, “we
will
continue our progress
of the past two years during the bal-
ance of 1963. At the present time we
are enthusiastic over such top-selling
product as the Duke Ellington,
Billie
Holiday,
Herbie
Mann,
Art
Blakely
and
Charlie Mingus
Jazz
packages;
our
Tale-Spinners
For
Children
re-
leases and our pop packages such as
Ferrante and Teicher’s “Keys To Her
Apartment”
and
the
Sound
Track
from
“Phaedra”
to
mention
only
a
few. During the balance of the year
we
will
be
working
with
top
film
music from major United Artists re-
leases,
as
well
as
carefully
planned
product from our regular artists with
proven
sales records.”
violinist,
internationally
acclaimed
band
leader,
radio
director,
and
re-
cording
manager,
was
honored
last
Thurs.
(14)
at
a
retirement
dinner
attended by many
tradesters.
Approximately 200 people were on
hand
at the
St. Moritz
Hotel,
includ-
ing representatives from
the Ameri-
can
Fedei-ation
of
Musicians,
the
music
publishing
and
record
indus-
tries,
all
departments
of
the
Victor
record
division,
and
the
Radio
Cor-
poration of America.
Keynote speakers at the dinner were
Norman
Racusin,
vice-president
and
operations manager of the label; J. Y.
Burgess,
Jr.,
vice-president
of
com-
mercial
sales; James P. Davis, record
operations
department,
and
John
Hammond, pop A&R
staff
producer,
at Columbia Records.
Ben
Selvin
began
studying
music
at the age of seven. At 21, while con-
ducting an
11-piece orchestra at the
famed
Moulin Rouge
night
club,
he
recorded
four
songs
for
the
Victor
Talking Machine Company—at a
set
fee
of
$100
per
song. One
of them,
“Dardanella,” became the
first dance
record to
sell over one million copies.
Other
hits by
the
Selvin
Orchestra
included
“I’m
Forever Blowing Bub-
bles,” “A Pretty Girl
Is Like A Mel-
ody,”
and
“Isle
of
Golden
Dreams.”
Throughout
his
career,
Selvin
has
recorded
more
than
9,000
selections
under
nine
different names
for nine
companies.
In 1927, established as an artist, he
left
night
clubs
to
become
musical
director
with
the
Columbia
Phono-
graph Company, was
eventually
ap-
pointed director of A&R, and assisted
in
the
formation
of
the
Columbia
Broadcasting
System.
After
serving
as vice president in charge of record-
ing and programming for the Muzak
Corporation from 1934 until 1941, Sel-
vin took
a leave
of absence
to work
with James Petrillo and the American
Federation of Musicians
in preparing
the
first
comprehensive
survey
of
recorded music.
After returning to Muzak, he joined
Majestic
Records
as
vice
president
and
in 1947, re-joined Columbia Rec-
ords in Hollywood as director of A&R.
In
February,
1953,
he
was
named
A&R
manager
for
Victor’s
Custom
Record
Department,
and
in
recent
years his primary duties have included
the
responsibility
for many
of
the
recordings made by the department in
the
United
States and
Europe.
Dis-
cussing
his
career on the
eve
of
his
retirement,
Selvin,
65,
stated:
“My
only regret
is that
I
didn’t join RCA
Victor as an executive in 1919 instead
of as an artist, since the last ten years
have been the most interesting of my
career.”
Master of ceremonies for the dinner
was Ralph
C.
Williams, manager
of
the custom
dept.
Discussing
Selvin’s
retirement he said: “During his career
at RCA Victor, Ben Selvin has served
the company well in an executive A&R
capacity. He
has made
a
significant
contribution
to
the
Record
Division
and Custom Records in particular, and
will be greatly missed.
It is our hope
that
his
future
plans may
well
call
for
a continuing
association with us
and
his many friends and
associates
in the music and record industry.”
Selvin, who
lives
in
Roslyn, Long
Island, has
long been
active
in
real
estate,
in
addition
to
his
musical
activities. He
plans
to
devote more
time
in
this
area,
plus
serving
as
a
musical consultant to the Top
of the
Fair,
Inc.
at
the New York World’s
Fair, among other ventures.

Dyer To New Posf Af
Capitol's Scranton
Plant
HOLLYWOOD—Forrest E. Dyer has
been appointed superintendent of the
main manufacturing plant of Capitol
Records, at Scranton, Pa.
He succeeds Robert C. Conniff, who
was recently transferred to New York
as export sales manager.
Dyer originally joined Capitol at its
Los Angeles plant as a matrix worker.
By 1953 he had worked his way up to
manufacturing superintendent of the
Los Angeles facility. In his new posi-
tion, he will report to David W. Law-
hon, Scranton plant manager.

Rockin'
Rebels
The
Rockin’
Rebels, who are
cur-
rently riding high on the charts with
“Wild Weekend” on Swan, do not in
any way typify the show
biz dream
of
an
overnight
success
story.
The
hard-working
group
was
organized
three years ago and they have been
perfecting their artistry ever since.
The
group
consists
of
Tony
Di
Maria, leader and drummer, Lee Car-
roll,
lead
guitar
and
singer, Kenny
Mills,
bass,
guitar
and
singer,
and
Eddy
Jay,
tenor
sax
and
drummer.
The
versatile
performers
are
all
chanters
in their own right and they
can
double on other instruments.
The
boys
received
their
first
big
break
recently when WKBW-Buffalo
spinner Tom Shannon discovered them
playing
a
date
in
Buffalo’s
Candy
Cane Lounge. Shannon was impressed
with
their distinctive sound and sug-
gested
that
they
record
his
theme
song,
“Wild
Weekend.”
The
rest
is
history.
Presently, the crew
is doing a tour
of one nighters and club dates
in the
New York area.
Mongo Santamaria
Latin
drum
star
Mongo
Santa-
maria, who
is currently scoring with
“Watermelon
Man”
(#53
on
this
week’s Top 100) on Riverside’s Battle
subsid,
is a native of Havana, Cuba.
Mongo
left
his
homeland
with
a
Latin revue ten years ago to seek his
fortune
and
on
his
arrival
in
the
United
States
was
quickly
snapped
up and featured by Perez Prado. Fol-
lowing a
stint with
Tito Puente,
the
artist joined Cal Tjader and contrib-
uted much to Tjader’s Latin jazz suc-
cess during the years he was featured
with
the group. Mongo
left
a
lucra-
tive job with Tjader to set out on his
own and has been working top Latin
and jazz spots ever since.
After
signing
with
Riverside
he
cut an album, “Go, Mongo.” His latest
single, “Watermelon Man” on
Battle,
is moving rapidly up the charts and
the label plans to issue an LP tagged
after the single later this month.

For the eighth year in succession, The Ivor Novello Awards have been made
to
those
responsible
for
the
writing-,
producing
and
exploitation
of works
which represent outstanding contributions to British popular and light music.
Headed by Hubert David, Vice Chairman of The Song Writers
Guild, a panel
of distinguished judges drawn from
all branches of the musical industry made
the following awards:
CLASS ONE—The Most Performed Work of the Year
“Stranger On The Shore”
Mr. Acker Bilk (Writer)
Sherwin Music (Publisher)
CLASS TWO—Disk Issued In
1962 Which Achieved Highest British Sales
“Telstar”

Decca Record Co. (Record Company)
Ivy Music (Publisher)

A special award was also made to publisher Lawrence Wright for Outstand-
ing Services to British Popular and Light Music.
The awards, in the form of bronze statuettes, will be presented to the win-
ners in each class during a special BBC TV programme early in May.
Oriole Records, leading British independent label,
is expanding
its activities
in the LP field with the launching of a new series “Realm.” Designed for fam-
ily listening with the retail price
set at 22/6d
($3.15),
it will be economically
possible for Oriole
to issue recordings by top
stars
in
all
fields
of music at
a price within the reach of the mass public. Material for the new series will
be drawn from
a
multiplicity
of

first
six LP’s
to be released
April 12th come mainly from the Oriole and Savoy catalogs including tracks
by Ray Charles, Lightning Hopkins, Sonny Terry, Smokey Hogg and Brownie
McGhee
all on one LP entitled “Rhythm and Blues;” “Come Dancing” by Phil
Tate, “Mambo In Mexico” by Ray Marquez; “Songs Of Couch and Consulta-
tion by Katy
Lee; “Songs Of Romance” by John Hanson and “Hamp Goes
Wild” the recording made by Lionel Hampton in Paris.
The “Realm”

in

“BLUE GENES” — The
Three
Sounds — Verve
V8513
Here
is a potent jazz offering from Verve by The
Three
Sounds
that
has
all
the
built-in
success
ingredients
to send
it straight to the best-seller
lists. Gene Harris
(piano),
Bill Dowdy
(drums)
and Andrew Simpkins
(bass)
display a whole lot
of
musicianship
and
subtly
blend
the
modern
jazz
idiom
with
a
pleasant
adherence
to
the
melodic
line.
Plenty
of
ear-arresting
listening
here
as
the
boys
unleash
their
instrumental
talents on “Autumn In New York,” “Blue Genes”
and “Red
Sails
In The
Sunset.” Jazz
buffs
will
surely dig the
set.
“JAZZ NOVA”—Paulo Alencar And His
Brazil-
ian All-Stars—Atco 33-153
Since the start of the bossa nova craze last
fall
there have been countless albums released utiliz-
ing the
Brazilian rhythms. Some
of these LP’s
were
first-rate
but
they
all
had
one
thing
in
common:
they
featured
an American
brand
of
Brazilian music. Now Paulo Alencar and his sex-
tet has come_ up with a superlative set using the
same improvisations, rhythmic patterns and per-
cussion effects as the modem Brazilian jazzmen.
The sounds here are
stricfly
jazz and
the' con-
tagious arrangements give the group ample
op-
portunity
to
wail. The crew
shines
on
“Ideas,”
“Hello America” and “Why Do I Remember.”
“LUIZ BONFA PLAYS AND
SINGS BOSSA
NOVA”—Verve V8522
Luiz
Bonfa, who
received
international
acclaim
for
his
magnificent
scoring
of
the
film
“Black
Orpheus,” has become a pioneer of music’s new-
est media, the bossa nova. The composer-guitar-
ist-singer
wrote
nine
of
the
melodies
included
here and co-wrote some of the others. The artist
is
a
superb spokesman
in
the language
of
the
bossa nova and
this new Verve
offering
should
win him
hordes
of
admirers.
Top-drawer
sides
here are “Adeus” and “Vem So.” Kudos to Lalo
Schifrin and Oscar Castro Neves for the
instru-
mental backing.
“OUT!” — Jack
Sheldon &
Quartet — Capitol
ST1851
This off-beat session of vocals and trumpet solos
by Jack Sheldon
is a happy combination of jazz,
pop and
wit geared
for
jazzophiles. The trum-
peter
cleverly
creates a tongue-in-cheek atmos-
phere on these tunes that comes
off
well. With
some
first-rate
assists
by
Shelly
Manne, Herb
Ellis and Jack Marshall,
the songster comes up
with some top-notch versions of “Love For Sale,”
“By
Strauss”
and
a
Sheldon
original
tagged
“Dandelion.”
“ELDER DON”—Don Wilkerson—Blue Note 4121
Don Wilkerson, who created quite a
stir in jazz
circles
a
while
back
with
his
first
Blue
Note
session, opens his talented tenor sax full-blast on
this, his second release. This time out the

is teamed up with Grant Green on guitar, Johnny
Acea on piano, Lloyd Trotman on bass and Willie
Bobo
on
drums.
Wilkerson’s approach combines
basic blues progressions, Afro-jazz and a potent,
danceable beat as he renders “San Antonio Rose,”
“Lone
Star
Shuffle”
and
“Poor
Butterfly.” A
talent to watch.

BELLINI:

The Met Prima Donna adds to a growing

Monti
and

Elkins,
this much
neglected work
is beautifully revived.

GERMANY
Billy Mo
is a young Negro from the islands who has been
in Germany for
many years as a singer and trumpet player. Although his popularity in clubs
and for one night stands has kept him going for many
years, he has never
made the top of the charts with a record. Now, his newest record, a comedy
song entitled “Ich Kauf Mir Lieber Einen Tirolerhut”
(I’d Rather Buy A Tirol
Hat) has taken off like widefire and made the number one position for the first
time this week. The young star who can imitate Louis Armstrong to a tee with
his trumpet and also his voice has a bright future
in store for him here.
To Tamoure
or not to Tamoure
is no longer a question
in Germany. With
the
Hawaiian rhythm
taking
off
like
crazy
through
the
indie
recording
of
“Wini-Wini” released on Polydor, the new sound
is making its way into record
grooves with many top
stars. Teldec has released no
less than
3 Tamoure re-
cordings by
prominent
artists
such
as
Caterina
Valente, Gerd
Boettcher &
Wynn Hoop.
The lineup for the 3rd German Pop Music festival to be held in Baden-Baden
on June 15
is almost set. Ariola will send Carmela Corren, Anita Traversi and
either Louis
Neffs
or Gunnar Wiklund. Carmela
is from
Israel, Anita from
Italy, Louis from Belgium and Gunnar from
Scandinavia.
Electrola
is being
represented by Greetje Kauffeld, Chris Howland and probably Conny. Greetje
is from Holland and Chris from England.
Metronome has nominated Ann-Louise Hanson, Rainer Bertram Dorthe and
Eurovision “Song For Europe”
contest winner
(^rethe Ingmann. Ann-Louise,
Dorthe and Grethe are from Scandinavia.
Polydor
is sending Lolita and Rene Kollo with a third artist still to be chos-
en. Lolita is from Austria. Teldec will be represented by Gerd Boettcher, Billy
Mo and Gerd Timmermann with Billy being from
the Carribean
islands.
In
all, over 50%
of
all the artists
at the German pop festival will not be Ger-
man!
Philips has
not yet deceided on
its
artists.
Teldec A&R man Werner
Muller, who was instrumental
in the career of Caterina Valente, has sent an
offer for a record contract to ex-Queen Soraya. She has not yet replied.
Ralph Maria Siegel reports that his musical “Herr Kayser And The Night-
ingale” will be produced for TV
in full length soon. He also reports that the
Bossa Nova craze has been very good for him. He’s got over 54 Bossa Nova
records
going
for him
in Germany
as
a
publisher.
“Desifinado”
alone
has
racked up 26 recordings and “One Note Samba” 18 waxings.
Klaus Teubig
of
Esplanade music
repoi^ts
that
the new
2
sided
Polydor
waxing of Mariona with songs written by Lotar “You, You, You”
Olias and
Kurt Schwabach
is taking
off
to
hitsville. The
firm
is
also working hard on
the new Hein Riess Seamen’s recording for Polydor and of course the high
flying Freddy recording of “Junge, komm bald wieder,” which
is nearing the
million mark in sales.
Presidential
pal
Paul
Siegel writes
that
he
visited
the White House and
received a golden
tie
clip of President Kennedy’s PT boat as a present. Paul
also guested on WWDC
in Washington with
his Teldec-Dot waxing
of “The
Minuteman” by the Oederland Orchestra.
The
first
Bert Kaempfert
production
of Brenda
Lee
in German
has
just
been released and critics have picked the record to enjoy great success
here.
Bernard Mikulski has opened the guns for the start of his CBS representa-
tion here. He has started by releasing 300 LP’s in stereo and mono, about 100
EP’s and over 50 singles.
Hans Gerig i^eports that the new Rex Giido waxing of “Maddalena” which
hit the number
6
slot in the hit parade this week finished
first in the Radio
Stuttgart “Schlager Scala.”
Theo Seeger of Peer Music reports that
his
2 push items of the week are
“Cha-Cha Dell’ Amore” sung in German by Cocki Mazzetti and “What Will My
Mary Say” by Johnny Mathis both released by CBS with the Mazzetti waxing
coming out on the Primary label.
Publisher-producer Hans R. Beierlein has started a big publicity campaign
for the French teenager star Francoise Hardy. The top German magazines and
papers have brought picture stories over the young gal and she
is being con-
sidered for the main
role
in an up and coming music film by CCC film here.
Francoise’s
first German recording released by Vogue
is just getting started
here.
A&R man Hans Bertram of Polydor has called to our attention the fact that
the reason that Margot Eskens did not represent Germany at the “Song For
Europe” contest is due to
illness. Margot was to replace Heidi Bruhl who was
sick, but then Margot caught a bad case of flu and Heidi was able to step back
into the picture in time for the festival
in England. Sorry for any false im-
pressions, Hans.
That’s
it for this week
in Germany.

ALBUM REVIEWS
“MOON GAS”—Dick Hyman/Mary Mayo—MGM
E4119
Dick Hyman indulges
in a bit of electronic trick-
ery
to
pi'ovide
some
interesting
backdrops
for
songstress Mary Mayo on this MGM outing. The
pianist-organist doubled as composer on some
of
the tunes here and intersperses them with some
time-worn oldies. Hyman’s playing
is effective as
are
the
vocals by
the
lark,
but
excessive gim-
mickry gets
in the wav. Included here are “Moon
Gas.” “Stella By Starlight” and “I’m Glad There
is You.”
“THE INTRODUCTION OF THE KNOB LICK
UPPER 10,000”—Mercury SR 60780
The Knob Lick Upper 10,000
is a new folk group
with
an
authentic,
colorful
old-time
bluegrass
style. The group does not attempt to carbon-copy
the
yet
bluegrass
artists. They
do
have
a
dis-
tinctive,
modern
folk
style
perfectly
suited
to
this country brand of music. Most of tunes here
like “The Cuckoo,” “Bowling Green” and “Kathy
Kline”
are
standards,
but the crew has
created
a new
batch
of
exciting
arrangements. A
fine
showing.

“FREE

1964

lections. Best bets here are “Propulsion,” “Dicho-
tomy” and “Man Alone.”
“THE
NATURAL
SOUL”—Lou
Donaldson
Blue Note
4108
Lou Donaldson has acquired quite an impressive

cursions but
this new teaming up with Tommy

Grant Green
on

portunity

CLASSICAL PICKS OF THE WEEK
“KILIMANJARO”—Quartette

As the album’s

is based on the traditional, primitive Afro-
beats. However, instead

throughout.
“THE SOUND OF HOROWITZ”—Vladimir Hor-
owitz—Columbia
For his second Columbia program Vladimir Hor-
owitz has chosen some especially soothing, lyrical
selections
from
Schumann,
Schubert,
Scarlatti
and Scriabin. Although the music, is for the most
part, slow and lyrical it is extremely intricate to
play. The pianist’s incredible keyboard sensitivity
and
commanding
style
is
highlighted
on
such
popular
selections
as Schumann’s “Scenes From
Childhood” and “Scarlatti’s “Sonata In E Major.”
A superior classical offering.

Rachmaninoff’s “Symphony No.

AUSTRALIA
Radio
stations 2SM
(Sydney)
and 3AK
(Melbourne)
joined
forces
some
months ago to introduce the
first
direct landline
interstate disk-jockey show
featuring Bob Rogers. The project has obviously been successful because both
stations are again
co-operating and are now
issuing
the
first National Top
100 Chart to appear in Australia;
the chart
is prepared each week and
dis-
tributed from both
stations. The chart
is based on record
sales
in both Mel-
bourne and Sydney
(between them
these two
cities account for
better than
75% of Australia’s total population) and gives
local recording artists
in both
cities a chance
to get chart ratings
in
other
States. 2SM
compiles the
best
selling
singles from
Sydney and 3AK
does
the same from Melbourne—the
two
lists are then broken down
to prepare the 2SM-3AK National Top
100.
This means that a local record rating well in Sydney
is assured of chart action
in Melbourne and vice versa—thereby giving the local artist some much needed
national recognition and
action.
_ American entertainer Frances Faye has returned to Australia for her second
nightclub season here in the last six months. She was a sensational success on
her first visit to this country and
it was announced then that she would return
as
soon
as
her commitments
in
America
were
cleared. From
all
reports,
Frances
is repeating the success she enjoyed on her
first
visit.
For sorne
time, Sydney and Melbourne music men have been concerned
at
the “barrier” being erected between Melbourne and Sydney
resulting
in
the
output of each city receiving little or no support in the other. With this situa-
tion damaging the prospects of local works overseas, Norman Whiteley of the
Belinda organization flew to Melbourne recently to confer with leading execu-
tives in the recording and publishing fields and with television producers. Firm
proposals were discussed for a complete reversal of relations between the two
-centers and announcements
can
be
expected
soon which
could
have
a
far-
reaching
effect on the future of Australian and New Zealand music both
at
Rome and
overseas. On
his
return, Whiteley commented
that he
believed
it
possible to establish a co-operation between Melbourne, Sydney, Brisbane and
Wellington such as the business had never known and was ready to go ahead
as soon as he got the green
light from Melbourne. With that established he
was then ready to bring in Adelaide, Perth and Hobart to the “common front.”
Already Belinda
is
sponsoring
the
publication
of Adelaide works—including
Rrass band material—^^in New Zealand and Australia
for eventual
export
to
United Kingdom and Europe generally. With the Johnny Devlin Music’s “Surf-
side” released on both Capitol and Bigtop Records
in USA and the UK and
others
to
follow,
the
Belinda Group
is making
big headway
with
its
1963
"“crash export” program.
It
is
true
that the Australian composer has never
had more opportunity but this
is
all the more reason why we should put our
own house in order between
States.
Dick Harkness
of the AWA
office (RCA
distributors)
in Melbourne organ-
ized a contest with Cann’s
(a leading retail house)
to promote the Elvis Pres-
ley film “Girls, Girls, Girls,” which
is now showing at the Barclay Theatre
in
Melbourne. They are searching for a girl who looks most like Laurel Goodwin,
ivho plays opposite Presley in the movie. Prizes include wearing apparel, fash-
ion and beauty courses and soundtrack albums from RCA.
Festival Records has issued an unusual and well produced single by famous
Australian
film
actor Chips
Rafferty. The “A” deck
is
called
the “The Big
Fight” and was written by popular vocalist Jay Justin. With worldwide con-
troversy raging over the
fight business,
it seems
likely that this release will
-catch heavy
action.
It should be noted
that “The Big Fight” was
recorded
and released before the match which resulted
in the recent death

in the United
States.

NARAS ANNOUNCES GRAMMY FINALISTS
Jew York, April 15—A total of 240 records in 39 different categories are com-
leting for the annual “Grammy” Awards, according to
final ballots being re-
eived today by members
of the National Academy
of Recording Arts and
Sciences. (NARAS).
Appearing most often on
this year’s
lists
of outstanding
artistic
achieve-
nent award
nominations
are
three
vocal
records,
two comedy
albums
and
ne instrumental performance
in
the pop and
jazz
field, and a
recording
of
iolin selections plus two symphonies
in the classical segment.
Battling for “Record
of the Year” and
also named
in
several
other
cate-
:ories are singers Tony Bennett with
“I Left My Heart In San
Francisco,”
lay
Charles with
“I
Can’t
Stop
Loving You” and Sammy
Davis,
Jr.
with
What Kind Of Fool Am I?” plus saxist Stan Getz and guitarist Charlie Byrd
,nd
their bossa nova
version
of
“Desiginado.” Nat King
Cole’s “Rambling
lose” and Joe
Harnell’s “Fly Me To The Moon Bossa Nova” complete the
ecord of the year nominations.
Bennett, Charles and the Getz-Byrd duo are also listed among the
five “Al-
lum
of

with

omni-present comedy

lations. Biggest vote-getter of

in eight categories.
Vladimir Horowitz’s album

nd two symphonies by Gustav Mahler,

“REX GILDO”—Capitol T10338
Rex Gildo
is one of West Germany’s most popular
chanters, and the young songster makes a strong
bid
for American
acceptance
with
this
premier
Capitol LP outing. With a long list of screen and
disk
credits
to
his name,
the
singer
delivers
a
string of American and. European hits in a highly
professional way exhibiting a gimmick-free, easy-
going
style.
Easy-listening
bands
here
are
“Speedy
Gonzales,”
“Walk
On
By,”
“On
The
Street Where You Live” and “Rosina.” The Ger-
man teen
idol could make
it big on this
side too.
“FOLK SONG FESTIVAL”—Walter
Forbes —
RCA Victor LSP 2670
Perhaps,
one
of
the most
glaring
traits
lacking-
in
today’s
crop
of
folksingers
is
authenticity.
Newcomer Walter
Forbes
displays
a
feelingful,
sensitive,
authentic
understanding
of
the
folk
idiom
on
this
his
Victor LP bow. The
chanter-
guitarist has a rich, wide-range voice and an im-
pressive,
natural
delivery.
While
backed
by
a
chorus, Forbes dishes up top-drawer reading of a
fine batch
of both
old and new folk items. Best
bets here include “Little Margaret,” “Jane, Jane”
and “Pastures Of Plenty.”
“SURF
DRUMS”—The
Lively
Ones—Del
Fi
DFLP1231
The
popularity
of
surfing and
its music
on
the
West coast has brought a deluge
of
surfin’ LP’s
to the market, but its acceptance
is
still primarily
West
coast.
'This
instrumental
group
unleashes
its talents on a bag of tunes with the hard-drivin’,
momentum gathering rhythm that typifies
surf-
ing.
Included
here
is
the
current
biggie,
“Wild
Weekend” along with lesser known items such as
“Surfer Boogie,” “Shootin’ The Pier” and
“Hill-
billie Surf.” The teen dance set should get plenty
of enjoyment from the disk.
“THE LUSTY TRUSTY BUSTER”—Peggy Lord
—Stereoddities C1903
Peggy Lord
is
a
modified Rusty Warren,
Belle
Barth
etc., who
sings
slightly naughty songs
in
an
engaging
manner. Accompanying
herself
on
the guitar, the husky-voiced lark displays an
in-
fectious vocal quality and polished delivery as she
dispenses folksy ditties in an off-hand way. Plenty
of chuckles and good humor to be had here as the
thrush
renders
“When
Your
Lover
Has
Gone
Astray,” “How To Judge A Nightclub” and the
highlight
track, “Mortgage Man.” The disk
is a
pleasing
session
that
should win
the
songstress
lots of new admirers.
“THE POET OF THE ORGAN”—Jesse Crawford
—Vocalion VL3692
Jesse
Crawford
steps
out
with
a
bright,
easy-
listening package of tunes on the electronic organ
for
Vocalion.
Plenty
of
keyboard
artistry
and
musicianship here as the instrumentalist delivers
some
sparkling
arrangements
of
such
melodic
items as “Hawaiian Honeymoon,” “The March Of
The Matadors” and “Harlem Holiday.” The
disk
is a pleasant late hours mood companion.
“SING OUT! HOOTENANNY”—Various Artists
—^Folkways FN 2513
A hootenanny
is
folk getogether and
this
Folk-
ways session boasting the accomplished talents of
such
luminaries
as Leon
Bibb, Fred
Hellerman,
Betty Sanders and Pete Seeger should find favor
with
a
host
of
folkniks. Most
of the
sides
here
were in 1950-55 period but their spirit is as mean-
ingful today and when they were
first recorded.
Best bets here include “All
I Want
Is Union” by
Pete
Seeger, “This Land
Is My Land” by Leon
Bibb
and
“Commonwealth
Of
Toil”
by
Betty
Sanders.
JAZZ PICKS OF THE WEEK
“AFRO-BOSSA” — Duke
Ellington —
Reprise
R 6069
The multi-talented Duke
Ellington
increases
his
range with this self-produced, swingin’ bosa nova
set. Ellington does not attempt to render the bossa
nova rhythms
in an “authentic” Latin
style.
In-
stead, the vet jazzman has woven the new sounds
into the complex microcosm of his Afro-oriented
big band. The effect comes
off amazingly well as
the
ork
dishes
up
first-rate
readings
of
“Silk
Lace,” “Pyramid” and “Eighth
Veil.”
All
of El-
lington’s many fans should come out in force for
the package.
“MIDNIGHT BLUE”—Keny Burrell—Blue Note
4123
In
the past few
years, Kenny
Burrell has come
into the national limelight as one of the best jazz
guitarists
around. On
this
Blue Note
entry the
versatile musician showcases his
ability to make
valid jazz-blues statements. Burrell
is teamed up
with an accomplished group
of musicians includ-
ing Stanley Turrentine on tenor sax. Major Hol-
ley on bass. Bill English on drums and Ray Bar-
retto
on
conga.
Burrell
takes
the
lead
as
he
renders
some
highly-personal
renditions
of
“Mule,”
“Soul
Lament”
and
“Saturday
Night
Blues.” A standout showing.
“STRAIGHT AHEAD”—Terry
Gibbs Quartet-
Verve V 8496
Terry Gibbs has earned many laurels
in the past
with
his
distinctive, unpretentious brand of jazz
and this new Verve set ranks as one of the vibra-
phonist’s most satisfying disks
in
quite a while.
Gibbs
does
not
utilize
gimmicks
but
breezes
through
the
selections
here
in
a
relaxed,
free-
flowing, easy-on-the-ears fashion. Among the best
tracks are “Hey Jim,” “On Green Dolphin Street”
and “For Keeps.”
“TRUMPET
CALIENTE”—Don
Goldie—Argo
LP 708
“Hot Trumpet,” which
is
this album’s
tag,
per-
fectly
characterizes
Don
Goldie’s
vibrant,
swingin’ trumpet stylings. But that
is only part
of
Goldie’s
artistry. The
jazzman’s
middle-road
style
couples mellow
tone,
technical
ability and
sensitivity. While backed by a small, professional
combo,
Goldie
turns
in
top-flight
readings
of
“Fast Thought,” “I Hear About A Rhapsody” and
“There
Will Never Be Another You.”
Pleasant
late mood hours companion.
CLASSICAL PICK OF THE WEEK
“RICHTER
IN
ITALY”—Sviatoslav
Richter—
Angel S36104
Sviatoslav
Richter
plays
three works by
Schu-
mann on
this
excellent Angel
disk. The
pianist
displays
his
typical
verve
and
forcefulness
on
these works which run the gamut from exciting
and
thunderous
to
soft and
somber. As
an
in-
terpreter
of Schumann, Richter
is
sensitive and
dynamic. This
recital includes the Sonata No.
2
in G
Minor,
Papillons and
Carnival
of
Vienna.
Considered by some
to
be
a
bit
heavy-handed,
Richter’s brilliance and genius cannot be
denied.
A potent classical offering.
pii?gMTr.
“COUNTRY & WESTERN CONFIDENTIAL”—
Gene Martin—Starday SLP226
Gene Martin perpetrates a country music expose
on
this Starday album geared for fun
listening.
The guitarist-chanter spoofs many of the biggest
idols
of the
country music
fans, the Grand
Ole

Pye Records will launch a new series devoted to Rhythm and Blues. Material
will be drawn from the American Chess, Checker and Argo catalogs and
will
feature such artists as Bo Diddley, Sonny Boy Williamson, Chuck Berry, etc.

as American
stars new British r&b exponents

dis-

field

I Treat You” (Howlin’
Wolf)
; “Help Me” (Sonny Boy Williamson) and Britain’s Cyril Davies’ “Coun-
try Line Special.” This

left for a three-week

inde-

ALBUM REVIEWS
nviejca
Crtl-JNO
“FESTIVAL OF FAITH”—Fred Waring—Capitol
ST1848
Fred Waring and his' Pennsylvanians sing a host
of
the
traditional
songs
of
faith
on
this new
Capitol outing. With a series of religious holidays
coming up, the album should get plenty of sales
action. Frank Davis
is
the featured
soloist here
and some
first-rate arrangements were provided
by Roy Rin^ald and Harry
Simeone.
Included
in the long list of sacred songs are “God Of Our
Fathers,” “Sholom Alechem,” and “Battle Hymn
Of The Republic.”
“THE SWEETEST SOUNDS” — Wayne King —
Decca DL 4368
Although new dance crazes come and go, there is
still a potent market for the easy-listening tradi-
tional terpsichorean sounds of Wayne King. The
vet orkster reaches into his rich bag of danceable
tunes and comes un with a delightful selection of
tunes
culled from Broadway
and
flicks
on
this
outing. The band breezes through some top-notch,
lush
arrangements
of
“The
Sweetest
Sounds,”
“Days
Of
Wine
And
Roses”
and
“Al-Di-La.”
Pleasant late hours mood companion.
“IN MEMORIAM PATSY CLINE”—Everest 1217
Patsy Cline’s tragic death last month has sparked
a renewed interest
in her earlier recordings, and
this session from Everest spotlights some of her
earlier hits. The country songstress surveys some
soulful
country-oriented
tunes
with
polish
and
feeling
as she
includes
such
oldies as “Walking
After Midnight,” “Honky Tonk Merry Go Round”
and “Let The Teardrops Fall.” The lark’s
legion
of admirers will surely want to add this album to
their collections.
“PRESENTING THE HUNTSMEN” —
Briar
International M 106
Part of the current revival
in folk music can be
attributed
to
interest from
the
nation’s
college
students. It
is not sui-prising that groups of
col-
lege folksingers should spring up. The Huntsmen
are one such group. On this their initial LP entry
these four youngsters display a feelingful, moving
understanding of the folk idiom as they render a
dozen
sturdies with
the assurance
of
a crew of
long-successful
pros. Among the
best
tracks on
the disk are “Sinner Man,” “Dark As A Dungeon”
and “500 Miles.”
“TO MY SOMEONE”—Marty Bronson—Norman
NL 108
Marty Bronson, who is the owner of a popular St.
Louis night
club,
is
also
a
fine
versatile
singer
if this, his premiere LP,
is any indication
of his
talents. The chanter has
rich, deep, wide-range,
legit-styled
baritone
voice
and
a
commanding,
professional
delivery. With
a
top-flight backing
supplied by Frank Harris, Bronson turns in stand-
out readings of “My Coloring Book,” “They Call
The Wind Maria” and “Goodnight My Someone.”
Loads of potential here.
“RIVIERA”—Bruno Canfora—Vesuvius 4412
Here
is a
session
of happy, moodful tunes with
an
Italian
flavor by
orkster Bruno
Canfoi'a
on
Vesuvius.
Lots
of relaxing mood music
here
as
the orchestra plays the familiar melodies symbolic
of the
Mediterranean.
Lots
of
lush
strings add
to the warmth of such pop melodies as “La Mer,”
“Volare,” “Torna A Surriento” and “Santa Lucia.”
The disk
is a pleasant late hours listening com-
panion.
JAZZ PICKS OF THE WEEK
“HOBO FLATS”—Jimmy Smith—Verve V 8544
In the past few years, Jimmy Smith has made a
significant
contribution
to
jazz with
his
distinc-
tive, highly-personal organ stylings. On this new
Verve
session Smith proves that
his
vital, fresh
style
is
still present by refusing to carbon-copy
even
himself.
Oliver
Nelson
has come up
with
first-rate arrangements
this time out and, while
backed by
a
big band, the
organist swings
su-
perbly
on “Hobo
Flats,” “Walk
Right
In”
and
“The
Preacher.”
Disk
should
score
in
both
the
jazz and pop markets.
“THE NEW SOUNDS OF MAYNARD FERGU-
SON”—Cameo C 1046
Maynard Ferguson kicks olf this Cameo bow with
a
spirited,
swingin’
reading
of
“Take
The
‘A’
Train” and
sets a polished pace which he main-
tains throughout the
set. As on his previous ses-
sions
the
tirnmneter fronts
a
12-piece band
but
the
individual
musicians
get
a
chance
to
wail
in the solo spotlight. There’s something for every-
one
in this varied jazz program from bossa nova
to
evergreens. Among
the
best
bets
here
are
“Gravy Waltz,” “At The Sound Of The Trumpet”
and “Danny Boy.” Disk should move quickly.
“UP & DOWN”—Horace Parian—Blue Note 4082
In today’s competitive jazz world, many pianists
are
inclined
to
be
sloppy under
the
banner
of
soulful
sounds.
Fortunately, Horace Parian
is
a
delightful
exception
to
the
rule.
The
talented
88’er
possesses
the
ability
to
communicate
in
straight-forward
technically
competent
state-
ments. Parian is in top-drawer form on this new
Blue Note
set of jazz-blues
selections. Best bets
here
include “Up And Down,” “The Other Part
Of Town”
and
“Lonely
One.” A
splendid
jazz
offering.
“THE GROUP—RCA Victor LSP2663
Here
is the premier LP on Victor by The Group,
a
trio
of vocalists with a fresh approach and
a
cohesiveness
that marks them
as
an
important
addition
to
the
world
of
jazz
singing.
Lyrical
ballad readings and rhythmic
scat deliveries are
included
on
this top-drawer
session.
Slick
sides
here are “Joey, Joey, Joey,” “Something’s Com-
ing” and “The Second Time Around.” Watch this
one for early acceptance.
“BOLA SETE BOSSA NOVA”—Fantasy 8349
That
special,
elite group
of bossa nova
experts
from
Brazil and
this
country must
include
the
name Bola Sete, an authoritative exponent of the
Brazilian
beat,
and
a
first-rate
guitarist.
The
artist makes
his LP debut on Fantasy with this
program
of bossa nova stylings that
reflect
his
sensitivity for the music. The guitarist plays his
own compositions along with those of Jobim and
Bonfa on this
set which includes “Sweet Thing,”
“Manha De
Carnival” and
“Without You.” The
disk is a distinctive bossa nova offering.
CLASSICAL
“THE GOSPEL ECHOES” — Warner
Brothers
W1499
Gospel music has become a potent force
in both
folk
and
pop
music
contributing much
in
the
areas
of melody,
lyric and rhythm.
This
excep-
tionally fine group. The Gospel Echoes, effectively
pinpoint this importance and are topnotch spokes-
men for gospel music. On
this Warner Brothers
LP, the
trio
sings and
plays
the
songs
of Jim
(Chief) Wetherington of the Statesmen Quartet.
Easy-listening bands here are “Wake Me Shake
Me Lord,” “The Future Looks Brighter To Me”
and “Tell Them What It’s All About.”
HAYDN : Six Canzonettes, Peter Pears, Benjamin
Britten—London OS25321
Six
short songs by Haydn and
six piano
frag-
ments by Johann
Christian Holderlin are
deftly
performed by Peter Pears
(tenor) and Benjamin
Britten
(pianist) on this excellent classical offer-
ing from London. The
classical purity of Haydn
and the lyrical line of Holderin’s works add up to
a bit of pleasant old world esoterica. Both artists
here reflect
sensitivity and understanding of the
respective
compositions. The
disk

^^x<^RGENTINA>
Instead of regular news, here’s information about a very interesting study
about the biggest part of the Argentine record market, and some comments
that will give Cash Box readers a very clear idea about the record scene
in
this country.
This
study was made by an
independent recording company
in
an
effort
to know
better
what’s
happening with
record
sales
in
Argentina, who
are
the
buyei's, and
so
on.
Several
questions were presented
in written form
to
more than one hundred
record
dealers
in Buenos Aires and
its
neighboring
cities, which account for a very big part of the whole
sales
in the
country.
These were the questions, and the most repeated answers:
Which is the record brand you sell best?: A great majority reported that CBS
is the label they
sell
best. There were some RCA and Odeon answers,
too.
Which
is
the
size and
speed
preferred
by
your customers?
:
The
single
33
record won
this
part.
It must be noted
that this
record has been extremely
successful
in Argentina, while
the
single
45 disappeared
after a very short
struggle. In general, the 45 single had very big trouble during all its existance,
while
the
single
33 became popular
in
a few months.
Double
33’s
are
also
becoming good
sellers, although
in
this
field
the
7” 45 rpm record has
still
some
force, and
some
diskeries
continue
releasing
novelties
on
this
speed.
78 rpm records have practically disappeared
in big
cities and
for promotion
uses.
Which type of music do you
sell best?
: Most retailers answered “twist”,
al-
though
it seems
certain
that by
this word they mean
the
current
type
of
chart
riders
(Anka,
Sedaka, Enrique Guzman). The word
“ballad”
is
very
little used in the country.
Who buys more records?
: The average age of the customers
is
surprisingly
low. Of
course,
it’s
no
secret that many
of them
are
teenagers. But
there
are younger buyers,
too!
It results that there are a
lot of 8 and
9 year
old
buyers, who
are
directly
impressed
by TV
programs
and
afterwards
ask
their parents
to buy them
the
records. We have
personally noted that even
artists
like
Antonio
Prieto,
whose
program
has
been
mainly
directed
to
grown up
people
capable
of buying
a
Rambler,
are
tremendously
popular
among children.
Which
is the main sales force for records: the tune or the artist?; The tune
outnumbered the
artist.
In some
cases, a very popular artist may
sell fairly
well a poor
single, but two or three bad waxings may “kill” an
artist. New-
comers have no trouble in reaching the charts when they present a good record.
Who are the most popular Classical music Composers?
: In this order, Beeth-
oven, Tchaikovsky and Chopin. During
1961 and
1962,
the market for other
“more
difficult”
classical music composers
widened, allowing
to
release
rec-
ords
like
the
“Archive”
series,
and
others
of more
specialized
type
than
regular
classical music
releases.
Do you
sell modern tango music?
In
general, the answer
is
yes.
This part
of the market
is
also wider than two years
ago. Astor
Piazzolla,
the much
discussed modern
tango
leader,
has
fair
sales. Eduardo
Rovira
has
also
a
good group
of
“fans”.
In standard tango
music,
there
are no
trends, nor
a
definite favorite
artist.
Who are the best selling folk music groups?
: No changes on this matter: Los
Fronterizos, Los Chalchaleros, Los Cantores de Quilla Huasi and newcomers
Los Huanca Hua, who started last year and have been selling well since then.
Which
is the best way
to promote record sales?
: A great majority answered:
Radio
Promotion, and
in some
cases:
live TV. Newspaper
ads,
posters and
other printed ways
of promotion weren’t too
well
considered.
Do the customers
prefer price or quality ?
: The answers were more
inclined
to “price” than
to
“quality.” As we have reported before, one
of the reasons
maybe
that
there
isn’t
really
a
big
quality
difference
between
low
priced
albums
(there are no low priced
singles)
and standard
LP’s,
since
in many
cases
“promotional”
albums
are
better
presented
than
standard
ones,
and
the pressing is always the same. Only high priced
lines (Grand Award, Audio
Fidelity, United Artists and Time)
are may
claim
a big
difference between
its
packing
and
the
“promotional”
records
one.
Besides,
prices
of
regular
albums are too high for teen buyers, who cannot ask their parents 500 pesos
“to buy
a
record”
excepting very few
justified
cases. The
“Club
del
Clan”
series
(priced
at
199)
didn’t
find
this
trouble, and
this
helps them
to
build
huge
sales.
Do you believe there may be some new idea to be applied to records?
: Strange
as
it may seem,
retailers seem afraid
of new ideas
in records. Most of them
should prefer the 33
single and 33 LP records remain unchanged.
Which
is
the
radio program
you
have heard about most?
:
“Escalera
a
la
Fama” by Ruben Machado, on Radio Excelsior. “Escala Musical,” same radio,
also got several answers.

JOHN HAMMOND
NEW YORK—Columbia Records has
promoted John Hammond
to
the po-
sition
of Director
of Talent Acquisi-
tioning,
according
to
an
announce-
ment from David Kapralik, pop A & R
director. Hammond,
a
longtime
jazz
disk
producer-authority,
will
be
re-
sponsible nationally for scouting, au-
ditioning and recommending potential
talent
for
the
Columbia,
Epic
and
Ohek
labels.
He
will
also
maintain
liason with artists,
artists’ managers,
agents
and
representatives
of
night
clubs,
concerts,
music
festivals
and
motion
pictures.
In
addition, he
will
arrange
and
conduct
auditions
throughout the country.
Hammond
will
direct the
adminis-
tration and review of musical material
submitted
to
Columbia,
and
he
also
will serve
in an advisory capacity
to
the Archive series of classic jazz per-
formances, a series which he created.
He
also
will
select
participants
for
Columbia’s
Teen
Talent
Auditions.
Commenting on his new post, Ham-
mond
said,
“.
.
.
I
consider that the
recording
industry
is
the
greatest
talent-developer
in
the
country. The
radio
and
television
industries
have
forfeited
their
leadership
by
their
heavy
reliance
on
talent
developed
through
recordings.”
“I
think,
he
added,
“the
time
is
right for bringing back
to the popu-
lar
music
scene
the
challenges
that
can
only happen with
the
discovery
and
development
of new
talent.
.
.”
He has been associated with Colum-
bia
since 1932 when he produced the
first
recordings
of
Fletcher
Hender-
son. During
this
period, he
also
re-
corded
Bessie
Smith, Duke
Ellington
and
Mildred
Bailey.
He
discovered
Billie Holiday when
she was
fifteen,
and was producer of most of the now
classic Teddy Wilson and
Billie Holi-
day

of

through
1938.
Other

PHILADELPHIA—At

Particular

(rec-
ord

and

hold meetings with each NARM
rec-
ord

ule.

“This format has proven one of the

chandiser
members,
urging' them
to
check their figures
of

the product which sold well and profit-
ably for them, and come prepared to
place orders at the mid-year meeting,

The NARM

uct,

to

“most

25,000

"ON THE BANDSTAND”—Buck Owens—Capitol
ST1S79
Here is a first-rate package of country tunes that
aptly showcase the vocal-instrumental
talents
of
Buck Owens. The songster
is backed in his efforts
by Don
Rich, Jay McDonald, Kenny
Pierce and
Ken
Presley. The
session
kicks
off with
a
duet
by Owens and
Rich and continues with
easy-lis-
tening
versions
of
such
country
standards
as
"King Of
Fools,”
“Cotton
Fields” and
“Kickin’
Our Hearts Around.” The
chanter’s fans should
come out in strength for this one.
“LOTSA BOSSA NOVA”—Kenny Burrell—Kapp
KL1326
The Kenny Burrell Octet unleashes its talents on
a dozen
oldies and newies with
a
distinct bossa
nova
flavor on
this Kapp outing. Launching the
session with
the
Glenn
Miller
favorite, “String
Of
Pearls,” the boys continue with some
stand-
out
versions
of
‘“The
Sweetest
Sounds,” “Two
Different Worlds” and “Star Eyes.” The
disk
is
geared for both dancing and listening and should
score in the marketplace.
“GERMAN HITS”—Rhinelanders—Cameo
C10.53
Conductor
Ted
Tyle
leads
his
Rhinelanders
through a merry, melodic romp
of oom pah pah
biggies that span four decades. Some of the tunes
here are traditional and others came
into popu-
larity
since WW
II. There
is plenty
of listening
and dancing pleasure to be had here as the band
essays
“Liechtensteiner
Polka,”
“Lili
Marlene”
and “O Mein Papa.” Lots
of dual-market appeal
here.
“THE LATIN BIT”—Grant
Green—Blue
Note
411
Grant Green perfectly combines the free-flowing
elements
of
the

idiom
with

jazz-
blues sounds on this

entry.
The guitarist is backed by a crew of accomplished
jazzmen
including Johnny Acea on

dell Marshall on bass and Willie Bobo on drums.
The
mood
here
is

and

as

“Mama
Inez.”
Jazzophiles
should

“TEN
DUETS FOR TWO
GUITARS ”—Music
Minus One 4011
Here is another instructional package from Music
Minus One aimed at would be guitarists. The set
includes
lead guitar arrangements
for ten
ever-

The novice can play along with Carl Kress on this

“My Blue Heaven.” Plenty of interest here.
“A NIGHT AT MEXICO

The music of El Zarco and his Mariachi Autland

“Las

“POLKAS FROM THE ALPS”—Hans Hansberg-
er—United Artists UAS 6259

“SHEARING BOSSA NOVA”—George Shearing

1873

of sales power.

Roelants, salesmanager and De Bie, artistic director and
his wife. Greene was

wife. He was very pleased
to hear how popular he was
with Belgian televiewers. CB had the opportunity to have breakfast with Bel-
gian capital. He was disappointed to hear that Belgian audiences cannot re-
ceive “Bonanza”
in

ecent years to the personal management of TV star Andy Griffith, will be
ling an annual
benefit show at Ohio University for
his Richard 0. Linke
ilarship Fund
for the

stints, a similar show for the scholarship
i

“SOMETHIN’ SLICK”—Brother
Jack McDuff—
Prestige 7265
Jack McDuff is a major example of the new front-
seat status of organ artists
in the mainstream of
modern jazz. McDuff successfully couples techni-
cal excellence with a fresh, original emotional ap-
proach. On this
set he
is
fine company including
Kenny Burrell on guitar and Joe Dukes on drums
as
he
offers
rousing
versions
of
“Our
Miss
Brooks,” “How
High
The Moon”
and
“It’s A
Wonderful World.” Deejays should really dig the
set.
“LET FREEDOM RING”—Jackie McLean—Blue
Note 4106
Although there are many new-wave
alto
saxists
around today, there are few who are as
original
as
Jackie
McLean.
The
talented
jazzman
has
molded the musical approaches of a dozen current
and while-back wallers and comes up with a style
that
is obviously all his own. On this set, McLean
is backed by a first-rate crew of jazzmen includ-
ing Walter Davis on piano, Herbie Lewis on bass
and
Billy Higgins on drums. But the
solo
spot-
light is firmly on McLean as he offers
“I’ll Keep
Loving You,” “Rene” and “Omega.” Superior jazz
fare.

“THE MEDIEVAL JAZZ QUARTET”—Classic
Editions CE1050
This
offbeat
entry from
Classic
Editions
fuses
medieval chamber music with the contemporary
jazz idiom with some very
effective
results. The
quartet
plays
the
recorder
and
gets
a modern
assist from George Dvivier on
bass, A1 Schack-
man on guitar and Paul Motian on drums. Way
out “Hip” liner notes complete this unusual pack-
age. Included are “How High The Moon,” “Nature
Boy” and “Autumn Leaves.” The idea was
origi-
nated and arranged by Bob Dorough. An
inter-
esting
offering.

“WONDERLAND OF OPERA”—Andre
Koste-
lanetz—Columbia CL 1995
Andre
Kostelanetz
has
helped

in-
terest
in

re-
leases but this new LP containing selections from
18 world-famous

The

is exactly right and the members
of the

Highlights

and

SAINT-SAENS: Symphony No.
3, Marcel Dupre,
Detroit
Symphony
Orchestra,
Paul
Paray/Con-
ductor—Mercury SR90331
This
two-part
classical
offering
from
Mercury
features
Marcel
Dupre
at
the
organ
playing
Saint-Saens third symphony and the Detroit Sym-
phony
Orchestra
with
Paul Paray
at
the helm
performing Symphony in B Flat Major by Ernest
Chausson. The subtle romanticism of Saint-Saens’
opus
and
the
fiery
emotionalism
of
Chausson’s
work make for sharp contrast
here. Both works
are beautifully performed and classical
devotees
should
find
it
a
worth-while
addition
to
their
collections.

######## cb 1963-05-18 p47  [african\s+beat]

Philips Records has started a big sales promotion for the new dance rhythm,
Tamoure, introduced here from
Tahiti and catching the
interest
of our fans.
Nippon Victor, representing Philips here, released the
first Tamoure LP from
the catalog of Smash Records. Also, the label
is going to offer Tamoure dance
courses
all over the
country,
with
representative
dancers
and
the Tamoure
twin
sisters going along.
“All
Star
Festival”
thfe UN album,
released here
at
the end
of February
through
the
cooperation
of
all
our recording companies,
has
been
enjoying
fantastic
sales. Many of our famous
artists
also have been doing work even
bigger success. Yukio Hashi, Nippon Victor’s No.
1 singer, attended the charity
sale held at a department store in the center of Tokyo, presenting poetry cards
with his signature to every customer who bought the
record, and
helped get
an excellent
sale of hundreds of copies
in thirty minutes.
Goodyear Tire Co., American
tire maker,
is presenting records through
its
sales
agencies
in Japan. The aim
is
to promote
the
tire
industry image
to
music fans, and,
accordingly,
the
prices
are much cheaper than
those
of
re-
cording companies. The sales route
is not only recoi'd shops but chain
stores,
gasoline shops, automobile parts shops and car dealers. The
first
issue
is an
LP
of
14
compositions,
including
the Duke
Ellington
Band’s
“Take
The A
Train.” Bobby Hacket Band’s “When
the
Saints Go
Marchin’
In.” Goodyear
plans to issue
13 LP’s
in
tw'o years. Second
issue features Louis Armstrong,
3rd Eddie Condon. Performances
are newly recorded by
the
artists
under
a
special
contract.
The Mexican
vocal group,
Candilejas,
arrived here May
11. The members
are Raguel Michael Talento, Guillemo Romero Zaraboza, Leon Bernal and Ibar
Leonel Barraza. As Latin songs are quite popular here in Tokyo, their arrival
was eagerly anticipated by many of our music fans.

BELGIUM
World famous trumpet player, Chet Baker, stopped over
in Brussels for a
day. His
visit was related to the preparation of a Chet Baker broadcast for
the weekly jazz program of Roger Adams at Flemish radio station and called
“Jazz in Beligum.” The program lasted a whole hour. It is interesting to note
that three Belgium
soloists participated: Jack Pelzer,
alto,
flute and soprano,
Benoit
Quersin,
base, and Rene Thomas,
guitar.
Also
on
the program was
American drummer John Harris, who played with Horace Silver at one time.
Top
event
recently
in
connection with SA Gramophone
activity, was the
appearance of a new Helen Shapiro record—a single. 'The side that has a spe-
cial appeal
is the one featuring “Woe
Is Me.” Helen went to Nashville, Ten-
nessee, to record this and other tunes. Also on the market is a new Cliff Rich-
ard song (Columbia)
called “Lucky Lips.” A new name on the Capitol label as
far as Belgium
is concerned—is Dick Dale. Mr. Kirsch, general manager for
SA Gramophone, had a business talk with Mr. Rouzies, general manager for
Bathe Marconi records. There is a great demand for the newest Adamo single
with “Amour perdu” as the battle-horse, the revei-se side showing “J’aime une
fleur.” On the
first day more than
10,000
disks went to the
dealers. Adamo
has been guest at the Olympia theater in Paris, together with
Cliff Richard
and The Shadows.
On her way to the film festival in Cannes, American movie star Bette Davis,
accompanied by director Robert
Aldrich, stopped
over
at
Brussels National
Airport for two hours. She talked with the press at a reception.
Ray Charles gave a concert at the Palais des Beaux Arts
in Brussels. The
Genius was loudly cheered by thousands
of jazz fans who
often interrupted
his show by shouting and by rhythmic handclapping. Also on the stage were
The Raylettes and the Ray Charles orchestra. 'The day after he performed in
Antwerp. He granted interviews
to Flemish TV, one for the weekly “Echo”
program,
presented by Jan Bauwens and
the
other
to
Frans Romeyns
(of
Cash
Box), who
introduces
the record program
called “Good
Records, Good
Friends” (Leuke Plaatjes, goede Maatjes”).
News of Palette records (and World Music)
is of a rather unusual nature:
Andre, guitar soloist of The Cousins
(hit: “Dansevise”) had his guitar stolen
out of his
car. He discovered the loss just before leaving for Lille where the

gp'oup arrived

to bon'ow a new

back

called;
the thief had tried to

strument
is now
in
the
custody
of
the
law. The
Cousins
meanwhile
have
turned out a French version EP, featuring “Marche Tout Droit” (Walk Right

is one of the best ren-
derings of the Eurovision success.

“Pro

CLASSICAL PICK OF THE WEEK
BEETHOVEN: String Quartet No. 12 in E Flat
Major; The Budapest
String Quartet—Columbia
ML5783
Beethoven’s String Quartet No. 12, written toward
the end of his career when he was already deaf,
is an abrupt departure from
the noiimal string
quartet patterns and requires more serious listen-
ing than some of his earlier works. The Budapest
String Quartet performs this four movement opus
with sensitivity and
sincerity. Devotees of cham-
ber music will find this an important addition to
their classical
shelves.

Surfin'
Push
LOS ANGELES—In an unusual three-
way tie-up, Del-Fi Records, the Music
City retail chain and KFWB last week
launched a “surfin’ hearse” promotion
to
call attention to the label’s line of
surfing albums and singles and
spot-
lighting
its
top
surfing
artists,
the
Lively
Ones.
Stunt
originated when
Del-Fi prexy Bob Keene learned that
southeim
California
teenagers, num-
bering
some
100,000
surfers,
have
been buying up used hearses
to
cart
their
surf
boards
to
the
beach, and
decided
to give
one away
to
attract
attention to his firm’s surfing catalog.
Clyde Wallich’s Music
City joined
in
with heavy in-store Del-Fi displays in
their three
stores, where any young-
ster can
pick up
his
entry blank
to
win
the
hearse,
a
1948
Packard,
or
second
prizes
of
new
surfboards.
KFWB tied-in with the promotion by
scheduling hourly plugs on the “surfin’
hearse” from
all their deejays. Keene
(second from
left)
is shown* with the
Lively Ones and Del-Fi surfin’ queen,
Rachel Roman, in the above pic.

Liberty's Promo & Sales
Department Are One Now
HOLLYWOOD—Under
the
direction
of Don Bohanan, national sales man-
ager of Liberty Records, an “entirely”
new
concept
in
the
handling
of
the
label’s 45RPM product goes into effect
immediately.
Bohanan
revealed
that
in
addition
to Bob Skaff’s duties as national pro-
motion
director
of
the
firm,
he
will
now
be responsible
for single record
sales including the schediuling of their
release dates.
Bohanan explained the move as an-
other step
in his firm’s climb “toward
single
sales
supremacy.” He
further
commented that
“promotion now
be-
comes
an
integral
part
of
the
sales
picture” and that he (Bohanan) would
continue to helm the sale of all Libeidy
products.
“Combining promo and
sales in the
single record market has proven suc-
cessful in a series of tests made earl-
ier,” said Bohanan. “A promotion man
can spot trends and,
if
in a
position
to
expedite
decisions,
would
be
as-
sured of a maximum
effort.”
To
assist him
in
his new
venture,
Skaff has appointed west coast promo
director Bud Dain
as
his
promotion
assistant.
Simultaneously
he
named
Bob Fead to coordinate the sales phase
of his expanded operation.

A major event for all Belgian singers in particular, and for singers of light
music with inteniational fame in general, took place
in Brussels a few days
ago. What we refer to
is the launching
of the production company Cine TV
Tecnic, which will produce show films, offering ample opportunities to Belgian
artists. Other kinds
of production are planned,
similar to the widely appre-
ciated “Dick Powell Show.” These
will be made available to TV
stations
all
over the world. The launching of this company, which
is considered as
quite
important and
is
without
precedent
in
our
country—as
probably
in many
other
countides
as
well—is
the
result
of
a
close
cooperation between
Staf
Knop, a joui-nalist on an important Flemish newspaper, and R. Devaux, a pro-
fessional photographer. While the former has written several successful plays,
the
latter
is well known
in show
circles as the regular photographer of the
Martini Terrace
in
Brussels, where
every
artist has
at
least
once been the

reception. Knop
will
act as the
artistic
director, whose main
task will consist
in seeking out talent, writing the
scripts and looking after
the realization. One of the
initial activities of the new company he told Cash
Box, will be the production of shows in the Far and Middle East. A
fii-st star-
studded show
is planned
in Beyrouth,
in the Lebanon, with the participation
of several famous
artists. We are looking forward to the
results which
the
new company will achieve. It will provide singers with an opportunity to gain
intemational acclaim and could in show business make quite a name for itself.
Its address is; Cine TV Tecnic, Department Cine de la S.A.R., Devaux, 35 rue
de Lausanne, Brussels
6.

“ANNETTE’S BEACH PARTY’’—Buena

BV3316
Annette tags this Buena Vista album outing after

The songstress exhibits a warm, lyrical voice and

on

Her many
admirers
should
dig
her treatment
of “Treat Him

“BEYOND THE SUNSET”—Hank
Williams—
MGM E 4138
Although Hank Williams’ tragic death cut short

is

presei’ved
for

countless

of
fans
through

like

set
the chanter
offers
a dozen

ratives in the best traditional country

liams
shines
on
“Pictures

“GOOD NIGHT SWEETHEART”—Morton Gould
—RCA Victor LM 2682
Morton
Gould, who has eamed many

of
evergreens
on

Victor mood
album.
The orkster has created some

ments for his big band which shines on “Tea For
Two,” “I Can’t Get Started” and “Through Your
Eyes To Your Heart.” Fine fare for dancing
or

“TROUBLE’S

cun-ently

outing

“BUHAINA’S DELIGHT”—Art Blakey &

Messengers—Blue Note 4104
Although

Messengers
swing

in

“Contemplation,” “Shaky Jake” and “Moon

Jazzophiles
should

for
