“THE MIRACLES ON STAGE”—Tamla 241
Here
is
another
in
Tamla’s
series
of reprded
“live”
disks—this
time
featuring
the
Miracles
who
are
constantly
represented
on
the R&B
charts with money-making
singles. On
this
ses-
sion the group recreates some of
its recent and
while-back
biggies
such
as “A
Love
She
Can
Count
On,”
“What’s
So
Good
About
Goodbye”
and
“You’ve
Really
Got A
Hold On
Me.” The
disk should score heavily in r&b markets.
“OFF
SHORE”—Santo
&
Johnny—Canadian-
American 1011
Santo & Johnny turn to the sea for the theme of
this new Canadian-American album geared espe-
cially for warm weather listening. The guitarists
gets some top-drawer backing from the orchestra
and chorus
of Mort Garson and come up
with
some ear-captivating renditions
of “Beyond The
Sea,” “Ebb
Tide” and “Beyond The
Reef.” The
boys could strike paydirt.
“CHUCK BERRY ON STAGE”—Chess LP1480
The
Chuck
Berry
originals,
“Memphis”
and
“Surfin’ USA” have
gotten
plenty
of
action
in
recent weeks, the latter a top ten tune. The com-
poser delivers them in rockin’ fashion on this ses-
sion cut “live” at the Tivoli Theater
in Chicago.
The excitement
is abundant here as the chanter
puts a jump tempo to good use on “Maybelline,”
“Brown
Eyed Handsome Man”
and
“Trick
Or
Treat.” The songster’s fans will dig the session.
“HITSVILLE, U.S.A.”—Sammy Lowe—RCA Vic-
tor LSP 2770
Sammy Lowe, who acquired quite a reputation as
an r&r arranger-conductor, comes up with a de-
lightful
instrumental
sampling
of
today’s
crop
of teen
hits. Lowe has created his arrangements
with eye out for dancing tastes and
his ork and
chorus
(on some
tracks)
is
in
superb form
on
“I Will Follow Him,” “He’s So Fine” and “South
Street.” Both
kids and
oldsters
should
dig
this
lively package.
“I REMEMBER YOU”—Jack La Forge—Regina
R 282
In
a
world where carbon-copy
imitators
are
a
rule of thumb. Jack La Forge is a breath of fresh
air. The
pianist’s
distinctive keyboard approach
successfully
blends
elements
of
the
pop,
jazz,
classical
traditions
into
one
cohesive
fusion
of
harmonious
interplay. On
this new
Regina
set
La
Forge
gets ample
opportunity
to
showcase
his
versatility by
projecting
a wide
variety
of
musical moods. The 88’er
is
in winning form on
“I Remember You,” “My
Foolish Heart” and
a
fine self-penned original called “Blues On Velvet.”
“WHERE HAVE ALL THE FLOWERS GONE?”
—Nina &
Frederik—Atco
33
154
Along
with
the
current
revival
in
folk
music
many new groups have come on the
scene. For
the most part, these
artists
utilize a variety
of
vocal gimmicks
to
achieve
their
desired
effects.
Nina and Frederik are a delightful exception
to
the
rule. These
artists have
a
straight-forward,
delicate refreshingly honest approach to the folk
idiom. The duo turns
in top-notch
renditions
of
“The Time Of Man,” “Where Have All The Flow-
ers Gone?”
and “Seven
Daffodils.” An
impres-
sive performance.
“THE
BLACK
SAINT AND
THE
SINNER
LADY”—Charlie Mingus—Impulse A-35
Perhaps
the most important aspect
of Mines’
music
is
its highly-personal nature. The bassist-
88’er communicates through
his music a variety
of emotions which he feels. Although this might
be limited, the jazzman’s artistry and
skill trans-
form
his
music
into
some
amazingly
concrete
universals. On this new Inpulse set Mingus
is
in
his best form in recent years. While backed by an
accomplished group of musicians the artist swings
on “Solo Dancer,” “Duet For Solo Dancers” and
four
other
self-penned
selections.
Jazzophiles
should really dig the LP.
“JAY AND THE AMERICANS”—United Artists
UAS6300
The
“in” thing for performers
is the
“live”
re-
cording session and Jay and the Americans get on
the bandwagon with this program cut at the Cafe
Wha in Greenwich Village. The boys direct their
attention to a hodge podge of melodia from folk
to pop, none of which are up to their usual stand-
ards of performance. Included are “I Hear Music”
and “Girls, Girls, Girls.”

“MORE”—Clark Terry—Cameo SC 1064
In recent months jazz tunes have made frequent
appearances on the
best-seller charts and Clark
Terry picks up on this trend by including several
“commercial” tracks on this his premiere Cameo
LP. The trumpeter’s easy-going, relaxed brand of
jazz
is
effectively showcased on
this
set which
runs the gamut from bossa nova to funky blues.
The
sextet
really gets
cookin’ on “More,” “The
Good Life” and “Hobo Flats.” Disk should appeal
to a wide variety of record buyers.

REUNION”—^Various
Artists—Swing-
ville 2037

ork

of
“Blues
I

“Roseland

Playing with a small combo that includes Martin

“VIRTUOSO FAVORITES”—Erick

RCA Victor LM2671
Erick Friedman
brilliantly

clas-
sical pieces that have become concert favorites of

The

vored with color. Friedman is artistic without be-
ing flashy and this program is sure to win him a

Superb
bands
are
“Spanish

cholique.”

“SCHUBERT:
Octet For Strings & Winds, Op.
166; Fine Arts Quartet & New York Woodwind

All the

of

is preserved by some
stunning cleverly-balanced counterpo'int portions.
A superb chamber music
entry.

“WASHINGTON BLOOPERS”—Kermit

—Jubilee WPMB
11
Kermit
Schafer
cashes
in
on
the
mistakes
of
luminaries
in high places on this often hilarious
session
of bloopers from
the
nation’s

Jubilee. The
columnist-radio producer
has come
up with dozens of slips of the lip to make up this
15th volume in the Blooper series. All of the pre-
ceding blooper LP’s have been big sellers and this
one
should
follow
a
similar
course.
The
disk
might
encounter
airplay
difficulties
but
many
comments are suitable for laff-programming.
“THE EXPLOSIVE SOUND OF LES BROWN”
—Columbia CL 2030
Les Brown and his Band of Renown, with the aid
of the arranging talents of J. Hill, take a delight-
ful swing into the classics on this new Columbia
set.
Hill has taken some popular
classical
selec-
tions
and transformed
into
the
swingin’
brand
music
long-associated
with
the
ork.
The
band
shines
on
“Bizet
Has
His
Day,”
“Debussy’s
Dream”
and
“Liszt
Les.”
Fine
fare
for
either
dancing or
listening pleasure.
“MR. BLUES”—B.
B. King—ABC-Paramount
ABC 456
The
vet
pop-r&b
chanter
unleashes
his
potent,
wide-range
vocal
talents
full-blast
on
this
top-
notch
teen-oriented
set
from
ABC-Paramount.
King’s
straightforward,
gimmick-free
soulful
style
is
firmly
showcased
on
first-rate
chorus-
backed readings of “Young Dreamers,” “By My-
self” and “On Your Word Of Honor.” All of the
artist’s legion of fans should really dig the pack-
age.
“GOLDEN FOLK SONG HITS—VOLUME 2”—
Johnny Mann Singers—Liberty LST 7296
Cashing-in on the universality of the current folk
trend,
the Johnny Mann
Singers come up
with
their second outing of pop-folk items. The group
does not read
the tunes
in
their
original
styles
but
offers
their own
distinctive
full
ork-backed
lush
renditions. Among
the
highlights
here
are
“If
I Had A Hammer,” “Greenback Dollar” and
“Walk Right
In.” Deejays should
find plenty of
spinnable material
here.
“THE BEST OF RUTH BROWN”—Atlantic 8080
Ruth
Brown, who
scored
some
time
ago
with
“Teardrops From My Eyes,” belts her way thru
a
bevy
of
rhythm
and
blues
tunes
in
soulful
fashion. The blues-singer handles these
14 tunes
with the ease and self-assurance that has become
her trademark. In addition to her biggie, the lark
smoothly essays “Mama He Treats Your Daugh-
ter
Mean,”
“Oh What A Dream”
and
“Lucky
Lips.” Solid r&b programming fare here.
JAZZ PICKS OF THE WEEK
“DISCOVER
TUPPER
SAUSSY”—Monument
MLP 8004
Once every few years a jazz 88’er emerges with
such drive and
vitality that he stands head and
shoulders above his peers. Tapper Saussy is such
a
pianist. The
talented young keyboard
stylist,
who
is
also
a
fine
writer,
has
a
free-flowing
modern
style which combines basic jazz melodic
changes and classical overtones into one cohesive
fusion
of
harmony.
While
backed
by
a
small
combo the artist shines on his own “Yellow Sum-
mer,” “Contrary Waltz” and “Too Very
Soon.”
A talent to watch.
“NOW!”—Sonny Stitt—Impulse A-43
Ace
jazz
saxist Sonny
Stitt teams up
with
an
accomplished
group
of
sidemen
including Hank
Jones on piano, A1 Lucas on bass and Osie John-
son
on

on
this
new
swingin’
Impulse
entry.
Sitt’s
hard-driving mainstream
approach
couples
vitality with
free-flowing
melodic
senti-
mentality. The crew
in top-notch form on “Sur-
fin’,”
“Please
Don’t
Talk About Me When
I’m
Gone” and “I’m Getting Sentimental Over You.”
One
of
the
best
sets that the
artist has
cut
in
quite
a
while.
“MO’ GREENS PLEASE”—Freddie Roach—Blue

Freddie Roach comes up with a second Blue Note
album, this time geared for dancing—everything
from

bird
to

nova. The

showcases his artistry at the electronic keyboard
in a variety of ways and tempos and gets some
first rate assistance from Kenny Burrell on gui-
tar, Conrad Lester on sax, Clarence Johnston on
drums and Eddie Wright on
guitar.
Jazz
buffs
addicted
to dancing
will
find
this
a

session.
Included
are
“Party

and
“Un-
chained Melody.”

“SOMETHING TENDER” — Bud Freeman —
United
Artists 15033
Here
is
an
easy-listening
jazz
package
from
United
Artists
featuring
the
saxophone
talents
of
veteran Bud
Freeman.
Assisted
by

of George

tain Greenery”)

CLASSICAL PICKS OF THE WEEK
“THE SURFER’S BEAT”—Calvin Cool—Charter
CLM103
The country is being deluged with “surfin’ ” LP’s,
many
of which
are making the
best-seller
lists.
Calvin
Cool and the Surf-Knobs make
their big
“splash” on
Charter with
this package
of
surf
standards
and
newies.
This West
Coast
group
displays the hard-driving rhythm that has become
the
trademark
of
the
authentic
surfing
bands.
The proceedings begin with “Surf City” and con-
tinue with such familiars as “Surfin’ U.S.A.” and
“Pipeline.”

series of very successful

world. The pianist has a commanding knowledge
of the composer’s works and executes them with
authority and
feeling.
This
excellent version
of
the 3rd Concerto ranks with
the best, and Ash-
kenazy’s handling of the 2nd and 3rd movements
is exciting and
brilliant.
Set
is a welcome
addi-
tion to the classical catalog.

Kyu Sakamoto Arrives In The United States For PA’s
HOLLYWOOD—Over 4,000 teenagers stormed Los Angeles International Airport last week to witness the arrival
of Japan’s leading pop vocalist, Kyu Sakamoto, whose Capitol recording of “Sukiyaki” recently reigned the num-
ber one single in the nation. Shortly before the chanter’s
arrival
from
Tokyo,
airport
officials
feared
that
the
crowd was beyond
control and emergency measures were taken to insure the
artist’s safe conduct through the
milling fans. However, through the pleas of KFWB-Los Angeles deejay Wink Martindale, the huge crowd was
persuaded to clear a path for Sakamoto. Among those
on hand
to greet the songster were: Glenn
E. Wallichs,
chairman
of the board of Capitol Records, Helen Funai,
“Miss
Nisei” and Lloyd W. Dunn,
the
label’s veep
in
charge
of
international
activities.
Pictured
(left
to
right)
in the left pic are Martindale, Helen Funai, Sakamoto
and Wallichs. Martindale
is shown passing out copies of Sakamoto’s latest hit, “China Nights,” in the right photo.

“CANADIAN SUNSET BOSSA NOVA”—Eddie
Heywood—Liberty LST 7313
Eddie Heywood has earned many
laurels
in the
past
for
his
distinctive piano
stylings but
this
new Ray Ellis-arranged bossa nova set ranks as
one
of
the
pianist’s
best
dates
in
recent years.
The
relaxed,
easy-going
melodic Heywood
key-
board approach
is firmly evidenced on “Canadian
Sunset,”
“St.
Louis
Blues”
and
“So
In
Love.”
Deejays should find plenty of programmable ma-
terial
here.
“PAUL LAVALLE AND THE BAND OF AMER-
ICA PLAY BROADWAY SHOW STOPPERS”—
MGM E 4148
Here’s
a
delightful program
of popular Broad-
way
selections
rendered
in
spirited,
marching
tempos by Paul Lavalle and his ork. George
Si-
ravo has
created some
colorful, imaginative
ar-
rangements for the band. Among the best tracks
here
are
“Get Me To The
Church On
Time,”
“There
Is
Nothing
Like A Dame” and “Strike
Up
The
Band.”
Loads
of
listening
enjoyment
here.
“NEW DIMENSIONS IN BANJO AND BLUE-
GRASS”—Eric Weissberg, Marshall Brickman
Elektra EKL 238
In the past several years there has been a major
revival
of bluegrass music with
city-based
folk
musicians. Among the leaders of this movement
are
Eric
Weissberg
and
Marshall
Brickman,
While
backed
by
Gordon
Terry
on
fiddle
and
Clarence White on guitar, the boys dish-up some
first-rate
fast-moving
traditional
bluegrass
sounds on this new Elektra LP. Highlights of the
set include “Pony Express,” “Old Joe Clark” and
“Mountain Dew.”
“12 STRING GUITAR ”—Various Artists—World-
Pacific
1812
Here’s an
interesting offering of
folk blues and
blue
grass
featuring
the
12
string
guitar
of
Glen Campbell backed by Rod Dillard on guitar,
Doug Dillard on banjo and Dean Webb on bass.
The
tunes
served
here
on
World-Pacific
are
folk-bluegrass
warhorses
that
have
stood
the
test of time plus some of the modern
favorites.
The
set should get plenty of dual-market action
with items such as “If I Had A Hammer,” “Walk
Right In” and “Blowin’ In The Wind” performed
with artistry and feeling.
“MUSIC OF MISS AMERICA”—Bernie Wayne—
Ice Blue 670
Bernie Wayne has come up
with
a package
of
ten
tunes
dedicated
to
the
hopeful
lovelies who
enter
the Miss America
contest each
year. The
composer-conductor
(he
performs
both
chores
here)
opens with
the Miss America theme that
has become the trademark of each winner, and
continues with “Everybody Can’t Be A Winner,”
“The Magic Of Miss America,” “Queen Of The
Ball” and
six more in the same vein. The album
is timely and should spark some interest.
JAZZ
PICKS
OF THE WEEK
“FULL NELSON”—Oliver Nelson—Verve V 8508
The
multi-talented
Oliver
Nelson
(he arranges,
conducts and plays tenor sax) displays
all of his
accomplished
talents
on
this new
big band
set
from
Verve.
Nelson
does
not
utilize
gimmicks
but
offers
the various
selections here
is a free-
flowing,
straight-forward
midstream
style.
The
crew
shines on “Miss Fine,” “Cool” and “Paris
Blues.” Superior listening throughout.
“TOWN HALL CONCERT”—Charlie Mingus —
United Artists UAJS 15024
The far-out, avant-garde jazz talents of Charlie
Mingus
are
effectively
showcased
on
this
top-
drawer
set cut live at a Town Hall concert last
year. Fans
of the bassist
will
find some of the
material here conservative compared to previous
Mingus
disks
but
the
artistic
quality
is
high
throughout. Among the outstanding tracks here
are “Clark In The Dark,” “Freedom” and “Don’t
Come Back.”
“DO NOTHING "TIL YOU HEAR FROM ME”—
Johnny Griffin—Riverside 462
Tenor saxman Johnny Griffin is joined by bassist
Monk Montgomery
and drummer Buddy Mont-
gomery for this top-flight jazz session on Riyer-
side. Unlike many of his jazz colleagues,
Griffin
adheres
to a more
lyrical approach to jazz that
makes
this
session an extremely pleasant listen-
ing experience. The saxman unleashes his talents
on
a
swinging
version
of
the
title
tune, “Do
Nothing ’Til You Hear From Me” and then rides
easily into a soulful treatment of “The Midnight
Sun Will Never
Set.” Jazz buffs will surely dig
the
set.
“CLEOPATRA-FEELIN’ JAZZY” — Paul Gon-
salves—Impulse A 41
Ace tenor saxist Paul Gonsalves teams_ up with
an
accomplished
group
of
jazzmen
including
Hank
Jones
on
piano,
Dick Hyman
on
organ,
George Duviver on bass, Kenny Burrell on guitar
and Roy Haynes on drums on this swingin’
set
of tunes from
the “Cleo”
flick and other
selec-
tions
of a
similar
feeling. The boys wail
effec-
tively
in a potent midstream style on “Blue For
Liz,”
“Anthony
And
Cleopatra
Theme”
and
“Cleo’s
Asp.”
Jazzophiles
should
really
dig the
disk.
CLASSICAL PICKS OF THE WEEK
“THE LORDS PRAYER”—The Patterson Singers
—Vee Jay 5032
The
Patterson
Singers, under the very capable
direction
of
pianist-director
Robert
Patterson,
offer up some top-drawer gospel tunes in a vein
closer to the folk spiritual than the usual gospel
fare heard today. The songs are delivered
in a
rhythmic,
fervent
spiritual
manner
with
some
feelingful
arrangements
by
Patterson.
Bright
bands here are “Were You There,” “I’ve Got To
Make It To The Promised Land” and “The Lord’s
Prayer.” An Excellent gospel entry.
BRAHMS: Violin Concerto In D, Heifetz/Reiner,
Chicago
Symphony
Orchestra — RCA
Victor
LM1903
RCA Victor presents a deluxe package edition of
Jascha Heifetz’s memorable recording of Brahm’s
Violin Concerto in D with Fritz Reiner conduct-
ing
the
Chicago Symphony
Orchestra. The
at-
tractively
boxed
set
includes
an
informative
brochure on the virtuoso and
a complete
list of
his
recordings.
The
violinist’s
handhng
of
the
concerto
is masterful and executed with faultless
precision. The
classical devotee will
find this an
excellent item.
“20,000 LEAGUES UNDER THE SEA”—Adven-
ture Records
1
Here
is
a
first-rate
kiddie
series
of
adventure
stories
in
sound
from
Adventure
Records,
dis-
tributed by Sherman
Sales which
also
handles
Amy-Mala.
This
issue
is
one
of
six which
also
includes “The Invisible Man,” “The First Man In
The
Moon,”
“Journey
To
The
Center
Of
The

stories
are
excellently
told
with
superb
stereo
effects
and a complete cast of characters for each

A very educational
series that should
see brisk
sales during the coming holiday season.
BRAHMS: Symphony
No.
2
in D

Orchestra—Philips

035

K. Ziegler Named To Head
N.Y. Automatic Canteen
Operation
CHICAGO—The appointment of Rich-
ard
K.
Ziegler
as
Executive
Vice
President
and
General
Manager
of
New York Automatic Canteen Corpo-
ration,
a
newly-acquired
subsidiary
of
Automatic
Canteen
Company
of
America,
was
announced
here
by
Patrick
L. O’Malley, Automatic Can-
teen
President.
O’Malley
said
that
Ziegler,
a
cor-
porate
Vice
President,
will
assume
his
new
duties
immediately
at
the
subsidiary’s
headquarters
in
New
York
City.
Ziegler, formerly Director of Trade
Development for the company, joined
Automatic Canteen in 1950 as a sales-
man
in York,
Pa.,
after many years
of managing independent vending op-
erations.
In
1952,
he moved
to
the
firm’s Washington,
D.
C.
office
han-
dling branch sales and military liason.
In
July,
1955,
Ziegler
transferred
to the company’s national
sales
staff
in Chicago as an executive sales rep-
resentative and was promoted
to
as-
sistant to the Vice President of Sales

ALBUM REVIEWS
“SONGS OF THE SEA”—“Tim Buck & Two-
Request RLP 8052
Once in a great while new folk performers come
on the scene who are worthy of special mention.
Tim Buck
and Two
are
just
such
artists.
The
songsters
display
a
fresh,
electric
polished
ap-
proach and a sensitive understanding of the folk
idiom
as they
offer top-drawer versions
of such
popular items
as
“I’ll Go No More A-Whalin’ ”
“My
Nancy
Is
Waitin’ ”
and
“A-Rovin.”
Disk
should create some fast excitement.
and his
CARAVAN
of
k ^USiC
MUU
I
“CARAVAN OF AMER-ABIC MUSIC”—Eddie
Kochak—Georgette 828
With the rise of Arabic and oriental night clubs
in
the
past
few
years, new
interest
has
been
sparked in eastern music., Eddie Kochak has been
playing
the
seemingly
strange
quarter-notes
all
, of his adult
life and fully understands
all shades
of Arabic music. On
this new Georgette
session
Kochak
and
his
band
turn
in
some
top-flight
readings
of
“Honey
Song,”
“1000
Years Ago”
and
“Oriental
Cha
Cha.” A
fine
ethnic
per-
formance.
“SOMETHING NEW”—Tex Beneke, Ray
Eberle,
Modernaires—Warner Bos. WS1505
Tex Beneke, Ray Eberle and the Modernaires with
Paula Kelly
recall some of the nostalgia created
by the country’s number one dance bandsman, the
late Glenn
Miller. The ork and
the singers have
adapted the Miller
style
to some current biggies
along with
a few
oldies. Ray
Eberle comes up
with a strong vocal on
“Call Me
Irresponsible”
and the band and the Modernaires are
first-rate
on “Up A
Lazy
River”
and
“Crazy
Rhythm.”
Sound dancing and
listening pleasure.
“GOLDEN
FAVORITES”—Ted
Weems—Decca
DL 4435
Although Ted Weems
is dead his memory
is pre-
served
for
his
countless
legion
of fans
via
fine
nostalgic
recordings
like
this
fine
Decca
set
of
swing
style
evergreens.
The
distinctive
lush
Weems
orchestral
touch
is
firmly
evidenced on
“Heartaches,”
“That
Old
Gang
Of
Mine”
and
“Moonlight.” All the tunes here are arranged for
easy-going dancing pleasure. Good item
for
old-
sters.
“BLUES
HOOT”—Lightnin’

Launches New Product,
Sales Meetings
The
color
and
atmos-
p
ere
of a national
political conven-
tion
invaded
International
House
in
New York, the Flying Carpet in Chi-
cago, and
the Beverly Hilton
in Los
Angeles
last week
as
Mercury
Rec-
01 ds moved in with its fall sales meet-
in?^.~c?nc^uc^ed
throughout
with
a
political convention theme and
called
Mercury Records
1963
Convention.”
Vote Mercury
for A
Sales Land-
slide
was the overall slogan for the

by
Kenny
S.
Myers,

in

of

in

as
“national
chair-

A
discount

called
“Rally
Round
the
Stars,”
includes
a 10%

all
LP’s,
including new
entries
(see below).
It ends
Oct.
15.
The meetings opened with a “Keynote
Address” by Irving
B.
Green,
presi-
dent,
who
reviewed
Mercury’s
pro-
gress
in
the past year
in
the
areas
of artist acquisition and development,
and
outlined
plans
for
the
coming
year.
Green stressed the fine balance that
Mercury
is maintaining
in
its
artist
roster,
not
only with
the

of
name
talent such
as Johnny
Mathis,
the
Chad
Mitchell
Trio
and

in
the development
of
key
chart
artists
such
as The Smo-
thers
Brothers,
Brook
Benton,
Ray
Stevens,
The
Platters,
and
Faron
Young.
He pointed out the drive to develop
teen talent, led by Lesley Gore, Diane
Ray and The Pixies Three.
Green
explained
the
extension
of
Mercury’s A & R arm
by
working
closely with independent producers all
over
the
country,
and by
searching
out hot masters.
Irwin H.
Steinberg, executive
vice-
president, in his “State of The Union
Address.”
pointed
out
the
excellent
business
climate
today
and
stressed
how the many arms of distribution
in
the record industry can work together
to
maintain
the
record
dealer
as
a
major and potent force. (See separate
story.)

were

and
David

in New

and
Chicago,
and Jack Tracy in Los Angeles. The

lations agency.

Mercury s Steinberg, Myers Cover
Industry’s State In Sales Speeches
CHICAGO—The state of today’s disk
industry was
sized-up
with
cautious
optimism made
by
Irwin
H.
Stein-
berg and Kenny Myers at sales meets
held
last week on behalf
of Mercury
Records’ new fall program
(see sepa-
rate
story).
Steinberg,
exec
veep,
in
a
“State
of the Union” address, declared that
the
retailer
is
still
a
vital
force
in
the
record
business
and
shows
“strong evidence” of continuing to be
a
vital
force.
Steinberg
said
that
the
dealer
is
growing because of a number of fac-
tors, among them greater newspaper
and
radio
advertising
due
to
dis-
counting
practices
and
record
clubs,
more
radio
programming
based
on
records,
low-price
phono
equipment
of higher quality,
diversity of record
product and better merchandising on
the
part
of
labels.
He
added
that
“the dealer
is putting up a great and
winning
battle
to
survive
as
retail
outlet thru
diversification.” Steinberg
stated that in 1962 record dealers did
about 49%
of the
total record
dollar
volume
as
compared
to
approxi-
mately 84%
of
the
dollars
in
1955,
but
that
dollar volume
on
the 49%
was $325 million compared
to
1955’s
dollar volume of $191
million. “Thus,
today,” Steinberg noted, “record deal-
ers
are
doing
approximately
60%
more dollars in records than they did
in
1955.”
Steinberg also noted the growth
of
the rack-jobber (30%
of the disk
in-
dustry’s business, 40%
of retail sales
if
clubs
and
juke box
operators
are
eliminated)
and
the
one-stop,
which
he termed a product of
a “bad mar-
riage between the distributor and the
marginal account.”
“This
marriage,”
he
said,
“pro-
duced an unwanted
child, adopted by
what
is now known as the one-stop.”
“And
because
of
the
one-stop,
the
marginal account, the unwanted child,
has grown
into
a
healthy, strapping
adult.”

32)

Handleman Co. Makes
Secondary
Stock Offer
NEW YORK—Handleman
Co.,
the
large rack-jobber & owner
of
distrib
outlets in Detroit & Cleveland, is mak-
ing a 330,000-share registered second-
ary
offering common
stock
at
$12
a
share.
Proceeds
on
the
sale,
being
made through an underwriting group
head
by
E.
F.
Hutton &
Co.
and
Baker, Simonds &
Co., accrue
to
five
members
of
the
Handleman
family,
not to the company.
When
the
sale
is
completed,
total
ownership of Handleman common and
Class B
stock by
all
officers &
direc-
tors will be 44.96%.
The
firm
has
experienced
a
profit
in
each year
since
the
business was
established
by
Phil
Handleman
in
1936.
In
1937,
Phil
Handleman
and
his
four
sons, present
officers
of the
firm, formed a partnership to conduct
the business and in 1946 the company
was incorporated
in
Mich.
For the
fiscal year ended April
30,
1963,
the
company
earned
$960,000
after
taxes
on
$30
million
in
sales.
In
1953, Handleman, which had dealt
primarily
in
the
drug &
toileteria
business,
began
merchandising

Transistors
Highlight
Of N.Y.
Hifi Show
NEW YORK—A
$70
million
a year
industry—hifii
components—went
on
display
before
the
public
last week
(11-15)
in the form of the New York
High
Fidelity Music Show, with the
tiny transistor making the big news
for
consumers,
predications
of
con-
tinued growth of the industry making
tradesters happy.
A number of firms, including such
well-known
outfits
as
Fisher
Radio
Coi-p.,
Harman-Kardon
and
Bogen,
displayed
transistorized FM
stereo
tuners
and
amplifiers.
While
such
equipment,
ready
for consumer pur-
chases,
is expected to be 20% to 30%
higher than
tube components, Avery
Fisher
of
Fisher
Radio,
predicted
that within six months “you’ll see the
advent
of
substantial
amounts
of
transistorized equipment.”
Transistorized equipment has
such
advantages
over
tubes
as:
smaller
components,
less
heat, elimination of
background
“hum,”
loss
distortion,
say proponents
of
transistors, which
have already revolutionized the port-
able radio
field.
According
to
Raymond
V.
Pope,
president
of
the
Institute
of
High
Fidelity
Manufacturers,
sponsors
of
the show, housed in
the Trade Show
Building,
this
year’s
hifi
equipment
sales
are running 15%
ahead
of the
1962 pace.

NEW YORK—With its new fall push,
“The
Mad,
Mad,
Mad,
Mad
Plan,”
United Artists Records is going along
with the not-so-mad idea of disk price
stabilization.
As announced at the label’s
distrib
3-day meet at the Flamingo Hotel in
Las Vegas
last week—where 25 new
albums made their debut—the label is
offering a 10% discount with the pro-
gram, a reduction from previous deals
in which discounts
of 15%
or better
have existed.
The diskery feels that
its develop-
ment of a “widely accepted” catalog
of pop, film music, jazz and kiddie al-
bums has enabled a solidification of its
price structure.
The
program’s
title
takes
its
cue
from
the UA
flick
company’s
big
Stanley Kramer-directed
effort,
“It’s

score
of which

the new
LP’s.

track entry

“Radio Diffusion Week” began
Sept. 30 in Mexico City with the assistance
of all owners and managers of radio stations in the country. The president of
the Chamber of Radio, E. Guillermo Salas, organized this event and his annual
report
is one of the best ever. Present on one of the work days
of this con-
vention was
the
President
of
Mexico,
Adolfo
Lopez
Mateos, whom
all
the
members of the convention thanked for his cooperation in many ways.
Making her debut in Mexico recently was Dorothy Dandrige at the Terrazza
Cassino, and
she
appeared
on
the
Nescafe TV
show,
with
Mexican
comic
Manuel “Loco” Valdez.
A big event was the arrival to the Mexican capital of Liz Taylor and Rich-
ard Burton, accompanied by
little Liza Todd. Burton came
to
film
the new
picture “The Night Of The Iguana,” also starring with Sue Lyon, Ava Gard-
ner and Deborah Kerr. Camera man
is well known Mexican Gabriel Figueroa.
Also due last week in Mexico was Bobby Darin and his wife Sandra Dee.
From Lima Peru we received a letter from young Mexican singer Dyno, who
will
also appear
in Argentina,
the country from where we
received
a
post
card from the Mexican duet Los Yorsys, who as usual are having a wonderful
success m that country. Their voices appear on Musai’t Records with the songs
“Pica Piedra” and “Giro Pera Loca,” the latter having a strong acceptance on
radio stations.
Big German hit “Danke Schoen” was recorded at CBS
in a sensational
ar-
rangement made by Chico O’Farrill and his orchestra
in a tropical
style. On
the other side, Chico picked “Watermelon Man.”
Two new young singers appeared on
the
Peerless
label.
Their names
are
Guillermo Covarrubias, who sung the song “Walk Like A Man,” and the other
one
is Beto Canedo recording, “Be My Girl Again.” Both have nice voices.
Neil Sedaka
is getting stronger each day with his Spanish
diskings.
First
was “Es Dificil Decir Adios,” later was “Soy El Amor” and now
is “Recuer-
dos De Ipacarai.” It would be wonderful
if Neil came to Mexico to do another
long play in Spanish. He
is now on top in
all the Latin American countries.
CBS announced the future arrival of its singer, Puerto Rican Di Marie, who
now is performing in New York. Several engagements are expected
in Mexico
City.
One of the best records ever made by Los Hermanos Carrion appeared on
radio
stations.
It
is
the
Spanish
version
of “Devil Woman,”
called “Magia
Blanca” and “Big Wind,” under the name of “Viento.” This group has
offers
to appear in Las Vegas, and they
will, no doubt, accept them.
Chuck Anderson, one of the best and most commercial arrangers we have
in Mexico
City, released
his fourth
long play
at CBS,
including
songs
like
“Eddie Eddie,” “Tell Laura
I Love Her,” “Speedy Gonzalez,”
“Let’s Dance,”
“No Anymore,” “Limbo Rock,” “Mangos,” “Run, Samson Run,” “Hey Ring A
Ding,” “El Ladron” and others. A
fine album for dancers.
One of the top German hits was recorded in Mexico at Gamma Records by
Oscar Madrigal. The song received
the name
of “Por Que”
(Why)
and
on
the other side, Oscar sings the song “Nunca Te Olvidare”
(I’ll Never Forget
You). Oscar
is
curi’ently one
of the busiest
artists, making two
pictures
at
the same time, and
it
is almost certain that he will record
in English.
From Italy arrived beautiful blonde Lorenza Lori, who already has prepared
two new songs to record
at RCA. Lorenza
also
will do a season
in theaters
and night clubs.
One of the most popular folk singers, Cuco Sanchez, left town to perform in
Santiago,
Chile,
invited by the Mexican ambassador. Cuco
will
continue
his
tour through several countries.
Campei Records announced two of its first recordings. With Myrta Cruz and
Los Yalace, the song “Te Burlaste,” and with
the rock and
roll
group,
Los
Esclavos, the theme “El Nene.”
Movie theme “El Cid” was recorded with Spanish lyrics by Alberto Vasquez
for the Musart label. On the other
side, a special arrangement of “The Moon
Was Yellow.”
Discos Universales will release very soon “Twilight Time” and “Only You”
recorded by The Platters in Spanish. These songs are part of an album made
by The Platters in Spanish, on which are included songs
like “Green Eyes,”
“Amor,” “Siboney,” “Maria Elena,” “Besame Mucho” and others.

JOHNNY MATHIS—MERCURY

60837
MATHIS’ MERCURY LP DEBUT A
CHRISTMAS DISK—For
his
album
debut
on
the Mercury
label, Johnny
Mathis
cut
a
collection
of
Xmas
songs, aptly called “Sounds of Christ-
mas.”
Dealers
and
Mathis
fans
are
quite
familiar
with
the
sound
of
Mathis at Christmas Time, for during
his
long
association
with
Columbia
Records, Johnny recorded one
of the
all-time Yuletide
best-sellers, “Merry
Christmas,” which, naturally, got the
songster a gold disk from the Record
Industry
Association
of
America
(RIAA).
This
new
Mathis-Mercury
release
can
also
realize
the
same
happy reward for
sales achievement.

BEACH BOYS

5069)
The Beach Boys, who are making two-sided smashes
a happy
habit
(they’re
currently
represented
by
“Surfer
Girl”
and
“Little

Coupe”), should easily continue their merry chart ways here. One half’s
a thump-a-rock’er, tabbed “Be True To Your School,” that makes use of
the
‘sis-boom-bah’
school
chant.
The
other’s
a
tearful,
oh-so-smooth
ballad labeled “In My Room.” Another twin sales-giant for the boys.

SAM COOKE (RCA
Victor
8247)
Cooke’s long
list
of
chai-t
credits,
recently represented by
“Frankie
And Johnny,” should soon see the
hit addition
of “Little Red Rooster.”
It’s an infectious blues allegory that Sam and the Rene Hall-led (organ-

shuffle

in
engaging

More
top
shuffle-rhythm blues sounds on the “You Gotta Move”

are culled from Sam’s “Night Beat” package.

.

Mercury’s King Of The Month
i)ETROIT—Mercury Records new King
of
the Month, Tommy
Schlesinger,
general manager of J. K. Distributing,
is shown
receiving his trophies from
Brook Benton at a surprise party last week at the Grand Bar in Detroit where
the chanter was appearing.
According to Kenneth
S. Myers, the
label’s
vice
pres,
in charge
of
sales,
Schlesinger merited the award on the basis of his outstanding promo
efforts
on behalf of songstress Lesley Gore, as his was the initial market for “It’s My
Party,” which brought
the
lark
overnight
recognition.
Schlesinger received a permanent “King For A Month” trophy and his name
was added
to those engraved on the traveling “King” plaque. He was
also
presented with golf equipment and will receive a series of surprise gifts from
the firm during his month-long
reign.
Some of those attending the festive event were
(left to right)
: John Kap-
lan, president of
J.
K.; Brook Benton; Marc Avery
of WJBK; A1
Valenti,
J. K. promo chief; Schlesinger; and Morris Diamond, the label’s national pro-
mo chief.

tant performers ever signed to Colpix

Her

together with

all-
star line-up of writers and producers,
should create one of the most power-
ful
combinations
in
the
record
busi-
ness. During the past 10 months, our
writers have been responsible for an
all-time music
business
record
of
12
songs that have made the top ten.”
The
lark has appeared
in summer
stock,
in
Bi’oadway
shows,
and

guested on leading TV musical variety
shows. Her
first album release under
the Colpix banner will be “Jane Mor-
gan Seranades ‘The Victors’,” A single
will
also
be
issued
later
this month.
During her tenure with Kapp,
the
songstress had
hits
in “Fascination,”
“Love Makes The World Go ’Round”
and
“The
Day
The
Rains
Came
Down.”
In
the
above
photo,
Kirshner
is

congratulating
Miss
Morgan
on the new wax pact.
Music Biz Secretaries
Organize To Aid Kids
NEW YORK—A newly formed char-
itable organization
in the New York
area
called
M.A.R.C.H.
(Music And
Recording Companies Humanitarians)
has undertaken as its first project the
musical
needs
of

children
of
University
Settlement
House
on
Rivington
Street
in New
York.
The ten charter members are made
up
of
secretaries
working
for
per-
formers, publishers, A & R men and
other representatives of the music in-
dustz’y. Two
of
the
secretaries who
were
instrumental
in
the
formation
of the new group are Adrienne Law-
ner
(Connie Francis)
and Judy Tan-
nen
(Steve
and
Eydie).
They were
quickly
joined
by
others
including
Edy Sohmers, Adrienne Gilmore, Bet-
ty
Smith,
Rosallie
Miller,
Beverly
Weinstein,
Jeanette
Hendler,
Eve
Sasko and Cathy Favaro.
march’s present project is to pro-
vide

dren of University Settlement House.

and too tired to join the Peace Corps ?

The

Only through your help can we ac-

If you

Trip Based On
Sales Performance
CHICAGO—Rock-Ola
Manufacturing
Corporation will be without the serv-
ices of a large number of top distribu-
tors during the October 26-November
8 period but they couldn’t be happier.
The
distributors
will
be
enjoying
a
well-earned European “Trip for Two”
vacation
to
the
Mediterranean
and
Southern
Europe,
arranged
and
fi-
nanced
by
Rock-Ola
for
deserving
Distributors.
The
qualifications
are
based
on
“sales-above-quota”
figures
on the “Rhapsody 11” and “Capri II”
phonographs.
The distribs will jet to Madrid, Sat-
urday Oct. 26. On Oct.
30, the whole-
salers
plane
to
Nice.
On
Oct.
31st
they travel to Monte Carlo by motor-
coach and the next day make a stop
at Grasse. Saturday, Nov. 2 the group
will
arrive
in
Rome
staying
until
Tuesday when
they
will
depart
for
Tivoli.
The
Isle
of
Capri,
the
site
of
the
background
promotional
ma-
terial
used
for
the
current
phono-
graphs, will serve as host to the
dis-
tribs on Nov.
6. Back
to Rome from
ED
DORIS
Sorrento on the 7th and home for the
business at hand, the sale of Rock-Ola
machines.
Rock-Ola business
sessions
will be
conducted throughout the trip at vari-
ous
intervals. New
product,
factory
relations,
new
developments,
and
plans
for
the
future,
will be among
the topics
discussed.
Ed
Doris,
Rock-Ola
Executive VP,
will head
the
staff
of factory
execs
traveling with the group.

Severs Ties With Ainsworth
LONDON—Hal

former

and

ment here and in Australia, told Cash

a new company
to handle imports of

ports.
He
will
also
represent
kiddie
ride
manufacturers
in
this new endeavor.
The name of the firm
is Halel En-
terprises Ltd. and
will
deal with the
importing
of machines. Major-Matics
Ltd.
will
continue
to

equip-
ment.
The
firm
is
headed
by
Joe
Phillips
and
Mrs.
Eldridge,
wife
of
the
European
coin
man.
Eldridge
can
be

the
following address, while in the United

during

world

c/o

Post

California.
Eldridge
has
severed
all
ties with
Ainsworth.

performed by young keyboard artist John Ogdon*
on
this
new
Angel
classical
offering.
While
backed
by
the
Philharmonic
Orchestra
con-
ducted by
Sir John
Barbirolli, Ogdon
perfectly
captures
the
rapidly-changing
moods
of
the
poetic work. The second side of the disk features
the
pianist
reading
a
fine
sampling
of
Franck
Variations. A
splendid
achievement.

Erroll Garner’s “One World
Concert,” recorded
live
at the
Seattle World
Fair, was released
this month
in Holland
in an Octave-Philips co-production.
The
sales are supported by a large commercial campaign for Dutch record-
dealers
like window-displays and
special
ads. Garner came
to Holland Nov.
9th,
for
personal
appearances
on Dutch TV. On
the same
date,
Mercury’s
Jazz-saxophonist Roland Kirk visited Holland for a one-night-concert at the
Amsterdam
Concert-Hall,
Nov.
10th.
The
concert was
very
successful. As
Cash Box was informed by Kirk’s record-company Phonogram, Kirk record-
ings like “We Free Kings,” “Donine” and “Reeds and Deeds” are selling well.
The
death
of Edith
Piaf has caused
a
strong demand
in Europe
for the
recordings that made her famous
in her early
career. Under the
title “Les
Grandes Chansons
d’Edith
Piaf,”
Philips
has
released
here an album
with
such
historic
Piaf recordings
as “Mon
Legionnaire,”
“L’accordeeoniste” and
“C’est Toujours La Meme Histoire.” The album finds a ready market in Hol-
land, where Piaf was very much
beloved.
On
Nov.
5th Phonogram
welcomed
invited German TV-producers
to
the
Singer
Concert
Hall
at
Laren,
Holland.
Phonogram’s
P.R.O.
Jaap Stamer
was
host and
introduced Dutch
vocal
top-talent
to
the producers
of
Freies
Berlin, the W.D.R. and
the N.W.D.R. The
intention was that producers and
talent should meet to discuss the possibilities for TV-appearances in Germany.
Among
the Dutch
artists were Ria
Valk, Anneke Gronloh, Rob De
Nijs, &
The
Lords, Johnny
Lion & The Jumping
Jewels and
the newly
discovered
tenor Willy Caron. Mr. Stamer told Cash Box
that the contact had resulted
in
several
excellent
contracts. He
added
that Germany
shows
a
growing
interest for Dutch
musical
talent, and
he
pointed
out
that
the
latest TV-
appearance of The Blue Diamonds
in Germany had resulted
in a tremendous
sale of “Sukyaki” in the German version.
Bovema’s
Columbia-label
is about
to
release
Edith
Piaf’s memorial-album
“Je Me Souviens Edith
Piaf,” featuring
10
of her biggest
hits. Other high-
lights
in the books are
Cliff Richards’ Spanish
sing-hit “Maria Nomas” and
Frank
Ifield’s new version of “Mule Train.”
In Holland
Stateside now has 3 vocal groups of significance on the record
scene: The
Shirelles,
doing
fine
with
their “What Does A
Girl Do?” The
Chiffons (A Love So
Fine)
and
the Four Seasons, hitting upon
their “New
Mexican Rose.”
Bovema’s
Atlantic-label,
this week, rushed out the No.
1 U.S. Hit-Parader
“Deep
Purple” by
the
singing duo
April Stevens-Nino Tempo. Further jazz
items by The Jazz Messengers, Erroll Garner’s Trio and Herbie ‘Bossa Nova’
Mann have been entering the charts.
Gramophonehouse’s
Imperial-label
still
receives many
demands
for Imca
Marina’s popular “Lass Mein Herz Nicht Weinen.” She
will be the
star of
the Viennese “Leute von Heute”-show on Nov. 23rd, which
will be broadcast
to other countries.
Other
Imperial-artists were
featured
on Dutch TV
last week:
Comedian-
singer Henk
Elsink
enrolled
his
3rd TV-Show and
Rita
Corita was one
of
the
stars of the great musical-show “A Star
Is Falling”
last weekend.
The Hootenanny Show, a hit in the United States, presented
in Europe for
the
first time at the American Food and Agricultural Exhibition
in the RAI
building, Amsterdam, from Nov.
7th
to the
24th. Eighteen American
artists
are presenting the show, which
is being directed by Connie B. Gay, a former
official of the American Department of Agriculture. Artists include Katherine
Comas,
Fred
Benko, Mary
Klick, Bobby
Staff, Obrey
Wilson,
Elton
Britt,
Due Howington, the Willis Brothers and the Tennessee Haymakers.
Artone’s snhsid Funckler Records
is working overtime to meet the
terrific,
demand for Trini Lopez’ Reprise etchings. Helped by his outstanding perform-
ance
at the annual Grand Gala Du Disque—for which event the Dallas-born
singer and drummer-sidekick Mickey Jones were flown over by local Reprise
exec
Pete
Felleman.
Trini
is now
the
1
record
personality
in
the
Benelux
with
sales
of
“If
I Had A Hammer”
well
over
six
figures and
his
“Trini
Lopez At
P.J.’s” album
the
hottest LP on
the
market.
Additional
releases
already in the bestselling brackets: a two-sided reading of “La Bamba” on a
single and a
special Lopez EP which
includes “Hammer,” “Bye Bye Black-
bird” and
a medley
of two
standards.
Frank Sinatra’s brand new 1963-recorded Reprise version of his inimitable
classic “Nancy”
(originally waxed some
eighteen
years ago
for CBS) was
released on a
single
last week
in Benelux by Artone’s subsid Funckler, with
strong reaction
as an immediate
result.
Tune was
extracted from Frank’s
latest album
“Sinatra’s
Sinatra” which
shall be issued
locally later in Nov. “This one
is going to
outsell everything
‘The
Voice’
did
so
far—including
the
highly
successful
“Sinatra-Basie”
album.” said Pete Felleman.
Another Benelux release on Funckler
is Louis Prima’s new reading of the
oldie
“Angelina,”
the
first
single
the New
Orleans-born
vet
vocalist
and
hornman waxed
for his own
label. Fact
is, that
five years
ago,
his Capitol
recording of “Angelina” was a smash
locally.

ALBUM REVIEWS
“THE ROUTERS PLAY 1963’s GREAT INSTRU-
MENTAL HITS”—Warner Bros. WS 1524
1963 produced a banner crop of instrumental hits
and the Routers dish-up a fine sampling of some
of the year’s biggest sans words chart-riders on
this new entry from Warner Bros. The crew does
not attempt
to
deliver the tunes
in the
original
fashion.
Instead each
selection
is given a fresh,
distinctive danceable styling. The group shines on
“Wild Weekend,” “Telstar” and “Hot Pastrami.”
Eye the package for rapid teen acceptance.
“HERE HE COMES AGAIN”—Fats Domino-
Imperial LP 9248
Fats Domino
is
one
of
those
rare
artists with
amazing staying power. On
this
set, cut during
his
days
with
Imperial,
the
vet
chanter-pianist
offers
a
top-drawer
of program
of
blues
ever-
greens and Domino originals
all rendered
in the
artist’s
distinctive,
hard-driving
rockin’
style.
Highlights
of
the
disk
include
“Goin’
Home,”
“When
I See You” and “Your Cheatin’ Heart.”
ROlHNn ««AST£T
“HEY! HEARD THE HERD?”—Woody
Her-
man—Verve V 8558
Although jazz has taken many avant-garde turns
since
WWII,
one
refreshing
remembrance
of
things past is the Woody Herman big band. Even
in this era when musical abstractions are the rule
of thumb, the Herman crew continues to wail in a
r-elaxed swing-styled manner. The band
is in fine
foi-m
on
“Blue
Lou,”
“Men
From
Mars”
and
“Four Others.” Plenty of potential
here.
“THE ROLAND KIRK QUARTET MEETS THE
BENNY GOLSON ORCH.”—Mercury SR60844
What might appear
to be
a
strange wax mar-
riage, that of the Roland Kirk Quartet and the
Benny
Golson
ork,
proves
to
be
worthy
and
natural as the two come up with some first-rate
jazz blendings. Launching the set with a Mingus
original
tagged,
“Ecclusiastics,”
the
pair
con-
tinues with
a
variety
of pop and
off-beat
com.-
positions from Kirk, Golson and Cy Coleman. The
theme here is strictly modern jazz and the serious
jazz buff will surely dig their treatments of “By
Myself,”
“Roland
Speaks”
and
“I’ve
Got Your
Number.”
“ROMAN
ACCORDION”—Charles
Magnante
Command RS 852 SD
Ace
accoi-dionist Charles Magnante takes us on
a musical tour of Italy on
this sparkling album
from Command. Magnante
creates
a
rich
spec-
trum
of
different tones and sounds
as he plays
his
instrument
with
verve
and
polish.
While
backed by a small orchestra, Magnante turns
in
winning
performances
on
“Guaglione,”
“Non
Dimenticar” and
“Arrivederci Roma.”
“THE BOB HARTER SONGBAG”—Liberty LST
7330
Although Bob Harter has been involved in count-
less sessions, this
is his premiere solo effort. The
chanter has extremely rich, wide-range bass voice
aptly suited to the folk idiom. While backed by a
chorus and rhythm
section, Harter turns
in top-
flight readings of such folk favorites as “Hound
Dog,” “Fair And Tender Ladies” and “Pastures
Of Plenty.” A most promising entry.
“BROTHER JACK MCDUFF LIVE !”—Prestige
7274
Jack McDuff
unleashes
his
keyboard magic
on
this
album
session
recorded
“live” by
Prestige
in Chicago. The
organist,
already making
noise
with a single culled from this
set tagged, “Rock
Candy,”
is
sure
to reap a harvest of
sales with
this rhythmic and bright session. Backed by Red
Holloway on tenor sax, George Benson on guitar
and Joe Dukes on drums, McDuff
is at his very
best
on
“Whistle
While You
Work,”
“A
Real
Doodun’
” and “Sanctified Samba.”
“HUB-TONES”—Freddie
Hubbard—Blue
Note
4115
Freddie
Hubbard
has
created
a
stir
with
his
previous
albums
but
this
new
Blue
Note
set
clearly
marks
him
as
significant
mainstream
ai-tist to be watched. The trumpeter’s distinctive,
musical
approach
is
an
interesting
mixture
of
basic blues progressions and new-wave imagina-
tion.
While
backed
by
a
superb
small
combo,
Hubbard
renders
outstanding
performances
of
“You’re My Everything,” “Prophet Jennings” and
“Lament For Booker.”
“DOMINIQUE THE SINGING NUN’S SONG”—
Le Choeur Enfants
de Montmarte—Palace PST
767
Le Choeur des Enfants de Montmarte could well
cash-in
on
the
success
of
the
Philips’
Singing
Nun success with
this delightful album
of folk-
styled
items
sung
in
French.
In
addition
to
a
fine reading of “Dominique,” the chorus comes up
with fine renditions of “Marche Lorraine,” “Sam-
bre
et
Meuse”
and
“La
Berceuse.”
Disk
has
enough built-in commercial ingredients to create
an immediate
sales response.
“FRENCH
COOKIN’ ”—Budd
Johnson—Argo
LP 721
Budd
Johnson
teams
up
with
an
accomplished
crew of jazzmen on this new Argo
set including
Hank
Jones
(piano),
Kenny
Burrell
(guitar)
and
Osie Johnson
(drums)
as he
goes through
his
delightful tenor sax paces
in
a program
of
French-flavored
selections.
The
mood
here
is
funky and relaxed as Johnson dishes up first-rate
readings
of “La
Petite Valse,” “Le
Grisbi” and
“Under Paris
Skies.” One
of the best
sets
that
Johnson has cut in quite a while.
“TONY
WEBSTER’S MARRIAGE COUNSEL-
OR”—Verve 15040
The
recent
publicity
against and
in
defense
of
the marriage counselors sparked this Verve album
written and produced by Tony Webster. Featuring
a cast of six that includes George Coe, Lovelady
Powell, Joan Darling etc., the Marriage Counselor
becomes
the
butt
of
ribs
and
barbs
hurled by
gag-writer
Webster. Format
is
a
series
of
in-
terviews between the counselor and
clients on a
wide variety of marital problems. Lots of laughs
to be had here.
“PEARL WILLIAMS AT LAS VEGAS”—Riot
R303
Pearl Williams serves up songs and humor on this
new
Riot
outing recorded
“live”
in Las Vegas.
Most
of
the
laughs
here
are
“Borsht
Belt”-
oriented and clearly labeled for adults only. The
laffgal has an easy, off-hand delivery calculated
to
put her
audiences
in a good mood
in
short
order. Although
the
disk
is
unsuitable
for
air
play, the holiday season could spark some brisk
sales.
CLASSICAL PICKS
“A VERDI COLLABORATION”—Anna
Moffo.
Franco Ferrara—RCA Victor LM 2685
The
“collaboration”
in
this
disk’s
tag
is
the
teaming up
of Anna Moffo and Franco Ferrara,
who conducts the RCA
Italiana Symphony. This
is obviously a labor of love for the
singer who
is
in superb voice throughout. The concept here
was to give the orchestra proper importance and
not, as so many Verdi offerings do, regulate
it to
a back-seat status. Among the highlights of this
top-notch
album
are
selections
from
“Ernani,”
“II
Travatore”
and
“Otello.”
Classical
buyers
should come out
in force for the package.

“CONCERTOS FOR THREE PIANOS”—Robert,
Gaby & Jean Casadesus, Phila. Orch./Ormandy
Columbia ML5895
This potent
classical
disk from Columbia boasts
the
talents
of
the
Philadelphia
Orchestra
con-
ducted by Eugene Ormandy and pianists Robert,
Gaby
and
Jean
Casadesus
playing
the
Mozart
Concerto
in F
Major,
the Bach
Concerto
in D
Minor and the Bach Italian Concerto in F Major.
Classical product gets
its highest turnover dur-
ing the holiday buying season and
this package
should attract the classical devotees.

JAPAN — Review
1963
The biggest topic of 1963 in our re-
cording world was
the
establishment
of
a new company. For many years
six recording companies existed in the
business,
each
representing
foreign
labels,
more
than
sixty,
while,
of
course, releasing Japanese records on
their own
labels. The incentive given
to
the not-so-big recording world by
the development of the new company,
backed up by one of our biggest finan-
cial systems of Mitsubishi Electric, in-
fluenced us to a great extent.
The
connections
between
electric
makers
and
the
recording
industry
have already been common
in Amer-
ican and European markets, while
in
Japan also we have the cases of Tosh-
iba
Records
with
Toshiba
Electric
Company,
Nippon
Victor
with
Mat-
sushita
Electric,
and now
this
new
company Nippon Crown with
Mitsu-
bishi has spurred
the
trend. As
this
company enters
into production next
year,
the competition for
a
share
our market will be more hectic.
Next topic is the great hit of “Suki-
yaki,” which was almost the first case
of a Japanese song proving the pos-
sibility of export, against the time of
only
one-way
business
with
foreign
markets importing
songs. And,
since
then,
our
publishers
and
recording
companies, are exerting themselves to
follow-up on “Sukiyaki.” On the other
hand, there was not enough room for
publishers,
as
hit
records
increased
year by year, replacing the ranks very
quickly. Only “Hey Paula” was a big
hit on the Japanese charts comparable
to,
say, “Pretty
Little Baby”
of
last
year,
while
the
top
singers
of
the
world
like
Elvis
Presley
and
Connie
Francis have sold also in our market.
Foreign
Artists who
visited Japan
in 1963:
Jan.
Feb.

"I'M GOIN' TO SING SIXTEEN SPIRITUALS" 
-Robert Shaw Chorale-RCA Victor LM 2580 
Robert Shaw directs his musical attention at 
American spirituals on this new Victor offering 
and leads his Chorale in fine program of feeling- 
ful evergreen laments. The big chorus displays an 
amazing understanding of the gospel -folk idiom 
as they render superb versions of "That Lone- 
some Valley," "Steal Away" and "My Soul's Been 
Anchored." 'Deejays should find the material here 
an interesting change of pace. 
"THE BEST OF JESSE CRAWFORD"-Decca 
DXSB 7171 
Jesse Crawford, one of the most consistent best- 
selling organists in the country, demonstrates his 
masterful keyboard technique on two dozen tunes 
that span the musical spectrum on this deluxe 
two -disk set from Decca. The organist plays pop, 
sacred and the classics here on a wide variety of 
melodies that include "Softly, As In A Morning 
Sunrise," "Merry Widow Waltz," "Ave Maria," 
"Wedding March" and many others. Crawford 
fans should come out in force for the set. 
"THIS IS GENE STRIDEL"-Columbia CL 2115 
Gene Stridel makes an impressive wax debut on 
Columbia with this package of ballads and blues 
tunes geared for easy listening. With arrange- 
ments and conducting chores handled by Marty 
Manning, the chanter eases his way through such 
melodic goodies as "After You've Gone," "The 
Sweetest Sounds" and "How Blue The Night." 
The songster has a big emotion -packed voice that 
merits attention from buyers and spinners. 
"MORE OF THE BEST OF JIMMY REED"- 
Vee Jay VJ 1080 
Vet blues songster Jimmy Reed unleashes his po- 
tent, wide -range vocal talents full -blast on this 
top-notch Vee Jay program of blues, evergreens 
and self -penned while -back Reed triumphs. While 
backed by a fine funky combo the chanter -guitar- 
ist really wails on "Baby What's Wrong," "Down 
In Mississippi" and "Caress Me Baby." Disk 
should sell strongly in the r&b markets. 
"SPIKE JONES NEW BAND"-Liberty LRP 
3349 
Spike Jones, who made an abrupt departure from 
his usual musical bill -of -fare with his last Liberty 
LP outing, continues in the same vein with this 
new outing directing his talents to some old and 
new hits. The orkster effectively combines a folk 
flavor with "trad jazz" in an ear -arresting man- 
ner on such oldies as "Kansas City," "Deep Pur- 
ple" and "Charade." Top-notch programming fare. 
"GREAT GOSPEL SONGS"-Tennessee Ernie 
Ford & Jordainaires-Capitol ST 2026 
Tennessee Ernie Ford, with a half dozen best- 
selling religious LP's to his credit, joins the Jor- 
danaires and Boyce Hawkins' gospel piano on 
this package of gospel songs from Capitol. The 
chanter and the quartet effectively combine rev- 
erence with good spirits on these happy tunes as 
they liltingly offer "Hide Me, Rock Of Ages," "A 
Beautiful Life" and "I Can Tell You The Time." 
Brisk sales are indicated. 
"CONCERT AT NEWPORT"-John Lee Hooker 
-Vee Jay VJ 1078 
One of the highpoints of last summer's Newport 
Folk Fest was the appearance of vet blues 
chanter, John Lee Hooker. On this new Vee Jay 
offering, cut live at some of his Newport concerts, 
the artist is presented in a varied program of 
blues laments. While backing himself on the gui- 
tar, Hooker turns in some top-notch performances 
of "I Can't Quit You Now Blues," "Bus Station 
Blues" and "Talk That Talk Baby."

COUNTRY HARMONICA 
JIMMY RIDDLE 
"COUNTRY .HARMONICA"-Jimmy .Riddle- 
Cumberland SRC 69511 
Although less familiar than the guitar as a folk 
instrument, the harmonica has a rich heritage as 
a musical country -folk communicator. On this 
lively Cumberland set Jimmy Riddle displays a 
top-drawer, rhythmic contagious style as he 
breezes his way through a flock of standards in- 
cluding "John Henry," "Careless Love" and "Lit- 
tle Brown Jug." Loads of listening enjoyment here. 
JAll PICKS MMIZIMIZIe 
"GERRY MULLIGAN MEETS BEN WEBSTER" 
-Verve V 8534 
Although the wax marriage of two jazz artists is 
nothing new, this session so skillfully blends the 
midstream baritone sax sounds of Gerry Mulligan 
with the more subdued progression of Ben Web- 
ster's tenor sax that it ranks as the finest thing 
that either man has done in quite a while. Neither 
artist kowtows to the other here. Instead, each 
lyrically compliment the other as they swing to- 
gether on "Chelsa Bridge," "The Cat Walk" and 
"Tell Me When." Jazzophiles should dig the set. 
"McCOY 
TYNER 
LIVE AT NEWPORT"- 
Impulse A-48 
Jazz 88'er McCoy Tyner has earned many laurels 
in the past but this sparkling set cut live at the 
while -back Newport jazz fest and featuring Bot 
Cranshaw, Mickey Roker, Clark Terry and Charlie 
Mariano showcases him in his most thoroughly en- 
gaging setting set. Tyner is obviously in the same 
groove with the boys as he turns some top-drawer 
imaginative readings of "My Funny Valentine,' 
"All Of You" and "Monk's Blues."

Tenor saxman Harold Vick steps into the spot-

"GROOVY GOODIES" - Various Artists - 
Prestige PR 7298 
Twelve of the country's top jazz artists perform 
an equal number of swingin' tunes on this new 
offering from Prestige. Some of the sides here are 
culls from the individual LP's of the artists but 
all are geared for top listening enjoyment. In- 
cluded here are "Rock Candy" by Brother Jack 
McDuff, "Stardust" by John Coltrane, "Seed 
Shack" by Gene Ammons, "Dig" by Miles Davis 
and eight other Groovy Goodies. The set is a 
jazzophile's delight.

Leinsdorf-RCA Victor LM 7030 
The plethora of memorial disks to the late Presi- 
dent have decidely run their course but this nu: 
perb recording of the recent solemn pontificar 
mass for JFK celebrated by Richard Cardina. 
Cushing of Boston and featuring the Boston Sym- 
phony rendering Mozart's "Requiem" under the 
baton of Eric Leinsdorf should attract many 
classical buyers. The conductor reads the moving 
work in an appropriate sweeping fashion with 
heavy emphasis on its qualities of sorrow. A 
standout achievement.

Liberty Ups Ray Hill, 
Brings In Abe Kesh 
NEW YORK-Liberty Records has 
made several changes in its promo 
dept. Ted Feigin, promo director, has 
announced the promotion of Ray Hill, 
previously 
southern 
Calif. 
promo 
head, to concentrate on the south and 
some midwestern markets. He has 
transferred to Cincinnati to handle 
his new chores. 
His former post has been taken over 
by Abe Kesh, who joins the label 
after three years as promo director 
at Eric Distributors in San Francisco,

Calif. 
Prior to his tenure with Eric, Kesh 
worked the Detroit area for Music 
Systems in sales and promo.

MEXICO 
The biggest promotion ever for a Mexican artist is now at CBS Records 
for folk singer Irma Serrano. This promotion will last several weeks, and 
the artist will tour the whole country, welcomed in each place by big displays, 
radio and TV spots, photos, records, contests, etc. Irma has a nice voice and 
a provocative style. 
Back from their first trip to a foreign country, Caracas, Venezuela, is the 
Mexican duet of the Hermanas Jiménez, at the same time that their third 
long play was released by Orfeon Records. The Jimenez sisters had successful 
appearances in Venezuelan night clubs and on TV. 
From Argentina we received a post card from rock and roll group 
Los Teen Tops, who are performing now in that country, which has taken 
very much to Mexican artists of the new wave. CBS released their latest 
record, the spanish versions of "Everybody" and "Dee Dee Dinah." 
Gamma Records released the winning song of the recent "San Remo Festi- 
val." The song is "Non Ho L'Eta" (Too Young To Love You) and is sung 
by its San Remo performer Gigliola Cinquetti in perfect Spanish. This young 
Italian singer, who is still a teenager, also recorded several songs in our 
language and Gamma Records is trying to popularize her. 
Panamericana de Discos released an extended play with four of the most 
popular songs sung by the sensational group, The Beatles. Those songs are 
"I Saw Her Standing There," "I'll Get You," "She Loves You" and "I Want 
To Hold Your Hand." 
Los Hermanos Carrión, one of the most popular romantic groups of the 
new Mexican wave, recorded at CBS two new songs "Las Cerezas" (The 
Cherries) and "Las Sombras" (The Shadows). On the first song they accom- 
pany themselves and on the second the Chuck Anderson orchestra performs. 
Los Hermanos Carrión will leave town very soon to perform in Argentina 
and other South American countries. 
Alberto Videz left PHAM publishing to accept a job as sales manager 
of CAMPEI publishing, where we were informed that Jack Mills (of the 
publishing company) will arrive very soon to the Mexican capital. 
CBS -Columbia had a cocktail party to present the first long play recorded 
by the famous Mexican actor Ignacio Lopez Tarso. In this album, Ignacio 
reads popular narrations of the Mexican revolution with a wonderful feeling. 
The production of this record was made by Fernando Z. Maldonado and some 
parts of Ignacio's narrative were supported musically by the fabulous Dueto 
América. I am sure that this album will have a strong demand with the 
Mexican population of the United States and some Latin American locales. 
Johnny Mathis arrived in México City to debut on February 20 at the 
Terrazza Cassino. The place is crowded every night, and it is possible that 
Johnny will choose several Mexican songs to record when he returns to his 
country. 
Based on the world famous song "Dominique," a Mexican producer will do the 
film with the life of the Singing Nun. They just don't know who will be the 
actress, Angélica María or Rocío Dúrcal. Both of them are singers of "The 
New Wave" and very popular in México. 
The Gay Clooners recorded at RCA Victor with a big orchestra background 
the song "El- Robot," which also represents a new rhythm. 
Popular comic duet Los Mimos recorded at Peerless Records two new 
creations, "El Baile De Las Poquis" and "El Beisbol" (The Baseball). This 
last record is a narration of the baseball game made by a Cuban, a French- 
man, an Argentinian, a Brazilian and a Spaniard.

HOLLAN D 
Philips' Phonographic Industries has released a double -LP album of a 
"St. Mark Passion" by Bach's contemporary and compatriot Ceorg Philipp 
Telemann. (Telemann has written more than 1500 religious vocal works). 
The hitherto forgotten work has been recovered by the German conductor 
Kurt Redel, who leads the Pro Arts Orchestra of Munich, a Youth Choir and 
soloists among whom Heinz Rehfuss sings the (baritone) part of the Evange- 
list. Otto Glastra van Loon, classical pro of Phonogram, told Cash Box that 
a large press -campaign has started in the Dutch press, and that the work 
will be performed for TV during Easter -week. 
In the Dutch Philips GR -series (10 inch LP's) two interesting LP's were 
released of performances by The Minneapolis Symphony conducted by Antal 
Dorati. They are: Gershwin's "Rhapsody In Blue" and "An American In Paris" 
(featuring pianist Eugene List), and the popular "Young Person's Guide To 
The Orchestra" by Britten with Morton Gould's "Spirituals for Orchestra." 
Andre Previn's music for the film -version of "Irma La Douce," was released 
by Phonogram in the form of a magnificent United Artists -album. The film 
is a great cash -box success in Holland. 
Johnny Hallyday still belongs to the five best -sold foreign artists in this 
country for ten continuous months already. He has three fast -selling singles 
in the Dutch hit-parade at this moment: "Pour Moi La Vie Va Commencer," 
"Ma Guitare" (both tunes from his first movie) and "Tes Tendres Annees," 
the French version of The Tender Years. Hallyday's latest 12" LP album 
is also a quick seller: a live -performance at the Parisian Olympia Theatre. 
Holland's most important traditional Jazz Band is the Dutch Swing College, 
lead by clarinetist/saxophonist Peter Schilperoort. The Band started in 1945 
as a combo for a Jazz Club at the Hague, being professional already two 
years later and doing world-wide tours since 1948. The late Sidney Bechet 
used to play very often with the DSC and even composed a tune for the 
Band. In 1949 the DSC made a couple of 78 rpm's, of which the 45 single 
pressings are still selling well these days, 15 years after recording dates. 
One of them is "At The Jazzband Ball" b/w "Margie," of which Philips made 
a special single -release again. 
Two important American jazz -LP's were released by Phonogram this month: 
"Woody Herman 1963" on Philips and a re-release of Sarah Vaughan's 1954 
recordings for Mercury with Clifford Brown. Since she did a live performance 
here last year for TV (Grand Gala du Disque, with Doug Duke at the Ham- 
mond -organ) there is also a demand for her earlier recordings. Furthermore, 
Frank Visser of Phonogram's Press Dept. reported the rush release of the 
following US -hits: "Dawn" by The Four Seasons (Philips), "Going Going 
Gone" by Brook Benton (Mercury) and "24 Hours From Tulsa" by Gene Pitney 
(United Artists). 
Bovema's Atlantic -label exclusively handling all MJQ-albums in this country, 
reports that the group will appear in Holland in the course of April next. 
Concert dates and places have not yet been set so far. In the pop area, the 
new April Stevens -Nino Tempo -Hit "stardust" will be out very soon. 
Also in the can for Atlantic is the in -person visit of bassist Charlie Mingus 
and a sextet on April 10 in Amsterdam (Concertgebouw). Mingus will be 
presented here by impressario Paul Acket, who also plans to bring altoist 
Omette Coleman in the coming season. 
Famous pianist Annie Fischer performed Schumann -works from February 
17-19 in Amsterdam. Bovema's Columbia -label strongly promotes her Schu- 
mann-pianocerto under Klemperer on the occasion.

"THE THINGS THAT TROUBLE MY MIND"- 
Dick Weissman-Capitol ST 2033 
Dick Weissman, who served his pop -folk appren- 
ticeship with the Highwaymen, spread his wings 
as a solo performer on this top-drawer set of 
message -songs. Weissman displays a rich, wide - 
range voice and ethnic delivery as he goes 
through his paces with polish and verve. While 
backing himself on the guitar, the chanter dishes - 
up splendid readings of "He Had A Long Chain 
On," "Portland Town" and "Wartime Blues." An 
impressive performance. 
"LOS INDIOS TABA-JARAS"-Aravel AB 2001 
Although Los Indios Taba -Jaras first gained an 
international reputation with their recording of 
"Maria Elena" on RCA Victor, the duo also has a 
fine understanding of the Latin folk idiom as 
evidenced by this top-notch disk from Aravel. The 
duo's infectious, rhythmic vocal and instrumental 
style is effectively showcased on "Canoita," 
"Aracuan" and "Meu Piao." Delightful listening 
throughout. 
"FOREIGN FILM FESTIVAL"-Jo Basile- 
Audio Fidelity AFLP 2124 
Fourteen melody -laden themes from recent flicks 
are surveyed by the orchestra of Jo Basile on this 
album entry from Audio Fidelity. The orkster 
employs a potent rhythm section as the fitting 
complement to the organ, piano and sax solo 
flights. Loads of top listening and dancing enjoy- 
ment to be had here. Rhythmic tracks here are 
"Charade," "Mondo Cane," "Boccaccio 70" and 
"Black Orpheus." 
"DICK SHAWN SINGS WITH HIS LITTLE 
PEOPLE" -20th Century Fox 4124 
Dick Shawn adds another facet to his versatility 
on this program of tunes on which he is joined 
by his Little People. That Shawn is a comic is 
much in evidence here as his approach to these 
tunes is part juvenile, part tongue-in-cheek, but 
wholly entertaining. The comic and the kids are 
obviously enjoying themselves with their treat- 
ments of "La Plume De Ma Tante," "High is 
Better Than Low" and "The Kockamamie." It's a 
delight for kids of all ages-including the elders. 
"SONGS THAT MADE HIM FAMOUS"-Clyde 
Moody-Starday SLP 262 
Clyde Moody's long legions of country fans 
should really dig this Starday album on which 
the vet chanter -guitarist offers a program of his 
previous hits. The songster demonstrates that he 
still has a potent, rich, wide -range baritone voice 
as he renders "Nobody's Business," "Whispering 
Pines" and "What It Means To Be Lonesome." 
Plenty of potential here. 
"HALLELUJAH THE HILLS"-Original Sound- 
track-Fontana MGF 27524 
Adolf Mekas' "Hallelujah The Hills" has been 
hailed as one of the crowning art -film achieve- 
ments of the year. The off -beat, wacky comedy 
was greatly enhanced by an almost as absurd 
score composed by Meyer Kupferman. The music, 
which, for the main, has an interesting semi- 
classical flavor, is divided into various distinctive 
segments each of which underlines a significant 
action in the flick. A thoroughly delightful listen- 
ing experience. 
"DEDICATED TO YOU"-Tommy Dorsey-RCA 
Camden CAS 800 
The Tommy Dorsey band of the thirties and 
forties surveys ten tunes which were typical of 
the times on this issue from Camden. In addition 
to some fine vocals by Frank Sinatra, Jack Leon- 
ard and Edythe Wright, there are some first-rate 
solos by Joe Bushkin, TD, Buddy Rich and Ziggy 
Elman. Lots of nostalgia here with such oldies as 
"Just As Though You Were Here," "Snooty Lit- 
tle Cutie" and "Will You Still Be Mine."

"JAZZ IMPRESSIONS"-Vince Guaraldi-Fan- 
tasy-3359 
Vince Guaraldi made a strong chart showing a 
while back with his "Jazz Impressions Of Black 
Orpheus" set, and could very well repeat that 
success with this first-rate package of jazz items. 
The pianist's highly distinctive style is evident at 
every moment as he serves up captivating rendi- 
tions of some old, some new tunes including "Yes- 
terdays," "Room At The Bottom," "Willow Weep 
For Me" and "Autumn Leaves." Could be an- 
other winner for Guaraldi. 
"PORTRAITS"-Gerald Wilson-Pacific Jazz 80 
The jazz big band era is decidedly over, but Ger- 
ald Wilson and his large crew continue to pro- 
duce exciting, valid musical statements in a large 
group context. The composer -arranger's mid- 
stream orientation is captured on a fine program 
of originals and evergreens including "So What," 
"Ravi" and "'Round Midnight." One of the best 
sets that Wilson has cut in quite a while.

"3 GIANTS"-Sonny Rollins With Clifford Brown 
& Max Roach-Prestige PR 7291 
Although all three of the jazz luminaries here 
have gone their separate ways (Clifford Brown 
died in '56) but their distinctive brand of bebop 
swingin' displayed on this fine Prestige set makes 
for some fine jazz listening. All three men per- 
fectly compliment each other as they blend their 
talents into one cohesive musical unit on "Valse 
Hot," "Kiss And Run" and "I Feel A Song Com- 
ing On." Jazzophiles should dig it. 
"DEBUT IN BLUE"-Gene Shaw-Argo 726 
Gene Shaw, who made his album debut on Argo 
with a set tagged "Breakthrough," follows it with 
this second stanza of jazz tunes delivered in the 
same potent manner. The trumpeter is backed 
throughout by rhythmic section lashing out with 
a heavy beat, some with a strong Latin flavor. 
Jazzophiles will dig these ultra -modern sounds, 
especially the tag tune, "Karachi," "The Gentle 
Princess," "When Sunny Gets Blue" and "Thieves 
Carnival." 
"FIVE ON EIGHT"-Rufus Jones-Cameo 1076 
Rufus Jones bows on Cameo with this package 
of jazz tunes served up in pulsating fashion by 
the drummer and his backdrop combo. The drum- 
mer shines in the solo spotlight along with sax- 
ists Joe Farrell and Seldon Powell on such instru- 
mental goodies as "My Special Dream," "Ebb 
Tide," "A Secret" and "Just About That Time." 
Jazzophiles will dig the set. 
CLASSICAL PICKS 
"OPERATIC RECITAL"-Robert Merrill-Lon- 
don 5833 
The Met's Robert Merrill demonstrates his op- 
eratic versatility on this solo debut on London. 
The baritone delivers arias from seven different 
operas displaying vigor and emotional intensity 
throughout, and his voice is rich with power and 
color. Devotees of Merrill and the opera will 
surely want to hear his interpretations 
of 
"Credo" from Otello, "Il Balen Del Suo Sorriso. 
from Il Trovatore and "Si Puo" from Pagliacci - 
SMETANA: The Bartered Bride: Rudolf KemPe 
conducting the Bamberg Symphony Orchestra- 
Angel 3642 
Bedrich Smetana's one hundred year -old bucolic 
opera is given an impressive reading by Baku 
Kempe conducting the Bamberg SymphonyfOr- 
chestra on this superb classical offering 
Angel. The disk features a host of fine singing 
talent including Pilar Lorengar, Fritz Wunder- 
lich, Gottlob Frick, etc. All of the work's sweep- 
ing, romantic statements are faithfully repro' 
duced on this recording. Classical opera buyeli 
should come out in droves.

Pick of the Week 
"CAN'T BUY ME LOVE" (2:12) 
[Northern Songs Ltd. ASCAP-Lennon, McCartney] 
"YOU CAN'T DO THAT" (2:33) 
[Northern Songs Ltd. ASCAP-Lennon, McCartney] 
THE BEATLES (Capitol 5150) 
Here's a Capitol offering that just can't miss. Orders for this brand 
new Beatles' deck, waxed in England for simultaneous release through- 
out the world, have already zoomed past the million mark. One half, 
tabbed "You Can't Buy Me Love," is a driving, beat -filled rocker that 
sports the foursome's famed 'Liverpool' sound. "You Can't Do That," on 
the other end, is a pulsating stomp'er bound for chartdom. Watch 'em 
take off. 
"THAT'S THE WAY BOYS ARE" (2:13) [Earth BMI-Barkan, Raleigh] 
"THAT'S THE WAY THE BALL BOUNCES" (2:22) 
[Bonjour ASCAP-Hamlish, Liebling] 
LESLEY GORE (Mercury 72259) 
The thrush, who has nothing but 'top ten' smasheroos, is a cinch to 
have another one in this follow up to "You Don't Own Me." The newie, 
labeled, "That's The Way Boys Are," is a contagious, multi -tracked 
handclapper that Lesley and her choral-ork support shuffle thru in ultra - 
commercial manner. The tear -compelling, philosophical romancer on the 
other end takes an easy cha cha beat ride. Credit for the stellar arrange- 
ments on both ends belong to Claus Ogerman. 
"MAKE ME FORGET" (2:18) 
[B. F. Wood ASCAP-Merrel, Harris, Douglas] 
"LITTLE GIRL YOU'VE HAD A BUSY DAY" (2:17) 
[Fajob ASCAP-Mendoza, Wisner] 
BOBBY RYDELL (Cameo 309) 
It looks (and sounds) like Bobby Rydell has another big "Forget" hit 
on his hands. The songster, who's coming off his hottest deck in some 
time, "Forget Her," can make it two smashes in -a -row with "Make Me 
Forget." It's another sentimental tear -compelling cut -in -England tune 
that moves along at a bright thump -a -twist pace. Coupler's a soft beat 
cha cha charmer that can also step way out. 
"THE MATADOR" (2:35) [Curtom, Jalynne BMI-Davis, Butler, Lance] 
"GONNA GET MARRIED" (2:12) [Curtom, Jalynne BMI-Mayfield] 
MAJOR LANCE (Okeh 7191) 
Lance follows his latest smash, "Um, Um, etc," in a string of smashes 
with another sensational Okeh stand that has the goods to make it his 
4th giant in -a -row. This one's a beat -filled affair about a new dance, 
tabbed "The Matador." The dandy J. Pate arranged deck's loaded with 
the hit sounds of his previous successes. The inviting cha cha -like un- 
dercut's a weeper labeled "Gonna Get Married." 
"KISS ME SAILOR" (2:25) [Saturday ASCAP-Rambeau, Rehak] 
"SOFT-SPOKEN GUY" (2:35) [Saturday ASCAP-Crewe, Rambeau] 
DIANE RENAY (20th -Century -Fox 477) 
Lark, who celebrated a huge success with her 20th -Fox tribute to 
"Navy Blue," is a cinch to be in for more way -up -on -the -chart festivi- 
ties this time out. Side to watch is another nautical jump delight, tabbed 
"Kiss Me Sailor," that Diana and the Calello-led ork-choral outfit serve 
up in ultra -commercial manner. The captivating, hush -voiced coupler 
takes a fetching cha cha beat route. 
"(THE BEST PART OF) BREAKIN' UP" (2:35) 
[Mother Bertha, Hill & Range BMI-Spector, Poncia, Andreoli] 
"BIG RED" (2:00) [H.P.S. ASCAP-Spector] 
THE RONETTES (Philles 120) 
The Ronettes, who have "Be My Baby" and "Baby, I Love You" under 
their hit belts, should soon be adding another solid sales item to the 
collection with "(The Best Part Of) Breakin' Up." It's a tantalizing 
shuffle -thumper that the gals knock out with loads of teen appeal. 
Stand out, percussion -led rock -a -rhythmic arrangement supplied by 
Jack "Specs" Nitzsche. As usual, the companion piece is a catchy all- 
instrumental swinger with jazz overtones. 
"STAY AWHILE" (1:58) [Flamingo -Hawker, Raymonde] 
"SOMETHING SPECIAL" (2:20) [Rogers -Springfield] 
DUSTY SPRINGFIELD (Pihlips 40180) 
The lark, who has a high -riding chart item on both sides of the At- 
lantic in "I Only Want To Be With You," can duplicate that success 
with this new one-already zooming up the best seller list in Great 
Britain. It's another up tempo driver, tabbed "Stay Awhile," that Dusty 
carves out in top notch multi -voiced manner. Superb choral -instrumental 
showcase rounds out the winner. Dusty's the cleffer of the charming cha 
cha beat opus on the flip.

Pick of the Week 
"SHANGRI-LA" (2:03) [Robbins ASCAP-Sigman, Malneck, Maxwell] 
"WARM AND TENDER" (2:01) [Metric BMI-Newman] 
VIC DANA (Dolton 92) 
Dana, who had the big vocal version of "More," a few months back, 
can do the same with "Shangri-La," the beautiful Bobby Maxwell -penned 
instrumental hit. Side features a top drawer vocal effort by Vic, who's 
backed in big, "Stripper" beat style by the Ernie Freeman ork-chorus. 
Tune, a Jackie Gleason TV theme, is already getting around the charts 
via both the Dana and Maxwell versions. The lovely tune on the flip 
moves along at a "More" clip. 
"VANISHING POINT" (2:00) [Wrist BMI-Gordon] 
"BOREALIS" (2:00) [Wrist-Rickland BMI-Motola, Page] 
THE MARKETTS (Warner Bros. 5423) 
The Marketts follow their recent sales giant, "Out Of Limits," with 
another fascinating instrumental that could quickly follow suit. This 
one's tabbed "Vanishing Point," and it's a steady beat thumper that once 
again sports those 'out of this world' instrumental sounds. The very 
pretty, soft cha cha beat coupler's titled "Borealis." Watch it, too! 
"THE PINK PANTHER THEME" (2:35) 
[Northridge & United Artists ASCAP-Mancini] 
"IT HAD BETTER BE TONIGHT" (1:56) 
[Northridge & United Artists ASCAP-Mancini, Mercer] 
HENRY MANCINI & HIS ORCH-CHORUS (RCA Victor 8286) 
The prolific flick composer has written the music for the new Peter 
Sellers -starred comedy flick, "The Pink Panther." His main -title creation 
is a strong, jazz -minded big -band swinger, while a gay Italian -flavored 
tune, "It Had Better Be Tonight," also from the pic, sports a lyric by 
his Oscar teammate, Johnny Mercer. Mancini's diskings of his own efforts 
are most often chart sounds, and he seems to have a two -for -the -money 
deck here. 
"CALL HER UP" (2:25) [Merrimac BMI-Garvin, Wilson] 
"THE KICKAPOO" (3:02) [Merrimac BMI-Wilson, Fann] 
JACKIE WILSON (Brunswick 55263) 
Wilson can have his hottest deck since "Baby Workout" in this new 
Brunswick stand. One half's a swinging shuffle -twist sentimental ro- 
mancer, labeled "Call Her Up," that Jackie and the Dick Jacobs' ork- 
choral outfit belt out with loads of coin -catching, pop-r&b enthusiasm. 
Ditto for the sizzling new rock -a -rhythmic dance step, "The Kickapoo," 
on the Alan Lorber-arranged companion piece. 
"TODAY" (2:44) [Miller & Heritage ASCAP-Sparks] 
"MISS KATY CRUEL" (2:35) [Heritage ASCAP-Podell, Woods] 
NEW CHRISTY MINSTRELS (Columbia 43000) 
The New Christy Minstrels can quickly get back in their money -making 
ways with this very commercial release, "Today," from the soon -to -bow 
MGM flick, "Advance To The Rear." The tune is a slow -moving, haunt- 
ingly plantive ballad about the painstakingly difficult progress of man- 
kind. The flip, "Miss Katy Cruel," is a lively, hard -driving, rhythmic up- 
dating of moving folk evergreen. Also merits a close look. 
"LET HER GO" (2:34) 
[Leeds ASCAP-Tepper, Bennett, Modugno, Zambrini] 
"LOVE'S GONNA LIVE HERE" (2:00) [Blue Book BMI-Owens] 
STEVE ALAIMO (ABC -Paramount 10540) 
Alaimo can again cop Top 100 laurels, this time via his ABC -Para- 
mount bow, "Let Her Go." Tune, which lists Domenico "Volare" Modugno 
as one of the cleffers, is an emotion -packed affair that the chanter puts 
across with telling effect. Excellent martial beat -like setting supplied 
by Bill Justis. The engaging coupler's (a current country click for Buck 
Owens) is delivered in a Bobby Darin "Mack The Knife" swing fashion. 
"WE'LL NEVER BREAK UP FOR GOOD" (2:13) 
[Couch, McDuff, Wilburn] 
"CRAZY LITTLE THINGS" (1:58) 
[Le Bill & Jackpot BMI-Beavers, Smith] 
PAUL & PAULA (Philips 40168) 
Chances are Paul & Paula will be chart -mates once again. The duo's 
latest, "We'll Never Break Up For Good" (an obvious reference to their 
off-the-record doings), is an extremely pretty, soft shuffle ballad ro- 
mancer that they carve out with touching sincerity. The complete change - 
of -pace coupler moves along at a contagious quick beat clip. 
"SHOUT" (2:28) [Wemar BMI-O'Kelly, Isley, Isley, Isley] 
"LITTLE GIRL" (2:22) [Just BMI-Greenberg, Baer] 
DION (Laurie 3240) 
From the Laurie vaults comes another Dion (Di Muci) offering that 
can make a big splash on the sales scene. It's the while -back sensation 
(for the Isley Bros.), "Shout," that opens in sizzling style quiets down 
to a whisper and then builds up again, in frenzied fashion. Backing's a 
pretty, easy-going weeper.
