EVERYTHING IN
THE GARDEN
The Grads (A&M)
MILLS MUSIC,
INC.
HOLLYWOOD—Liberty
Records
has
acquired
its own tape duplicating fa-
cilities
with
the
purchase
of TDC
Electronics
of Omaha, Nebraska,
ac-
cording
to
A1
Bennett,
president
of
the
label.
TDC was
founded
four
years
ago
by
its president, Leo Colvin, and vice-
president,
Stan
Nick.
It
is
involved
in the manufacture of four and eight
track
cartridges
as
well
as
the
reel-
to-reel
variety. TDC
has
thirty
em-
ployees
and
utilizes
two
duplicating
lines of a master and ten slaves each.
The
company’s
future
plans
include
the
addition
of
at
least
two
more
duplicating
lines as soon as
possible.
TDC uses the Telepro 4-track cartrige
and the Lear 8-track unit.
Bennett
said
he
was
“particularly
gratified
with
the
purchase,
because
we were able
to retain the
fine serv-
ices
of
Leo
Colvin
and
Stan
Nick.”
Colvin will remain on as general man-
ager
while
Nick
will
serve
as
chief
engineer.
TDC will handle Liberty tape manu-
facturing and continue to offer custom
services to other recording companies.
The TDC
acquisition
is
not
unlike
Liberty’s
Research
Craft
buy
last
year.
Its
founder,
Allen
Ellsworth
was
also
retained.
Research
Craft
presses
a
considerable
amount
of
product
for
Liberty
in
addition
to
handling
orders
for numerous
other
manufacturers.
Liberty’s growth
pattern
this
past
year has continued
to
accelerate. Be-
sides Research Craft and TDC, Liberty
also
acquired
World
Pacific—Pacific
Jazz Records, which has since grown
into one of the parent company’s most
successful divisions. It also established
a new economy
line, Sunset Records.
Other important Liberty divisions are
Imperial
Records
and
the
vast
pub-
lishing holdings of Metric Music.
Hershfield To Head
Sales
At General
Recorded Tape
SUNNYVALE,
CALIF. —
Herbert
Hershfield has been appointed to the
newly
created post
of
national
sales
manager for General Recorded Tape,
Inc.,
according
to
Alan
J.
Bayley,
president.
Hershfield,
who
joined
the
local
stereo tape manufacturer April
1, had
been
president
of
International
Pro-
motions Inc., Chicago-based tape sales
and distribution firm.
Bayley said creation of the national
sales manager
post was
part
of
the
company’s
expansion
into
production
and marketing of tape cax-tridges for
auto
tape
players. The
firm
expects
to
introduce
its
first
series
of
tape
cartridges later this month.
Hershfield will be based at General
Recorded
Tape’s
corporate
head-
quarters here. He will assume some of
the
sales
responsibilities
formerly
shared by Bayley and marketing vice-
president
John
Spellman.
Prior to heading International Pro-
motions
Inc., Hershfield had been na-
tional
sales
manager
and
central
regional
tape
specialist
for Ampex
Stereo Tape, based in Chicago. He will
locate
here
immediately,
and
will
move
his
family
to
the
Sunnyvale
area at the close of the current school
year.

Vinton & Klein Buy Stampers
NEW YORK—Bobby Vinton and
Al-
len Klein have announced the purchase
of The
Village Stompers from Duke
Niles.
The
Stompers
earned
a
gold
disk
in
1963 with
their
first
release,
“Washington Square” and have gone
on to accumulate world-wide LP sales
totalling
3,000,000.
The
undisclosed
price
is believed
to have reached into
six
figures.
Vinton, who
holds
a music degree
from
Duquesne
Univ.,
had
his
own
band until
1962 when he recorded the
million-seller, “Roses Are Red,” as
a
vocalist
for
Epic,
to
which
he
had
previously been signed as an orchestra
leader. He plans
to direct and super-
vise
all
future
waxings
of
the
Stompers,
noted
for
their
original
“folk-Dixie”
sound.
The
acquisition
of
the
group,
also
Epic
pactees,
re-
flects
the
resurgence
of
interest
in
instrumental
recordings,
a movement
spearheaded
by
the
recent
successes
of Herb Alpert’s Tiajuana Brass.
Allen Klein and Company,
Inc. has
assumed
direction
of
The
Village
Stompers, who
have
been
a
popular
attraction
on
the
nation’s
campuses
and fairgrounds,
as
well
as frequent
guests on major television shows and
headliners at top cabarets.

SMASHING—Sixteen hundred of the

BURBANK, CALIF.—With

recently

1 million; the disk is current smash in

and
Australia, with

Rose will be making his first trek to
WB and Reprise licensees on behalf of

a

with Louis Benjamin, managing direc-

Negram in Holland.
Discussions will concern themselves
with new marketing strategy and mer-
chandising plans for the coming year,

ners and Reprise Fall program.
Both Maitland and Rose
will

in

Gulf & Western Buys
Muntz Stereo Pak
VAN NUYS — Muntz
Stereo
Pak,
claimed by
its founder and president
Earl
W.
Muntz
to
be
the
world’s
largest
producer
of
stereo
and
car-
tridge tape products
for cars, homes
and
boats,
will
be
acquired by
Gulf
& Western Industries, a $150 million
a
year
sales
firm
in
mining, manu-
facturing, auto part
distribution and
aerospace.
Acquisition of Stereo Pak’s net as-
sets involves an agreement, according
to G&W
exec vp David A. Judelson
and Muntz, that provides for the
is-
suance
initially
of
10,000
shares
of
class B
convertible
preferred
stock
of G&W and
the
issuance
of
25,400
additional shares over a
six year pe-
riod.
This
deal
is
subject
to compli-
ance
with
the
requirements
of
the
California
Corporation
Act
and
ap-
proval
of
the
board
of
directors
of
both
companies.
Plans
call
for
all
the
operations
and assets of Muntz Stereo Pak to be
placed into a wholly owned subsidiary
of G&W and that the present Stereo
Pak management will continue
to
di-
rect the operations and businesses of
the
new
subsidiary
subject
to
the
policies
of G&W.
Muntz
says
the
company
houses
the
world’s
largest
tape
library,
estimated
at
30,000
titles,
and
is
currently
producing
approximately
10,000 cartridges
daily at
its
7-plant
complex
near
Los
Angeles.
Muntz
Stereo Pak was formed
in
1963 and
is currently represented nationally by
1,500
accounts.
Fiscal
1966
sales
for
the company
are
estimated
at
$20-
million.
Muntz employs 200
technical, mar-
keting,
sales and administrative
per-
sonnel and also produces stereo prod-
ucts under
its Audio/Stereo
Division.
The
Van
Nuys
operation
includes
separate
divisions
for
cartridge
as-
sembly, cabinet making and finishing,
tape
loading,
duplicating,
labeling,
shipping, engineering, quality control,
car
installation and
retail
sales.

are next in line for the big, big club.

SScTARGENTINA
Very soon the
first pre-recorded tapes
will be
available
to
the customers,
while up to now' the only way to get tape music was by importing it from the
United States and Europe. Although the quantity of existing tape recorders is
small, the market
is expected
to develop
into something important
in a few
years. Philips will market a budget record
player, which
will even be given
free
if the customer orders a not yet
specified amount
of
records.
Besides,
Phonogram
will
start
selling
a
ten
record
set
(to be
paid
in ten months)
through the Philips home appliance
dealers, many of whom regularly do not
sell records. The set
is tagged “Argentina Sings This Way” and contains a
story of tango and folk music from 1810 to the present.
Nestor
Selasco, Music Hall’s prexy, has started a ten week tour that will
include Lima (Peru), Medellin (Colombia), Caracas (Venezuela), Los Angeles,
New York, Vancouver, Tokyo, Hong Kong and Honolulu. Selasco’s purposes are
to sign renewals and new contracts with the diskeries he represents here, and
mainly to study the latest improvements in recording equipment, for applica-
tion in the label’s new studios, now under construction.
CBS
organized
two
gatherings
this
week:
one
honoring
tropical
music
chanter Tito Rodriguez, currently visiting here, and another one
to present
Leo Dan
writh
his
second
gold
record,
for another one
million
sales mark.
Rodriguez’ dinner took place at the Golf Club, while Dan’s cocktail party was
held at the Alvear Palace Hotel.
RCA is improving its share in the jazz music field with a series of releases
under the Vintage
series banner. Latest additions
to
this
series
are “Count
Basie In Kansas City,” recorded with the Bennie Moten band, and Duke Elling-
ton’s “Daybreak Express.” The
diskery’s part in
this branch
of the market
has been growing steadily during the past months, along with other strong
editions coving old tango and folk music recordings.
A detailed report from Odeon states that Atahualpa Yupanqui has recorded
a new album, which
will be launched
soon. Atahualpa will
travel
to Japan,
where Argentine
folk music
is
well
appreciated. Two
other
strong
artists,
Ramona Galarza and Nestor Fabian, will make a tour of the province of Santa
Fe and start a new program,
titled “Our Party.” Frank Pourcel’s “Avec,” a
top seller during several months, has passed the 100,000 mark; Poursel’s latest
recording, “El Cordobes,” seems also an extremely strong bet.
Latest
releases from Trova
include
a Folkways album
recorded
in
Spain
with typical music from that country, and another one by the
Fisk
Jubilee
'
Singers, along with Elenco albums
(recorded in Brazil)
carrying versions by
Lenny Dale with the Sambalanco Trio, and guitar player Rosinha de Valencia.
On the Classical music side there is an LP with music by Wilhelm Friedemann
Bach, recorded by 88’er Heida Hermanns.
Disc Jockey Records is releasing the first album by Benny Barbara, trumpet
player who recorded with Harry James. Benny was born
in Argentina and
lives currently in Canada, and these recordings were done for Elysee Records
of that country. Also from DJ
is another album by “The Smallest Orchestra
in The World”: Cesar Bo (Guitar) and Alberto Alcala (Drums). Local orkster
Lucio Milena, on his side, has recorded “La Boheme” and “Michelle.”
Microfon is outing an EP tagged “Tango en Cano 14,” named after the well
known night spot where tango music
is played. The recording has been done
by the Hector Stamponi orchestra, with singers Ruth Durante and Marcelo Paz.
Johnny
Allon has
recorded
another
single:
“Everybody
Loves The
Clown,”
while newcomer Zachary has “Look At Me” as new title and the Trio Oriental
recorded “Cuando El Amor Se Va” and “Guajira Guantanamera.”

NEW YORK—Chappell

For years, Dreyfus has owned and

known as Chappell’s, and in this
role
over the years, he became a producer
of many
hit
musicals
and
a
record
man,
as
well
as
a
successful
music
publisher and nurturer of writing and
producing
talent.
Today, Dreyfus operates both com-
panies
in
addition
to
branches
in
Paris,
Munich,
Sydney,
Toronto
and
Milan.
He
commutes
three
or
four
times a year between New York and

to

the vast
opera-
tions.

his
age,
the
veteran
music man keeps a
close eye on
the

The way things are shaping up here it won’t be long before Mrs. Elva Miller
is grabbing her share of national chart rating in Australia with her just re-
leased single
(Capitol)
of her rather unique versions of “Downtown” and “A
Lover’s Concerto”; pre-release airplay has reached almost unbelievable propor-
tions, but
this
is usually the case with most novelty
records. EMI
plans
to
issue the album, “Mrs. Miller’s Greatest Hits,” within the next couple of weeks.
Australian pop music groups will be offered a great opportunity to achieve
international recognition in the national “Battle of the Sounds” to be conducted
in July by radio station 3UZ. Forty-one commercial stations
all over Australia
will conduct elimination heats on a regional basis. The eventual State winners
will all gather at Festival Hall in Melbourne for the Grand Final to be held on
Sunday, July 17. The judging panel will be:
Normie Rowe, Festival/Sunshine recording artist; Neville Smith, Australian
manager of the recording division of Astor Electronics Pty. Ltd.; Fred Tolley,
chief music librarian of 3UZ; Ray Bean, program manager of
station 2UW
;
Kenn Brodziak, Aztec Services; Maggie Makeig, editor of “Disc”; Horrie Dar-
gie, managing director of D.Y.T. Services Pty. Ltd.
The ultimate winner will receive a trip to England with the Sitmar shipping
line; four weeks accommodation in London; $1,000 spending money; a record-
ing contract with Go!! Records, and a definite overseas engagement. The 3UZ
national “Battle
of the Sounds”
is being sponsored by Hoadley’s
Chocolates
Ltd; and the “Battle”
is open
to
all Australian groups whether amateur or
professional.
Little
local
girl Lori celebrated her tenth birthday on May
14th.. To mark
the occasion her recording company, RCA, released her new single “Poor Little
Black Sheep” and “If I Knew You Were Cornin' I’d Have Baked A Cake.” The
former is a composition by local writer John Parks.
Ron Gillespie, chief executive of W & G Records, says things look good for
the first record by local boy A1 Styne, who was recently signed to a long-term
pact with the company. Titles on the debut release are “Look For My True
Love” and “Don’t Ever Leave Me.” In an exclusive interview with Cash Box,
Gillespie remarked “If we can judge the potential by the measure of entice-
ment being offered to that artist (A1 Styne) by other record company people
then Styne is made. Hardly had the pressings of his record cooled before Styne
was being given the full treatment by other record men.” Gillespie continued,
“It’s a pity that in a country the
size of Australia this kind of sniping has
been introduced.”
After releasing one record through RCA
(on the ATA label) Col Joye, one
of Australia’s most popular artists over a long period, has renewed his asso-
ciation with the Festival group. Col Joye Enterprises Pty.
Ltd., will produce
future
releases on the ATA
label for which
Festival have
the
distribution
rights for Australia, and the Far East including Japan. In addition to Col Joye,
the ATA label will produce records by Judy Stone, the Joy Boys, Sandy Scott,
Brian Henderson and others. They even have an album by Father Kevin O’Con-
nor entitled “Introducing Father Kevin O’Connor—The Singing Priest Of The
Outback.”
Tony Troraeros
of Phono-Vox records
is
elated over the
success he
is
en-
joying with the Francoise Hardy release “Only You Can Do
It,” which Tony
has issued on the Vogue
label. Tony reports that as a result of an overseas
phone
call with Leon Cabat
(president of Vogue Records
of
Paris)
he
will
shortly receive two films of performances by Francoise Hardy, which will be
placed with national television pop music shows. The demand for albums by
Francoise Hardy is also very strong and each imported shipment
is
sold out
almost the minute it arrives here. Tromeros says he is receiving great co-oper-
ation from Cabat and Madame Colette De Nattes at Vogue headquarters
in
France. Phono-Vox have decided that Vogue
will be the only overseas
label
that they will represent.
It is known that Phono-Vox will soon embark on a
program of recording Australian talent
(in English) and several artists have
already been signed up.
Recent releases through the Astor company include “My Life” by the Over-
landers, and the “Michelle” album by the same group. “Juanita Banana” by
the Peels was released on the Karate label. The Astor boys are working on two
former
No.
1 American
hits
in “Daydream”
by
the
Lovin’
Spoonful,
and
“You’re My Soul And Inspiration” by the Righteous Brothers on Verve.
Following the surprisingly big volume of business done by W & G with their
series “Steam Action”
(authentic sounds of Australian locomotives)
the label
has just launched an album entitled “Australian Bird Calls.” The package fea-
tures location recordings of many Australian birds, and the album jacket car-
ries a “live” four-color shot of the Australian lyrebird.

ABC-Par Purchase
Of Dunhill Finalized
Liberty Buys Blue Note Lube!
NEW YORK—Long-standing rumors
of
the
purchase
of
Dunhill
Records
by
ABC-Paramount
were
confirmed
last
week
in
California
by

Newton,

of ABC-Par who
flew
to the west coast
to

the
deal, and Dunhill principals Jay Las-
ker,

and

Roberts.
Involved
in

are

Records,
Trousdale
Music
and
Dun-
hill
Productions.
Negotiations
were
completed
during
the
afternoon
of
last Wednesday (18)
in Beverly Hills.
Dunhill Productions and Trousdale
Music
were
formed
less
than
two
years
ago
and
Dunhill Records
cele-
brated
its
first
birthday
last month
(April).
Also
included
in
the
pur-
chase are the services of Jay Lasker
and Lou
Adler, who
will continue
to
run the Dunhill operation, while Bob-
by Roberts, one
of the foremost per-
sonal managers
in
the
business,
will
devote
all of his time
to
his manage-
ment firm and
to production of films.
The
initial
success
of
Dunhill
started
with
Dunhill
Productions,
formed
by
Roberts
and
Adler, who
will

Liberty Buys All-Disc
LOS
ANGELES—Liberty
Records
has acquired All-Disc Records, a lead-
ing
eastern
pressing
plant.
Move
follows
last year’s
acquisition by
the
label of Research Craft, a west coast
pressing
plant,
and
the
recent
pur-
chase of TDC, a tape duplicating com-
pany
in
the
midwest.
According
to Al Bennett, president
of
Liberty,
an
agreement
has
been
signed
with
Ivan Amo
which
calls
for the business and substantially
all
of
the
assets
of
All-Disc
as
well
as
the services of Amo, who will operate
the company
as
general manager
of
the new
division.
Located
forty-five
minutes
from
Times Square in Roselle, New Jersey,
All-Disc
produces
records
for many
leading indie labels, including Disney-
land, Twentieth Century Fox and An-
somia.
Founded
in
1960
by Amo,
a
technical engineer, the company orig-
inally utilized four presses
in a 5,000
square feet plant.
It has
since grown
into
a
facility
which
encompasses
30,000
square
feet on two
acres and
houses 20
presses. Eighty people
are
employed by All-Disc for three
shifts
which operate twenty-four hours daily.

Linsky To Pickwick
As Product Manager
LONG
ISLAND
CITY,
N.Y.—Herb
Linsky
has
been
appointed
product
manager
for
Pickwick/33,
“Instant”
Learning- and Pickwick tapes.
Linsky will plan and promote prod-
uct
sales
and
assume
full
responsi-
bilities for merchandising and market-
ing the lines assigned to him from the
completed
packaging
of
the
product
until
it
is purchased by the ultimate
consumer,
according
to
Cy
Leslie,
president of Pickwick.
The concept of a product manager,
while
almost commonplace
in
heavy
industry,
is relatively new to the rec-
ord field and Linsky’s post
is an inno-
vation
in
the
Pickwick
corporate
structure,
Leslie
noted.
Leslie
indi-
cated that the growing complexity of
our
business
and
the
demand
for
executives who can go
into
the
field
and put together programs that
pin-
point
effort
and
concentration
as
though they were
operating
a
small
business of their own
is “increasingly
important.”
Linsky, at 37 a youthful veteran of
the
record
industry,
has
served
in
various
sales
and
promotional
posts
with RCA
Victor,
Epic, London
and
Kapp
since
coming
into
the
record
field
in
1955.
He
has
traveled
ex-
tensively
and
been
involved
in
all
areas of national sales and promotion.
Pickwick/33, Linsky’s chief respon-
sibility,
is
Pickwick
International’s
$2.
($2.50
classical)
label
composed
of
selections
from
the
catalogs
of
fourteen
full-price
record
com-
panies
including
Capitol,
Warner
Brothers-Reprise,
ABC-Paramount,
Everest,
etc.
Extensively
advertised
and
publicized,
Pickwick/33
is
re-
garded as one of the most successful
new economy priced
labels
in the
in-
dustry and one of the most important
lines
in
the
Pickwick
International
sales structure.

FOCUS oiir jazz
illlllllllllllllUllllllllllllllllllllilllilllllllllllllllllllllll^
For years we have heard the
cry,
“Bring back the big bands!”. As far
as
live
performances
are
concerned,
there
is no indication that such a re-
turn is imminent. However, if we may
draw an inference from what the rec-
ord companies have been doing lately,
it might be safe
to say that on rec-
ords, at least, such a state of affairs
is not only imminent, but already upon
us.
Recently,
the
record
companies,
major and independent alike, have be-
gun to showcase their key jazz artists
in big band settings, much in the tra-
dition that has long been Duke Elling-
ton’s. This approach
is
not the
con-
ventional big band sound that we have
come
to know from regular working
bands of the past and present. In most
big bands the emphasis is always on a
smooth, cohesive ensemble sound, with
short, rather than extended, solo play-
ing by any particular performer. Ad-
mittedly, there have been exceptions,
but these have been rare; these were
usually characteristic to some special
work, written and performed for the
express
purpose
of
exhibiting
the
special talent of some deserving per-
former.
As
examples,
Benny
Good-
man’s
“Sing,
Sing,
Sing” for Harry
James
and
Gene
Krupa,
or
Artie
Shaw’s “Clarinet Concerto,” or Duke
Ellington’s “Concerto For Cootie” for
Cootie Williams. You might say that
what is happening now in the jazz re-
cording
field
is
an
extension
of
the
Ellington concept, which had been to
feature his solo artists, using the band
as a graceful attendant.
Big band album
production
neces-
sarily means an increase in cost, some-
times a prohibitive cost which makes
the break even point very
difficult to
attain. Why would the companies em-
bark on
a program which would
in-
crease the hazard
of breaking even?
Perhaps they feel that there has been
a saturation of small group jazz
re-
cordings.
Or
do
the
companies
feel
that the record buying public has be-
gun
to
feel
that
there
is
a
certain
anonymity
about much
of the
small
group recordings that have been pro-
duced with such abundance? Do
rec-
ord producers feel that big band jazz
is an easier introduction to the other-
wise non-jazz buying public? Maybe
the companies
feel that they have a
better chance of having their product
played on the
air
if
it has that BIG
sound which seems to please so many
program
directors
at
radio
stations.
With the fierce competition in the re-
cording
industry,
do
the
companies
sense
that
the
customer might
feel
that he is getting more for his money
when
he
buys
a
big
band
record ?
Whatever the reasons,
it becomes
in-
creasingly apparent that record pro-
ducers are leaning more and more to
the big sound in recorded jazz.
Among the recent releases that
il-
lustrate the big band
setting for an
artist known
primarily
as
a
small
group jazzman is guitarist Wes Mont-
gomery’s latest album, “Goin’ Out Of
My Head” (Verve
8642). On
this
al-
bum Montgomery is surrounded by an
array
of top jazzmen, with excellent
and
varied
arrangements
by
Oliver
Nelson. Montgomery, who burst upon
the jazz scene in the late fifties, after
having
been
a
long-time
legend
in
Indianapolis,
gained
his
reputation
making trio and quartet albums. Yet,
in his brief association with Verve, he
has already done two big band record-
ings. On
each album Wes
has
been
given
the
opportunity
to
show
his
lyrical
ballad
style,
as
well
as
his
ability
to
play
hard
swinging
jazz.
Oliver
Nelson’s
charts
afford
Mont-
gomery
full
freedom
to
exploit
his
Montgomery and Nelson forge from
“Chim Chim Cherie,” by way of Dis-
ney’s Mary Poppins. Wes’ solo playing
is immensely
exciting and
is
in no
way restricted by the larger setting.
“Jazz Dialogue”
(Atlantic 1449)
is
another recent
release
that
offers
a
small jazz group that rarely records
in
a
big band
context. The Modern
Jazz Quartet, considered by many to
be the essence of small group jazz, is
heard here with an
all-star band
of
twelve. The album
is aptly titled be-
cause, in effect, this is a jazz dialogue
between
The
Quartet
and
the
big
band. John Lewis, the musical
direc-
tor of The MJQ, did all seven arrange-
ments, and
it
is
interesting
to
note
that six of the seven vehicles recorded
on this album have been recorded pre-
viously by The Modern Jazz Quartet.
Thus, what we have is an opportunity
to
compare how
these
newly
struc-
tured
big band
sides
compare
with
what had been done originally by the
small
group.
“Jazz
Dialogue”
is
an-
other
strong
argument
for
the
re-
newed
interest
in
big band
jazz
re-
cording.
Stanley Turrentine, one of the most
original sounding and energetic of the
younger
tenor
sax
men,
has
been
working
for
the
past
several
years
with his wife, Shirley Scott, in a small
jazz group, usually a quartet. His re-
cordings, too, for the most part have
been
in
that same
small group
con-
text.
“Joyride”
(Blue Note
4201)
is
evidence
that
the
independent
jazz
label owners feel the necessity of pro-
ducing some big band jazz. Blue Note
could not have selected a more deserv-
ing artist for such exposure than Tur-
rentine. Once again the arrangements
have been written by
Oliver Nelson,
who conducts the
dates, as well. The
sixteen man
big band
reads
like
a
who’s who of jazz, including men like
Clark Terry, Jay Jay Johnson, Kenny
Burrell,
Herbie
Hancock,
and
Phil
Woods,
each
of whom
has
been
a
leader on his own recording dates. The
calibre of such sidemen
is an indica-
tion of the quality of this album, and
it
should
be
thus,
because
Stanley
Turrentine
outdoes
himself
on
this
“Joyride.”
The
final
album
for
discussion
is
Ahmad
Jamal’s
latest,
“Rhapsody”
(Cadet 764). This recording is a com-
bination
of
trio
sides
(five)
and
trio
accompanied by a fifteen piece orches-
tra of violins, violas, and
celli
(four).
The string tracks were arranged and
conducted by Joe Kennedy, himself an
accomplished
violinist, and
a
gentle-
man whose
star
as an arranger has
yet
to
ascend.
The
opportunity
to
listen alternately to just the trio and
then the
trio with the
string accom-
paniment points up how emphatic
is
the wedding
of the two
sounds. The
program
piaterial
on
this
album
is
especially
attractive,
too, comprising
seven
standards
and
two
originals.
Jamal
has
never
been
recorded
in
better form, and the ease with which
the
strings are blended with the trio
is
a
joy
to
the
ear. “Rhapsody” by
Ahmad Jamal is another strong argu-
ment for more such big band settings
for jazz artists.
Hopefully,
the
trend
toward
big
band recording by jazz luminaries will
continue.
This
direction
will
be em-
braced
by
the
buying
public
if
the
record
executives
will
recognize
the
latent
danger,
that
of
taking away
the
jazzman’s
identity
and
turning
him into a pop artist. If the jazz per-
former
is
allowed
to
maintain
his
identity,
the
stalwart
jazz
buying
public will continue to buy, and so will

Or-
chestra, Handel’s Latin psalm
“Dixit
Dominus” and completing the release
is a program of Hungarian folk-songs
by Zoltan Kodaly and Bela Bartok.

ENCINO, CAL.—Enrique Lebendiger,

in

has won an honor for producing the

record. Lebendiger accepted the award
at a special assembly for this purpose

Paulo on Mar. 31. The work achieving
this
distinction was “An
Anthology
Of
Brazilian Authors” arranged and
played by the native pianist, Eny Da
Rocha. The RGE recording
is
distrib-
uted
throughout
South
America
by
RCA Victor.

ENTINA
Music Hall
is launching the Pye catalog this week
in Argentina, through
four albums recorded by some
of
the
top
artists belonging
to
this
British
label. Names
are
Sounds
Orchestral,
the
Searchers,
the Kinks and
Sandie
Shaw, and Luis Calvo, one of the diskery’s toppers, announced that there will
be a corresponding number of singles to reinforce promotion of these
artists.
MH’s prexy, Nestor Selasco,
is continuing his world wide
tour, and has
re-
ported
the arrangement
of new
contracts with
labels Ember,
Alegre,
Cox,
and Ce.
Each new release by Palito Ortega—currently in Europe—is news, and the
most recent RCA outing, “Convivir,” seems to be heading to big sales marks,
as have most of the artist’s previous efforts. As we commented before, Palito’s
album with the music of “Mi Primera Novia,”
his
latest
film,
will probably
appear among the top selling albums of 1966, thus continuing a success
last-
ing about five years, something exceptional for pop music in this country. Of
course, RCA
is devoting plenty of promotion to this record.
Lucio Milena’s Milrom organization reports that a promotion campaign
is
being held in behalf of “Lei Mi Aspetta,” Italian song originally cut by Gene
Pitney
(here released by CBS) and Nicola De Bari
(Fermata),^ and here by
Claudio and the same Lucio Milena (Disc Jockey), los Cinco Latinos (Quinto)
and Claudia (Odeon Pops).
Odeon
is releasing the well known Mexican
hit, “La Banda Borracha,”
in
two versions: by tropical music group
los Wawaned and by regional
artist
Canuto. Among the diskery’s best selling records appears the previous record-
ing by los Wawanco, “Quiero Un Sombrero,” along with several waxings by
the Beatles (Michelle), local artist Yaco Monti (“Siempre Te Recordare”) and
Claude Ciari’s instrumental, “La Plage.”
Public Relations man Roberto Quirno infos that Brazilian
artist Yuyu Da
Silva will stay during 1966
in Buenos
Aires, recording for Disc Jockey and
shooting a film
directed by Carlos Borsani under the
title
of “Panchito En
Buenos
Aires”. She has recorded two
of the
tunes, which
will appear as
a
single:
“La
Hormiguita”
and
“El
Chupetin”.
Another DJ
artist,
Rosamel
Araya, has been considered
“the most popular pop
artist”
after a research
made by one of the local public opinion organizations.
CBS reports the inking of teen actor and singer Sergio Mas, born in the
province of Cordoba, and the recording of his first singles for the
label. Mas
performs weekly on Channel
13, in the “Sabados Circulares” Saturday after-
noon spot, and will soon appear on the same Channel as actor. Melodic singer
Robetro Yanes will soon start a new tour. Next July he’ll jet to Bogota, Cara-
cas, Puerto Rico and Miami, returning to San Pablo, Rio and Buenos Aires after
three months
of
travelling. He’s currently performing on Channel 9 and
is
recording a new LP.
Phonogram
is releasing the
first album
of folk songstress Mercedes
Sosa,
one of the main names in the new stream of artists in this
field. The LP
in-
cludes
titles
like “Zamba Del Riego”, “Quena” and Chilean traditional tunes
“Tonadas De Manuel Rodriguez”. Other outings are a new LP by Edmundo
Rivero, “Espectacular”, and the second album hy Mina, “Studio Uno”.
H y R Records is outing an album by tango lark Mercedes Simone, featuring
several
standards
like “Motivo
Sentimental”, “Tu
Llegada”
and,
of
course,
“La
Cumparsita”, Arrangements
and
the
orchestra have
been
directed
by
Emilio Brameri, and several doubles and
singles have been
culled from
this
album. Other HyR items are two LP’s cut originally by Combo
in
Italy by
the
Stella Alpina Chorus and
Calabrese
artists
Franco
Mazzitelli,
Daniela
Zagarese, and Mario Lombardi.
From San Juan, Puerto Rico, we have received a postcard from the Mac Ke
Mac’s, reporting good success
in their appearances at the Caribe Hilton and
WAPA-TV. The contract will last a couple of weeks, and afterwards the group
will continue its tour.
Lagos Publishers informs us
that next month they
will print a
series
of
fifteen kiddie songs, written by Carlos Guastavino and Leon Benaros. Maria
Helena would record these songs for use at school, since they cover different
aspects of teaching. The purpose
is to renew the material currently available
for first-grade school, considered too old for practical use.
Trova continues its plan of strong jazz releases, with the labels
it represents
and several interesting local recordings. Some of the latest Contemporary re-
cordings are “Relax”, by Gerry Wiggins, and “Jazz Giant” by Benny Carter,
while under the
Pacific Jazz banner the news
is an LP by tenor saxist Bud
Shank.
Julio Korn Publishers
reports that they have
the
rights
to
several tunes
appearing in the “Un Disco Per L’Estate” RAI TV Contest, which
is being
held in
Italy.
Titles are “La Porta Dell’Amore”, “Cuando La Prima
Stella”,
“Non Vorrei Volerti Bene”, “Se La Vieta E Cosi” and “L’Uomo D’Oro”, and
have been recorded
originally by Betty
Curtis,
Orietta
Berti, Franco
Tozzi,
Tony
del Monaco and Caterina
Caselli. For
its record
division,
Diskorn, JK
arranged the representation of US label Hickory.
Liliana Paz of Smart Music reports that the pubbery has the rights to three
songs from the repertoire of Brazilian star Altemar Dutra: “Somos Iguales”,
“El Telefono” and “Sei La”. Dutra
is a good
seller in this market and good
results are expected from these tunes.
Ricardo Romero
of
Belter,
recently established
in Argentina,
sends word
about the success of the two first LP’s of this label released in Buenos Aires:
Lola Flores and Manolo Escobar. Other LP’s are ready for marketing in the
near future, and Romero hopes Belter will establish itself firmly in this coun-
try.
Surco reports the release of a
single by the Young Rascals, with their re-
cent US hit, “Good Lovin’ ” and “Mustang Sally”. On the European side, Surco
is releasing an album with several cabaret tunes recorded by artists such as
Paul Morgan, Marlene Dietrich and Hilde Hildebrand. This LP was recorded
originally by Telefunken.
Fermata Publishers report that new group los In has recorded for CBS the
oncoming Lennon-McCartney
hit,
“Girl”, as part
of their
first
single. Para-
guayan group los Teen Agers has cut “Cunado Mas Lejos Estoy”, “Una Casa
En La Cima Del Mundo”, “Michelle” and “lo Ti Daro Di Piu”, for new label
Neptuno, while Segio Ponti, for Music Hall, has cut also “Girl”. The pubbery
has also the rights to “7 Uomini D’Oro”, included in a film being screened on
these days, and French hit “Mon Credo”.
Neumann Publishers reports the recording of “Tan Solo Un Loco Amor”, by
Nito Mores for Music
Hall, who
will
also
cut “Desnudate”,
another tango
premiered by Nestor Fabian and now recorded for Odeon by Hector Beltran.
“Desnudate” will be also recorded by Tango Orchestra Di Paulo for RCA and
Fulvio Salamanca on Music Hall.
Ala Nicky Records informs us about the release of a single by Italian artist
Armando Docetti: “La Spiaggia Sara Vuolta” and “La Pioggia E Diventata
Nieve”, recorded
originally for Primo
of that country, and another one by
tango Orchestra Osvaldo Piro: “Dice Una Guitarra” and “Disonante”. For folk
fans there is a single by el Bagualero Salteno: “El Patron” and “La Linduara”.

Some
years
ago,
Bob
Crewe,
a
highly
talented
composer,
felt
that
in order to get ahead
in the strongly
competitive
music
and
recording
business,
it
would
be
a
great
ad-
vantage
for
a
writer to also produce
records.
And
so
Bob
Crewe
com-
bined
writing
with
arranging
and
producing.
He
achieved
great
suc-
cess,
and
now
both
Crewe
and
his
companies are known throughout the
world.
Russ
Miller,
profressional
man-
ager
of
Crewe's
publishing
firm,
Saturday
Music,
Inc.,
is
in complete
agreement
with
this
principle.
He
makes
it a
rule to select writers who
can
also be developed as producers.
This
policy
has
been
tremendously
effective
for
both
writer
and
pub-
lisher.
Russ
Miller, and Bob Coogan,
as-
sistant professional manager of Sat-
urday
Music,
are
always
on
the
lookout
for
writers,
and
since
it
is
known

they

in-

the other
hand, record producers from around-
the-globe
have
beaten
a
door
to
Saturday Music
in search of material
for
their
own

sessions.
They
have
found
that
this
is
one
publishing
firm
that
really
has
its
finger
on
the
pulse
of
the
record
buying
public.
Outstanding
producers
who
have
found
that
they
can
always
count
on

Music coming
up

the

Platters
The Platters have been on the mu-
sical scene since 1953 when the group
was
formed
by Herbert
Reed.
Since
their
first
hit, “Only You,” on Mer-
cury,
the
group
has
been
carrying
such
hits
as
“The
Great
Pretender”
and “Magic Touch”
(to name just
2)
to the ear of the music listening pub-
lic. The
Platters have
just completed
a college tour and are currently mak-
ing their way to Los Angeles via Bos-
ton, Baltimore, and Detroit. The group
is
scheduled
to
appear
in
Bermuda
and Japan before the end of Summer.
Herbert
Reed,
Sonny
Turner,
and
David Lynch are originally from L.A.
and
Sandra Dawn
and Nate
Nelson
are from New York. Sandra was with
the Shantells before joining the Plat-
ters
and
Nate was
lead
singer
for
the
Flamingoes.
Nate,
who
plays
drums on the
side,
also produces
re-
cords
and
writes
songs
like
“Hear,
Speak, See No Evil” which
is the flip
side of the
Platters’ Current Musicor
outing
“I
Love
You
1,000
Times”
(number 42 on
this week’s Top
100.)
Susan
Christie
Susan Christie has been singing for
most of her 23-years and somewhere
along the line developed a proficiency
on
the
Fender
bass.
The
pert
lass
teaches guitar as a sideline in Moores-
town,
N.J. John
Hill, who
is
Susan’s
husband, produced her Columbia
out-
ing
“I
Love
Onions”
while
engaged
in graduate studies in the music
field
at
Temple
University.
The
Onion
loving thrush was graduated from the
University of Penn, and in seemingly
almost
un-American
co-ed
fashion,
met her husband in high school rather
than in college.
Bratrice
(that’s the real name) has
often
been
featured
on
Philadelphia
television and
is presently
set for
a
Herman Spero TY’er. Long a regular
on
the
Philadelphia
entertainment
scene, Susan
Christie was
a member
of a folk group called the Highlanders
and in recent years she has been tour-
ing the U.S. with a pop group called
the Encores.

Dynamite Productions
Signs MGM Indie Pact
NEW
YORK—Richard
Perry
of
Dynamite Productions has negotiated
an independent production
deal with
Lenny
Scheer
of MGM
Records.
Under
the
pact
Perry
will
produce
several Dynamite
artists for
release
on MGM and its subsid labels.
First
act
to
be
recorded
will
be
Forestina & Roy. Their
first release,
“Suddenly,
It’s Love,” will be waxed
this month.
Columbia
Stages
3rd
Golf Tourney
NEW
YORK—Columbia
Records’
third annual golf classic was recently
held
at
the Knollwood Country Club
in
Elmsford,
N.Y. One hundred and
fifty golfers participated
in
this, the
firm’s
largest
tournament
to
date.
The golf
classic was
hosted by
label
veep
Bill
Gallagher.
In
addition
to
Gallagher,
those
in
attendance
at
the
tournament
in-
cluded a number of Columbia Records
executives;
representatives from mu-
sic trade publications, radio and tele-
vision personnel; Broadway producer
George
Abbott;
golf
pro
Art
Wall;
Columbia artists Robert Goulet, Steve
Lawrence and Jerry Vale; and noted
personalities Gary
Marshall, Tommy
Mercer, George Siravo, Dick Williams
and Kai Winding.
Each
year,
one
of
Columbia’s
re-
cording artists
is selected to serve as
tournament chairman.
This year, the
honored
post
was
filled
by
Robert
Goulet.
The highest award, the President’s
Flight
Perpetual Trophy for
golfers
with
registered
U.S G.A.
handicaps,
was won by Endo Corsetti, with a low
gross of 80. Corsetti
is affiliated with
D&H Distributors
in Harrisburg, Pa.
The Robert Goulet Fairway Flight
Cup, named in honor of the chairman,
for golfers without registered handi-
caps was won by Art Schwartz, with
a low net of
70.
The tourney was divided into three
categories for the purpose of award-
ing
trophies.
These
categories
in-
cluded Division
1—Recording Artists,
Division
2—Radio-TV
Personnel,
Di-
vision 3—Music Trades.
In Division
1,
1st Low Gross went
to Tommy Mercer, 2nd went to Robert
Goulet and 3rd was awarded to Gary
Marshall.
George
Siravo
took
the
prize for low net.
In
Division
2,
1st Low
Gross was
copped by Pat Digilio, 2nd was taken
by Irwin
Schlussel and
3rd by Mort
Becker. Low net went to John Yotts.
In
Division
3, Bob Wells
took
1st
Low Gross, Fred Scrutchfield took 2nd
and Dick Aultman 3rd. Harry Singer-
man walked off with Low Net.
Golf pro Art Wall scored a gross of
69
in
the
celebrated
Robert
Goulet
Foursome.
The
day’s
competition
was
high-
lighted by
a banquet headed by
Bill
Gallagher,
Jack
Loetz
and
Gene
Weiss.
Entertainment
was
provided
by Eddie McGuinness and Gege Renzo
and
their
orchestra,
and
Columbia
Records
artists
Les
Paul
and
Van
McCoy.

Jerry
Ross
Joins Mercury
As A&R
Staff Member
NEW
YORK—Jerry
Ross,
veteran
indie producer from Philadelphia, has
joined
the
Mercury
A&R
staff.
Charles Fach, vp and
director
of
re-
corded
product
for
the
diskery,
in
explaining
the A&R
addition,
said
that
Ross’
supervision
of
the
first
Bobby
Hebb
recording
session
JERRY ROSS
brought about the
appointment. The
session resulted in the surging Philips
single, “Sunny.” Fach also cited Ross’
consistent
track
record
which
con-
sists of such national successes as the
Dreamlovers’
“When We
Get
Mar-
ried” and “You Gave Me
Somebody
To
Love”;
Candy
and
the
Kisses’
“The
81”;
and
the
Sapphires’ “Who
Do You Love?” Ross will be involved
in the recording activity of such Mer-
cury
talent
as Wayne
Cochrane and

Sensational
C.
C.
Riders,
Jesse
Colin
Young,
and
Spanky
and

Gang.

CHICAGO—Following the resignation

ALAN MINK
the record business

“objectively
a
number of business propositions.” He

as

ager,

Mercury’s national promo

ager

a Kapp
subsid, and spent two
years
as
mid-west
regional
promo

disk business with M.
S. Distributing
in Cleveland as a local promo man.

WJRZ, WWVA Cancel
Stadium C&W Concert
NEWARK—The
giant country
spec-
tacular planned for Yankee Stadium
on Aug.
5, has been
canceled, Cash
Box learned from WJRZ-Newark pro-
gram director Ed Neilson.
The concert, a joint venture between
the
Newark
station
and WWVA-
Wheeling, was to have been the larg-
est entertainment package of its kind
ever to be assembled in the New York
metropolitan area and had a scheduled
lineup that included Roy Acuff, Buck
Owens, Webb Pierce, Flatt & Scruggs,
Ray
Price,
Stonewall
Jackson,
Roy
Drusky, Warner
Mack,
Pete
Drake,
Dick Curless, Dottie West and Johnny
Dollar, among others.
Neilson,
who
just
returned
from
Nashville,
where
he
consulted
with
such C&W
personages
as
deejay-
radio
consultant
Joe
Allison,
talent
packager
Hubert Long
and Pamper
publishing
chief Hal
Smith,
told CB
that “the consensus of opinion seems
to
indicate
that
the
station
is
not
ready for a show of such proportions.
This does not preclude stadium spec-
taculars
at some
future
date, but a
package such as the one planned for
Yankee Stadium will have to be post-
poned for at least a year.
“To do a show of these proportions,
I
feel
that there
are
a
great many
major
details
to
consider. The
show
has to be staged and produced prop-
erly in order to benefit the promoters
and
a
definite
value
to
the
ticket-
buying public. We feel that we’re not
quite ready
to
give
the
audience
its
full
dollar value.”
Neilson also stated that he was ex-
ceptionally thankful to those in Nash-
ville, particularly Hal Smith, who had
taken
time
to
advise
him
on
the
matter.
Together
with
Lazar
Emanuel,
prexy
of WJRZ,
Neilson
has
gone
into meetings with Fred
Podesta
of
Management Enterprises, where they
have begun planning a series of coun-
try concerts for the summer months.

WILLIAM B. WILLIAMS
Herman,

of WNEW,

also

the founding

Proceeds from the affair benefit the

of

B’nai
B’rith Lodge. Tickets and reservations

Marilyn
Larsen,

Roy Orbison's Wife
Killed
In Cycle Crash
GALLATIN, TENN.—Claudette Ches-
ter
Orbison, wife
of record
star and
songwriter, Roy
Orbison, was
killed
here
last Monday
evening
(6)
in
a
motorcycle
accident.
The
accident
occurred at 7:00 p.m. as the Orbisons
were
returning
on
separate
motor-
cycles from a racing function in near-
by Bristol, Tenn.
Orbison,
riding
slightly
ahead
of
his
wife, had passed an
intersection.
Mrs. Orbison was unable to stop her
cycle when
an
auto moved
into
the
main
thoroughfare
without
stopping
at the intersection. Her cycle crashed
into
the
side
of
the
car.
She
was
rushed
to
Sumner
County
Memorial
Hospital,
in
Gallatin, where she
died
two
hours
later.
The
driver
of
the
auto
is being held by
local
police on
charges of involuntary manslaughter.
Services were
held
at
10:00
A.M.
Wednesday (8) at the Philip Robinson
Memorial
Chapel
in
nearby Hender-
sonville. Interment was
at Woodlawn
Cemetery,
Nashville.
Pallbearers
in-
cluded William Chester, Mrs. Orbison’s
brother; Sam
Orbison, Roy Orbison’s
brother;
Billy
Sanford;
Bill
Dees,
Orbison’s
songwriting
and
singing
teammate;
and
Ron
and Don
Gant.
Don Gant
is
a
record
producer who
has
been
associated
with
Orbison’s
recordings.
Honorary
pallbearers
included
a
host
of
well-known
persons
on
the
Nashville music
scene. The
list inclu-
ded Wesley Rose, head
of the Acuff-
Rose
interests
in
Nashville, who
is
Orbison’s
personal
manager;
Lester
Rose,
sales manager of Hickory Rec-
ords, a part of the Acuff-Rose organi-
zation; Bud Brown, vice president of
Acuff-Rose;
Jim
Vienneau,
Orbison’s
record
producer
for MGM
Records;
Chet
Atkins,
guitarist
and
record
producer
for RCA
Victor, who
has
been
associated
with
a
number
of
Orbison’s
recording
dates;
Bob
Mc-
Cluskey, assistant to the president of
Acuff-Rose;
Howard
Forrester,
head
of the Acuff-Rose Artist Corporation,
Orbison’s
booking
agency;
attorney
Dick
Frank;
Fred
Foster,
head
of
Monument Records, with which Orbi-
son v/as associated for several years;
and Jack Kirby, a member of the Mon-
ument
staff.
Mrs.
Orbison was
born
September
5, 1941 in Odessa, Texas, and was the
daughter
of
Mr.
and
Mrs.
Frady
Chester. She was the
oldest of three
children. Her
brother
William
is
21
and
her
sister,
Paulette,
is
15.
In
addition to her mother, father, brother
PJ

CADET
RECORDS
FOCUS ojir jazz
The
serious
jazz
record
collector
pursues
his hobby with
a
passion,
a
passion
that
sometimes
borders
on
grim
determination. As with
all
col-
lectors, whatever the area, his great-
est delight is the acquisition of some-
thing that none of his fellow collectors
own.
Jazz
record
collectors
have
been
known to take excursions to relatively
unknown towns, and having arrived in
these
foreign
surroundings, begun a
house
to
house
canvas,
inquiring
of
the
owners,
“Do
you
have
any
old
records that you would
like
to sell?”
When told that there were some rec-
ords
to
be
bought,
our
impassioned
collector would take
oflP his coat,
roll
up
his
sleeves, and leaf through box
after box of old records in an attic or
a basement, hopeful
of finding some
gems that would enrich his collection.
For
the most
part,
these
searchings
dealt with 78 rpm records, very often
on obscure labels; obscure, that
is, to
the
general
public,
but
to
avid
jazz
enthusiasts things that were rare pos-
sessions.
Things have a way
of coming
full
cycle, and such a phenomenon
is now
taking
place
in
the
record
business.
Perhaps
not
in
the
record
business,
per se, but it is happening in the busi-
ness of buying records. You see, there
is a renaissance of interest in 78 rpm
records.
This
renewed
interest
in
shellac recordings
is spoken about
in
hushed
tones, primarily because jazz
record
collectors
are
a
very
zealous
lot,
and
also
because
78’s
have
not
been pressed in a long time. The ab-
sence of supply, coupled with this bur-
geoning
interest
in
old
recordings,
has made the available supply dimin-
ish with the passing of each shopping
day.
Most
of the material found on
old
78’s comes from the vaults of our ma-
jor record
labels. These
vaults
liter-
ally bulge with classic jazz recordings,
recordings
that
had
been
available
only on shellac pressings.
It must be
assumed
that
these
companies
have
become aware
of
the
jazz
collector’s
interest,
witness some
of
the major
labels have embarked on re-issue pro-
grams, some
in
depth,
others
super-
ficially. We shall attempt to point out
some of the more significant ra-issues
that have been made available to the
public.
Victor’s Program
RCA Victor’s Vintage Series
is one
of the most complete attempts to re-
lease many of the great recordings for
which jazz collectors have been known
to commit near mayhem. The Vintage
program
is
under
the
direct
super-
vision of Brad McCuen, himself a jazz
enthusiast
of
long
standing,
and
a
very knowledgeable one, too. McCuen
has
gleaned
from
the
rich
Victor
stockpile a wealth of much of the best
jazz that Victor ever recorded. Thank-
fully, the sound has not been phonied
up in an attempt to compete with the
high, high fidelity of today’s product.
The sound
is that of the original re-
cording, made better to hear only
in
that
there
is an
absence
of
surface
noise. There
is none
of the manufac-
tured “enhancement” which, while
it
might make for a bigger, fuller sound,
is completely uncharacteristic of what
the
original
recording
sounded
like.
The Vintage
Series does not concern
itself with any particular style, or any
special
era.
Thus
far,
McCuen
has
tried to touch
all the bases, from The
Coon
Sanders
Nighthawks
to
Dizzy
Gillespie of the late Forties. Included
in
the
Victor
re-issue program
are
previously
rare
things by Duke
El-
lington,
Don
Redman,
Fats
Waller,
Benny
Goodman,
Jack
Teagarden,
Earl
Hines, Count
Basie, and
forth-
coming in a July release, more Dizzy
Gillespie,
Harland
Leonard
&
His
Rockets,
and
King
Oliver
In New
York.
Columbia ‘Omnibus’
Columbia Records approach
to the
re-issue program
is unique; here, the
omnibus
approach
has
been
taken.
With the exception of three
releases,
all
of Columbia’s excursions into the
past have been released in two, three,
and four album packages, boxed, and
each
with
a
well
documented
enclo-
sure. The printed booklet that accom-
panies each release is annotated, punc-
tuated with many great photographs,
and also
a complete
listing
of
dates,
personnel, and
all
other information
that makes
the
listening
that much
more enjoyable.
Columbia’s
re-issue
program
is
headed up by Frank Driggs, who, like
Victor’s McCuen, is an avid student of
early
jazz
recordings.
Thus
far,
Driggs
has
packaged
sets
of
early
recordings
by
Billie
Holiday,
Duke
Ellington, Gene Krupa, Fletcher Hen-
derson,
Mildred
Bailey, Woody
Her-
man,
to name a few.
Also, Columbia
has
re-issued
a
series
called
Jazz
Oddysey,
of which
three
have
been
released,
to
date:
Jazz Oddysey
#1,
The
Sound
Of New
Orleans;
Jazz
Oddysey #2, The Sound Of Chicago;
Jazz
Oddysey
#3,
The
Sound
Of
Harlem. Each
is a musical anthology
of that
area, featuring many
of the
prime
contributors.
Commodore To Mainstream
The
Commodore
label,
long
re-
spected as one of the most fruitful of
jazz producers, was
sold a couple
of
years
ago
to
Mainstream
Records,
which
is owned by Bob
Shad.
Shad
has re-issued just about all the great
early sides by people like Billie Holi-
day, Lester Young, Coleman Hawkins,
Teddy Wilson, Red Norvo, Art Tatum,
Roy
Eldridge,
Ben
Webster,
and
many
other
jazz
greats
of
the
late
Thirties and
early
Forties.
This
re-
issue
program
has
been
met
with
overwhelming enthusiasm by jazz col-
lectors all over the world.
Emarcy, a subsidiary label of Mer-
cury
Records, has
recently begun
to
unloose some of the many good things
that they own. The most significant of
these
old
sides are the
original Key-
note
recordings
that
were
produced
in
the
mid-Forties
by
Harry
Lim.
Highlighting
this new
prog:ram
are
some
especially
precious
recordings
by Lester Young. Also
in
the newly
activated
Emarcy
re-issue
program
are some Coleman Hawkins
sets, and
some Roy
Eldridge
sides. Word has
it that Emarcy will make more good
things available on a regular basis.
Decca’s
Vaults
Decca Records, which owns a veri-
table wealth
of ^eat
early
jazz
re-
cordings,
has,
with
a
couple
of
ex-
ceptions,
failed
to
embark
on
any-
thing resembling a re-issue program.
They
did
release
some
early
Savoy
Sultan
recordings,
and
some
Chick
Webb
sides,
but
that
is
about
all.
Even these were almost forced by
a
hungry public to be released, a public
that literally petitioned Decca to un-
lock
the
warehouse.
Decca,
with
its
subsidiary
labels, owns
so many im-
portant early jazz
recordings, and
it
should be made known
to them that
collectors
all over
the world
are
ea-
gerly
awaiting more
re-issues
from
them.
Contact,
a
small
independent
jazz
label, has re-issued several important
albums,
recordings
that
were
done
originally on
the
Signature
label by
Bob Thiele in 1943-4. Among the Con-
tact recordings are some monumental
recordings by Lester Young and Cole-
man Hawkins.
So, maybe the
activities of 78 rpm
jazz record collectors have had some
influence on the thinking of companies
which have so much of this good prod-
uct
to
offer.
Necessarily,
the
dollar
volume
that
is
to
be
enjoyed from
these re-issues will determine whether
or
not
the
companies
will
sustain
their
respective
programs.
Much
of
the
responsibility
for
the
success
of
these
re-issue programs
will
fall
on
the record buying public, who, if they
do
not respond
saleswise,
will
again
find
themselves
without
so much
of
this good music
that
should
be
per-
petuated.
Further,
responsibility
will
rest with radio stations whose format
permits
them
to
program
this
fine
music
of
yesterday.
Unless
it
gets
played and
heard,
the
chances
of
it
being
bought
are
very
remote,
be-
cause these days about the only way
the public knows what
is available to
them over the counter is by what they
hear being played on
radio.
So, pro-
gram
directors and record promotion
men,
please take
note!

POP BEST BETS
PHYLLIS
McGuire
sings—ABC-Paramount
552/S 552
Phyllis McGuire steps out from the trio format
for this warm, easy to listen to LP. The lark, who
is the lead singer in the famous sister act, does a
set
of
standards
on
this
disk with
“Vaya Con
Dios,” “I Can’t Give You Anything But Love” and
“Who Can I Turn To (When Nobody Needs Me)”
being among the
finest. Folks who have enjoyed
the McGuire Sisters should also enjoy this sweet
set.
THE “MODS” SALUTE HERB ALBERT & THE
TIJUANA BRASS—Modernaires—Columbia
CL
2490/CS 9290
The
Modernaires,
longtime
veterans
in
the
music world, have aimed a musical salute toward
a group of red-hot “newcomers,” Herb Alpert &
the Tijuana Brass, with this Columbia LP. Mark-
ing the first time that many of these tunes have
been recorded
with
lyrics,
the
set
features
the
group
(with Paula Kelly)
giving their sparkling
adaptations
to
such
grooves
as
“Tijuana

Phonogram organized a party last week to present
to the press and show
business people
its new production, “Argentina Canta Asi,” a ten-12" LP
set
with a selection of folk and tango music. Felix Luna took part in the selection
of the folk recordings, and Catulo
Castillo has been
in charge
of the Tango
part. The
set
will be
sold
at about $30 through
Philips
dealers and
regular
retailers, and good sales are expected.
Tape
cartridges
are
“the
talk
of
the town” and
there
certainly
is some
reason for
it:
there
is already one
local manufacturer ready
to market
car-
tridge tape recorders, which would be sold at about $200 and could be used in
cars and at home, while several record companies are studying the production
of pre-recorded tape and
its
possibilities. The main
discussions are
centered
around
artist and composer’s
royalties, and big news
is expected within
the
next weeks.
Currently there
is some importing
of tapes from
the
U.S. and
Japan, but in small quantities.
Composer Ben Molar is heading a movement towards the production of tango
music by well known writers and composers who generally do not devote time
to this work. The
first production thus obtained
is “Milonga Para Los Orient-
ales,” penned by Jorge Luis Borges and Jose Basso, and other tunes, this time
with the cooperation of Adolfo Bioy Casares and Florencio Escardo, are on the
way.
A delicate situation has come up at SADAIC, the
Society
of Authors and
Composers
of
Argentina,
in
charge
of
collecting
mechanical
and
artistical
royalties
for
repertoires
in
this
country.
Its
director.
Dr. Ramon
Jueguen,
named by the government a year and a half ago, has been charged with com-
plaints of mismanagement and improper use of funds by a group of members
of the
society, just before his departure to the ClSAC meeting
in Praga. At
press time no further information was available.

Hcsindteman Declares
3-For>2 Stock Split
NEW YORK—The board of directors
of
the
Handlenian
Co.,
the
large
Detroit-based rack-jobber, have voted
a
three-for-two
stock
split
on
the
1,002,960 shares of common stock and
Class B common
stock
outstanding,
subject
to
stockholder
approval
at
the company’s annual meeting
to be
held in Detroit on Aug.
1, 1966. After
the
split,
there
will
be
1,504,440
shares of common stock and Class B
common
stock
outstanding. The
pro-
posed three-for-two stock split is pay-
able Aug.
19, 1966 to stockholders
of
record Aug.
2,
1966.
This
is the
first stock
split for the
company since its shares were initially
offered to the public in 1963. Based on
a
three-for-two
stock
split
1,053,108
shares of common stock will be
eligi-
ble
to
receive
dividends
instead
of
702,072 shares as previously.
It
is the intention
of the board
of
directors,
at
their
next
quarterly
dividend meeting to be held on
Sept.
7, 1966, to declare a quarterly dividend
of
.20
per
share
on
the new
shares
then outstanding following the
split.
Such
board
action
will
necessarily
depend on general business conditions,
and
the
earnings
and
financial
con-
dition of the company.
According to Paul Handleman, pres-
ident,
the company
expects
to
soon
report a new high in sales and earn-
ings for the fiscal year ended Apr. 30,
1966.

Clamike Charges Plagiarism
Against James Brown, King
NEW YORK—Clamike
Records
has
brought
suit
against James
Brown,
King Records and Dynaton Music
in
the Southern District (New York)
of
United States District Court for dam-
ages
in
a
purported
copyright
in-
fringement
of
a
tune
called
“It’s A
Man’s World.”
The suit of the plaintiffs was stimu-
lated by a recent successful recording
by James Brown, “It’s A Man’s Man’s
Man’s
World,”
on
the
King
label.
Dynaton
Music
publishes
the Brown
Version.
According to the complaint, in Sept,
of
1964,
Betty
Newsome
wrote
an
original
musical
composition
which
was
duly
registered
and
identified
from
the
Register
of Copyrights by
Camike
Music,
a wholly-owned
divi-
sion of the plaintiff.
The
complaint
further
states
that
the defendants infringed on said copy-
right by
utilizing,
assigning and
li-
censing
without
permission
the
me-
chanical
reproduction
rights, and by
mechanically
reproducing,
manufac-
turing, distributing and selling mech-
anical reproductions “embodying sub-
stantial
portions”
of
the
song.

For NAMM Show In Chi
CHICAGO—William
R.
Gard,
execu-
tive vp of NAMM, has predicted that
attendance at the annual music show
will be in excess of the 20,000 mark.
This
prediction
was
based
on
the
record
number
of
advance
reserva-
tions
pouring
in
for
the
big
music
and home entertainment event which
is
slated
to
begin
Sunday,
July
10,
at Chicago’s Conrad Hilton Hotel.
Gard said: “The 65th annual music
show
will
without
question
be
the
biggest
in our history by
all
indica-
tions.
Every
bit
of
space
available
for exhibits has been sold out and we
have been hard put
to
contend with
the flood
of requests for room
reser-
vations
at
hotels
close
to
the
show.
We are taking every possible step to
handle the record crowds with maxi-
mum
efficiency
in
order
to
provide
easiest access to exhibits and to avoid
congestion
wherever
possible.
Ad-
vance
reservations
plus
relocation
and
enlargement
of
the
registration
area will help the
situation and
pre-
vent inconvenience.”
Promotional
activity
will be
spot-
lighted at the 5-day show and a
full
program of business sessions covering
key questions in the music and home
entertainment industry has been
set.
The
major
emphasis
in
this
year’s
show
-will be on cooperation and
co-
ordination in the
sales of both music
and home
entertainment
products.

$1 Mil High In Jan.-May
NEW YORK—A new high
in
collec-
tions
for
a
five month
period—more
than
$1
million—was reached by
the
American
Guild
of Authors & Com-
posers for the period ending May
31.
This figure represents about
$200,-
000 more than in the same period last
year. According to Miriam Stern, exec
director of AGAC, which
collects for
its writer members mechanical royal-
ties, improved data processing, Guild
“prodding” and the continuing AGAC
auditing program
are
the main
rea-
sons for the record
collection.

Currently holding down a comfortable

is certain

similar response with this Victor LP.
Highlighted by that same
single, and featuring
strictly heartbreak items, the album
is a feeling-
ful,
sensitive
performance
that
should
do
very
well. Other tracks include her recent hit “Before
The
Ring
On

Turns
Green”
and
“Baby.”

on

should

slice
of
that sales action. Highlighted by grooves by the

AFTER THIS MESSAGE—Mitchell-Ruff Trio—
Atlantic 1458
Part of this group (then known as the Mitchell-
Ruff
Duo)
joined
the
Yale
Russian
Chorus
in
order to bring American jazz into Russia in 1959.
The
trio
is made up of Dwike Mitchell on piano,
Willie Ruff on bass and French horn, and Helcio
Milito on drums. “After This Message,”
“I Got
Rhythm,” and
“Solo For Unaccompanied
Bass”
are among
the
better
tracks. The
jazz market
will welcome this one.
I
JAZZ BEST BETS
MOSE ALLISON PLAYS FOR LOVERS—Pres-
tige/PR-7446
This package
is comprised of popular American
ballads. All love songs, but of different attitudes,
they have been
tied together by Mose
Allison’s
distinctive
combination
of
urban
sophistication
and rural wit.
“I Told Ya
I Loved Ya, Now Get
Out,” “You Belong To Me,” and “My Kinda Love”
are blue ribbon efforts. Not an overly sentimental
love
song
album,
this
one
is
likely
to
do
well.

recorded

outing which

FOCUS ON MZZ
llllllllllllllllllllilllllllllllllllllllililllllllllllli
Part
of the Newport Jazz Festival
of 1964 was an afternoon panel
dis-
cussion
which
concerned
itself
with
how
the
interests
of
jazz
and
the
people who perform
it could best be
served.
The
panel
included
per-
formers, commentators, disk jockeys,
night club operators, artist and reper-
toire men, and concert promoters,
all
from the world of jazz. Because of the
varied
interests
of
the
participants,
myriad
points
of view were
offered.
One
of
the
panelists,
a
disk
jockey,
took
a
very adamant
stand,
stating
that
the
single most important
ele-
ment
in
the
development
of a
jazz-
man’s career in today’s market is the
recording. His contention was that a
successful
recording
career was
the
catalyst for
a
well-filled calendar
of
personal appearances, night club, con-
cert,
television,
et
al.
Let’s
concern
ourselves with the expansion of that
sentiment,
the
ever-increasing
im-
portance
of
the
recording
industry
and its satellites in the launching and
the sustaining of the career of a jazz
performer.
Disks Launch P.A.’s
There has been a startling inversion
of events
that governs
the very
ex-
istence
of
a
performer, and
particu-
larly a jazz performer. Years ago,
if
an
artist had a
successful track rec-
ord, based on his appearances at night
clubs,
dances,
or
concerts,
it
would
evoke sufficient interest on the part of
record company executives to want to
record that artist. The philosophy ob-
viously was
that
after
the
exposure
our
performer
had
enjoyed making
personal
appearances,
there
would
certainly be many potential customers
for his recordings. Today, the people
who engage performers for personal
appearances
want
a
pre-fabricated
audience,
one
that has
been
created
by the recordings that have made the
artist known
to
the
audience
before
he
has
ever
been
seen
or heard
in
person.
Thus,
the
inversion!
Where
previously
it had
been
appear
first,
then
record, now
it
is
record
first,
then
secure
engagements
on
the
strength
of whatever
successful
re-
cordings are out there, endearing you
to the listening audience.
So, what
it
actually amounts to
is that the book-
ing people want to
rid themselves
of
the element of risk when they hire a
performer; that security has to come
from best-selling recordings.
Even the most ardent champion of
jazz will acknowledge that there are,
with
each
passing
day,
fewer
and
fewer
clubs
where
jazz
is
pro-
grammed
on
a
regular
basis.
For
whatever reasons,
this
situation does
exist. Perhaps
the
availability of
so
much jazz on record has helped bring
this about. With the increase in sales
of jazz recordings and the decrease in
the number of clubs offering jazz, that
might be one of the reasons. However,
in
defense
of
live
jazz
presentation,
let us
state
that the
college campus
scene has become a very fertile area
for jazz performers.
In
a
sense, the
college
campus
has
filled
the
void
created
by
the
shuttering
of many
jazz clubs. Wherever
it is performed,
the demand
for an
artist
is
created
by his recordings. That is for sure!!!
To further expand
the importance
of
recordings, we must concern
our-
selves with
the
significance
of play-
back equipment. Not too long ago, the
person who
owned
a
high
fiedelity
system was the envy of all his friends
and
neighbors. And
understandably,
because
it wasn’t that long ago that
such
systems were
prohibitively
ex-
pensive,
and
because
they
were
re-
served only for those who could afford
that outlay of money. Today, with the
decrease in cost of comparable equip-
ment, just about everyone can afford
a modest
hi-fi
system. As
a matter
of fact, if one admits to not owning a
hi-fi
today, he
is looked
at, askance.
This means
that
there
is
a
greater
potential record buying public and the
record companies are certainly taking
advantage of that potential. The con-
stant
outpouring
of
the
increasing
number of record companies is almost
inundating, and somewhat confusing,
because where
can
all
these
record-
ings be heard? No
longer
is
it
cus-
tomary to be able to walk into a local
record store and listen to a recording
before you buy
it. There might
still
be some stores that offer that service,
but they are very rare, indeed.
Deejay Exposure
That leads us to the very important
role the disk jockey plays
in the de-
velopment of a jazz artist’s career. To
begin with, there are not that many
jazz programs on the air, and because
there
aren’t,
the
jazz
listener
seeks
out each one with a
passion. Where
else
will
our
listener
and
potential
customer be
able
to be kept abreast
of
the
latest
releases?
Where
else
will he be made aware of a new talent
on the scene? Where
else
will he be
given the opportunity to listen before
he
buys?
Actually,
the
jazz
deejay
probably exercises the greatest single
influence in establishing a performer’s
worth at the box office, be it a concert
hall,
a
night
club,
or
at
a
sales
counter in a retail record shop. Unlike
pop jockeys, most jazz deejays retain
the
freedom
to program what
they
choose, and this autonomy only height-
ens the importance
of what they
do.
Experience shows that most jazz disk
jockeys are basically jazz fans, and as
such, they feel a great responsibility
to themselves, their audience, and
to
the
artists
whose
recordings
they
play.
Of
course,
if
it
isn’t
in
the
grooves,
no
matter how
much
our
deejay likes
it, or how often he plays
it, the chances
of a
record breaking
out are very remote. But
if
it
is in
the
grooves,
our
deejay
is
the man
who can
get
it across
to
the
public.
Therein
lies
his
strength.
A
classic
illustration
of how
im-
portant the right record can be to a
jazz
artist
is
the
record,
“The
In
Crowd” by The Ramsey Lewis
Trio.
This
record
comes
to mind
because
it
is
of
a most recent vintage;
cer-
tainly, there have been others
like
it
in the
past. Ramsey and
his fellows
had, up until “The In Crowd” break-
out,
been
a
regular working
group,
with a better than average following
among the jazz
set, and a group that
commanded
a
reasonably good
price
for
personal
appearances.
(Dame
the
BIG
record,
and
the
asking
price
tripled, there were
television appear-
ances by
the
dozens,
and
the name
Ramsey Lewis became almost as well
known at The Beatles. What stronger
case can be made for the importance
of
recordings
for
the
success
of
a
good performer?
Deems Taylor
Dies
NEW YORK—Deems
Taylor
(80),
composer, critic, and former president
of ASCAP died July 3 at the Medical
Arts
Center
in New York. Taylor
is
perhaps best remembered for having
composed
two
operas,
“The
King’s
Henchman”
and
“Peter
Ibbetson.”
“The King’s Henchman” was commis-
sioned
in
1925
by
the
Metropolitan
Opera Company, and set a record for
new American
operas by being
per-
formed
for
three
successive
seasons
after
its
debut
at
the Met
in
1927.
Taylor
is
survived
by
his
daughter
and grandson.

TALENT ON STAGE
RAWLS
NEW YORK—Lou
Rawls
says
that
he has been “an up and coming young
blues singer for
five
years,” but now
that he
has
a
hit album
for
Capitol
(“Lou
Rawls
Live”)
they
tell
him
“you
ain’t
singing
blues,”
but
it
doesn’t
matter
what
you
call
the
music
that Rawls
finds himself
sing-
ing,
it’s great by any name.
Lou
has
reached
a
point
of
pure
professionalism
in
his
act,
which
is
interspaced with some of the
liveliest
and
funniest
patter we
have
heard
from
a
singer
in
quite
some
time.
And
his
songs,
by
they
Broadway
ballads or low, bluesy tales of broken
hearts
and
homes,
are
moving
and
powerfully displayed by Rawls’ melo-
dious, highly elastic voice that ranges
from
the
dramatic
to
the
comedic
with equal
ease.
Lou Rawls can no longer be an up
and
coming
young
blues
singer
be-
cause
as
everyone
in
that
big room
at
the
Village
Gate
knew, from
the
start
to
the
finish
of
his
act, he has
arrived.
RONNETTES
NEW YORK—The
Ronnettes,
who
have for quite some time been one of
the top girl groups
in the rock music
field,
made
their
first
major
New
York
club
bow
recently
at
Basin
Street
East,
with
a
new
act
and
seemingly a new perspective on what
their fans v ant to see them
do.
In
addition
to
such
big
hit
tunes
as
“Walkin’
In
The
Rain”
and
“Be
My Baby”
the
girls’ new
renertoire
holds
a
host
of
standards
plus
well
known
soul
songs
the
likes
of
“Shout.”
Though
they
shined
with
their
hits,
despite
a weak
orchestral
backing,
the
trio
lost
much
of
the
excitement that
it can, and does, gen-
erate when
it strayed from the music
that
the
girls
obviously
enjoy most
and do their best
at.
The
inclusion
of
standard
tunes
does not ipso facto, make for a more
adult
and
appealing
act.
The
finest
entertainment
comes
from
artists
who do
the
best with what they can
do
best, and
the
Ronnettes
can
rock
an audience
like very few others can.

JOHNNY MATHIS
LOS
ANGELES—“Tender
Is
The
Night”
was
the
second
tune
in
Mathis’
delicate bag
of
ballads
per-
formed
at
the
pop
concert
series
opener
at
the
4,400
seat
city owned
Greek
Amphitheater.
It
could
have
been
the
title
song
for
this
evening
under the
stars.
Just a year short of a decade since
this
San
Francisco
College
student
burst
upon
the
record
scene
with
“Wonderful!
Wonderful!”
and
“It’s
Not For Me To Say” (both simultane-
ously on the charts in ’57) Mathis has
more than
increased
his considerable
stature as an
artist. He
is today vir-
tually
without
peer
as
a
master
of
the
earressive
ballad.
He
embraces
each
lyric
with
affection,
reaching
for notes
that would vanquish
lesser
men. He
does
it
so
effortlessly
that
you momentarily wonder
if he might
not,
after
all,
be
deceitfully
syn-
chronizing to a backstage tape.
A
dozen
or
so
ballads
are
per-
formed during the two hour program
with
just
enough
brighter
tunes
to
balance
the
evening.
In
addition
there’s some
fine backing from Jack
Feierman’s
Orchestra
as
well
as
a
kind
of unrelated King Family
in
a
group called Our Younger Generation.
These
six
boys
and
eight
girls
ex-
uberantly back
the
star,
occasionally
performing on their own and particu-
larly
effective
with
medley
of
con-
temporary
rockers.
Hardly
a
tune
that Mathis has been associated with
over
the
years
has
been
neglected.
There
is, of course, “Maria,” his usual
closer. It is
all but eclipsed a moment
later by “The Man
Of La Mancha”
medley,
which
concludes
with
that
aspiring
phrase
“to
reach
the
un-
reachable
star.”
In
a
nigh
perfect
evening
Mathis comes
awfully
close.
JOHNNY TILLOTSON
NEW YORK—There’s
an
entertain-
ing
propagandist
for
country
music
at
the
Copacabana
these
days.
This
soft-sell
lobbyist
for
the
country
sound
is MGM
songster Johnny
Til-
lotson, a country boy himself who
is
now
a smooth and
polished example
of urbanized
sophistication. Although
he does well with some
straight pop
standards,
including
a femme name-
song medley, the apex of his act
is a
tribute
to
the
influence
of
country
music among yesterday’s and today’s
pop
music
scene.
This
bit
is
built
around a re-write of the old Gershwin
song,
“Love
(Country)
Is
Sweeping
The
Country,”
and
recalls
such
familiar items that originally made
it
country-wise
as
“Anytime,”
“Oh
Lonesome
Me,”
“Tennessee
Waltz,”
“Half
As
Much,”
“Don’t
Let
The
Stars
Get
In Your Eyes”
and, more
recently, “King Of The Road.”
Earlier, Tillotson offers a poignant,
guitar-in-hand
rendition
of
one
of
Hank Williams’ great
songs, “I’m So
Lonesome
I
Could
Cry.”
The
artist
also
offers
a
medley
of
his
teen-
oriented
hits, some of which also owe
a
debt
to
the
country
field
(eg.
“Heartaches By The Numbers.”)
Tillotson’s
affable,
boy-next-door
bent
is one of his prime assets as an
artist.
It
looks
like
his
first
Copa
showcase
is
but
just
one
of
a
long-
series
of
engagements
in
years
to
come.

MIDNIGHT
SESSION—Damita
Jo—Epic
LN
24202/BN
26202
Damita Jo has come up with a top-notch mu-
sical
offering
in
this
album
session,
recorded
‘live’
at Basin
Street
in New York.
Kicking
off
the performance with “That Wonderful
Feeling
Of Love” the lark uncorks a healthy platterful of
her own wonderful feeling in her typical vibrant,
infectious
style.
Other
tracks
include
“You’re
Nobody Til Somebody Loves You” and “The Best
Things In Life Are Free.”
THE PROMISE
OF THE DAY—Corrie
Folk
Trio & Paddie Bell—Elektra EKL-304/EKS-7304
The
folk songs
of
Scotland and
Ireland have
been
performed
by
innumerable
artists
on
this
side
of the ocean but they come
to
their
finest
glow when
in the hands
of such a
fine group of
musicians
as
the
Corrie
Folk
Trio
and
Paddie
Bell. The
authentic twang
of
the
highlands
fill
this
lovely
disk
of some
well known and some
obscure
tunes.
Folk
fanciers
will
love
“Roddy
McCorley”
and
“The
Leaving
Of
Liverpool”
as
well as the other tracks.
Solid
sales
here.
LONESOME
IS ME—Charlie
Louvin—Capitol
T/ST 2482
Once again
Charlie Louvin
offers an excellent
selection
of
items
for C&W
audiences.
Heart-
break and loneliness top the
bill of fare
in
this
session,
with
the
songster
adding warmth
and
feelingful stylings as extra
spice on each tender
morsel.
Among
the
standout
tracks
here
are
his
former
charters
“To
Tell
The
Truth”
and
“You
Finally Said Something Good (When You
Said Goodbye),”
in addition to the
title track.

KITTY WHITE—Clover CL 1229
Here’s
a
session by
Kitty White
that
should
help
build
a
fine
following
for
the
songstress.
Displaying an innate sensitivity and a rich, emo-
tion-packed style, the lark lets loose with a string
of well-chosen grooves all spiced with a beguiling
ork
backing. Among
the
top
grooves
included
in
this
one
are
“Happiness
Is A Thing
Called
Joe,” “Mood Indigo” and “Summer In The City.”
KADDISH—Allen Ginsberg—Atlantic
4001
This
is a package containing Allen Ginsberg’s
well known narrative poem, “Kaddish,” read by
the
poet himself. The album
is
sure
to be well
received, not only by Ginsberg’s many fans, but
by students of American
literature and verse as
well.
JUST ABOUT EVERYTHING—Bob Dorough—
Focus 336
Lively sounds featuring the piano and vocal of
Bob Dorough, with his incisive phrasings as high-
lights
of
the
package.
“Don’t Think
Twice”
is
spearheaded by
A1
Schackman’s
guitar.
“Balti-
more Oriole,” “Lazy Afternoon,” and “The Craw-
dad Song” are blue ribbon tracks. Good listening
all
the way
through,
this
one
is
likely
to
find
favor with jazz as well as pop fans.
JAZZ BEST BETS
DREAM WEAVER—Charles Lloyd Quartet—At-
lantic S/SD-1459
A delightful jazz offering by the Charles Lloyd
Quartet,
this album was recorded
in the
U.S.A.
just
prior
to
the
group’s
debut European
tour.
Lloyd on tenor sax and flute,
is backed by Keith
Jarrett on piano, Cecil McBee on bass, and Jack
DeJohnette
on
drums.
The
title
song,
“Bird
Flight,” and “Love Ship” are
all blue ribbon
ef-
forts.
This
one
is
sure
to
find
favor with
jazz
buffs everywhere.
DIZZY GILLESPIE—RCA Victor LPV 530
This
is the latest addition to the growing RCA
Vintage Series catalog, a collection of repressings
of old folk, blues, and jazz recordings. The pack-
age
the
sides
Gillespie’s
big bands
cut
for
the
diskery between 1947 & 1949 and chronicles
the
decade when Dizzy emerged from the position of
a promising talent on the Philadelphia scene to a
position of national prominence. Sure to be sought
after by
those
interested
in
the
early
develop-
ments
in jazz.
OH BABY!—Big John Patton—Blue Note 4192
A jazz package featuring the Hammond Organ
as played by Big John Patton while being backed
up by Blue Mitchell on trumpet, Harold Vick on
tenor sax, Grant Green on guitar, and Ben Dixon
on drums.
This
is Big John’s
fourth album
for
Blue Note. “One To Twelve,” “Night Flight,” and
“Each Time” are outstanding tracks. A good one
for jazzophiles and pop fans.
THE WEARY TRAVELER—King Fleming Trio
—Cadet LP-4053
This
is an offering of
quiet,
lyrical jazz tunes
enhanced
by
King
Fleming’s
straight-forward
and
uncluttered
approach
to
the
piano.
King
Fleming
is backed up by Bugs Cochran on drums
and Melvin Jackson on
bass. “Taking A Chance
On
Love,”
“Green
Leaves
Of
Summer,”
“One
O’Clock Jump,” and the title song are outstanding
tracks. A must for the jazzophile.
CLASSICAL PICKS
BEETHOVEN/BRAHMS—Conrad Hansen, Hein-
rich Geuser, Arthur Troester—Mace M/MS-9038
This package features Conrad Hansen, Heinrich
Geuser, and Arthur Troester playing Beethoven’s
“Trio In B Flat Major Op. 11” and Brahms’ “Trio
In A-Minor Op. 114.” Both of these selections are
for piano, clarinet and violoncello. This one
is a
must for the
classical music
enthusiast.
SCHUBERT—SYMPHONY NO. 9 (‘THE GREAT
C MAJOR’)—Sir John Barbirolli—Angel S-36328
Sir
John
Barbirolli
masterfully
conducts
the
Halle
Orchestra
in
Schubert’s
“Great C-Major”
symphony,
which
is
so
called
to
distinguish
it
from an
earlier symphony
in
the same
key. On
this recording, the
last movement
is particularly
outstanding;. A package
destined
to be added
to
many
classical
record
libraries.
