FOCUS ON jazz
This month marks the seventh an-
niversary of the passing of Billie Hol-
iday. Even though the
definition of a
jazz
singer remains
a very nebulous
thing,
Billie’s
acceptance
as
undis-
puted
champion
is
virtually
uncon-
tested. And
it
isn’t
as
though
this
legend
has
grown
since
her
death;
Billie was a legend in her own time.
Too
often we’re prone
to forget
the
great ones of the past, in deference to
the stars of the moment. Today, as a
token repayment for all the great mu-
sic
she
left us
as a legacy, we
shall
concern ourselves with Lady Day, as
Billie
Holiday came
to
be
known.
We’re fortunate
to have an abun-
dance of recorded works by Billie Hol-
iday, spanning an
era from
1933
to
1958. Admittedly, some
of what
she
recorded in the twilight of her career
left something
to be
desired, but
in
the light of comparison, even her less-
than-best
efforts
dwarfed
most
of
what
was
being
recorded
by
other
so-called jazz singers. She had an in-
defineable
quality
which
was
never
approached by any other female sing-
er; the fact that no other female sing-
er has had the temerity to try to imi-
tate
Billie Holiday
is
eloquent
testi-
mony to her uniqueness.
Always Recorded
with
the
Best
The
major
portion
of
Billie’s
re-
cordings can be found on three labels:
Columbia,
Decca, and Verve, and
in
that
chronological
order.
The
sides
she did for Columbia covered the pe-
riod from 1933
to 1942, and on these
recordings
she
surrounded
herself
with
such
jazz
notables
as
Benny
Goodman, Teddy Wilson, Ben Webster,
Bunny
Berigan,
Lester Young, Buck
Clayton,
Chu
Berry,
Roy
Eldridge,
and countless others of that high cali-
ber. One
thing was
for
sure:
Billie
Holiday never went into a recording
studio with anyone but the best! The
Holiday
sides on Columbia have, for
the most part, been consolidated into
two packages. The Golden Years, Vol.
1
and
Vol.
2.
Each
of
these
boxed
packages is made up of three albums,
and each box contains an
illustrated
brochure,
complete with many
valu-
able
photographs
and
all
the
perti-
nent data concerning each recording.
There
is
reason
to
believe
that
Co-
lumbia
still has a sufficiency of sides
to make up another volume.
From
the
mid-forties
to
the
very
early
fifties we have many
excellent
things
that
Lady
Day
did
for
the
Decca label. Most of these recordings
were done with large
orchestrations,
although there were some done
in
a
small
group
setting. The
Decca
re-
cordings included such legendary Hol-
iday
offerings
as “Lover Man,” “No
More,” “God Bless The Child,” “Crazy
He
Calls
Me,”
“You’re My
Thrill,”
and “Por^.” While she recorded for
Decca
Billie
did
some
wonderful
things with Louis Armstrong, a wed-
ding of talents that was so completely
right that
it defies description.
Billie Holiday’s last affiliation, with
the exception of two albums that she
did
for
Columbia
(her
last
two
al-
bums), was with Norman Granz and
his Clef
label, now Verve. There
are
those who feel that these are the best
she did, in spite of a lessening of that
pure sound that she
evidenced
early
in her singing career. In the absence
of that pure sound there was a much
more mature and emotional
delivery.
Again,
as
always.
Miss
Holiday
re-
corded only in the company of the top
jazz musicians of the moment. Some
of the Verve things were recorded in

recorded

in the studio. She re-

identified, things

“Strange

I

Holiday approach.

Reprint of Eulogy
I
This
writer
had
the
privilege
of
j
writing the following for a program
!
of
the
1959
Randall’s
Island
Jazz
Festival:
DON’T EXPLAIN
Today
I
said, “Goodbye, Lady, and
Thank You.” As
I
sat
in the chapel
where
Billie
Holiday
lay
in
state,
I
observed
the
never-ending
lines
of
friends who came
to pay
their
last
respects
to Lady Day, who gave
so
much and
asked
so
little
in
return.
It was
obvious
that
these were
not
morbid
thrill
seekers who
came
to
see the Billie Holiday who was vilified
by
the
press,
even
as
she
lay
at
death’s
door.
Instead,
these
were
mourners
from
every
walk
of
life,
rich and poor, Negro and white, silent
and weeping, come
to repay
in some
small way the many gloriously
thril-
ling
moments
that
she.
Lady,
had
given
so
generously.
It has been said that Billie Holiday’s
voice was
like
a
piece
of
rare
silk,
with a tattered edge, and
so
it was,
filled with the emotion and the poig-
nancy
that
she
breathed
into
every
lyric. There was a tender and delicate
sincerity that made you feel that she
was
singing her
song,
ballad,
blues,
or
whatever,
just
for
you, and
you
alone.
It was
as though
she wanted
you to share her happy moments and
to
help
her
endure
her
sad
times.
Those
who
enjoyed
the
privilege
of watching the Lady work know the
magic she possessed; how, when it was
time for her
set, no matter how low
she felt, she became an articulate and
plaintive
teller of stories. There
is a
certain
indefinable
something
that
separates
the
great
from
the
near
great, and
this
quality,
call
it what
you will, was Billie Holiday’s heritage.
Much has been written about Billie
Holiday’s
life,
but
always
with
the
taint
of
sensationalism,
so
that
for
the
many,
her
very
existence
was
merely a source for tabloid exploita-
tion. This
I reject vehemently! What
about
Billie,
the
sincere,
Billie
the
warm, Billie the love kind of person?
Do you suppose
that she
could have
attained
that
pinnacle
of
greatness
that made her the peerless performer
without
all
these
qualities,
plus
the
inner
beauty
with
which
she
was
blessed?
Billie Holiday was a beauti-
ful person and a great artist, perhaps
the
greatest we
shall know
in
her
idiom;
I choose to respect and vener-
ate her memory for this, and for this
alone.
To sympathize
is not to condone, to
be
sure;
but
sympathy
and
under-
standing were owed
to
Billie;
unfor-
tunately, she received
little of either.
She
had
her
inadequacies
and
her
excesses, none will deny that, for she
was a mortal, even as you and
I, and
she
fell
prey
to
the
frailties
that
plague us
all. How many times, over
the
years, must she have asked
her-
self,
“What’s
the
use?” From
her
early childhood on, even as an estab-
lished
star,
the
indignities
heaped
upon
her must
have
taxed
her
re-
straint. Her experiences while travel-
ing
as
featured
vocalist
with name
bands,
both Negro
and
White,
have
been recounted so often as to be com-
monplace, as have her encounters with
the
law. However, one
incident
of
a
more recent vintage took
place
in a
large
Midwestern
city
where
Billie
was
performing,
and
this
incident
should
be
made
known.
While
she
was out having supper, her dressing
room
was
illegally
entered,
ran-
sacked,
and
her
expensive
wardrobe
slashed in fruitless search for damag-
ing evidence that would result in her
arrest.
This
hostile
attitude
was
Billie’s welcome wherever
she
went,
wherever she worked. Is it any wonder
she despaired, and asked, “What’s the
use?”
We should consider ourselves priv-
ileged
to have known
Billie Holiday,
the
singer,
from
her
performances,
both
live
and
recorded. We
should
consider
ourselves
even more
privi-
leged
to have known
Billie
Holiday,
the
Lady,
and
I,
for
one,
shall
be
eternally
grateful
for
her
legacy,
a
library of her recorded
efforts, which
I
shall
treasure
as
one
of my most
prized
possessions. Thank
you, Lady
Day, and
.
.
.
don’t
explain.

is releasing a big stack of

are

is now heading for

Dallas To Tower
Nat'l.
Sales Head
HUGH DALLAS
HOLLYWOOD—Hugh Dallas has been
appointed
national
sales and promo-
tion manager for Tower Records
ac-
cording
to Bud
Fraser,
president
of
the label.
Dallas, a veteran of 15 years in the
record
business,
leaves
his
post
as
national sales and promotion manager
of
Philips
in
Chicago
to
join
the
Tower staff in New York. He replaces
Vito
Samela, who
left
the company
several months
ago.
Simultaneously,
Fraser announced the appointment of
Sal Licata as assistant national sales
manager.
Licata, who
was
Eastern
regional Sales and Promotion Manag-
er for the
label,
will continue
to op-
erate out of the New York
office and
will report directly to
Dallas.
A native of Detroit, Dallas got his
start in the music business as a sales-
man for Florida Music Sales
in 1954.
Two years
later he joined Command
Records
as
Mid-Western
sales man-
ager. In 1960 he became Mid-Western
regional
promotion
director
for
Co-
lumbia Records, a post which he held
for three years prior to joining Philips
in
1963.

Lion Cubs Aid
'Born
Free'
Soundtrack LP Promotion
NEW YORK—A1 Abrams
of Harold
N. Lieberman Distributors
in Minne-
apolis
hit
upon
an
unusual
idea
to
publicize the MGM sound track album
of “Born Free.” He borrowed two lion
cubs from
the
local
zoo
and
placed
them
on
display
in
the
window
of
Music
City Record
Shop,
one
of the
big
stores
in downtown
Minneapolis.
The window display featured blow-ups
of
the
sound
track album
cover
as
well
as photographic
scenes
in
color
from the “Born Free” cinema venture.
Both
A1
Abrams
and
Music
City
reported
that
“the
‘live’
display
boosted
sales on the album
consider-
ably.”
Kim Joins Monument As
Creative Director
HOLLYWOOD—Ken
Kim
has
been
retained
by
Monument
Records
as
Creative Director for all album covers
and allied areas effective immediately,
according
to an announcement made
by label prexy Fred Foster last week.
Kim
has
been
involved
in
the
re-
cording industry for the last 10 years,
having
done work
for
Capitol,
Dot,
Liberty, World Pacific, Dolton, Warner
Bros, and
Reprise. Kim has received
eight
L.A.
Art
Director’s
Club
awards for various album covers and
was nominated for a Grammy for his
cover of the Allen Sherman “My Son,
The Folk Singer” LP.

Shure Markets New
Mike/Instrument Mixer
EVANSTON,
ILL.—Shure
Brothers,
has
announced
a
significantly
new
microphone/musical instrument mixer
which according
to the manufacturer
makes
it
practical,
efficient and
eco-
nomical
for
musical
groups
to
use
up
to
five
electric
guitars,
basses,
consolette organs, or microphones, or
any
combination
of
five,
with
an
existing guitar or P.A. amplifier. The
new
device,
called
the
Shure
Model
PE68M,
has
a
standard phone
jack
output
for
connection
to any
guitar
amplifier;
a
Cannon
connector
for
high
or
low
impedance
microphone
inputs;
and
a
phono
jack
for
con-
nection
to
an
auxiliary
high
level
input on a P.A.
amplifier.
It
is fully
transistorized
and
portable.
Size
is
2-%" x 11-%"
x 5-%e", and
weight
is
only
4
pounds.
List
price
of
the
unit
is
$97.50.
Indicative
of
the
versatility
de-
signed
into
this
new
mixer
is
the
fact
that
if
more
than
five
inputs
are required, two or more mixers may
be
interconnected
to
accommodate
even
more
instruments
and
micro-
phones. Each input on the mixer has
a separate volume control. These sep-
arate
controls
allow
balancing
the
volume
between
instruments
or
be-
tween
instruments
and
vocalists.
There is also a master volume control
that simultaneously controls the gain
of
all
inputs.
Lenny Bruce Dead At 40
HOLLYWOOD—Lenny
Bruce, highly
controversial comedian, who recorded
for the Fantasy
label, and whose act
has lead him
to numerous
legal
dis-
putes over the years, was found dead
in his Hollywood home last Wed.
(3).
An
autopsy was
scheduled
to
deter-
mine the
cause
of
death.
Bruce was
reportedly preparing
to
move
in
federal
court
to
obtain
the
right
to appear
in New York again.
He
has
been
absent
from
the
city
since
being
convicted
of
giving
an
obscene performance
at the Cafe Au
Go Go
in
1964.
Bruce
is
survived
by
his
mother
and
11 year
old daughter Bonnie.

is all smiles as he receives a citation from Thomas
R. Sard, director of the Washington, D.
C. Department of Corrections for his
performance, (26) at the Lorton Prison Jazz Festival. More than 2,000 convicts
attended as Charles put on a two hour

of

Chaplains, who

the

Acuff-Rose/Chappell Link-Up
Exceeds Expectations Thus Far
NEW YORK—Chappell and
Co. has
rounded
out
the
first
six months
of
its publication agreement with Acuff-
Rose
International
this
week,
with
sales
of
a
host
of
different
publica-
tions from tthe well-known Nashville
catalog “far exceeding even the most
optimistic
earlier
sales budgets,”
ac-
cording
to John
Cacavas,
Chappell’s
director of publications. Cacavas and
Chappell
president
Louis
Dreyfus
negotiated
the arrangements for the
Old
Line
publisher
to
handle
the
production and merchandising of the
Acuff-Rose printed editions.
Disclosing that “the crash program
we
undertook
when
we
closed
the
deal
with
Acuff-Rose
last February
saw printed copies of many types
of
arrangements
within
two
months,”
Cacavas
said that Phase One
of the
program
is now drawing
to
a
close.
He added that he will be in Nashville
Monday
(15)
for
several
days
of
meetings with Acuff-Rose prexy Wes-
ley
Rose, and
his
assistant Bob Mc-
Clusky
to
discuss Phase Two
of the
operation,
which
will
involve
plans
for
intensive
sales,
promotion
and
merchandising
campaigns
on
the
product
now
available
as
well
as
material due
off the presses
shortly.
More than 40 publications of Acuff-
Rose
material,
arranged
for
stage
band,
marching
band
and
choral
groups, aimed primarily
at the
edu-
cational
market
have
already
been
turned out. In addition, several folios
of up
to 30
different songs
each,
ar-
ranged for organ, trumpet, piano and
guitar
have
been
printed.
One
of
these, “Tuff Guitar
Goes
Nashville,”
is now
in
its
third
printing,
accord-
ing to Pete Wollery, who heads up the
Chappell publication sales.

BMI Makes
Largest
Int'l.
Distribution
In
Its
History
NEW YORK—Robert B. Sour, presi-
dent
of
BMI,
announced
last
week
that
a
total
of
$1,175,000
has
been
paid out to writers and publishers by
the collection agency in the 19th semi-
annual distribution of monies received
from
foreign
performing
rights
so-
cieties
for
the
use
of
BMI
music
abroad. The sum
is
the
largest ever
distributed
by BMI
in
any
similar
period.
After deduction of a 10% adminis-
tration fee for handling of these reve-
nues, BMI
paid
$952,000
to
writers
and $223,000 to publishers. The lower
payment
to
publishers
is
due
to
the
fact that most
of them
are
paid
di-
rectly through their foreign
affiliates.
Writers are paid on the basis of per-
formances
tallied by
the
foreign
so-
cieties and reported to BMI.
BMI began
collection and adminis-
tration
of
foreign performance
pay-
ments
to
its
affiliates more than
10
years
ago.
Today,
it
has
reciprocal
agreements with 24 foreign
societies.
Bud Powell Dies
NEW
YORK—Pianist
Bud
Powell
died
(3)
in a Brooklyn hospital from
a
combination
of
malnutrition
and
tuberculosis.
The
41-year-old
artist’s
early
recordings
with
Charlie
Bird
Parker and Dizzy
Gillespie are
cred-
ited by many
with
having
been
re-
sponsible for the emergence of modern
day jazz from the swing era.

At The White House
NEW
YORK—Rudolf
Serkin
per-
formed
at the
W’hite House on Aug.
2nd at the request of President John-
son.
Serkin’s

The

Festival
in Vt., has recently returned
from
a European
concert
tour.

FOCUS ON JAZZ
A fairly recent development in the
field of recorded jazz is the increasing
number
of
releases
that
are
“Afro-
Latin”
oriented.
True,
it has always
been
possible
to
obtain
recordings
that featured
a wedding
of the two
sounds, jazz and
Latin rhythms, but
it would appear that of late there has
been
a
deliberate
endeavor
on
the
part of the record producers to make
a more overt attempt to romance that
particular segment of the record buy-
ing public.
Was
this
increased
interest
in
rhythmic
influenced
jazz precipitated
by the tremendous popularity
of
the
Bossa Nova movement several seasons
ago? Prior to the wholesale exposure
that Bossa Nova
enjoyed,
there was
always a small hard core of listeners
who
championed
the
Afro-Latin
sound, but the only air play that such
music
received was
on
specific
pro-
grams. Rarely,
if ever, was this type
of music played on the so-called popu-
lar music
stations. Came
the
Bossa
Nova and suddenly a whole new hori-
zon was opened;
consequently, a new
market was
created, and
the
efforts
of the record producers indicate that
their
current
product
is
geared
for
that new market.
Jazz that embodies
the Afro-Latin
rhythms
is
hot music
and,
as
such,
invites
participation
on
the
part
of
the
listener.
It
really
doesn’t matter
if the music
is being danced
to, per
se. There
is that basic pulsation that
invites one
to become involved, either
physically
or
spiritually.
Coupled
with
the
pronounced
rhythmic
im-
pulses,
there
is
also
usually
a
very
strong melodic content;
consequently,
there
is a greater inducement for the
listener
to become
involved, because,
in
essence,
this music
is more
basic
for
the average listener.
As
suggested,
isolated examples
of
the
Afro-Latin
jazz
sound
have
al-
ways
been
available.
Because
of
the
infrequency of this type of recording
it
was
considered
special
material.
There were some jazz
artists who in-
corporated the Latin rhythms in some
of
their
work.
Dizzy
Gillespie must
be considered an innovator because he
was one of the
first to popularize the
incorporation
of
Latin
rhythms
to
jazz.
Gillespie,
even
in
the
Forties,
blended
his
special
jazz
talent
with
the
Latin
influence,
using
authentic
Latin
percussionists
who
lent
their
native sound
to the wedding.
Charlie
Parker, another
of the
titans
of
the
jazz
world,
recorded
an
extended
Afro-Cuban
jazz
suite
with
Machito
in
the
Fifties.
George
Shearing
al-
ways
journeyed
into
the
Afro-Latin
sound
as
an
integral
part
of
his
program
material.
Johnny
Richards,
composer
and
arranged
par
excel-
lence, wrote, arranged, and conducted
his
own
suite,
“Cuban
Fire,”
which
Stan
Kenton
recorded
in
1955
with
an augmented
orchestra. Art Blakey,
whose
Jazz
Messengers have
always
been
in
the
vanguard
of
the
jazz
scene,
is another who has always
in-
vestigated the Afro rhythms with his
bands.
Cal
Tjader,
who
played
with
George
Shearing
in
the
mid-fifties,
has, probably, more consistently than
any
other
jazz
leader,
pursued
the
Latin
jazz
sound.
Tjader
didn’t
use
the
Latin
influence
as an
adjunct
to
his
regular
jazz
book.
On
the
con-
trary,
the
performance
of
a
vehicle
without
the
Latin
overtone was
the
departure from
the norm, instead
of
vice
versa.
During
his
association
with
the
Fantasy
label,
his
record-
ings
were
almost
exclusively
Latin
flavored,
and
because
there
was
a
dearth
of
that type
of
recording
at
that time, Tjader’s albums were pur-
chased in great volume. Actually, Cal
Tjader
might
have
been
considered
the
bulwark
of
the
Fantasy
cata-
logue, a testimony to his great popu-
larity
and
a
premature
indication
that there was a great market to be
sought
with
Afro-Latin
Jazz.
Since
his
affiliation
with
the
Verve
label,
Tjader’s
concept
has
remained
ba-
sically
the
same. We
say
basically,
because for a time the policy makers
at Verve made
an
abortive
attempt
to
take
Cal away from
the formula
which
had
made
him
so
successful
with Fantasy. However, we may
as-
sume
that Verve
has
taken
an
ac-
counting
because
his
last
three
al-
bums
have
proven
big
sellers
for
Tjader,
and
each
has
been
in
the
idiom that
first brought him to great
popularity, Afro-Latin jazz.
Mongo Santamaria, an alumnus
of
a Cal Tjader group
of the
late
Fif-
ties,
is a current favorite among jazz
afficianodos who
prefer
their
music
with
a
strong
rhythmic
impulse.
Mongo’s
music
is
less
subtle
than
Tjader’s
or
Shearing’s
because
he
uses more
conventional instrumenta-
tion, namely, reeds and brass. Mongo
Santamaria
emphasizes more
of
the
full sound, the urgent, almost relent-
less
sound
that
characterizes
good,
insistent, rhythmic music. Mongo has
been very consistent in his approach.
From his very first recordings on the
Battle label to his current recordings
on Columbia
his sound has been
al-
ways
the
same.
The
only
difference
that might
be
observed
is
that
his
current
recording
program
includes
many more
songs from
the
popular
field, where
in
his
early work most
of what he recorded was original ma-
terial from the members of his band.
This can only be construed as an
ef-
fort on the part of Columbia to make
Mongo
Santamaria’s
more
univer-
sally acceptable because of the famil-
iarity of the material being played.
Willie Bobo, another alumnus of a
Cal Tjader group,
is rapidly gaining
favor
as
another
leader
of
a
Latin
jazz group. Bobo, a great percussion-
ist, made
several
albums
as
leader
for
Roulette,
but
nothing
of impor-
tance seemed to happen for him. Re-
flecting
on
those
efforts,
they
were
more
jazz
than
Latin
and
because
they were they had no
specific
iden-
tification
for
that
audience
which
wants
its Latin LATIN. What Willie
Bobo and
his band
is now recording
for
Verve
is
readily
identified
as
Afro-Latin
jazz,
strong,
invigorating
music that makes you want
to do
it
to
it.
There are several other current re-
cordings
that
fall
into
the realm
of
Afro-Latin jazz which
are worthy
to
mention.
Montego
Joe,
a New York
based
percussionist
whose
talent
is
heard on many recordings
as
a
side-
man, has made two
excellent albums
for Prestige Records, ARRIBA CON
MONTEGO
JOE
and
his
latest,
WILD AND WARM. His
first album
for
Prestige was made up
of fewer
tracks
and
more
extensive
blowing
space
for
the
soloists.
Joe’s
latest
album
is made up
of
shorter
tracks
with
more
emphasis
placed
on
the
ensemble sound and
less on
the
solo-
ists.
Here
again, we must draw
the
inference that
this
is an overt
effort
on the part of the record company to
get some
play on
the popular music
stations,
who,
for
whatever
reason,
refuse
to
play
tracks
that run
over
three minutes. Long tracks
or
short,
these two albums by Montego Joe are
excellent
and
should
be
included
in
any library of Afro-Latin jazz.
Another
entry
into
the
field
of
Afro-Latin
jazz
is
the
Mira
al-
bum, INTRODUCING THE AFRO-
BLUES
QUINTET
PLUS
ONE.
This group
falls somewhere between
the
Tjader
sound
and
the
Mongo
Santamaria.
One
member
of
the
group,
Jack
Fulks,
doubles
on
alto
sax and flute; when he plays alto the
band takes on a much more muscular
sound,
a
harder
sound. When
Fulks
plays
flute, the sound
is very charac-
teristic
of the Tjader approach. The
material
on
this
album
is
excellent
and the pacing of the program makes
it completely enjoyable. One listening
convinces you that the group has been
working
together,
and
with
good
results.
There
is
every
reason
to
believe
that Afro-Latin
jazz has
only begun
to flourish in popularity. As a further
measuring
device
of
its
popularity,
one might
listen
closely
to
its
influ-
ence
on
the
groups
playing rhythm
and
blues,
or
if you bother
to
listen
to
commercials,
notice
how
often
these
rhythms
are
incorporated
into
the
background
music.
There
is
no
doubt
about
it,
Afro-Latin
jazz
is
here
to
stay.
WE’RE
TEUJW’
IT LIKE
ITUS!

Execs Back In N.Y.;
Label Bows Three LP's
EW YORK—Kapp
Records’
flying
sales
team
returned
to
their New
York home base
last week, following
Fall
product
presentations
to
every
Kapp
distrib.
The
visits
took
place
over a period of more than two weeks,
and resulted in what sales vice presi-
dent,
Sid
Schaffer,
described
as
“the
highest initial sales orders for any al-
bum release
in the Arm’s
history.”
Noting
that
more
than
half
the
firm’s distributors have already placed
second
and
third
reorders,
Schaffer
also announced a supplemental release
of
three
additional
albums
to
com-
mence shipping on the 15th and to be
added to the basic
Fall release of 15
albums.
The three sets include one by Gun-
ter Kallmann’s Chorus with Orchestra
and
French
maestro,
Raymond
Le-
fevre,
has, “You Don’t Have To Say
You Love Me,” and lastly, in the sup-
plemental
release
is
organist,
John
Gart’s newest LP, “Back Home In In-
diana.”
But
the
excitement
for
the Kapp
sales team was not limited to product
reaction.
The
close-out
visit
of
the
presentation tour in Detroit last week
was
capped
by
a
last-minute bomb
scare aboard an aircraft about to take
off for New York. Debarked from the
plane along with the other passengers
were
Schaffer, A&R
chief, Hy
Grill;
National
Sales Manager, Joe Berger.

Musicor To
Handle
Dixon's Cheetah
Label
NEW YORK—Musicor Records com-
pleted negotiations last week for the
national distribution of Cheetah Rec-
ords, owned by indie producer, Luther
Dixon.
Dixon,
well-known
for
his
string of producing successes for the
Scepter
label,
produced
the
recent
smash
revival
for
the
Platters,
“I
Love You
1,000
Times,”
as
well
as
their new release, “Dervi,” issued last
week.
Cheetah will be released under the
Musicor label with a separate Cheetah
logo. First release will be by the well-
known
duo, Inez and Charlie Fox. A
new group, the Pigeons, will also have
a single out on Cheetah.
Dixon, who has just completed
re-
cording the Platters’ follow-up single,
“Dervi,”
for
Musicor,
will
produce
most
of the upcoming recordings
in
Detroit, where he now lives.
Another project
in which Dixon
is
busily engaged,
is planning
the
ses-
sions for Musicor by Eartha Kitt, who
recently
signed
with
the
label.
Rendezvous Ballroom Burns
BALBOA, CAL. — The Rendezvous
Ballroom,
once
a mecca
of
the
big
bands that had
in more recent years
catered to rock bands, was destroyed
by fire on Sunday, Aug.
7. Ironically
the last group to play the Rendezvous
was a rock band known as the Cinder-
men.

Roland
Kirk Released
From Mercury Contract
CHICAGO—Roland Kirk has been re-
leased
from
his
affiliation
with
the
Mercury Record Corp.
as
of Aug.
1.
The artist, who plans to free-lance for
the
present,
is
scheduled
for an
ex-
tended European
concert tour which
will begin
in England. His European
itinerary has not been
definitely
set
as yet.
Rodgers &
Parker
In
Dot
Production
Pact
HOLLYWOOD—Singer Jimmie Rod-
gers, who also holds an A&R position
with Dot
Records, and Dick
Parker,
bass player with the Shenandoah Trio,
have entered a partnership to produce
for the Dot logo. The
first joint ven-
ture of the production pact
is a rock
single
from
Parker’s
pen
entitled
“What’s Your Game.” The deck, which
was recorded by Craig Carr, is sched-
uled for immediate release.
Henry Tobias Music Forms
NEW YORK—Henry
Tobias
is
con-
solidating
his music pubberies
into a
single
parent
firm
to
be known
as
Henry Tobias Music Co. The ASCAP
firm will control the publishing inter-
ests of Patore Music, Charlen Music,
and PAT

The constant growth of the recording
industry
imposes
ever-increasing
re-
sponsibilities
on
the
people who
are
I
in
a
position
to
influence the buying
I
habits
of
the
public.
That
area
of
influence
includes
buyers
for
retail
I
record
outlets,
critics,
disk
jockeys,
j
and
jazz
journalists. In the midst of
the growing number of new releases,
it becomes very easy
for
a
particu-
larly deserving album
to become
lost
in the
shuffle and go unnoticed. Such
would be highly inequitable, from the
points of view of the
artist, the pro-
ducer,
and
the
listener who
enjoys
knowing about the exceptional. So, in
an endeavor to preclude
this happen-
ing, periodically
it shall be a function
of
this
column
to
highlight
several
albums which
are worthy
of
special
comment. Necessarily, the selection of
these albums
will
reflect
the
opinion
of this writer and the high standards
of Cash Box.

[
cause Willie Ruff plays both bass and
'

horn, and each one
expertly,
i
Mitchell’s piano is considered by many
j
to be the epitome of jazz on that in-
I

is
facile,

I

is a complete mu-
!
sician. The fact that these men don’t

1 many

i MARQUIS DE SADE—LALO SCHI-
FRIN—VERVE
8654
Don’t
let
the
:ongue-in-cheek
title
of
this
album
fool
you!
This
is
substantial
music.
Last year Schifrin won a Grammy for
his
writing
of
“Jazz
Suite
On
The
Mass,” which was performed by Paul
Horn on Victor
This Verve album
is
his first effort since then. To describe
the flavor of the music
in
capsule,
it
is
a
modernization
of
the
baroque
music
of yesterday, always imagina-
tive,
always
swinging.
Lalo
and
his
music are portrayed in three different
settings: in a small group, in a string
setting,
and
in
a
brass
setting.
To
obtain
all
the
colorations
that
char-
acterize baroque
music,
Schifrin
has
used harp, harpsichord, and a
single
voice. Worthy
of
special
mention
is
rhe playing of Jerome Richardson on
flute. Gene
Bertoncini on
guitar, and
Richard Davis on bass. The main force
is
Lalo
Schifrin’s
writing
and
his
playing,
and
in
this
day
when
so
much begins to sound alike, this album
is a welcome departure into new pas-
tures. The Marquis de Sade certainly
would have dug
this album, and you
will,
too.
MACK THE KNIFE AND OTHER
BERLIN
THEATRE
SONGS
OF
KURT WEILI^THE SEXTET OF
ORCHESTRA U.S.A.—VICTOR
3498
This
small
band
from
within
The
Orchestra has gleaned from the
rich
library of Kurt Weill seven songs and
has endowed
each
with
a
rewarding
jazz treatment. The Sextet, under the
direction
of
Michael
Zwerin,
must
have enjoyed every moment spent
in
the recording studio at Victor, witness
the vitality that practically jumps out
of the grooves. Zwerin’s bass trumpet,
an instrument
that we hear
too
sel-
dom,
is featured, as
is the playing of
the late Eric Dolphy. This album also
affords
us
the
opportunity
to
hear
two
members
of
The
Modern
Jazz
Quartet, John Lewis and Connie Kay,
in
a new
setting.
Naturally, “Mack
The Knife”, “Bilbao Song”, and “Bar-
bara Song”
are
included
in
the
rep-
ertoire, but we also get the chance to
hear
some
of
Kurt
Weill’s
lesser
known works, “Alabama
Song”, “As
You Make Your Bed”, “Pirate Jenny”,
and “Havana Song”. One of the
out-
standing aspects of this album
is the
fact
that
it was
recorded
with
two
different groups, and
yet the
overall
feeling remains
completely
identical.
This must be considered as
a
tribute
to
the
solid
musicianship
of
all
the
performers.
RCA
Victor,
George
Avakian, Bob Prince, and the gentle-
men
of the ensemble
are
to
be
con-
gratulated
for
a
job
magnificently
done.
TIME WILL TELL—JOHN ANDER-
SON—TANGERINE
1506
One must
draw the inference that John Ander-
son
is
a
strict
disciplinarian,
other-
wise how could he have achieved such
a tight big-band sound from nineteen
men
who
obviously
don’t
work
to-
gether on a regular basis
Anderson,
a veteran
of the big band scene and
himself
an
accomplished
trumpeter,
although he
doesn’t play on
this
al-
bum, has put together what might be
the big band “sleeper” album
of
the
year. The
section work
bristles,
the
soloists are outstanding, and the ma-
terial is muscular whether it is at up,
medium, or down tempo. Of particular
interest
is the use of piccolo,
itself a
depai’ture from the normal instrumen-
tation, and an
instrument
which,
as
it
is used here, makes the altogether
sound even more
incisive.
Hopefully,
some
deejays
and program
directors
will
read
this
very
enthusiastic
cri-
tique and, as a consequence, will seek
out
this
John
Anderson
album
and
give
it some much deserved air play.
Music like this should be heard by the
many, not the few.
JUST ABOUT EVERYTHING—BOB
DOROUGH—FOCUS 336 In 1956 Bob
Dorough
recorded
a
vocal album
on
Bethlehem,
one
titled,
“Devil
May
Care.” By
now,
this album
has
be-
come
a
collectors’
item
In
spite
of
its scarcity and the fact that a decade
has elapsed, it continues to receive air
play from many discerning program-
mers.
Dorough’s
latest
album,
com-
prised
of
ten
vocals,
is
a
veritable
potpourri
of
good
music,
featuring
standards, ballads, jazz originals, and
a couple
of jazz
infected folk
songs.
By
some
standards.
Bob
Dorough
might
not
be
considered
to
have
a
good voice, at least not in the accepted
sense
of
the
word,
voice.
However,
let us hasten to add that Bob Dorough
is a great singer, one whose phrasing
is
completely
unique,
and
a
singer
whose understanding
of
a
lyric
is
a
joy to behold, especially
in the midst
of so many vocalists who
don’t seem
to
understand
the
meaning
of
the
words they sing. Dorough’s colleagues
on this recording are
all seasoned and
sympathetic
players:
A1
Schackman
on guitar, Percy Brice on drums, and
Ben Tucker on bass. It was with Ben
Tucker
that
Dorough
collaborated
several
seasons
ago
on
the
hit,
“Cornin’ Home, Baby”. On this Focus
album two more Dorough-Tucker
ef-
forts can be heard, each a jazz
orig-
inal by Tucker to which Bob Dorough
has
added
his
engaging
lyrics.
The
Dorough
piano
is very much
in
evi-
dence
throughout
the
album
and
it
fortifies the opinion, often expressed,
that no one can accompany a singer
better than
the
singer
himself.
This
Bob Dorough
vocal
album
signals
a
welcome return to the recording scene
for
one
of
music’s most
gifted
per-
formers,
a
singers’
singer,
a
musi-
cians’ singer, and, perhaps most impor-
tant
of
all, an
appreciative
listeners’
singer.

Milestone
Records
Bows
With
Emphasis On Jazz
NEW YORK—Milestone
Records,
a
new
label with
the announced
inten-
tion
of
concentrating
on
“quality
album product,” has just begun activ-
ity,
with
headquarters
in New York
City.
Milestone
plans
to move most
heavily
into
the
jazz
market,
and
has
stressed
this
point by
acquiring
the
services
of
jazz
producer
Orrin
Keepnews.
The
label’s
first group
of
releases
is
currently
being
shipped.
Included
are:
jazz
album,
“Mean What You
Say,”
by
the
Thad
Jones/Pepper
Adams
Quintet;
“Lead
Me,
Guide
Me”, by the
Duncanaires, a Chicago-
based
gospel
and
spirituals
group;
and “Classic Delta Blues”, by Missis-
sippi-born
blues
singer Big Joe Wil-
liams. The
first two
were newly
re-
corded
by
Keepnews,
with
the
Big
Joe
disc
being
produced
by
blues
man
Pete
Welding.
Subsequent
re-
leases, although emphasizing
current
jazz,
will
also
include
“important”
reissue
packages
as
well
as
further
material
in
the
blues
and
gospel
fields.
Distribution has been
set for most
key
territories,
and
organization
of
the
national
sales
picture
is now be-
ing completed, with
a
tape
cartridge
affiliation and overseas licensing deals
now also under discussion.
Keepnews,
vet
record
executive,
A&R
producer
and
jazz
voice
has
been retained to
supervise
all phases
of
initial
organization,
in
addition
to
serving
as
Milestone’s
recording
director. Keepnews
is best known for
his
long
association
with
Riverside
Records. One
of the founders of that
company,
he
was
instrumental
in
building
it
into
a
leading
jazz
label,
functioning as
its creative head until
1964. He has also been merchandising
manager
of Colpix
Records
and
has
most
recently
been
operating
as
an
independent producer.

NEW YORK—The
London
group
is
currently
intensifying
promotion
on
the singles front. The outfit has issued
nearly
20
singles
in
the
past
few
weeks
and,
according
to
sales
chief
(singles)
Walt
Maguire,
is
pushing
the entire product. The recent London
group releases are highlighted by Los
Bravos
with
“Black
Is
Black”
and
Flip
Cartridge with “Dear Mrs. Ap-
plebee.” These artists are on the Press
and Parrot labels, respectively.
The
binge
of
indie
production
ac-
tivity reflects a broad range of styles
from
groups
to
girl
singers
to
an
international novelty hit from Ireland,
titled “Up
Goes
Nelson,”
a
sort
of
musical
documentation
of the
recent
destruction of Lord Nelson’s statue in
Dublin. The London side
is by the Go
Lucky Four and has been reported to
have been number one in Eire.
Nine
of the new
sides
are on
the
Parrot
label.
These
include
the new
release by the
Ides
of March,
titled
“Roller Coaster,” and produced in Chi-
cago
by
Mike
Considine;
Britisher
Tom Jones’ latest “What A Party;” a
slow rock version
of “Hi-Lili Hi-Lo,”
by Britain’s Alan Price Set, one of the
newer favorites there; “Cajun Honey,”
by
the
well-known
Clarence
(Frog-
man) Henry, produced by Peter Paul
and Bob Astor; and “Melody For An
Unknown
Girl,” by the Unknowns, a
West Coast group cut by singer-pro-
ducer, Steve Alaimo.
Also among the Parrot
releases
is
the new Coast group, the Daily Flash,
with a Bob Dylan song, “Queen Jane
Approximately,” produced by Charles
Green and Brian Stone
of York-Pala
Productions;
Jonathan
King’s
“Just
Like A Woman”;
“I Can Only Give
You
Everything,”
by
the
British
group. Them; and the Zombies’ disk-
ing of “Indication.”
On the London label, in addition to
the novelty Irish
side, are: Marianne
Faithfull’s “Counting,” a song by Bob
Lind;
Noel
Harrison
in
“The
Man
Behind The Red Balloon,” written by
P.
J.
Sloane;
and
a
country-styled
effort
by
Margaret
Whiting,
“The
Wheel Of Hurt.”
Joe Cuoghi’s Hi
label
in Memphis,
another member of the London group,
has Willie Mitchell’s newest, “Mercy,”
a strong R&B pop effort, “Without A
Reason,” by Janet and the Jays; and
Ace
Cannon’s
“More,”
which
was
rushed
out
as
a
single
after
deejay
play of the side from an album.
Another new effort by Freddy Scott
on the Marlin label in Miami
is titled
“Pow
City.”
This was
produced
by

HOLLYWOOD—CRDC has formed a
creative products

of

to
Stan
Gortikov,

partment
as
CRDC’s
national man-
ager
of
creative products. Mynatt
is

20-year

of

of the merchandising

ing as Capitol’s western custom sales

Gortikov stated that the integration

into

is

for

ing facilities, and programming serv-
ices.

Award Winners

%Hit With $1 Million Suit
-
PHILADELPHIA—The
Cyrkle,
hit
Columbia
Records
group,
and
their
managers, Brian Epstein and Nathan
Weiss, have been sued for more than
$1
million
in
the
Court
of Common
Pleas
in Philadelphia.
The
plaintiff
is
Sheryl
Records,
which claims that the members of the
group—Earle
Pickens,
Don
Danne-
mann,
Thomas
Dawes
and
Martin
Fried—had recorded for Sheryl, head-
ed by Jerry
Ross,
as
the
Rhondells
and were released through ABC Rec-
ords.
According
to
the
complaint,
the
boys’
contract with
Sheryl was
dated
Nov.
7,
1964,
with
renewal
rights through
1969, and
called
for
the group to record for Sheryl on an
exclusive
basis.
Ross
contends
that
the contract had been renewed for at
least one year through Nov.
of
this
year.
When Brian Epstein formed Nem-
peror Artists' Ltd., an American man-
agement
firm,
with
Nathan
Weiss
several months ago, it was announced
that
the
Cyrkle would
be
the
com-
pany’s first act. The singers have had
two
big
singles
hits,
“Red
Rubber
Ball” and “Turn Down Day.” Jerry
Ross is the producer of the number
1
single
in
the
country, Bobby Hebb’s
“Sunny” on the Philips label.

Ampex 1st Qtr. Profits
Sets Record High
NEW
YORK—Ampex
Corp.
sales
rose
31
percent and
net eanings
34
percent
in
the
first quarter
of
fiscal
year
1967, compared
with
the same
period last year,
it was annouced last
week by
William
E.
Roberts,
presi-
dent and
chief executive.
Sales
for
the
three months ended
July 30, 1966, totaled $46,061,000, up
31
percent from
$35,273,000
a
year
ago.
Net
earnings
after
taxes were
$1,887,000,
or
20
cents
per
share on
9,455,196 average shares outstanding,
up 34 percent from $1,408,000, or
15
cents per share on 9,295,376 shares.
The company’s backlog of product
orders
at the end
of the period was
$51,000,000, up
43
percent from
this
time
last
year,
even
though
record
shipments were attained in the quar-
ter, reflecting gains by
all
divisions.
Roberts
said
continued
high
de-
mand for videotape
recording equip-
ment
for broadcasting, industry and
education,
consumer
audio
recorders
and
accessories
for home
entertain-
ment and magnetic tapes of
all types
contributed most heavily
to
the
first
quarter gains.

ENZO STUARTI
NEW YORK—There
is a new, com-
pelling
side
to
singer Enzo
Stuarti.
The songster, who has built a strong
nitery
following
with
overpowering
renditions
of
romantic
songs,
un-
veiled a “soft and
sentimental”
side
at his Copacabana opening here last
week
(18). The phrase “soft & senti-
mental” just happens
to be the
title
of an upcoming Epic LP by the artist.
It should win him many new fans, if
his Copa preview
of
the album was
any
indication.
While
Stuarti
gives
patrons
a
generous
supply
of
his
more familiar high-register warbling,
much
of the standing ovation he
re-
ceived at the end of his stand seemed
an appreciation of the new LP med-
ley. The
album
contains
such
items
as
“Yesterday,”
“The
Shadow
Of
Your
Smile” and
“I
Will Wait For
You” from the “Umbrellas
of Cher-
bourg.”
Intimate
and
thoughtful,
Stuarti
performed them
with
a
so-
phistication that neither previous
re-
cordings
or
nitery
dates
have
re-
vealed.
Epic,
it
seems, now has
the
big ballad
voice
it has been
looking
for.
Stuarti now has a new kind
of
artistry that should open up
an
en-
tirely new audience to him.

HOLLAND
The number one position on the Dutch hit-parade went early in August to
Karin Kent with her
lively rendition
of “Dans Je De Hele Nacht Met Mij”
(Dance All Night With Me) on the Decca label. The music for this song, edited
by U. A. Music-Altona in Amsterdam, was composed by Bert Baccarach and
could
be
heard
in
the
original
instrumental
version
in
the
U.
A.
picture
“What’s New
Pussycat”.
Via
a German
version
that
did
not
develop
into
greater popularity, Karin Kent picked out the song with Dutch lyrics by Willy
Rex for her repertoire to be sung at the recent Knokke Song Festival in Bel-
giurn, where the young lady from Amsterdam conquered
the
multi-linguistic
public. A
large
publicity campaign
in
close cooperation with
leading Dutch
daily paper “Het Vrije Volk” was the
second phase, and
also Belgium
took
over the release immediately with a great deal of success. “Dans Je De Hele
Nacht Met Mij”
is the fastest selling Dutch-sung single Phonogram has
re-
leased so far this summer.
Holland
is among the countries with
the best
classical LP
turn-over, Leo
Boudewijns of Phonogram told us, and among the most beloved classical com-
posers
in Holland
he mentioned
Vivaldi and Mozart
emphatically, and
also
Bach,
Beethoven
and
Haydn.
The
active
general
label-manager
was
quite
happy to announce the releases of a P. P.
I. production of new Vivaldi-inter-
pretations
by
I
Musici
(five
concertos)
and
a
Philips-album
featuring
the
brilliant Quartette Italiano with four of Joseph Haydn’s most popular string-
quartets.
Phonogram was proud to introduce the new French singer Georgette Lemaire
on the Dutch market. Otto Vriezenberg, label manager for Dutch Philips, told
us that the young woman
is considered in France as the sharpest competitor
in carrying
the
Edith
Piaf
torch.
Discovered
in
a
cafe where
“the
singing
lady”
(as she was called in her French village) used to sing along with juke-
box chansons. Georgette Lemaire won
the
first
prize
in
the
Tele Dimanche
contest, and was contracted by
S. P. P. in France. Released are her LP: “Mon
Premier 33 Tours” and her introductory^single “Et
Si
C’etait Vrai”. The LP
is already a big success in France.
The Sextet of the world-wide popular Dutch Swing College
(the line-up with
Oscar Klein and Dick Kaart,
brass,
leader
Peter
Schilperoort,
clarinet, and
rhythm-section Arie
Lighthart, Bob van Oven and drummer Lu
Sanet)
are
conquering the market with a highly commercial single taken from a previous

Ellingtoned
“East

Louis Toodle-Oo” and

bluesy “From

that well-chosen

of the
D.
S.
C. band, released
in
the proper
times,
keep up an unbroken chain of popularity-continuation in both the home-market
and abroad.
“The Best of Jim Reeves” by Faron Young
in his splendid Mercury-album
that was considered by the
official Dutch Jim Reeves Fan Club as one
of the
most
exciting and
fascinating C & W productions by
the Mercury
diskery.
Also released here was the Mercury-album by Clebanolf’s Ork with the amus-
ing

Julie Felix, the attractive and highly gifted American folk-singer, switched
from Decca to Fontana and consequently came on the Dutch market with her

It seems that American music (top hits)
is getting popular again and several
radio stations in the country have changed their programming to this type of
music. Anyhow, the percentage
is no higher than a 20%.
Gabriel Pardo, manager of the famous Mexican rock and roll group the Loud
Jets,
is preparing a modern music festival at the National Auditorium, with
the performances of Frank Sinatra Jr., the Tommy Dorsey band, Duane Eddy,
the Supremes and some other artists. At the moment, nothing
is sure.
Brazilian group
the Tamba
Trio
offered
a
cocktail
to
the
press and
disk
jockeys of Mexico City, to introduce new arrangements which belong to a new
long play that will be released on the Philips
label.
It is said that Connie Francis will arrive in town very soon. She will perform
at a nightclub and
record
in
the
Spanish
language. The recordings
will
be
released on the MGM label and be distributed by DUSA record company.
Capitol Records cut the latest Beatles album titled “The Beatles Yesterday
And Today”, with songs
like “Yesterday”, “Nowhere Man”, “Act Naturally”,
“Day Tripper” and others. Most of them have been released already.
The Puerto Rican female group,
the De Castro
Sisters,
is performing
at
the “Terrazza Cassino” nightclub. On the same show
is Dutch singer Andrik,
who has settled since about a year in town.
Gamma Records released at the moment four LP’s by Johnny
Rivers,
the
singer who
is supposed to perform
in some nightclub
of Mexico City by the
first days of September. “Susie Q”
is
still his most popular record here.
Kapp Records released “Strangers In The Night” and “Weekend”
in a new
single record. On the same label we received “Younger Girl” and “Gone For
A While” in the version of the Critters.
Spanish
singer Mayte Gaos, who
has
settled
in Mexico
with
her
family,
wrote to inform us that she will record an LP in Madrid, with songs written
by Agusto Alguero, and two written by herself. Mayte also told us that when
she returns
to Mexico she
will adopt the Mexican nationality.
Maybe by this time the veteran singer and actress Judy Garland has arrived
at the Mexican International Airport. She will perform for two weeks at night-
clubs, on TV, and at the National Auditorium.
The famous Mexican group of Los 11 Hermanos Zavala returned to Mexico
after a long season in Puerto Rico. Now they will do an LP at Capitol Records
under the direction and arrangements of one of the 11 brothers, Jose Antonio
Zavala.
About the latest RCA releases in 45 rpm are “Vagabundo” and “Nosotros”
with veteran singer Fernando Fernandez, “Amor Desesperado Amor” and “Sa-
bras Que No Me Quieres” with Las Hermanns Navarro,
“Chicotito,
Si” with
Los Dugs Dug and “Cloudburst” and “Cry Girl” with the Kan Dells.
Johnny Albino, the
first voice
of the world-known Mexican Trio Los Pan-
chos, left the group forever because he
will
live
in
his country, Puerto
Rico,
where he has a
lot of business. This
is the fourth
first voice that leaves the
trio in 22 years. El Guero Gil and Chucho Navarro are the two elements of the
group who always have belonged to
it. Now
it is possible that a Mexican will
be the first voice in the trio.
Argentinian
singer Ambar Lafox made her
debut
in
a
nightclub
of town
and
it is possible that she will do a series of recordings for CBS records.
Los Apson Boys cut at Eco label an LP where they play songs
like “Susie
Q”, “Fuiste A Acapulco”, “De Hoy En Ocho”, “Ya No Hay Beatles”, “Con El
Tiempo Y Un Ganchito”, “Fue En Un Cafe” and
others.
On the music market appeared the
first single recorded by Monna
Bell
in
Spain at the Hispavox-Gamma
labels. The themes are “El Sabor Del Amor”
and “The Shadow Of Your Smile”.
Female folk singer Irma Serrano cut at CBS records a new album with some
of her latest
hits
like “Puente Roto”, “Quisiera Ser
Pajarillo”,
“Carinito De
Mi Vida”, “El Recadito”, etc.

Liberty launched Ruben Rodriguez’ (& Guadalajara Kings) “Cucurucu Paloma”
featuring the exciting “Mariachi Rock” sound.
Bovema’s Columbia label manager Cees Pompe told CB that Liberty-singer
Julie London will not appear at the Grand Gala du Disque
of early October
next. The company’s label
is, however, happy to announce that popular singer
Richard Anthony,
a
Parisian
of Turkish-English
birth,
will be added
to the
all-star presentation.
Other Columbia-artists already signed for the Gala-roster are the Japanese
twin-sisters the Peanuts and Britain’s Georgie Fame, who hit the charts with
“Get Away” and his new LP “Sweet Things” very recently.
Imperial, now preparing a variety of new albums both
in the
classical and
pop area for release
in
the
fall, launched
a
7" record featuring the
barrel-
organ “De Turk” playing the latest Dutch
hits.
On the World Festival for Brassbands by Kerkrade—on TV almost daily this
week—Columbia’s G. U. S. Footwear Brass Band from Kettering, England, got
358 out of the maximum 360 points. It has consequently become a real favorite
for the
Festival’s
1st
Prize,
still
in the hands
of an
Israelian Youth Band,
last year’s winner.
Roel Kruyze, Capitol chief

It Be Nice”
hit the
stands.
